title: Drunk Bragging Trump Staffer Started Russian Collusion Investigation
text: House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes is going to have a bad day. He s been under the assumption, like many of us, that the Christopher Steele-dossier was what prompted the Russia investigation so he s been lashing out at the Department of Justice and the FBI in order to protect Trump. As it happens, the dossier is not what started the investigation, according to documents obtained by the New York Times.Former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos was drunk in a wine bar when he revealed knowledge of Russian opposition research on Hillary Clinton.On top of that, Papadopoulos wasn t just a covfefe boy for Trump, as his administration has alleged. He had a much larger role, but none so damning as being a drunken fool in a wine bar. Coffee boys  don t help to arrange a New York meeting between Trump and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of Egypt two months before the election. It was known before that the former aide set up meetings with world leaders for Trump, but team Trump ran with him being merely a coffee boy.In May 2016, Papadopoulos revealed to Australian diplomat Alexander Downer that Russian officials were shopping around possible dirt on then-Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton. Exactly how much Mr. Papadopoulos said that night at the Kensington Wine Rooms with the Australian, Alexander Downer, is unclear,  the report states.  But two months later, when leaked Democratic emails began appearing online, Australian officials passed the information about Mr. Papadopoulos to their American counterparts, according to four current and former American and foreign officials with direct knowledge of the Australians  role. Papadopoulos pleaded guilty to lying to the F.B.I. and is now a cooperating witness with Special Counsel Robert Mueller s team.This isn t a presidency. rewritten_article_text:
Papadopoulos Conversation Helped Prompt Russia Investigation

House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes has argued that the Christopher Steele dossier played a central role in the FBI’s investigation of possible ties between Russia and the Trump campaign. But reporting and congressional documents indicate that the inquiry began before the dossier was provided to the bureau.

Former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos told Australian diplomat Alexander Downer during a 2016 meeting in London that Russian officials had obtained information that could damage Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton. The conversation later became significant to investigators examining Russian efforts to interfere in the election.

Papadopoulos held a foreign-policy role with the campaign and was involved in efforts to arrange contacts between Trump’s team and foreign officials. The campaign later described him as a minor volunteer, though his activities included outreach to foreign representatives and discussions about possible meetings involving Trump.

In May 2016, Papadopoulos spoke with Downer at the Kensington Wine Rooms. The precise details of the conversation remain unclear, but Australian officials passed information about it to their American counterparts after material from hacked Democratic emails began appearing online two months later, according to officials familiar with the matter.

The information helped prompt the FBI to examine whether members of the Trump campaign had coordinated with Russian efforts, a probe that later became the subject of special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation. Papadopoulos pleaded guilty in 2017 to lying to the FBI and cooperated with investigators.

The episode became part of the broader dispute over the origins of the Russia investigation and the role played by intelligence reports, foreign contacts and information about the stolen Democratic emails.

David Clarke Draws Online Mockery After Posts About Critics

On Friday, former Milwaukee County Sheriff David Clarke faced renewed online criticism over a January encounter with a fellow airline passenger and a series of aggressive posts about media coverage of the incident.

The passenger, Dan Black, was questioned by police after leaving a flight on which he had encountered Clarke. Clarke acknowledged contacting law enforcement, while Black disputed the circumstances of the detention. Authorities later investigated the incident, and reports said a search warrant had been sought for emails related to the case.

Clarke rejected reports about the investigation as “fake news.” In a series of tweets posted December 30, 2017, he wrote that he was “UNINTIMIDATED” by what he called attempts by the media to discredit him. He added that he would “poke them in the eye with a sharp stick” and “bitch slap” his critics.

He followed that post with another message saying that when the media published what he considered false reports, the response should be to “go right at them” and “make them taste their own blood.”

The posts quickly drew criticism and mockery on social media.

“This is your local newspaper and that search warrant isn’t fake,” one user wrote, arguing that the investigation could continue even though no charges had initially been filed.

Other users mocked Clarke’s rhetoric, his former law-enforcement image and his public profile. Some shared edited images of Clarke, while others criticized his decision to involve police in the encounter with Black.

The controversy added to scrutiny of Clarke, who resigned as Milwaukee County sheriff in 2017 after serving three terms. He had also been publicly associated with Donald Trump’s administration and was discussed as a possible candidate for a federal homeland-security position, although he was not appointed to the role.

Clarke’s tweets remained available online as critics continued to debate the airline incident and the investigation into his communications.

title: Pope Francis Just Called Out Donald Trump During His Christmas Speech
text: Pope Francis used his annual Christmas Day message to rebuke Donald Trump without even mentioning his name. The Pope delivered his message just days after members of the United Nations condemned Trump s move to recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. The Pontiff prayed on Monday for the  peaceful coexistence of two states within mutually agreed and internationally recognized borders. We see Jesus in the children of the Middle East who continue to suffer because of growing tensions between Israelis and Palestinians,  Francis said.  On this festive day, let us ask the Lord for peace for Jerusalem and for all the Holy Land. Let us pray that the will to resume dialogue may prevail between the parties and that a negotiated solution can finally be reached. The Pope went on to plead for acceptance of refugees who have been forced from their homes, and that is an issue Trump continues to fight against. Francis used Jesus for which there was  no place in the inn  as an analogy. Today, as the winds of war are blowing in our world and an outdated model of development continues to produce human, societal and environmental decline, Christmas invites us to focus on the sign of the Child and to recognize him in the faces of little children, especially those for whom, like Jesus,  there is no place in the inn,  he said. Jesus knows well the pain of not being welcomed and how hard it is not to have a place to lay one s head,  he added.  May our hearts not be closed as they were in the homes of Bethlehem. The Pope said that Mary and Joseph were immigrants who struggled to find a safe place to stay in Bethlehem. They had to leave their people, their home, and their land,  Francis said.  This was no comfortable or easy journey for a young couple about to have a child.   At heart, they were full of hope and expectation because of the child about to be born; yet their steps were weighed down by the uncertainties and dangers that attend those who have to leave their home behind. So many other footsteps are hidden in the footsteps of Joseph and Mary,  Francis said Sunday. We see the tracks of entire families forced to set out in our own day. We see the tracks of millions of persons who do not choose to go away, but driven from their land, leave behind their dear ones. Amen to that.Photo by Christopher Furlong/Getty Images.

Papa John’s founder John Schnatter stepped down as chief executive of the pizza chain in December 2017, weeks after criticizing the NFL’s handling of player protests during the national anthem.

Schnatter had become involved in the debate after players began kneeling during the anthem to call attention to racial injustice and police brutality. In November, he said the controversy had hurt Papa John’s sales and criticized the league’s leadership. The company later said Schnatter’s comments were not intended to blame players for the chain’s performance.

Papa John’s announced that Schnatter would leave the CEO position and be succeeded by Chief Operating Officer Steve Ritchie. Schnatter remained chairman of the company’s board at the time.

The announcement came amid public discussion about the relationship between corporate brands, political issues and consumer reactions. Papa John’s had previously been associated with conservative causes, and Schnatter had expressed support for President Donald Trump. However, the company did not publicly say that customer boycotts or political pressure directly caused his departure.

Companies often face challenges when executives comment on contentious social and political issues, particularly when those comments involve a brand’s customers, employees or business partners. In Papa John’s case, the company said it planned to focus on its operations and relationships with franchisees, employees and the NFL.

Schnatter’s resignation marked a change in the company’s leadership, but it did not resolve the broader debate over athlete protests, racial inequality or the role of businesses in political controversies. Those issues continued to shape public discussion long after the announcement.

Republicans continued to promote their tax bill as a measure that would provide financial relief to middle-class and working families, while critics argued that the legislation would deliver larger benefits to corporations and higher-income households.

In a December 2017 interview and social-media post, then-House Speaker Paul Ryan defended the law’s potential impact on families. Ryan cited an estimate that a family living paycheck to paycheck could receive about $2,059 more per year from the tax changes, calling that amount significant. He also acknowledged that the effect would vary depending on a household’s income and where it lived.

“If you’re living paycheck-to-paycheck … and you got $2,059 more from a tax cut next year, that’s not nothing,” Ryan wrote on Twitter on December 21, 2017.

The tax law’s effects differed by household circumstances, including income, deductions and state and local taxes. Analysts and critics debated whether families in high-tax states such as New York and California would benefit as much as households elsewhere, particularly because the law placed new limits on the deduction for state and local taxes.

The debate reflected broader disagreements over whether the legislation would meaningfully help struggling families or primarily benefit businesses and wealthier taxpayers.

**Disney Heiress Criticizes Republican Tax Bill, Saying Wealthy Americans Will Benefit**

Abigail Disney, a member of the family associated with The Walt Disney Company, criticized the Republican tax overhaul in a 2017 opinion article for *USA Today*, arguing that the legislation would increase economic inequality even as it reduced taxes for many Americans.

Disney wrote that the gap between wealthy Americans and lower-income households had widened since the Reagan administration and argued that so-called “trickle-down” economics had not delivered broad-based benefits.

“But nothing has brought the problem of inequality into sharper focus for me than the current proposals by Republicans to overhaul the tax system,” she wrote.

At the time, congressional Republicans were advancing what became the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Supporters said the legislation would reduce taxes, encourage investment and promote economic growth. Critics, including Disney, argued that the largest benefits would go to corporations and high-income households and that the law could increase the federal deficit.

Disney said the bill could leave middle-class families with limited savings while reducing government resources for programs and services. She also criticized provisions affecting deductions, health care and education, saying that cuts to public spending could offset some of the benefits taxpayers might receive.

“Republicans insist this plan will cut taxes for the middle class,” Disney wrote, while arguing that the legislation would reduce “the responsibility of the wealthy to contribute to the common good.”

She acknowledged that her own financial position could improve under the bill. Disney said the legislation would provide benefits to wealthy families, including her own, while potentially making it easier to transfer wealth to future generations. She also criticized provisions that she said would benefit private-jet owners and other affluent taxpayers.

The Congressional Budget Office projected that the legislation would increase federal deficits by roughly $1.5 trillion over 10 years before accounting for broader economic effects. Estimates of the bill’s impact on health coverage varied, but the CBO said the number of uninsured people would rise by millions over time if related changes were implemented.

Disney argued that the legislation would make economic mobility more difficult for people without significant wealth.

“With a suffocating education system, a dying infrastructure and a national debt that will be at least $1.5 trillion bigger, that social mobility will be far out of reach for people like you,” she wrote. “But I will be able to stay comfortably right where I am.”

Her opinion article was also featured in a video published by NowThis in December 2017. In it, Disney urged voters to consider the broader effects of the legislation rather than their immediate personal benefit.

“If democracy is just a bunch of people advocating for their own self-interest instead of the interests of the greater good, then we’re not a democracy,” she wrote. “This isn’t tax reform. It’s a heist.”

The controversy arose as Mueller investigated Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible contacts between Russian officials and people associated with Trump’s campaign and transition. The acquisition of the emails did not itself establish wrongdoing by Trump or members of his team.

The disagreement highlighted broader questions about how records created during a presidential transition should be handled when federal investigators seek them. It also added to the political conflict surrounding Mueller’s investigation, which Trump and some of his allies have repeatedly criticized.

The special counsel’s office continued its work while the transition team considered its legal options.

**SNL Mocks Roy Moore After His Loss in Alabama Senate Race (VIDEO)**

Democrat Doug Jones defeated Republican Roy Moore in the special election to replace Jeff Sessions in the United States Senate. Moore’s campaign was shaken by allegations from several women who said he pursued them when they were teenagers, including allegations of sexual misconduct involving minors. Moore denied the accusations.

Even before the allegations emerged, Moore was a controversial figure in Alabama politics. He was removed as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court twice, first after refusing to remove a Ten Commandments monument from the state judicial building and later after defying a federal ruling involving same-sex marriage. He also made a number of provocative statements about religion, homosexuality and the role of the judiciary.

Alabama had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1990, and Moore was supported by President Donald Trump and much of the Republican establishment. His defeat therefore came as a surprise to many political observers, particularly in a state that had generally favored Republican candidates in statewide elections.

Saturday Night Live addressed the result during a “Weekend Update” segment. Host Colin Jost joked about Moore’s defeat and the allegations that had surrounded his campaign.

“Congratulations to Alabama’s newest senator—not Roy Moore,” Jost said. “Doug Jones has become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Alabama in over 20 years.”

Jost then used the result to poke fun at Moore, saying, “Said Roy Moore: ‘Gross, over 20 years?’”

The segment also criticized Trump’s response to the election. Trump had endorsed Moore during the campaign, but after Jones won, he noted that Republicans would have another opportunity to contest the seat in a future election.

Jost joked about the president’s reaction, saying Trump had gone “all in” for Moore and then appeared to dismiss the loss. He also imagined Trump responding to other political developments with a similarly casual message, including a congratulatory tweet to special counsel Robert Mueller.

The Alabama election gave Democrats a narrow foothold in the Senate and was widely viewed as a setback for Trump and national Republicans. Jones served the remainder of Sessions’ term before losing the seat to Republican Tommy Tuberville in the 2020 election.

**Republican Senator Defends Call for Mueller Probe to Address Partisanship**

Senate Majority Whip John Cornyn (R-Texas) criticized former Attorney General Eric Holder’s warning about any effort to remove Special Counsel Robert Mueller, while also saying Mueller should address what he described as partisan conduct in the Russia investigation.

Holder tweeted Friday, “Speaking on behalf of the vast majority of the American people, Republicans in Congress be forewarned: any attempt to remove Bob Mueller will not be tolerated.”

Cornyn responded by retweeting Holder’s message and writing, “You don’t. You don’t.”

Bloomberg reporter Steven Dennis wrote Saturday that Cornyn’s criticism appeared to be directed at Holder rather than Mueller. Cornyn replied, “But Mueller needs to clean house of partisans.”

The exchange came as Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election continued. The special counsel had been appointed by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein in May 2017 after Attorney General Jeff Sessions recused himself from the matter. Mueller’s work had drawn criticism from some Republicans, while Democrats and other supporters defended the investigation’s independence.

Washington Post columnist Greg Sargent asked Cornyn on Twitter whether he would accept the findings of the Mueller investigation as legitimate.

“Makes sense to me to wait to see what they are first,” Cornyn responded.

Cornyn did not call for Mueller’s removal in the exchange, but his comments about alleged partisanship prompted criticism from some Twitter users who viewed them as an attempt to undermine the investigation.

“If you even THINK of firing Mueller I’ll make it my life’s mission to make sure this is your last term, buddy,” one user wrote.

Other users from Texas also criticized Cornyn and expressed support for Mueller.

“Carrollton, TX here. Ready and willing to help get Cruz and Cornyn out,” one commenter wrote, referring to Cornyn and fellow Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz.

“Garland, TX here. Same! Bye bye,” another user posted.

“Austin, TX. #IStandWithMueller,” a third commenter wrote, accusing Cornyn of representing his own interests. Those posts reflected individual opinions on social media and did not establish broader public sentiment.

“I stand with Mueller!” another user wrote.

One commenter questioned why Mueller would be dismissed if President Donald Trump had done nothing wrong, writing that firing the special counsel would appear to be an effort to cover up wrongdoing. The tweet referred to Trump as a “Russia pawn,” a characterization that was not established by the senator’s exchange.

Another user invoked the 1973 “Saturday Night Massacre,” when President Richard Nixon ordered the dismissal of special prosecutor Archibald Cox during the Watergate investigation, and warned Cornyn against supporting Mueller’s removal.

Other posts urged voters to put “country over party” and criticized Cornyn’s position. One commenter wrote, “He speaks for me, @JohnCornyn, and he speaks for the vast majority of American citizens who, you should remember, vote. See you in 2018.”

Some users also speculated about moving to Texas or campaigning against the state’s Republican senators, while others said Cornyn’s position would be judged by history.

At the time, Mueller’s investigation had not issued final findings, and Cornyn said he preferred to wait for its conclusions before evaluating them.

**Trump’s White House Christmas Party Draws Scrutiny on Sandy Hook Anniversary**

President Donald Trump’s White House Christmas party in December 2017 drew criticism after National Rifle Association chief executive Wayne LaPierre was reported to have attended on the fifth anniversary of the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting.

The December 14 event coincided with the anniversary of the 2012 massacre in Newtown, Connecticut, in which 20 children and six educators were killed. Trump did not make a public statement specifically commemorating the anniversary that day, prompting criticism from gun-violence prevention advocates and some victims’ families.

Meghan McCain Tweets Response To Steve Bannon Following Doug Jones’ Win In Alabama

As Democrat Doug Jones won a U.S. Senate seat in traditionally Republican Alabama, the result prompted reactions across social media, including from some Republicans. Jones narrowly defeated Republican Roy Moore in a special election for the seat vacated by Jeff Sessions after he was appointed attorney general.

Meghan McCain, the daughter of the late Sen. John McCain, directed a brief message at Steve Bannon, one of Moore’s prominent supporters, after the election results were announced:

“Suck it, Bannon.”  
— Meghan McCain (@MeghanMcCain), December 13, 2017

The three-word post quickly drew attention online.

Bannon spoke at Moore’s election-night rally and had endorsed Moore during the Republican primary, opposing Sen. Luther Strange, whom President Donald Trump supported. Bannon continued backing Moore after multiple women accused the Republican candidate of pursuing them when they were teenagers and, in some cases, of sexual misconduct. Moore denied the allegations and said he had not engaged in sexual wrongdoing.

Bannon had urged Republicans to support Moore and criticized those who declined to do so. Moore’s campaign and supporters rejected the allegations, while several national Republican figures withdrew their endorsements or called on him to leave the race.

On Dec. 12, Alabama voters elected Jones by a narrow margin, making him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Alabama since 1992. The outcome was widely viewed as a setback for Moore, Bannon and other Republicans who had supported his candidacy.

Jones’ victory also demonstrated that Democrats could compete in a state that had strongly favored Republicans in recent presidential and statewide elections. However, the result did not by itself signal a broad change in Alabama’s political alignment; Republican candidates continued to hold the state’s other Senate seat and most statewide offices.

McCain’s post reflected one of several reactions from Republicans and other conservatives who had opposed Moore’s candidacy. The election showed that, even in a heavily Republican state, allegations surrounding a candidate and divisions within a party could affect the outcome of a closely contested race.

**Liberal Group Uses Ivanka Trump’s Comments in Billboard Outside Trump Rally**

President Donald Trump appeared at a rally in Pensacola, Florida, on Friday night to support Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore. The event drew supporters as well as protesters, including a liberal group that highlighted comments made by Trump’s daughter, Ivanka Trump, about allegations against Moore.

American Bridge used a mobile billboard featuring Ivanka Trump’s criticism of Moore. The truck displayed the message, “There’s a special place in hell for people who prey on children,” alongside a photograph of Trump’s daughter.

“Happening now at @realDonaldTrump’s rally: we’re driving a mobile billboard promoting @IvankaTrump’s condemnation of Roy Moore,” American Bridge wrote on Twitter.

The group said the billboard also featured Ivanka Trump’s comment that she had “no reason to doubt the victims’ accounts.” A video posted by American Bridge showed the vehicle outside the rally.

“There is a special place in hell for people who prey on children,” Ivanka Trump told the Associated Press after allegations against Moore became public. “I’ve yet to see a valid explanation, and I have no reason to doubt the victims’ accounts.”

Several women had accused Moore of pursuing or initiating sexual relationships with them when they were teenagers, while Moore was in his 30s and serving as a district attorney. Moore denied the allegations. Trump endorsed Moore before the rally and spoke in his support, while saying the choice was ultimately up to Alabama voters.

The billboard was reportedly displayed near the rally and driven around the area by American Bridge staff members.

Trump had also faced public accusations of sexual harassment or assault from numerous women before and after his 2016 presidential campaign; he denied the allegations. The controversy surrounding Moore became a major issue in the Alabama Senate race, drawing national attention to the Republican candidate’s record and his treatment of the accusations.

BREAKING: Former Officer Sentenced in Walter Scott Shooting (DETAILS)

In the United States, police use of force and accountability have remained subjects of intense public debate, particularly in cases involving Black Americans. The deaths of Sandra Bland, Philando Castile, Keith Lamont Scott, Michael Brown and Freddie Gray, among others, have drawn nationwide attention and prompted calls for changes in policing and the criminal justice system.

One such case came from North Charleston, South Carolina, where police officer Michael Slager fatally shot Walter Scott, a Black man, after a traffic stop in April 2015. Scott was running away when Slager fired several shots. A bystander, Feidin Santana, recorded the encounter, and the video became central to the investigation.

The footage appeared to contradict Slager’s initial account that he had feared for his life. It showed him firing at Scott’s back as Scott ran away, then approaching and handcuffing him. The video also showed Slager placing an object near Scott’s body after the shooting. Prosecutors later described the object as a Taser.

Following the release of the video, Slager was arrested and charged in state court with murder. His first trial ended in a mistrial in December 2016 after jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict. In May 2017, Slager pleaded guilty in federal court to violating Scott’s civil rights and obstructing justice.

On December 7, 2017, U.S. District Judge David Norton sentenced Slager to 20 years in federal prison. The sentence was imposed under a plea agreement and included a finding that Slager had acted with malice. The former officer also received three years of supervised release.

The case drew national attention because the bystander’s video provided evidence that challenged the officer’s initial account. Scott’s family and civil rights advocates had called for accountability, while Slager’s family asked the court for leniency.

Slager’s conviction and sentence marked a significant development in a case that had become part of the broader debate over police shootings, the use of video evidence and equal treatment under the law. The outcome did not resolve those wider questions, but it demonstrated the role that independent recordings and federal civil rights prosecutions can play in cases involving police use of deadly force.

Questions were raised about President Donald Trump’s health after he appeared to slur some words during a speech announcing the U.S. decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. The White House attributed the moment to dry mouth, while commentators and social-media users suggested other possible explanations. A brief speech, however, does not establish that a person has a medical or mental-health condition, and no public medical assessment linked the incident to one.

Discussion of Trump’s behavior and communication had already intensified in the media. His frequent tweets and controversial comments, including his decision to retweet anti-Muslim videos posted by a far-right British group, drew widespread criticism. Some commentators and mental-health professionals offered opinions about his conduct, but public speculation is not a diagnosis, and professional organizations generally caution against assessing a person without a direct examination.

Questions about the president’s fitness also emerged amid pressure from special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into possible contacts between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. The investigation had expanded after former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI. Neither the investigation nor Flynn’s plea established that Trump was unable to perform the duties of the presidency.

The debate led some lawmakers and activists to discuss the 25th Amendment, which provides a process for addressing a president’s inability to discharge the powers and duties of the office. Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, supported legislation known as the Oversight Commission on Presidential Capacity Act, introduced as H.R. 1987. The proposal would have created a congressional commission that could play a role in the process described in Section 4 of the amendment. It did not itself remove a president from office, and the legislation was not enacted.

Under Section 4, the vice president and a majority of the Cabinet—or another body established by Congress—may declare that the president is unable to perform the duties of the office. Congress has never created the alternative body referenced in the amendment. At the time, Raskin and other supporters argued that such a mechanism was needed, while opponents questioned the proposal and said there was no established basis for invoking the amendment.

Palestinian officials condemned the announcement. Saeb Erekat, then the Palestine Liberation Organization’s secretary-general and a senior negotiator, said Trump had “destroyed any possibility of peace” and was pushing the region toward “chaos and violence.”

Palestinian officials have long sought East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state, while Israel claims the city as its capital. Most countries have not recognized Jerusalem as belonging exclusively to either side.

Leaders across the Middle East warned that the decision could increase tensions. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called Jerusalem a “red line” for Muslims, while Jordan’s King Abdullah II cautioned that changing the city’s status could undermine efforts to fight extremism and damage prospects for peace. Several governments also expressed concern about possible protests and violence.

Trump’s announcement was welcomed by many evangelical Christian supporters in the United States, who had urged him to fulfill a campaign promise to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. Israel’s government also praised the move, while Palestinian officials and other governments argued that it risked weakening the United States’ role as a mediator.

The embassy move was not immediate. The United States embassy formally opened in Jerusalem in May 2018, while the broader questions concerning the city’s borders, sovereignty and role in a future peace agreement remained unresolved.

title: Trump Only Cares About Trump; Why He Is Recognizing Jerusalem Today
text: President Donald Trump announced yesterday that he plans to formally recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. While this is left most pundits perplexed, the reasoning is clear. Trump wants to divert attention from Robert Mueller s investigation. It is no coincidence that the day after the news broke that Deutsche Bank has received subpoenas for information on the Trump family s assets, that this Jerusalem decision was announced. What could be a bigger news story than getting this information? A blow up in the Middle East.Look at the reaction world leaders have had to this announcement. American allies throughout the Middle East and Europe have asked Trump not to do this and have stressed how dangerous a statement this is. US News and World Report put this out today: The mere consideration of Trump changing the status quo sparked a renewed U.S. security warning on Tuesday. America s consulate in Jerusalem ordered U.S. personnel and their families to avoid visiting Jerusalem s Old City or the West Bank, and urged American citizens in general to avoid places with increased police or military presence. It is worth noting that while Trump will formally announce that the U.S. will recognize Jerusalem as Israel s capital, there is no movement underway to relocate the embassy from Tel Aviv. In fact, he has signed an order to delay that decision for another six months. This move is necessary due to the 1995 Jerusalem Embassy Act, which mandated the embassy be moved. It also allowed the president to delay that by six months and every president since that act became law has done so this way.The Atlantic has even compared this decision to Trump  wagging the dog,  a reference to a movie where a U.S. president goes to war with Albania to take the public s attention away from his own scandals involving a mistress. The film was viewed as a parody of President Bill Clinton s military actions in Afghanistan and Sudan after he acknowledged an affair with Monica Lewinsky.While whether or not Clinton attacked other countries to distract the nation from his actions with Lewinsky may be a point that is up for debate, it is clear that Trump likes to do things to distract the public s attention. Catherine Rampell wrote about this tactic late last year in the Washington Post. She wrote: Welcome to 2017, the ouroboros of distractions, where every terrible thing is a head-fake for a ruse for a diversion for a misdirection from something else much, much worse. Trump makes announcements, sends tweets and says things without any thought to the real world consequences that follow. Experts in the Middle East fear that the Jerusalem announcement will lead to real deaths. Many people worry  that his thoughtless and impetuous tweets will lead to a nuclear war. His thoughtless comments confuse and enrage many.By making such a move, for such purely personal reasons, Trump is proving, once again, that he is not fit to be president of a condo association, much less of the United States.Featured image by Andrew Burton/Getty Images.

**Watch: Trump-Supporting Coal CEO Says Senate Tax Bill Could Threaten Mining Jobs**

During his presidential campaign, Donald Trump promised to revive the coal industry and bring mining jobs back to struggling communities. After taking office, he signed executive actions aimed at reversing several Obama-era environmental policies, including the Clean Power Plan. Congress also repealed the Obama administration’s Stream Protection Rule in 2017.

“I made them this promise,” Trump said during the campaign. “We will put our miners back to work.”

But Robert Murray, a prominent Trump supporter and chief executive of Murray Energy, warned that the Senate’s version of the Republican tax-reform bill could harm coal companies and put mining jobs at risk.

Murray said the legislation would increase Murray Energy’s taxes by about $60 million a year, according to reports by CNBC and CNNMoney. He argued that the bill’s effects would be especially damaging to highly leveraged, capital-intensive businesses such as coal producers.

“This means that very capital-intensive, highly leveraged employers, like coal-mining companies, will be forced out of business, with tragic consequences for our families and for many regions of our country,” Murray said, according to CNNMoney.

“We won’t have enough cash flow to exist. It wipes us out,” he said in an interview cited by the outlet.

Murray argued that the proposed legislation could undermine some of the benefits he believed the Trump administration’s policies had provided to the coal industry. Murray Energy, based in Ohio, employed approximately 5,500 people at the time.

CNNMoney reported that Murray warned a bankruptcy could affect those employees and their families. Asked whether other coal companies might also face financial trouble, he responded, “Most certainly.”

Murray hosted a fundraiser for Trump during the 2016 campaign and was an outspoken supporter of the president. His criticism of the tax proposal highlighted tensions between some coal-industry interests and the broader Republican tax plan.

Murray’s comments were a prediction about the possible effects of proposed legislation, rather than evidence that the bill had already eliminated mining jobs.

John McCain Asked Twitter Users to Help Him Reach 3 Million Followers as Tax Vote Drew Criticism

Senator John McCain appealed to his Twitter followers on the morning of Monday, December 4, 2017, saying he was 74 followers short of reaching three million followers.

“We're only 74 Twitter followers away from 3M — spread the word & help us reach this big milestone!” McCain wrote.

The post came shortly after McCain joined most Senate Republicans in voting for a major tax bill. The Senate passed the legislation early on December 2, and the vote drew criticism from Democrats and some of McCain’s Republican critics.

McCain, an Arizona Republican, had also been one of the more outspoken congressional critics of President Donald Trump. His vote for the tax legislation nevertheless prompted some commentators to question whether his opposition to the president extended to the Republican Party’s central legislative priorities.

The bill, later signed into law by Trump, reduced corporate tax rates and changed individual tax provisions. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the legislation would increase the federal deficit by roughly $1.5 trillion over 10 years, before accounting for possible economic effects. The agency also projected that about 13 million more people would be uninsured by 2027, in part because of the repeal of the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate.

Critics also objected to the process by which the bill was approved. Senate Democrats released photographs showing handwritten changes to the legislation before the vote, and argued that lawmakers had not been given enough time to review the final text. Senator Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, posted an image of the documents on Twitter, writing that Republicans were making “handwritten changes to their already handwritten changes.”

Republicans defended the bill as a way to reduce taxes and encourage economic growth, while Democrats said it would disproportionately benefit corporations and higher-income households. The legislation passed the Senate 51-48, with McCain voting in favor.

After McCain’s Twitter post, some users responded by criticizing his tax vote rather than promoting his account. Several tweets used the hashtag #UnfollowMcCain, but the scale and effect of the effort were not independently established.

One post claimed that McCain had lost thousands of followers since the appeal and linked the change to his vote on the tax bill. Other users similarly accused him of supporting legislation they believed would harm access to health care.

“I’m a ‘no’ on that. You can have all the Twitter followers you want — AFTER you prove that you care more about this country than you do about the corrupt GOP & your stinking donors by voting *NO* on the #GOPTaxScam,” one user wrote.

Another critic said McCain’s vote had damaged his reputation as a Republican willing to challenge his party. The responses reflected the broader political reaction to the tax bill, rather than establishing that McCain’s request had caused a coordinated or unusually large loss of followers.

McCain was undergoing treatment for brain cancer at the time, but there is no clear evidence that his health or medical care was connected to the online reaction to his post. His appeal for followers remained a minor social-media moment amid the larger debate over the tax legislation and the closely divided Senate vote.

**Email From Trump Transition Official Referenced Russia’s Role in 2016 Election**

K.T. McFarland, who later became deputy national security adviser in the Trump administration, wrote in an email during the 2016 presidential transition that Russia had “just thrown the U.S.A. election” to Donald Trump, according to emails obtained or described by *The New York Times*. The message, written weeks before Trump’s inauguration, discussed the difficulty of easing relations with Moscow while sanctions remained in place.

The email does not by itself establish that Trump transition officials believed Russia had improperly influenced the election, and its meaning was disputed. A White House lawyer told *The Times* that McFarland was referring to the way Democrats had characterized the election results and Russia’s alleged role in them.

The newspaper reported that emails among senior transition officials showed that Michael Flynn was in contact with other members of the incoming administration before and after his conversations with Russian Ambassador Sergey I. Kislyak about U.S. sanctions against Russia. The exchanges included discussions of foreign policy and the transition’s approach to relations with Moscow.

McFarland sent the email to Thomas P. Bossert, who later became Trump’s homeland security adviser, and forwarded it to Flynn, future chief of staff Reince Priebus, future senior strategist Stephen Bannon and future press secretary Sean Spicer, according to reports by *The Daily Beast* and *The New York Times*.

The communications became part of broader scrutiny of contacts between members of Trump’s transition team and Russian officials following the 2016 election. U.S. intelligence agencies later concluded that Russia had sought to influence the election, while investigations examined whether anyone associated with the Trump campaign coordinated with those efforts. Those inquiries did not establish that the email alone demonstrated such coordination.

In a 2017 segment, HBO host John Oliver referred to the developing controversy as “Stupid Watergate,” describing it as a scandal with potentially serious consequences but involving repeated mistakes by those connected to it.

**Michael Flynn Pleads Guilty in Russia Investigation as White House Seeks to Limit Fallout**

While President Donald Trump was away from Washington, special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election continued. Former national security adviser Michael Flynn pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his conversations with Russia’s ambassador and agreed to cooperate with the investigation.

According to court documents, Flynn admitted that he was directed by a senior member of the Trump transition team to contact Russian officials in December 2016. The conversations included discussions about a United Nations resolution and U.S. sanctions imposed on Russia by the Obama administration. The documents did not establish that Trump, as a candidate or president-elect, ordered Flynn to contact the Russians.

Flynn’s plea marked the first criminal case brought by Mueller’s team against a senior member of the Trump administration. It did not, by itself, establish that the Trump campaign colluded with the Russian government. Flynn’s cooperation could nevertheless provide investigators with additional information about contacts between the transition team and Russian officials.

After the plea was announced, the White House said Flynn’s conduct did not implicate the president or other administration officials. White House lawyer Ty Cobb said Flynn had been fired after making false statements to Vice President Mike Pence and other officials about his contacts with the Russian ambassador.

“Nothing about the guilty plea or the charge implicates anyone other than Mr. Flynn,” Cobb said in a statement.

The White House also described Flynn as a former national security adviser who served for 25 days and as a former Obama administration official. Flynn had previously worked in the Obama administration, serving as director of the Defense Intelligence Agency before being asked to leave the post in 2014.

Former President Barack Obama reportedly warned Trump about Flynn during a meeting shortly after the 2016 election, expressing concerns about appointing him to a senior national security position. Trump nevertheless selected Flynn as his national security adviser. Flynn resigned in February 2017 after reports that he had not fully disclosed his conversations with the Russian ambassador.

Following Flynn’s resignation, Trump described him as a “wonderful man” who had been treated unfairly by the media. Flynn’s guilty plea and agreement to cooperate with Mueller added to the political pressure surrounding the Russia investigation, while leaving unresolved the broader question of whether members of the Trump campaign coordinated with Moscow.

Questions about Donald Trump’s mental fitness have periodically surfaced in public debate, particularly in response to his speeches, social-media posts and conduct in office. However, public comments and unusual behavior alone do not establish that a person has dementia or another medical condition.

On MSNBC’s *Morning Joe*, host and former Republican Congressman Joe Scarborough said that people who had been close to Trump during the 2016 campaign had privately expressed concerns about his mental state. Scarborough attributed the claims to unnamed individuals; they were not independently verified, and no medical diagnosis was presented.

Scarborough also urged members of the Cabinet to consider whether the 25th Amendment could apply if they believed the president was unable to carry out his duties. The amendment provides a constitutional process for transferring presidential powers when a president is unable to discharge the responsibilities of the office, although invoking it would require action by the vice president and a majority of the Cabinet, followed by procedures in Congress.

“If this is not what the 25th Amendment was drafted for, I would like the Cabinet members serving America—not the president—you serve America, and you know it,” Scarborough said on the program. “You represent 320 million people whose lives are literally in your hands.”

Trump Retweeted Videos From Britain First Deputy Leader, Drawing Criticism

President Donald Trump sparked criticism after retweeting three videos posted by Jayda Fransen, deputy leader of the far-right British group Britain First.

The videos, shared early on November 29, 2017, were presented by Fransen as evidence of violence involving Muslims. Their origins and descriptions were questioned, and at least one video was found to have been recorded in a different context from the one suggested in its caption.

Fransen welcomed the president’s actions in a message to her followers.

“THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES, DONALD TRUMP, HAS RETWEETED THREE OF DEPUTY LEADER JAYDA FRANSEN’S TWITTER VIDEOS!” she wrote. “DONALD TRUMP HIMSELF HAS RETWEETED THESE VIDEOS.”

Fransen had previously been convicted in the United Kingdom of religiously aggravated harassment. The case involved an incident in which she confronted a Muslim woman. Britain First is an anti-Islam political organization that has been described by civil-rights groups and news organizations as far-right.

One of the retweeted videos purported to show a Muslim man pushing a person from a rooftop. Reports identified the footage as having been filmed in Egypt during unrest following the 2013 removal of President Mohamed Morsi, rather than as a recent incident involving migrants in Europe. Another video showed a boy on crutches being attacked, although the circumstances and location presented in the accompanying post were also disputed.

The retweets prompted criticism in Britain and the United States. Paul Joseph Watson, an editor-at-large for the conservative website Infowars, wrote that the decision was “not great optics.”

British broadcaster Piers Morgan also criticized the president’s decision.

“Good morning, Mr President,” Morgan wrote. “What the hell are you doing retweeting a bunch of unverified videos by Britain First, a bunch of disgustingly racist far-right extremists? Please STOP this madness & undo your retweets.”

The videos and their captions also drew attention because of Britain First’s association with anti-Muslim activism. The group’s name has been linked to the 2016 murder of British Labour Party lawmaker Jo Cox, whose killer shouted “Britain first” during the attack. The group was not responsible for Cox’s murder, but her husband, Brendan Cox, said Trump’s retweets risked giving legitimacy to far-right politics.

“Trump has legitimised the far right in his own country, now he’s trying to do it in ours,” Cox wrote. “Spreading hatred has consequences & the President should be ashamed of himself.”

Trump’s retweets remained online for a time before being removed. The White House did not immediately provide an explanation for why the president shared the material. The incident renewed debate over Trump’s use of Twitter and the consequences of amplifying inflammatory or misleading posts to his large audience.

Trump Criticizes NFL Players’ Protests After Remarks at Native American Event

President Donald Trump renewed his criticism of NFL players who kneel during the national anthem on Tuesday, saying the protests showed disrespect for the country, flag and anthem.

“The American public is fed up with the disrespect the NFL is paying to our Country, our Flag and our National Anthem. Weak and out of control!” Trump wrote on Twitter on Nov. 28, 2017. He also claimed that at least 24 players had knelt that weekend and suggested that NFL stadiums were struggling to attract fans.

The tweet came a day after Trump spoke at an event honoring Native American veterans who served as code talkers during World War II. During the ceremony, he referred to Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren as “Pocahontas,” a nickname he has used to question her claims of Native American ancestry. The remark drew criticism from Native American leaders and others who said it was inappropriate at an event honoring Indigenous veterans.

Trump’s comments about the NFL also prompted criticism online. Some users accused the president of focusing on players’ protests against racial injustice while ignoring other forms of racial and political division. Others defended the players’ right to protest and argued that kneeling during the anthem was intended as a peaceful statement about police brutality and racial inequality.

According to figures compiled by The Associated Press from reporters at stadiums around the country, 23 players participated in protests that weekend, rather than the 24 cited by Trump.

One woman, Leigh Corfman, told *The Washington Post* that Moore initiated a sexual encounter with her when she was 14 and he was 32. Legal commentators and critics noted that the age of consent did not resolve all questions surrounding the allegations, including claims involving a 14-year-old and allegations that Moore used his position or reputation to approach young women. Time Magazine called to say that I was PROBABLY going to be named  Man (Person) of the Year,  like last year, but I would have to agree to an interview and a major photo shoot. I said probably is no good and took a pass. Thanks anyway!  Trump tweeted.Time Magazine called to say that I was PROBABLY going to be named  Man (Person) of the Year,  like last year, but I would have to agree to an interview and a major photo shoot. I said probably is no good and took a pass. Thanks anyway!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) November 24, 2017The only flaw with the President s claim was that not a single word of it was remotely true and he was called on it too, first by Time magazine, who were quick to point out that that s not how the selection or announcement process even works, something Trump should already be aware of, and then by Time s chief content officer, Alan Murray, who tweeted that none of what the President had tweeted was at all factual.The President is incorrect about how we choose Person of the Year. TIME does not comment on our choice until publication, which is December 6.  TIME (@TIME) November 25, 2017Amazing. Peter Souza, Barack Obama s former official White House photographer and an ardent Trump troll, took to Instagram to taunt President Trump. Souza shared a compilation of images consisting of 15 Time covers featuring the Obamas, originally posted by an account by the name of @michelleandbarack. To rub a little more salt into Trump s open and possibly septic wound, Souza also added the caption Someone has a lot of catching up to do  to his post, as well as hashtags such as #TwoTerms, #ThankYouObama, #ComeBackBarack, and #MyPresidentWasBlack. Trump Returns From Florida Golf Trip, Claims He Has Accomplished More Than Any President

President Donald Trump returned from a five-day holiday in Florida in November 2017 after visiting one of his golf clubs on each day of the trip, according to CBS News reporter Mark Knoller, who tracks presidential travel and golf outings.

Knoller reported that Trump had spent all or part of 87 days at one of his golf clubs since taking office, in addition to a visit to a golf course in Japan. He noted that the White House did not always disclose whether Trump played golf during those visits.

At a comparable point in their presidencies, Knoller counted 24 rounds of golf for former President Barack Obama and seven for former President George W. Bush. The figures reflect publicly reported outings and may not capture every round.

Trump frequently criticized Obama’s golf outings during the 2016 campaign and after taking office. “If I were in the White House, I don’t think I’d ever see any of the places that I own,” Trump said during the campaign, referring to one of his Florida properties. “I just want to stay in the White House and work my ass off, make great deals.”

On November 26, Knoller reported that Trump had visited his golf club for the fifth consecutive day during his Florida holiday. The press pool was taken to a nearby public library rather than given a photo opportunity at the club.

That evening, Trump again criticized coverage of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “Since the first day I took office, all you hear is the phony Democrat excuse for losing the election, Russia, Russia, Russia,” he wrote on Twitter.

Trump added that the economy was “booming” and that he had “possibly done more than any 10 month President.” The statement was a broad political claim, rather than a measure based on a standard comparison of presidential accomplishments. At the time, the Russia investigation led by special counsel Robert Mueller remained ongoing.

**Two Weeks Before Election, Trump Criticizes Doug Jones and Urges Alabama Republicans to Vote for Roy Moore**

Two weeks before Alabama’s special Senate election, President Donald Trump continued to campaign against Democratic candidate Doug Jones while supporting Republican nominee Roy Moore, who had been accused by several women of pursuing or touching them when they were teenagers. Moore denied the allegations.

In a series of November 26 tweets, Trump argued that Jones would be a “Schumer/Pelosi puppet” who was weak on crime and border security, opposed to the military and the Second Amendment, and interested in raising taxes. Trump also wrote that he had endorsed Luther Strange in the Republican primary but warned that Democrats could win the general election if Alabama voters did not support Moore.

The president’s messages focused largely on Jones rather than the allegations against Moore. Jones, a former federal prosecutor, had successfully prosecuted two Ku Klux Klan members involved in the 1963 bombing of Birmingham’s 16th Street Baptist Church, which killed four Black girls. During the campaign, Jones described himself as a moderate and expressed support for gun-rights protections alongside some expanded background checks.

Trump’s comments came as Republicans debated whether Moore should remain the party’s nominee. Several party officials and Republican lawmakers had withdrawn their support after the allegations became public, while others continued to back him or said voters should decide.

Trump and congressional Republicans were also pursuing a major tax bill at the time. His reference to Jones’s position on taxes reflected a central Republican campaign argument, but the tweets did not establish that tax legislation was the reason he continued to support Moore.

The Alabama race became a test of Republican unity and of Trump’s influence in a state he had won decisively in the 2016 presidential election. Democrat Doug Jones ultimately defeated Moore in the December 12 special election.

text: Over the last few weeks, I ve watched as the last shreds of the Republican Party s  family values  rotted away.As Alabama voters prepare to go to the polls in December they have two choices before them.They can vote for the Democrat and prove that they refuse to tolerate an accused child molester and sexual predator being in their party and in the Senate, or they can put political power over the morality they have long preached about.In other words, they can either put power over principles or put principles over power.They can t do both.And while they are damned if they do and damned if they don t, choosing the latter of those two options would be a far better and more honorable choice.Some things go above politics, and sexual assault is, and rightfully should, be one of them.Voting for Moore for the sake of political power throws every sexual assault victim under the bus. It will especially be a slap in the face of women across the country, a major voting block that has already been overwhelmingly voting Democrat for many years.If Republicans want to have any chance of surviving as a legitimate political party for many more decades to come, it is critical that they start by drawing a line in the sand when it comes to Moore and the people who defend him such as Donald Trump.This starting point alone can restore a little of the respect the GOP has lost. Perhaps then, they ll even be courageous enough to rejects the racists and the sexists and the Nazis, which will do more to grow the ranks of the party than the Southern Strategy ever did.And then the Republican Party can get past being a haven for extremists and anti-government zealots and get on the road to becoming a sane party with real ideas instead of simply opposing and obstructing at every turn, which has not been good for the country at all.America has lost its respect of the international community and our reputation has been seriously sullied. Letting Moore step inside the Senate would send a message to the world that America supports child molestation and the sexual assault and harassment of women.Such a message from the Republican Party smacks of hypocrisy. After all, we are talking about the same party that constantly bring up the sexual assault allegations against Bill Clinton.But just like how they constantly bring up Abraham Lincoln in an attempt to claim that the Republican Party must still be great, their rhetoric about Bill Clinton is old and tired and not really that relevant today. The GOP is far removed from the days of Lincoln. And Bill Clinton was president two decades ago and if he were running today he would not win. The sexual assault allegations alone would prevent him from even getting on the ballot.However, by supporting Donald Trump, who was accused by a dozen women of sexual assault during the 2016 campaign, Republicans committed a serious hypocrisy that undermines their Bill Clinton talking point.If Moore wins next month, Republicans will only be doubling down on that hypocrisy and they ll be past the point of no return. And the consequences will be severe.America is more diverse than ever before. Women have emerged as a force to be reckoned with after decades of old white guys running the show. Minorities are also set to become the majority of the population, and once that scale tips, the GOP will no longer be able to be the party of white people. It just won t work.It s just a matter of time, and time is running out for the Republican Party.And that s why they must rise above politics and stand for something bigger than themselves.Sexual assault and child molestation should not be rewarded with power and prestige. And that should go beyond the political arena as well, whether the behavior is coming from a corporate CEO or the part-owner of a website or a church leader or any other position of power.Republicans need to start practicing the  morality  they preach and they can do that by putting politics aside and do the right thing.That s what Republicans did in 1860 when they voted for a dark horse candidate as their flagbearer. Lincoln then put politics aside to assemble one of the greatest Cabinets in our history, bringing together liberal and conservative Republicans and even a Democrat or two.And even though Lincoln remained neutral at first and the politics of day made it really difficult, he made the decision to put politics aside and pushed for the passage of the 13th Amendment. Such a move at the time could have cost Lincoln a second term, but he did it anyway.Lincoln put principle over power in the face of an even more contentious and hateful political environment than we are experiencing today. It s time for Republicans to do the same now.Seven years ago, my first article for this site explained how Republicans have put power over principles for decades to the detriment of our progress towards a better future for everyone.Today, I want inform my loyal readers that this will be my final article for Addicting Info.It has been an honor and a privilege to write here for so many years. I must first thank my readers for making this job possible. Knowing that I was informing so many people across the country and around the world motivated me to make writing about politics my career. And now it is time to move on in order to further pursue that goal.It is hard to leave the best job one has ever had. Through the years, I have made friends and lost friends. I have been here through the struggles and the triumphs. And I have done that while drastically improving as a writer and a person along the way.With that being said, it is especially hard to leave the people I work with, and there are many, both past and present, who deserve a shout-out. I would like to personally thank Wendy Gittleson, Sarah Wood, Eve-Angeline MItchell, John Prager, Justin Acuff, Elisabeth Parker, Shannon Barber, Andrew Simpson, Conover Kennard, Jameson Parker, Ryan Denson, Patricia Colli, Randa Morris, Joe Fletcher, Dylan Hock, April Louise Childers, Justin Rosario, Shannon Argueta, Allison McHam Vincent, Christopher Blair, Oliver Willis, Kerry-anne Mendoza, Nathaniel Downes, Nurmi Husa, and David E. Phillips for enriching my life and helping me develop into the writer and person I am today. You have all been amazing friends and colleagues and I would not be where I am without you.Last, but not least, I want to thank Matthew Desmond for believing in me enough to give me my start and keep me around all these years. You have been the best boss I could ever have hoped for and your friendship and support has been invaluable to me. You ve been an inspiration and I will always be grateful and fiercely loyal to you. In the weeks before Alabama’s December 2017 special election, allegations against Republican Senate candidate Roy Moore became a central issue in the campaign. Several women said Moore had pursued them when they were teenagers, and one woman alleged that he sexually assaulted her when she was 16. Moore denied the allegations and said he had not engaged in sexual misconduct.

Alabama voters therefore faced a choice shaped not only by party politics but also by questions about credibility, character and the standards candidates should meet. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Doug Jones, argued that the allegations disqualified Moore from serving in the Senate. Moore and many of his Republican supporters rejected the accusations and described them as politically motivated.

The controversy created a difficult situation for Republican leaders. Some national Republicans withdrew their support or called on Moore to leave the race, while others continued to back him because they believed a Republican victory was important to the party’s control of the Senate. President Donald Trump ultimately endorsed Moore and urged Alabama voters to support him.

The dispute also revived broader arguments about the Republican Party’s emphasis on family values and personal responsibility. Critics said that supporting Moore despite the allegations would undermine the party’s stated positions on sexual misconduct and accountability. Supporters responded that the allegations had not been established in court and that voters should decide the matter.

The allegations against Moore also drew attention to the different standards Republicans had applied to prominent Democrats, including former President Bill Clinton. At the same time, critics noted that Trump had won the 2016 presidential election despite multiple women publicly accusing him of sexual misconduct. Trump denied the accusations, and he has not been criminally charged in connection with them.

Some Republicans viewed the Alabama contest primarily as a referendum on party control of the Senate and the policies of the Trump administration. Others argued that a candidate’s character and the credibility of accusations against him should be considered independently of political consequences.

The election also took place amid a national reckoning over sexual harassment and assault. In 2017, allegations against powerful figures in entertainment, media, politics and business led to public discussions about workplace misconduct, the treatment of accusers and the responsibilities of institutions that protect influential people.

Supporters of Moore said that the allegations should be evaluated carefully and that unproven claims should not automatically determine an election. Critics said the accounts were serious enough to require political accountability even without a criminal conviction. The disagreement illustrated the difficulty of balancing due process with the responsibility of political parties to decide whom they will support.

The contest was held in a state that had voted reliably Republican in recent presidential elections, but Democrats believed Jones had a chance because of the controversy surrounding Moore and the state’s history of electing Democratic officials. Jones was a former federal prosecutor who had led the successful prosecution of two men responsible for the 1963 bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham.

Republicans held a narrow majority, and a Moore victory would have preserved one of the party’s seats. A Jones victory would have reduced the Republican majority and offered Democrats an opportunity to challenge the party in a traditionally conservative state.

The controversy also prompted discussion about the future of the Republican Party. The United States was becoming more racially and culturally diverse, and younger voters and women were increasingly influential in national elections. Political analysts and party officials had differing views about how Republicans should respond to those changes, including whether the party should focus primarily on conservative policy positions or make broader efforts to appeal to voters who felt alienated by its rhetoric and candidates.

Decisions made during high-profile campaigns can influence public perceptions of a party for years, particularly when leaders appear to apply different rules to allies and opponents.

Lincoln’s presidency is associated with the preservation of the Union and the abolition of slavery, but invoking his legacy does not resolve contemporary disputes over candidates or party policy. Historical accomplishments cannot substitute for evaluating present-day allegations and political decisions on their own terms.

Ultimately, Alabama voters were asked to decide whether Moore should represent them in the Senate. They could treat the allegations as disqualifying, accept Moore’s denials, or weigh the accusations alongside their views on party control and policy. The decision belonged to voters, while the responsibility for presenting accurate information rested with the candidates, political organizations and news media covering the race.

On December 12, 2017, Jones defeated Moore in the special election. The result was widely attributed to a combination of factors, including the allegations against Moore, Democratic turnout and the Republican candidate’s difficulty consolidating support. Moore continued to deny wrongdoing after the election.

The Alabama campaign did not settle the larger questions raised during it. Political parties continued to face scrutiny over how they respond to allegations against candidates and officeholders, particularly when those individuals are important to the party’s electoral goals. The episode demonstrated that political power and institutional credibility can come into direct conflict, and that voters may make decisions based on both policy preferences and judgments about character.

Sean Hannity Defends Trump After Time Corrects His Account of Person of the Year Selection

Fox News host Sean Hannity criticized Time magazine after it disputed President Donald Trump’s description of a conversation about the publication’s Person of the Year selection.

Trump had said that Time contacted him to tell him he was “probably” going to be named Person of the Year and asked him to participate in an interview and photo shoot. He said he declined the offer because he did not have enough time.

Time responded on Twitter that Trump’s account was inaccurate, saying, “The President is incorrect about how we choose Person of the Year. TIME does not comment on our choice until publication, which is December 6.”

Hannity challenged the magazine’s statement in a series of tweets posted on Nov. 25, 2017.

“I call total Bullshit on Time. Answer the question; did you or did you not call the WH and say @realDonaldTrump @POTUS was being considered for person of the year and ask for an interview?” Hannity wrote.

He repeated the question in another post and later criticized the magazine’s credibility, referring to CNN and joking about climate change.

The exchange followed Trump’s public claim that he had rejected the honor. Time had not said that it never contacted the White House; its statement focused on the process of selecting and announcing Person of the Year and rejected Trump’s characterization of the conversation.

Social media users criticized Hannity for defending the president and questioned why he was focusing on Time’s statement rather than Trump’s account of the exchange.

Some users also referenced reports that Trump had displayed framed, altered Time magazine covers featuring himself at properties associated with his businesses. The covers resembled the magazine’s design but were not genuine Time covers.

Other commenters compared Trump’s media image with that of former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama, who had previously appeared on authentic Time covers. The responses reflected the broader political divide surrounding Trump’s relationship with the news media.

Time announced its 2017 Person of the Year on Dec. 6, naming “The Silence Breakers,” women who spoke publicly about sexual harassment and assault. Trump was not selected, although he appeared among the finalists.

The dispute illustrated the different accounts offered by Trump and Time about the contact between the White House and the magazine, as well as Hannity’s willingness to publicly challenge the publication on Trump’s behalf.

Donald Trump was not selected as Time magazine’s Person of the Year in 2017, though he had won the distinction the previous year. Before the 2017 announcement, Trump said on Twitter that the magazine had told him he was “probably” going to be named Person of the Year again, provided that he agreed to an interview and a major photo shoot.

The decision followed a period of increased public attention to allegations of misconduct in workplaces and other institutions.

Trump had been named Time’s Person of the Year in 2016, after his election as president. In his 2017 tweet, he appeared to suggest that he had declined the magazine’s recognition, while Time said it did not discuss its selection before publication.

The dispute came amid wider interest in potential candidates for the annual designation, including public figures and movements that had shaped the year’s news. Time’s Person of the Year is chosen by the magazine’s editors and is intended to recognize the person or group considered to have had the greatest influence on events during the year, whether positively or negatively.

### Questions About John McCain’s Walking Boot Prompt Online Conspiracy Theory

Senator John McCain (R-AZ) was treated at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in November 2017 for a minor tear in his right Achilles tendon, according to information posted on his website. He returned to work in the Senate and said he would wear a walking boot while the tendon healed.

“I can’t tell you how much I hate wearing this boot!” McCain wrote on Twitter on November 6.

McCain later posted a photograph from his daughter Meghan’s wedding in which the boot appeared to be on his left foot. In an earlier image, he had been seen wearing it on his right foot.

“Mother, father & puppy of the bride in beautiful Cornville #Arizona yesterday!” McCain wrote on November 22.

The apparent change prompted speculation among some conservative websites and social-media users. Gateway Pundit published a post about the “boot-switch,” while online commenters suggested, without evidence, that McCain was wearing an ankle monitor, faking an injury or otherwise concealing information.

“John McCain’s walking boot mysteriously appears to swap feet in latest photo,” one Twitter user wrote, using the hashtag #BootGate.

Other posts accused McCain of dishonesty and questioned whether the images had been altered. Some users connected the claims to broader conspiracy theories, although there was no evidence that McCain had been caught faking an injury or that he was under house arrest.

McCain addressed the confusion in a tweet on Thanksgiving Day.

“Thank you for your support & best wishes,” he wrote. “My left leg was doing extra work to compensate for the boot, so I’m giving it a break. I still hate wearing this boot, but it won’t slow us down from frying 7 turkeys today!”

McCain had announced in July 2017 that he had been diagnosed with glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, and was receiving treatment. There is no evidence that the tendon injury or the change in which foot wore the boot was part of a broader deception.
