More than a year ago, House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy was caught on a hot microphone suggesting that two people in Washington were being paid by Russia: Donald Trump and California Republican Rep. Dana Rohrabacher. McCarthy later apologized and said he was not being serious. Both men were still in office.

A report by The New York Times, however, described a long-running relationship between Rohrabacher and Russian officials, while stopping short of concluding that he was a Russian agent. According to the report, the FBI warned Rohrabacher in 2012 that Russian intelligence officers viewed him as a potential source and had assigned him a code name. The briefing occurred several years before Rohrabacher served as chairman of a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee focused partly on European and Eurasian affairs.

Rohrabacher did not appear to have a formal role in the 2016 Trump campaign, but his contacts with Russian officials and other figures drew political and investigative attention. The FBI and Senate Intelligence Committee were seeking to interview him about an August meeting with Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, Rohrabacher said. Special Counsel Robert S. Mueller III was also reportedly interested in a meeting Rohrabacher had held the previous year with Michael T. Flynn, who later briefly served as President Trump’s national security adviser.

Rohrabacher’s relationship with Russia went back decades. As a young conservative who worked in the Reagan administration, he welcomed the collapse of the Soviet Union and later developed a relationship with Vladimir Putin. In the 1990s, Rohrabacher said, he lost an arm-wrestling match to Putin, who was then a rising Russian political figure.

Rohrabacher denied that he was a Russian asset or that he had knowingly worked for Russian intelligence. He said he did not remember being told that Russian officials regarded him as a source. Former intelligence officials said the FBI and senior members of the House Intelligence Committee had warned him in the Capitol in 2012 that Russian spies were trying to recruit him. Rohrabacher recalled being told that he had been targeted for recruitment, but dismissed the suggestion that he had been acting improperly.

His contacts nonetheless attracted scrutiny. In 2016, he carried a memo concerning Democratic donors from a meeting involving Russian-linked individuals and delivered it to people connected with the Republican Party, according to the Times report. He also met with Assange and with Russian businessmen, including individuals who had faced allegations of criminal conduct. Those contacts, by themselves, did not establish that Rohrabacher was working as a Russian agent.

Rohrabacher said his objective was to improve relations with Moscow and enlist Russian cooperation in combating terrorism. Critics argued that his approach was too accommodating toward the Russian government and its allies, including Syrian President Bashar al-Assad.

Republicans sought to create some distance from Rohrabacher as scrutiny of Russia’s activities in the 2016 election intensified. His influence on the House Foreign Affairs Committee was limited, and he did not retain the subcommittee chairmanship in the next Congress.

Politically, the controversy posed a challenge for Rohrabacher. He was facing a competitive race in California, and opponents cited his positions on Russia and his meetings with Russian-linked figures.

Hans Keirstead, a stem-cell researcher and one of several Democrats seeking the party’s nomination to challenge Rohrabacher, criticized the congressman’s record on Russia and questioned whether his priorities aligned with those of his constituents. Rohrabacher rejected the criticism as a political attack and used the controversy in fundraising appeals.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and other Republican officials criticized a White House request for roughly $44 billion in additional disaster aid, saying it did not appear to meet the needs created by Hurricane Harvey and other recent disasters.

About 20 members of the First United Methodist Church had gathered for a holiday meal. Afterward, the group discussed firearms and how they should be handled in a church setting. The discussion reportedly followed similar gun-safety seminars held by a nearby sheriff’s department.

Tellico Plains Police Chief Russ Parks said the man showed the group a .38-caliber Ruger handgun he was carrying. He removed the magazine and cleared the chamber while demonstrating the firearm, according to authorities.

Later, as members of the group were cleaning up, another parishioner who had not seen the demonstration asked to look at the gun. The man handled the firearm, which still had a round in the chamber, and it discharged.

The bullet passed through the man’s hand before striking his 80-year-old wife, who was seated in a wheelchair beside him. Authorities said the bullet entered her lower abdomen, exited on the opposite side, and then struck her forearm before ricocheting off a wall and coming to rest beneath the wheelchair.

The shooting caused confusion inside the church, with some people initially believing that an armed attacker might be present. Church members called 911, and emergency responders took the injured couple to a hospital.

Both were flown to the University of Tennessee Medical Center for treatment. Authorities initially described their conditions as critical. Police said the shooting appeared to be accidental and did not report evidence of an active assailant.

The incident underscored the importance of treating every firearm as loaded and following basic safety procedures, including keeping the gun pointed in a safe direction and keeping one’s finger away from the trigger.

During Roy Moore’s 2017 campaign for the U.S. Senate, several women accused the Alabama Republican of pursuing or sexually harassing them when they were teenagers. Moore denied the allegations.

A separate account concerned Moore’s alleged presence at the Gadsden Mall, where he reportedly encountered young women while working as an assistant district attorney. Becky Gray, who said she worked at the mall and was in her early 20s at the time, described Moore’s repeated visits to her department.

Gray said Moore would stop to talk with her when he came through the store and that his attention eventually made her uncomfortable.

“I went to my manager and talked to him about it and asked him, basically, what could be done,” Gray said in an account reported by ABC News. She said a manager later told her that Moore had been banned from the mall.

Gray also recalled Moore spending time at the mall on Friday and Saturday nights, when many younger people gathered there. “It just kind of got creepy to me,” she said.

Another former mall employee, identified in reports as Greg Legat, also said Moore had been barred from the property. His account was presented as supporting Gray’s recollection, although the circumstances and timing of any ban were not independently established in the reports.

The mall allegations were separate from the accusations by women who said Moore pursued them or had sexual contact with them when they were teenagers. Those women’s accounts became a central issue in Moore’s Senate campaign, which he ultimately lost to Democrat Doug Jones.

Gray’s account does not by itself establish that Moore sexually harassed or assaulted anyone, and reports about the alleged mall ban did not provide definitive documentation from the mall. Moore rejected the broader allegations against him and questioned the accounts made public during the campaign.

The claims about Moore’s conduct remained part of the controversy surrounding his candidacy and prompted renewed scrutiny of his interactions with young women before he entered statewide politics.

Trump Administration Moves to Allow Some African Elephant Trophy Imports

The Trump administration announced in November 2017 that it would begin allowing the import of certain sport-hunted elephant trophies from Zimbabwe into the United States, reversing a suspension imposed during the Obama administration. The decision concerned permits issued under the Endangered Species Act and did not repeal the law or create a blanket authorization for elephant trophies.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said it had determined that importing legally hunted elephants from Zimbabwe could benefit conservation under specific conditions. The agency said revenues from regulated hunting may support local communities and wildlife-management programs, although conservation groups questioned whether the policy would provide meaningful protection for elephants.

The announcement drew attention in part because Donald Trump Jr. has previously hunted an elephant in Zimbabwe and posted photographs from the trip. His brother, Eric Trump, has also participated in big-game hunting. The president’s sons were not identified as applicants for permits under the new policy.

African elephants are protected under the Endangered Species Act, but the law allows the government to authorize imports when it concludes that hunting is legal, properly managed and contributes to the survival of the species. Each application must be evaluated separately, and the decision does not authorize the importation of illegally obtained trophies.

The policy was announced amid continuing concern over the decline of African elephant populations. The 2016 Great Elephant Census estimated that savanna elephant numbers fell by about 30 percent between 2007 and 2014, largely because of poaching and habitat loss. The United States and other countries have taken steps to restrict the ivory trade, while some African countries have argued that tightly regulated hunting and limited ivory sales could generate funding for conservation. Texas Sheriff Draws Criticism After Raising Possible Disorderly Conduct Charge Over Anti-Trump Sticker

Fort Bend County Sheriff Troy E. Nehls drew criticism after posting on Facebook about an anti-Trump sticker displayed on a truck frequently seen along FM 359.

“I have received numerous calls regarding the offensive display on this truck,” Nehls wrote. He asked anyone who knew the owner—or owned the truck—to contact him so they could discuss the matter.

The sheriff also said the county prosecutor had indicated that a disorderly conduct charge could be considered, although he suggested that the issue might instead be resolved through an agreement to modify the sticker. The post did not indicate that anyone had been charged or arrested.

The incident prompted questions about whether the sticker constituted protected political expression. Criticism of the president or other public officials is generally protected by the First Amendment, although speech can be subject to narrow restrictions in circumstances not involving the expression of a political opinion.

The Supreme Court addressed related issues in its 1971 decision in *Cohen v. California*. In that case, the court overturned the conviction of a man who had worn a jacket bearing an expletive directed at the military draft, ruling that the government could not punish him merely for displaying the message in public.

The case involving the truck remained a matter of public discussion after the sheriff’s post. The available account did not establish that prosecutors filed charges or that the truck’s owner agreed to change the sticker.

On Tuesday, Donald Trump told reporters a story about Air Force One and former President Barack Obama that appears to be incorrect. Before boarding the plane to return home from the Philippines, Trump said Air Force One had once been denied landing rights there during a trip by his predecessor because relations between the United States and the Philippines were poor.

Trump said Air Force One “never got to land” in the Philippines while describing his own relationship with the Southeast Asian nation as “very strong.”

“And as you know, we were having a lot of problems with the Philippines. The relationship with the past administration was horrible, to use a nice word,” Trump told reporters in Manila. “I would say ‘horrible’ is putting it mildly. You know what happened. Many of you were there, and you never got to land,” he continued. “The plane came close but it didn’t land.”

In September 2016, Obama called off a planned meeting with Duterte in Laos after Duterte directed an obscene remark at him. Duterte had objected to questions about his government’s violent campaign against illegal drugs.

Obama also visited the Philippines earlier in his presidency and signed an enhanced defense cooperation agreement with the country in 2014. Trump said that the relationship between the United States and the Philippines was “probably better than ever before.”

“So it’s very important that we get along with the Philippines, and we really do. We have a very good relationship,” he said. “I would actually say probably better than ever before.”

Duterte’s campaign against suspected drug dealers and users has drawn condemnation from human rights organizations and the United Nations. The number of deaths has been disputed, with Philippine authorities reporting thousands of fatalities and rights groups alleging that the toll was substantially higher. Duterte has defended the campaign and made repeated remarks supporting lethal force.

During Trump’s visit, human rights groups criticized him for not publicly pressing Duterte over the killings. The White House said the two leaders discussed issues including terrorism, trade and regional security. Trump’s account of Obama’s arrival in the Philippines, however, is inconsistent with records of the 2015 visit.

OOPS: Trump Judicial Nominee Faced Questions Over Failure To Disclose Marriage To White House Attorney

When the Senate Judiciary Committee approved along party lines Donald Trump’s nomination of Brett Talley to a federal judgeship in Alabama, questions emerged about information omitted from his disclosure materials. Talley is married to Ann Donaldson, who served as chief of staff to White House counsel Donald McGahn.

According to reporting by The New York Times, Talley was asked in his publicly released Senate questionnaire to identify family members and others who could present potential conflicts of interest. He did not list his wife.

The omission drew scrutiny because federal district judges can issue rulings involving the executive branch and its lawyers. During the confirmation process, Talley also described frequent contact with White House lawyers but did not identify Donaldson as his spouse in the questionnaire.

Talley’s professional qualifications also became a central issue in the nomination. He had not tried a case, and the American Bar Association rated him “not qualified” for the position in a unanimous assessment, an unusual finding for a judicial nominee.

The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced Talley’s nomination, but the full Senate did not confirm him. His nomination was later returned to the White House and was not ultimately approved.

The disclosure issue and the ABA’s assessment prompted criticism from Democrats and legal observers, who questioned whether Talley had sufficient courtroom experience and whether his personal and professional connections had been fully presented to senators. Supporters of the nomination argued that the Senate should evaluate his qualifications through the confirmation process.

The episode highlighted the scrutiny applied to judicial nominees’ experience, ethics disclosures and potential conflicts of interest. It also raised questions about how the Senate reviews nominees whose professional relationships include senior administration officials.

Trump Chuckles After Philippine Leader Calls Journalists “Spies” During ASEAN Summit

U.S. President Donald Trump and Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte exchanged friendly remarks during a bilateral meeting in Manila on Monday, despite international criticism of Duterte’s human-rights record.

Trump chuckled after Duterte referred to journalists as “spies” while reporters were being asked to leave the room. The exchange occurred as members of the press tried to ask about human rights.

“We will be talking on matters that are of interest to both the Philippines and the United States,” Duterte said, according to accounts from reporters present. “With you around, guys, you are the spies.”

Bloomberg reporter Jennifer Jacobs described the exchange in a post on social media. She wrote that Duterte made the remark as the press was being ushered out of the meeting, and that Trump chuckled.

When reporters asked Trump whether he would raise human rights with Duterte, the Philippine leader interrupted and said the gathering was not a news conference. Duterte later told reporters, “I would like for the media to leave us alone,” before they exited the room.

The meeting took place as Duterte faced international scrutiny over his administration’s campaign against illegal drugs. Philippine authorities have reported thousands of deaths in police operations, while human-rights groups have alleged that the number of victims is substantially higher and have called for independent investigations.

Duterte has repeatedly dismissed criticism of the campaign and has used hostile language toward journalists and political opponents. His relationship with the United States had deteriorated during President Barack Obama’s administration, after Obama expressed concern about human rights in the Philippines. Duterte responded with an insult directed at Obama and pursued closer relations with China and Russia.

Trump, by contrast, had adopted a warmer tone toward Duterte. During their meeting, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional issues, but there was no public indication that Trump directly challenged Duterte over the drug war or other allegations of abuses. Trump had also invited Duterte to visit the White House, an invitation that drew criticism from human-rights advocates.

The treatment of journalists at the Manila meeting attracted additional attention because the Philippines has long been considered a dangerous country for members of the press. International press-freedom organizations have documented numerous journalist killings there over several decades, particularly in connection with political and local government disputes. Impunity in many of those cases has remained a longstanding concern.

Trump had frequently criticized news organizations during his presidential campaign and continued to accuse some journalists of publishing “fake news” after taking office. Duterte has likewise attacked critical media outlets and reporters.

The brief exchange in Manila therefore prompted criticism from press-freedom advocates, who said the leaders’ lighthearted response contrasted with the seriousness of threats facing journalists in the Philippines. The White House did not publicly announce any new human-rights commitments arising from the meeting.

Biden Jokes That Trump “Married Very Well” During 2017 Interview

Former Vice President Joe Biden was asked by Matt Lauer on NBC’s *Today* in November 2017 to identify something Donald Trump was doing well as president.

Biden initially offered a qualified response, saying there were “a number of things” Trump was doing well, but that he objected to the tone of the administration.

“I think there’s a number of things he’s doing well. But even the things he’s doing well, it’s how he does them,” Biden said. “It’s more the tone of this administration that bothers me.”

When Lauer pressed him to name one specific example, Biden replied with a joke.

“Well, I think he married very well,” Biden said.

The remark referred generally to Trump’s marriage and did not specify which of Trump’s three marriages Biden meant. Trump was married to Ivana Trump from 1977 until their divorce in 1992, to Marla Maples from 1993 until their divorce in 1999, and has been married to Melania Trump since 2005.

Biden later discussed broader national-security issues and offered a more substantive response about the administration’s approach to military deployments, including the continuation of some U.S. personnel in the Middle East.

NBC News shared a clip of the exchange on social media:

“What do you think Trump is doing well?”

“I think he married very well.”

The interview came amid speculation about whether Biden might seek the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020. Biden said he was not ruling out a campaign, while also indicating that he was not prepared to accept the nomination at that point.

Biden had also criticized Trump earlier in 2017. In remarks reported in January, he urged the newly elected president to “grow up” and take seriously the responsibilities of the office.

“Grow up, Donald,” Biden said. “Grow up. Time to be an adult, you’re president. You gotta do something, show us what you have.”

The exchange reflected the political tension between Biden and Trump, who frequently criticized one another during and after the 2016 presidential campaign.

Convincing President Donald Trump to release his tax returns has proved difficult, but public financial disclosures have provided some information about his business interests and debts. A document released by the United States Office of Government Ethics lists sources of income, assets and liabilities connected to the president and his businesses.

The disclosure does not, however, establish that Trump violated the Constitution or accepted laundered money. It shows that he continued to receive income from businesses while serving as president and that he had significant debts, including obligations to domestic and foreign financial institutions. Whether those arrangements raise legal concerns under the Constitution’s Emoluments Clause remains a matter of debate and litigation, not a conclusion established by the document.

Among the institutions identified in reporting about Trump’s finances is Deutsche Bank, which has provided financing to Trump-related businesses over a number of years. In January 2017, the bank agreed to pay approximately $630 million in penalties to U.S. and British regulators over a Russian “mirror trading” scheme that moved billions of dollars out of Russia through trades involving its Moscow and London offices. The penalties concerned the bank’s compliance failures and did not establish that money from the scheme was lent to Trump.

Deutsche Bank has also extended loans to Trump and his companies, including financing associated with properties such as the Trump International Hotel in Washington, D.C. Public records and financial disclosures show a business relationship between the bank and Trump, but they do not demonstrate that the loans contained Russian funds or that Trump knowingly participated in money laundering. The timing of particular loans likewise does not by itself establish a connection to his presidential campaign or political advisers.

The bank has faced other major regulatory settlements. In December 2016, Deutsche Bank agreed to pay $7.2 billion to resolve U.S. claims related to residential mortgage-backed securities issued before the 2008 financial crisis. In April 2015, it agreed to pay roughly $2.5 billion to settle investigations into the attempted manipulation of global interest-rate benchmarks.

Those cases have drawn scrutiny to Deutsche Bank’s compliance and business practices, while Trump’s financial ties to the institution have prompted questions from lawmakers, journalists and ethics experts. But the available disclosures and regulatory settlements do not prove that Trump received laundered money from Russia. Further conclusions would require evidence beyond the information contained in the government filing and the bank’s separate enforcement cases.

**Trump Defends Putin’s Denial Despite U.S. Intelligence Assessment of Russian Meddling**

During a trip to Vietnam, Donald Trump again said he accepted Russian President Vladimir Putin’s denials that Russia interfered in the 2016 U.S. presidential election, despite a U.S. intelligence assessment that concluded Russia conducted an influence campaign targeting the election.

Asked by reporters whether he still believed Putin, Trump said the Russian leader had repeatedly told him that he had not interfered. Trump said he had asked Putin about the matter several times and believed Putin was sincere when denying the allegations.

U.S. intelligence agencies have assessed that the Russian government directed efforts to interfere in the election, including a hacking and disclosure campaign targeting Democratic organizations and a social-media effort designed to influence American voters. The 2017 assessment was produced by the CIA, FBI and National Security Agency, with the broader intelligence community supporting its conclusions.

Trump has frequently criticized former intelligence and law-enforcement officials who investigated Russia’s activities, including former CIA Director John Brennan, former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper and former FBI Director James Comey. During the exchange, Trump described them as politically motivated and accused Comey of lying and leaking information.

The findings about Russian interference were also examined by special counsel Robert Mueller and congressional committees. Mueller’s investigation documented extensive Russian efforts to influence the election but did not establish that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in those efforts.

Trump’s campaign and associates also faced scrutiny over contacts with Russians and other foreign nationals during the 2016 campaign. In June 2016, Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., met at Trump Tower with people who had offered information described as damaging to Hillary Clinton. The meeting included a Russian attorney and others with ties to Russian interests, though the participants did not provide the promised material.

That same summer, Trump publicly said, “Russia, if you’re listening,” and urged the country to locate emails associated with Clinton. Trump later said the remark was sarcastic, while Russian intelligence officers were subsequently accused by U.S. authorities of hacking Democratic accounts.

Trump has continued to reject allegations that his campaign improperly worked with Russia and has portrayed the investigations as politically motivated. His willingness to accept Putin’s denials while dismissing conclusions from U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement officials has remained a point of contention in the debate over election interference and national security.

Newsweek has frequently used provocative covers, and its November 10, 2017, issue drew attention for its satirical portrayal of President Donald Trump and members of his administration. The cover questioned whether the administration was among the most corrupt in U.S. history and featured the headline “Snakes on a Plane,” a reference to the 2006 film starring Samuel L. Jackson.

The cover story was promoted by Newsweek on Twitter on November 2, 2017:

“New cover story: Trump is leading the most corrupt administration in U.S. history, one of first-class kleptocrats.”

The illustration shows Trump straddling a jet labeled “Government Air” while throwing money into the air. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin appears behind him, with Mnuchin’s wife, Scottish actress Louise Linton, next in line. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos is also depicted, while former Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price appears falling away from the aircraft.

The figures reflect controversies surrounding government-funded travel during the early months of the Trump administration. Price resigned in September 2017 after reports that he had used taxpayer-funded charter flights for official travel. Mnuchin also faced questions over his requests for government aircraft, including travel connected to a European trip with Linton. The Treasury Department later reviewed the matter.

Inside the issue, Newsweek published an article by Alexander Nazaryan titled “Trump Is Leading the Most Corrupt Administration in U.S. History, One of First-Class Kleptocrats.” The article examined allegations involving travel, security arrangements and other expenses by members of Trump’s cabinet, while contrasting those controversies with Trump’s campaign promise to “drain the swamp.”

“[Trump’s Cabinet] were people, we’d been told, who were sacrificing lucrative private-sector posts to work in the service of the American people,” Nazaryan wrote. “Now, those very same ‘forgotten Americans’ were paying for [Secretary of the Treasury Steven] Mnuchin, worth as much as $500 million, because he apparently didn’t want to go through airport security.”

The article also quoted Zephyr Teachout, a Fordham University law professor and author of *Corruption in America: From Benjamin Franklin’s Snuff Box to Citizens United*, on the relationship between power and accountability.

“Power and stupidity are close companions,” Teachout said. “They are actually living in a world in which they can’t see the ways in which they are being corrupted. You’re so powerful that you don’t even understand that a chartered flight isn’t a right.”

The cover was presented as political commentary rather than a factual determination that the administration was the most corrupt in American history. Its striking imagery and pointed headline nonetheless prompted considerable discussion online before the issue reached newsstands.

title: Sunday’s Massacre In Texas Bumped Columbine Out Of The Top Ten Deadliest US Mass Shootings
text: It s been more than 18 years, but anyone who was alive at the time will remember when they first heard the news that Eric David Harris, 18, and Dylan Bennet Klebold, 17, two students from Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado, had shot and killed 12 of their fellow students, plus one teacher and wounded 21 additional people, before turning their guns on themselves in the school s library on that fateful morning of April 20, 1999. The pair were also packing almost 100 explosives in what USA Today described as a  suicidal attack [that was] planned as a grand if badly implemented terrorist bombing. At the time it was almost impossible to conceive a greater tragedy, two lonely teenage outcasts feeling the need to take so many innocent young lives on just a regular day at school. Sure, there had been other mass-shootings of a greater scale, but Columbine is still the worst US high school shooting on record, was the second-worst mass-shooting on any school campus at the time behind the 1966 University of Texas massacre, and the fifth-worst mass-shooting on US soil.Fast-forward less than two decades later and the murder spree at Columbine High School no longer even cracks the top-10 when it comes to the worst single-day mass-shootings in modern US history. What makes the statistics even more terrifying is that the five worst mass-shootings in the United States and six of the top-10, have all occurred in the last 10 years. To make matters worse, three of the top-5 were in the past 18 months.Here are the 10 worst single-day mass-shootings in modern US history, counting victims only. In each instance, the shooter s death has been omitted.Which brings us to Eric Harris, Dylan Klebold, and the Columbine High School massacre. To many, that is one of the worst tragedies the human mind can conjure up   Just a couple of misunderstood teenagers who sought the justice of who they saw as their transgressors by running riot on their school and shooting at anyone in their path, resulting in 13 deaths, before killing themselves. This incident is no longer one of the 10 worst mass-shootings in modern US history, but something needs to be done before it drops any lower.Featured image via screenshot

The 1999 attack at Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado, remains one of the most widely remembered school shootings in the United States. On April 20, 1999, students Eric Harris, 18, and Dylan Klebold, 17, killed 12 students and one teacher and wounded 21 others before taking their own lives. Investigators also found numerous explosives connected to the attack.

The 2017 elections produced a strong night for Democrats in Virginia and New Jersey, but they did not result in a complete Republican collapse. In Virginia, Republicans maintained control of the House of Delegates, while Democrats won the statewide offices and narrowed the legislative gap.

Maine Voters Approve Medicaid Expansion Through Obamacare

Maine voters approved a ballot initiative to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, rejecting years of opposition from Republican Gov. Paul LePage and state lawmakers.

The initiative, approved by nearly 60 percent of voters on Tuesday, directs the state to provide Medicaid coverage to adults under 65 with incomes at or below 138 percent of the federal poverty level. In 2017, that threshold was roughly $16,600 annually for one person.

The expansion could make approximately 70,000 Mainers eligible for coverage, according to estimates cited during the campaign. However, enrollment was not expected to begin immediately. State officials would need to submit an implementation plan and establish procedures for enrolling eligible residents.

Maine had previously declined to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, despite several legislative efforts. LePage had opposed expansion and vetoed related legislation, arguing that the state could not afford the costs. The ballot initiative allows voters to approve the policy directly, although its implementation remained subject to administrative and legal steps.

The vote made Maine the first state to adopt Medicaid expansion through a citizen-led ballot initiative. The result also came as congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump continued debating proposals to repeal or change the Affordable Care Act, including its Medicaid provisions.

Supporters of the Maine initiative said expansion would help low-income adults obtain health coverage and improve access to medical care. Opponents raised concerns about the cost to the state and the effect on Maine’s existing Medicaid program.

Medicaid expansion has been adopted by most states, while others, including Maine at the time of the vote, had not participated. The Maine result added to the broader national debate over the future of the Affordable Care Act and the role of Medicaid in covering low-income Americans.

The initiative did not itself repeal or modify the Affordable Care Act. Instead, it directed Maine to participate in the federal Medicaid expansion established by the law.

WATCH: Rick Santorum Criticizes Trump’s Response to Republican Election Loss

Former Pennsylvania Sen. Rick Santorum criticized President Donald Trump’s response to Republican candidate Ed Gillespie’s defeat in Virginia’s gubernatorial election.

Santorum, a former Republican presidential candidate and CNN political commentator, discussed the election results after Democrats won the governor’s races in Virginia and New Jersey on November 7, 2017.

After Gillespie’s loss, Trump wrote on Twitter that Gillespie “worked hard but did not embrace me or what I stand for.” Trump also pointed to Republican victories in four special U.S. House elections and cited the performance of the economy.

Gillespie’s campaign had emphasized issues including immigration, crime and opposition to the removal of Confederate monuments. Trump endorsed Gillespie during the campaign, though Gillespie did not make the president the central focus of his campaign.

The Virginia race was widely viewed as an early test of the political environment ahead of the 2018 midterm elections. Democrat Ralph Northam defeated Gillespie by roughly nine percentage points.

Santorum defended Gillespie during a television discussion, saying, “It’s not Ed’s fault. You’re blaming it on Ed, and I just don’t think it’s Ed’s fault. I think the bottom line is Donald Trump is not delivering on what he said he was going to deliver on, and that’s the problem.”

Santorum said Republicans needed to follow through on their policy promises and demonstrate that they could govern. His comments reflected broader debate within the Republican Party about the significance of the election results and the role of Trump’s agenda in the defeats.

The losses did not determine the outcome of the 2018 or 2020 elections, but they prompted discussion among Republicans about voter turnout, campaign strategy and the president’s influence on state and national races.

Tuesday’s off-year elections produced significant victories for Democrats, particularly in New Jersey and Virginia. The results offered the party an encouraging sign after Republicans had won several closely watched special elections for congressional seats earlier in President Donald Trump’s administration.

Democrat Phil Murphy defeated Republican Lieutenant Governor Kim Guadagno in the New Jersey governor’s race, succeeding Republican Governor Chris Christie. In Virginia, Democrat Ralph Northam defeated Republican Ed Gillespie in a closely watched contest. Gillespie emphasized immigration and public safety during the campaign and sought to associate Northam with national Democratic leaders, but Northam ultimately prevailed.

Danica Roem also made history in Virginia by becoming the first openly transgender person elected to a state legislature in the United States. Roem defeated incumbent Republican Robert G. Marshall, who had supported legislation restricting restroom access for transgender people. Her victory marked a notable change in representation in the Virginia House of Delegates.

In New York City, Democratic Mayor Bill de Blasio won reelection by a wide margin. With victories in New Jersey, Virginia and New York City, Democrats swept three prominent off-year races for the first time in decades.

The results reflected voter dissatisfaction with some of the themes associated with the Trump era, including harsh rhetoric on immigration and cultural issues. They also gave Democrats momentum as they prepared for the 2018 midterm elections. Party leaders and activists nevertheless faced the task of turning the off-year victories into broader gains in future contests.

Federal prosecutors Drop Case Against Woman Who Laughed During Jeff Sessions’ Confirmation Hearing

The Justice Department has ended its case against Desiree Fairooz, a Code Pink activist who laughed during Jeff Sessions’ 2017 confirmation hearing.

Fairooz was arrested after reacting to remarks by Sen. Richard Shelby, who described Sessions as someone who had treated people equally throughout his career. She was charged with disorderly conduct and disruptive conduct. A jury later acquitted her of one charge but convicted her of another, though a federal judge set aside the conviction and ordered a new trial.

In November 2017, prosecutors filed a notice of *nolle prosequi*, formally ending the case. Fairooz announced the decision on social media, writing, “What a relief! Guess they’ve got enough ‘laughing’ matters to deal with!”

Fairooz said her laughter was an involuntary reaction to Shelby’s remarks. She also described her conduct as an expression of opposition to Sessions’ record and policies, including his positions on immigration, LGBT rights and civil rights.

The case drew criticism from civil-liberties advocates and activists, who argued that prosecuting Fairooz over a brief outburst at a congressional hearing was an excessive response. Prosecutors’ decision to abandon the case ended a legal dispute that had continued for months.

Fairooz had previously been arrested during protests, but the case surrounding the confirmation hearing attracted particular attention because it involved conduct that supporters characterized as political dissent. The Justice Department did not pursue a retrial after filing the dismissal notice.

Trump Jr. Mistakenly Promotes Wrong Day Of Virginia Election On Twitter

Donald Trump Jr. mistakenly referred to the day after Election Day in several Twitter messages urging Virginia voters to support Republican gubernatorial candidate Ed Gillespie.

Gillespie had been endorsed by President Donald Trump during the 2017 Virginia governor’s race. On Tuesday, Nov. 7—the scheduled Election Day—Trump Jr. posted messages encouraging conservatives to vote for Gillespie and other Republican candidates, but repeatedly used the word “tomorrow.”

“Let’s take @EdWGillespie across the finish line tomorrow! Virginia: get out and vote for Ed & entire @GOP ticket,” Trump Jr. wrote.

In another post, he said, “Virginia, the future of the Commonwealth is at stake tomorrow. Find your polling place … to vote Ed for #VAGov.”

The messages prompted criticism and corrections from other Twitter users, who pointed out that voting was taking place that day rather than the following day.

“Think you mean today not tomorrow,” CNN journalist Jake Tapper wrote in response.

Other users also mocked the error and questioned Trump Jr.’s understanding of the election calendar. Trump Jr. later corrected the wording in a subsequent post, writing, “Today is Election Day in Virginia!”

The 2017 Virginia election was held on Nov. 7, with Democrat Ralph Northam ultimately defeating Gillespie in the governor’s race.

President Donald Trump’s support for a sweeping anti-corruption campaign in Saudi Arabia drew criticism from some social media users this week.

Over the weekend, Saudi authorities detained dozens of princes, current and former officials, and prominent business figures as part of an anti-corruption investigation ordered by King Salman. **Facebook Challenged Federal Warrants Seeking Information About Trump Protest Organizers**

Federal prosecutors served Facebook with search warrants seeking information connected to three accounts associated with protests around President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration, according to court filings. The requests included data from the “DisruptJ20” page, which was used to discuss and organize demonstrations.

The American Civil Liberties Union filed a motion to quash the warrants on behalf of three Facebook users. The organization argued that the requests could expose political associations and communications belonging to people who organized or participated in protests against the administration.

“What is particularly chilling about these warrants is that anti-administration political activists are going to have their political associations and views scrutinized by the very administration they are protesting,” ACLU attorney Scott Michelman said in court filings.

One of the users represented by the ACLU is Emmelia Talarico, who operated the DisruptJ20 page. The warrant reportedly sought information about people who visited or interacted with the page, potentially including identifying information and other account records. The page had been viewed by thousands of people, according to the filings.

Talarico said the request could give the government access to sensitive information connected to her account and to people who used the page to communicate about political events. The ACLU argued that the scope of the warrant raised First Amendment and privacy concerns because it could reveal the identities of people who merely viewed or interacted with a protest-related page.

The warrants also sought information from the accounts of Lacy MacAuley and Legba Carrefour. Carrefour, who described himself as a political activist, said he had participated in or helped organize numerous demonstrations and political events. He also expressed concern that his Facebook account contained private information about his personal life.

Facebook was served with the warrants in February and was initially prohibited from notifying the users involved. The company later disclosed the existence of the requests after that restriction was lifted. Court filings concerning the warrants and Facebook’s response remained subject to confidentiality rules as the legal challenge proceeded.

The case raised broader questions about how law enforcement can obtain social-media information related to political organizing and whether warrants seeking data from an entire page or group are too broad.

Journalist Paul Wood previously wrote that he had heard allegations of Russian kompromat involving Trump from sources before the dossier became public. In comments during the trip, Trump described his relationship with Abe and said that, after winning the presidency, he began receiving calls from leaders around the world.

Trump had not previously held elected office, and he frequently referred to that background when explaining his approach to government and foreign policy. His meetings with Abe focused on the U.S.-Japan alliance, trade, North Korea and regional security.

A video or transcript of the remarks does not establish that Trump was expressing surprise about the number of countries in the world. The wording in the original account presents an interpretation as a direct admission and adds criticism that is not supported by the available record.

The United Nations currently has 193 member states. The Holy See and the State of Palestine hold non-member observer status, leading some references to describe the total number of countries as 195, although there is no universally agreed definition of what constitutes a country.

Trump’s 2017 Japan visit was his first official trip to the country as president. Abe welcomed him for meetings and a state visit that included discussions of the two nations’ security partnership and economic relationship.

Trump also addressed the NRA’s annual convention in 2017, becoming the first sitting president to do so since Ronald Reagan. During his campaign, he praised the organization’s support, telling members, “You came through for me, and I am going to come through for you.”

The NRA has opposed many gun-control proposals and supported efforts to expand gun rights. Whether the Texas shooting will lead to new federal legislation remains uncertain. text: Who knew that Donald Trump would humiliate himself and us as soon as humanly possible with his trip to Asia? There was really no way to know that   this is one of the smartest men on the planet oh wait. This is Donald Trump. And in discussing North Korea s decision to fire ballistic missiles over Japan, he wondered why Japan didn t just shoot those missiles down.That, in turn, shows a complete and total lack of knowledge about how missiles work, about even our own military s capabilities, and about the optics of such an endeavor on ours and Japan s part. First off, it would have been extremely difficult for Japan to shoot them down due to their altitude and speed. Japan does have missile interceptors, but North Korea s missiles were very likely out of range.Then there are the optics: Japan would have been embarrassed alongside us. Our own capabilities to shoot down missiles are also limited, and tests on both systems have failed consistently. Watching us and Japan embarrass ourselves would have emboldened North Korea because it would have told them that we can t stop their missiles. An emboldened North Korea is the last thing the world needs right now.But that s not all. Trump also insulted all of Japan by saying that he couldn t understand why a country full of samurai warriors wouldn t want to shoot down North Korea s missiles. While the samurai are a part of Japan s long and rich history, Trump calling them  a nation of samurai warriors  just reinforces the rest of the world s belief that Americans are too stupid and too arrogant to bother learning about anyone else, and would rather just fall back on ethnic stereotypes.These remarks took place well before Trump actually headed to Japan; however, the news of it came out as he was en route. So, just like every other international trip on which the walking racist presidential impostor has gone, we have been embarrassed on the world stage. Again.Featured image via Mario Tama/Getty Images

Trump Questioned Why Japan Did Not Intercept North Korean Missile

President Donald Trump drew attention during his 2017 trip to Asia after questioning why Japan had not shot down a North Korean ballistic missile that had passed over Japanese territory. The remark came amid heightened tensions over North Korea’s missile and nuclear programs.

Japan had missile-defense systems capable of attempting an interception, including ship-based Aegis systems and land-based Patriot batteries. However, an interception is not guaranteed, particularly when a missile is traveling at high altitude and speed. Japanese authorities said they had determined that the missile did not pose an immediate threat to the country and therefore did not attempt to destroy it.

The decision reflected the limits and risks involved in missile defense. Interceptors can fail, and an unsuccessful attempt could create additional uncertainty during an already tense confrontation. The United States and Japan had also emphasized the importance of coordinating their response to North Korea’s launches.

Trump’s comments were criticized by some observers who said they oversimplified a complex military decision and risked suggesting that Japan had failed to respond adequately. Japanese officials, however, continued to work with Washington and Seoul on tracking missile launches and strengthening regional defenses.

The episode highlighted the difficult choices facing countries responding to North Korea’s weapons tests, as well as the challenges of discussing those decisions publicly during a diplomatic trip.

The Investigation Expands As Mueller’s Team Examines Former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn

The investigation into Russia’s role in the 2016 presidential election has led to charges against several people associated with Donald Trump’s campaign and transition team. Former Campaign Chairman Paul Manafort and his business associate Rick Gates were indicted on federal charges and surrendered to authorities. Foreign policy adviser George Papadopoulos pleaded guilty to making false statements to investigators and agreed to cooperate with Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s office.

Former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn has also remained under scrutiny in the investigation. NBC News reported that Mueller’s team was examining Flynn’s activities, including his work for the campaign and the Trump transition team. Flynn resigned as national security adviser in February 2017 after reports that he had discussed sanctions with Russia’s ambassador and had not fully disclosed those contacts to Vice President Mike Pence.

The investigation has also examined the role of Flynn’s son, Michael G. Flynn, who worked with his father and was involved with the transition. ### Hawaii Protesters Criticized Trump During 2017 Visit

Donald Trump stopped in Hawaii in November 2017 while traveling to Asia, where he visited Pearl Harbor and the USS Arizona Memorial. His visit also drew protesters, some of whom displayed signs criticizing his policies and his past promotion of the false claim that Barack Obama was not born in the United States.

Trump received limited support in Hawaii during the 2016 presidential election, winning about 29 percent of the vote. The state has also generally elected Democrats to statewide and federal office.

Among the signs seen near the Hawaii State Capitol were messages including “Welcome to Kenya,” a reference to the conspiracy theory Trump repeatedly promoted about Obama’s birthplace. Other signs reportedly read, “So bad you make Bush look good,” and “Aloha also means goodbye.”

The demonstrations focused on several issues, including immigration, climate change, racism, nuclear threats and Trump’s criticism of Hawaii officials during the controversy over Obama’s birth certificate.

Trump’s promotion of the so-called “birther” theory began before his presidency and continued for years. Obama released his long-form birth certificate in 2011, showing that he was born in Honolulu. Trump later acknowledged that Obama had been born in the United States, though the issue remained a source of criticism from protesters.

Some demonstrators also objected to Trump’s remarks about the military service of the late Sen. John McCain, a former prisoner of war. One protester wore a shirt reading “Trump for prison 2017.”

The administration’s request did not mean that the Supreme Court had found the ACLU lawyers violated court rules or committed misconduct. Any sanctions would have required further consideration by the justices.

The case drew criticism from civil-liberties groups, which said the government’s response could discourage attorneys from representing vulnerable people in urgent cases. Administration officials, meanwhile, maintained that they were entitled to seek judicial review and that the lower courts had acted too quickly.

The proceedings became part of a broader legal conflict over the treatment of unaccompanied minors in federal custody and the extent of the government’s authority over their medical care.

Republican members of Congress were defending a tax overhaul backed by President Donald Trump, even as public-opinion surveys showed that many Americans were uncertain about or opposed to key parts of the proposal.

The legislation, which included reductions in corporate and individual tax rates, was promoted by Republicans as a way to encourage economic growth, investment and job creation. Democrats and other critics argued that the bill would disproportionately benefit corporations and higher-income taxpayers while increasing the federal deficit.

Polls conducted during the debate showed mixed views about the proposal and the broader issue of tax reform. A CBS News survey found that many respondents questioned whether corporations would use tax savings to create jobs. Surveys from CBS and NBC News/Wall Street Journal also found that people were divided over whether the legislation would strengthen the economy.

Republicans emphasized that lower corporate taxes could eventually benefit workers through higher wages and increased investment. Some economists, however, disputed the administration’s projections about how quickly those benefits would reach employees.

When a Vox reporter asked Republican lawmakers about public opposition to the legislation, Rep. Chris Collins, a New York Republican, responded, “I don’t care,” according to the report. The exchange was presented as an example of the sharp disagreements between lawmakers and critics over how much weight should be given to polling on the tax bill.

Other Republicans offered more qualified responses. Rep. Mike Conaway of Texas said he did not believe the polls cited by the reporter. Rep. Jason Smith of Missouri said he would like to see the surveys, adding that they did not reflect the views of his constituents.

The lawmakers’ responses came as Republicans worked to build support for one of the party’s major legislative priorities. The tax bill had not yet been fully considered by Congress, and its provisions remained subject to negotiations.

Republican leaders argued that the proposal would simplify the tax code and promote economic growth. Democrats maintained that the measure favored wealthy Americans and corporations. The disagreement over public opinion reflected the broader political debate surrounding the bill and the competing claims about its likely effects on taxpayers and the economy.

As Congress continued considering the legislation, lawmakers faced pressure to explain how the bill would affect their constituents and how its costs would be addressed.

Trump’s Energy Secretary Said Electricity Could Improve Safety in Developing Countries

Rick Perry, then U.S. energy secretary, argued that expanding access to electricity in developing countries could improve people’s lives and contribute to greater safety, including by providing lighting in areas where people may otherwise be vulnerable to crime.

“From the standpoint of sexual assault, when the lights are on, when you have light that shines the righteousness, if you will, on those types of acts,” Perry said. “So from the standpoint of how you really affect people’s lives, fossil fuels is going to play a role in that. I happen to think it’s going to play a positive role.”

Perry’s remarks linked energy access and public safety, but he did not present lighting as a comprehensive solution to sexual assault. The statement drew criticism from people who said it oversimplified the causes of sexual violence and risked implying that assaults primarily occur because communities lack electricity.

Improved lighting can be one part of broader efforts to make streets, homes and public spaces safer. However, sexual violence occurs in many settings, including places with reliable electricity, and is influenced by factors such as abuse of power, coercion, discrimination and failures in prevention and law enforcement.

The comments also reflected Perry’s broader support for expanding fossil-fuel production and electricity generation. Perry has frequently promoted natural gas, coal and other conventional energy sources while emphasizing the importance of bringing electricity to communities that lack dependable access to it.

Critics of the secretary’s position argued that development policy should address energy poverty without suggesting that fossil fuels or electric lighting alone can prevent rape. They also noted that improving safety requires education, effective institutions, support for survivors and accountability for perpetrators.

Perry’s statement did not establish that fossil fuels would stop sexual assault. It expressed his view that expanded energy access could have positive social effects, including better lighting and potentially safer public spaces. The causes of sexual violence, however, are considerably broader than darkness or a lack of electricity.

Some players began kneeling in 2016 after Colin Kaepernick, then with the San Francisco 49ers, started the protest. The issue received renewed national attention in 2017 after President Donald Trump criticized the players and called on NFL owners to discipline those who refused to stand.

Papa John’s reported weaker-than-expected sales, and its stock price fell following the announcement. The decline reduced the value of Schnatter’s holdings by an estimated tens of millions of dollars, although the company’s results reflected a range of business factors and did not establish that the protests were solely responsible.

“Leadership starts at the top, and this is an example of poor leadership,” Schnatter said at the time. He added that the company was disappointed that the NFL and its leadership had not resolved the dispute “to the satisfaction of all parties.”

Those disputes contributed to public scrutiny of the chain, although claims that they alone caused a nationwide boycott or specific financial losses are difficult to establish.

Other restaurant companies did not report the same effect from the protests. Pizza Hut, another major pizza chain, said at the time that it had not seen a measurable impact on its business from the NFL controversy. Differences in marketing, customers and sales channels made direct comparisons difficult.

Schnatter remained a wealthy businessman and a major shareholder in Papa John’s, but the company’s stock decline and weaker sales put pressure on its leadership. 4 Reasons Why This Little-Known Trump Aide May Be More Relevant to the Russia Investigation Than Paul Manafort

On Monday, former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort was indicted as part of special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. The charges against Manafort and his business associate Rick Gates concern alleged financial crimes and violations of foreign-agent registration laws, rather than an alleged conspiracy with Russia.

The same day, court documents revealed that another former Trump campaign adviser, George Papadopoulos, had pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI. Papadopoulos is less well known than Manafort, but his case is directly tied to his contacts with people claiming connections to the Russian government and to efforts to arrange meetings between the Trump campaign and Russian officials.

That does not establish that President Donald Trump or the campaign conspired with Russia. But it explains why Papadopoulos could be significant to Mueller’s investigation.

First, Papadopoulos’s contacts took place while he was working as a foreign-policy adviser to the campaign. According to his plea agreement, he communicated with people connected to Russia who claimed to possess politically damaging information about Hillary Clinton. The agreement also describes discussions about arranging a meeting between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The documents do not say that Trump approved such a meeting or was aware of all of Papadopoulos’s communications. They do indicate that Papadopoulos discussed his efforts with campaign officials. One senior campaign official encouraged him to continue exploring the possibility of a meeting, according to the court filings.

Second, the timing of Papadopoulos’s outreach has drawn attention. His contacts with individuals claiming to have Russian government connections began before the June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower involving Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, Manafort and a Russian lawyer who was described as having damaging information about Clinton.

Trump Jr. initially said the meeting concerned Russian adoptions, but later released emails showing that the prospect of information about Clinton was a central reason for it. The meeting itself has not been shown to have produced an agreement or actionable information.

Third, Papadopoulos’s case intersects with broader questions about what campaign officials knew about Russian efforts to influence the election. U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that Russia conducted a campaign aimed at affecting the election, including the hacking and release of Democratic emails. Trump also publicly called on Russia during the 2016 campaign to find Clinton’s missing emails, a remark he later characterized as a joke. Neither event, by itself, establishes coordination between the campaign and the Russian government.

The fourth reason for Papadopoulos’s importance is that he is cooperating with Mueller’s investigators. His plea agreement says he agreed to provide information and documents and to testify if required. That makes his account potentially useful to prosecutors, although the public filings do not establish what additional evidence he has provided or whether it implicates senior campaign officials.

Manafort and Gates, meanwhile, face charges including conspiracy, money laundering and failure to register as foreign agents. Those allegations relate largely to their consulting work for Ukrainian political interests and financial activity. Prosecutors could seek cooperation from either man, but there was no public evidence at the time that either had agreed to do so.

Papadopoulos has acknowledged lying to the FBI about the timing and nature of his contacts with Russian-linked individuals. His plea agreement provides evidence that he had outreach involving Russia while serving on the campaign, but it does not prove that Trump knew about or authorized those efforts. His cooperation could make him an important witness, but its ultimate significance will depend on what investigators can corroborate.

title: Former Ambassador Accuses Trump Of Violating Constitution Every Time A Diplomat Visits
text: While the Trump administration is still reeling over the fact that Special Investigator Robert Mueller has now arrested three people with close ties to the administration over its ties to Russia, there is another serious alleged violation of the law that everyone should be making bigger headlines.According to a former Ambassador from Mexico, the Trump administration is *ahem* encouraging world leaders to stay at Trump properties while they are visiting in the United States.Arturo Sarukhan, who served as Mexico s ambassador to the United States from 2007 to 2013, tweeted on Tuesday that a former U.S. diplomat told him the U.S. State Department s protocol emphasizes to world leaders that they should use Trump s D.C. hotel for official visits.Sarukhan s tweet also uses the term  kakistocracy,  which means government by the worst people.Source: Think ProgressKakistocracia: ex funcionario EU me dice q Protocolo DptoEstado fue instruido a enfatizar a gobs? usar HotelTrump p/ viajes oficiales a DC  Arturo Sarukhan (@Arturo_Sarukhan) October 31, 2017If this is true, this is a clear violation of the Constitution s Emoluments Clause, which forbids U.S. officials from receiving anything of value from foreign leaders because it could lead to corruption. Of course, the ethics ship sailed away from the White House the moment Donald Trump took office, so it s pretty believable that Trump would strong-arm people to stay at his properties. He s been accused of doing it before.Back in May, someone projected  Emoluments Welcome  and  Pay Trump Bribes Here  on Trump s D.C. hotel.Had a lot of fun projecting #emolumentswelcome on Trump hotel pic.twitter.com/FlFr2ITJtj  robin bell (@bellvisuals) May 16, 2017Being projected on Trump Hotel in DC right now. #resist pic.twitter.com/RJEAqOnGgp  Tim Hogan (@timjhogan) May 16, 2017Trump is currently facing a number of lawsuits, including from members of Congress, about his violating the Emoluments Clause.In June, Think Progress said this:Trump s new downtown DC hotel has hosted embassy events for Azerbaijan and Kuwait, who switched to the Trump hotel from their original booking at the Four Seasons. The hotel hosted an annual conference sponsored by the Turkish state last month a conference that in previous years was habitually held at the Ritz Carlton. And, since Trump s election, a Saudi-backed lobbying campaign spent around $270,000 at the hotel for lodging and catering costs.When a federal official, especially the President, profits off of foreign dignitaries, conflicts abound. It s difficult to claim the moral high ground or to impose sanctions when our own government is running a pay-for-play scam, which is exactly what this is.Featured image via Win McNamee/Getty Images

While the investigation led by special counsel Robert Mueller was drawing attention to the Trump administration’s ties to Russia in 2017, another controversy involved the president’s Washington hotel and foreign diplomats.

Arturo Sarukhan, who served as Mexico’s ambassador to the United States from 2007 to 2013, tweeted on Oct. 31, 2017, that a former U.S. diplomat had told him the State Department’s protocol office was emphasizing President Donald Trump’s Washington hotel to foreign governments planning official visits.

Sarukhan’s post was not accompanied by documentation identifying the former diplomat or confirming the claim. It also used the term “kakistocracy,” which refers to government by the least qualified or worst people.

Source: ThinkProgress

“Kakistocracia: ex funcionario EU me dice q Protocolo DptoEstado fue instruido a enfatizar a gobs? usar HotelTrump p/ viajes oficiales a DC” — Arturo Sarukhan (@Arturo_Sarukhan), October 31, 2017

If officials were encouraging foreign governments to use a business owned by the president, the practice could raise ethical and constitutional questions. The Constitution’s Emoluments Clause has been the subject of legal disputes over whether the president may receive benefits from foreign governments, although courts and legal scholars have disagreed about the clause’s scope and how it applies to the Trump Organization.

Trump faced several lawsuits in 2017 alleging that his business interests created conflicts under the clause. The administration and Trump’s attorneys denied that the president had violated the Constitution.

The Washington hotel had also become a focus of criticism from ethics groups and opponents of the president. In May 2017, protesters projected messages referencing emoluments and alleged bribery onto the building.

“Had a lot of fun projecting #emolumentswelcome on Trump hotel” — Robin Bell (@bellvisuals), May 16, 2017

“Being projected on Trump Hotel in DC right now. #resist” — Tim Hogan (@timjhogan), May 16, 2017

ThinkProgress reported in June that the hotel had hosted events involving the embassies of Azerbaijan and Kuwait, as well as a conference sponsored by the Turkish state. The publication also reported that a Saudi-backed lobbying campaign had spent approximately $270,000 at the hotel on lodging and catering.

Those reports did not establish that foreign governments had been directed by the State Department to use the hotel or that any payments violated the Constitution. They did, however, add to concerns about potential conflicts of interest created by the president’s continued ownership of businesses that served foreign governments and diplomats.

Reports Describe Tensions Between Trump and Jared Kushner Amid Mueller Investigation

The White House faced renewed scrutiny after federal prosecutors announced charges against former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and his business associate Rick Gates, while former campaign adviser George Papadopoulos pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI.

The developments intensified attention on special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and possible contacts between the Trump campaign and Russia. Former Trump campaign aide Sam Nunberg said the investigation could examine financial dealings involving Kushner and the Trump Organization, though the scope of Mueller’s work is determined by the special counsel’s mandate and Justice Department oversight.

Reports published at the time, including by Vanity Fair, described disagreements within the White House over the investigation and over Kushner’s influence on the president. Kushner, who is Trump’s son-in-law and a senior adviser, was involved in major personnel and policy decisions, but there is no public evidence that Trump blamed him for Mueller’s appointment.

Mueller was appointed by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein in May 2017, following President Trump’s firing of FBI Director James Comey and the resignation of national security adviser Michael Flynn. The president has denied wrongdoing and has repeatedly criticized the investigation.

Some advisers and allies urged Trump to adopt different approaches to the investigation, ranging from cooperating with it to attacking it publicly. Others focused on improving the administration’s political standing. Trump’s approval ratings were low during this period, although comparisons with previous presidents depend on the poll and the time frame used.

Steve Bannon was a former White House chief strategist, not a president, and left the administration in 2017. He and conservative allies criticized Kushner’s role in the White House, while other Republicans defended the president and called for the investigation to proceed without political interference.

Roger Stone, a longtime Trump associate, also criticized the investigation and promoted calls for scrutiny of the so-called Uranium One deal involving the Clinton Foundation and a Russian company. Congressional inquiries into the matter did not establish that Hillary Clinton approved the transaction or that it demonstrated a criminal conspiracy. The subject was nonetheless cited by some Trump allies as a political counterpoint to the Mueller investigation.

Trump had the authority to remove Mueller but did not do so during the period described. Any attempt to interfere with the investigation could have carried significant political and legal consequences.

The reports about internal disagreements raised questions about Kushner’s influence and the administration’s strategy, but public evidence did not establish that Trump was making Kushner responsible for the investigation or for the scandals surrounding the White House.

**Russian-Linked Group Used Meme of Hillary Clinton Boxing Jesus in Facebook Campaign**

A meme depicting Hillary Clinton in a boxing match with Jesus Christ was among a collection of political advertisements linked to a Russian influence operation during the 2016 U.S. presidential election.

The advertisement, which circulated online before the election, was associated with the “Army of Jesus” Facebook page. The page was created and operated by the Internet Research Agency, a Russia-based organization accused by U.S. investigators of conducting a broad social-media campaign aimed at influencing American political opinion.

The ad was among the materials released by congressional investigators in October 2017 as part of their examination of Russian activity on Facebook. Democratic Senator Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, shared examples of the advertisements as the committee questioned representatives of major social-media companies about foreign interference.

Other ads and online pages connected to the operation addressed issues including immigration, race, religion, gun rights and regional political divisions. Investigators said the campaign often presented itself as American grassroots activism and promoted conflicting viewpoints in an effort to intensify existing disagreements.

The Senate Intelligence Committee later identified thousands of Facebook advertisements purchased by accounts linked to the Internet Research Agency. The company has said that the ads reached millions of users, although the material represented only part of the broader Russian social-media effort. Twitter and other platforms also found accounts and activity connected to the campaign.

The disclosures came as federal investigators examined Russia’s efforts to interfere in the 2016 election and possible contacts between Russian-linked individuals and members of Donald Trump’s campaign.

In October 2017, former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his contacts with individuals connected to Russia during the campaign. He agreed to cooperate with investigators. His case was one of several arising from special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation, which was continuing at the time.

The release of the advertisements underscored how foreign operators used familiar political imagery, religious themes and divisive messages to target American audiences. The material did not necessarily reflect the views of the people who created or paid for it, but was designed to encourage engagement and amplify political conflict.

Legal Experts Clarify Trump Lawyer’s Claim That “Collusion” Is Not a Crime

Donald Trump’s attorney Jay Sekulow defended the president during a Tuesday morning interview with ABC host George Stephanopoulos, arguing that the term “collusion” does not itself describe a specific criminal offense.

Sekulow was responding to questions about Trump campaign associate George Papadopoulos, who had pleaded guilty to lying to FBI agents about his contacts with people connected to Russia. Papadopoulos was a campaign volunteer and served on an advisory committee, Sekulow said, but the proposed meeting involving Russian contacts never took place.

“The end result is the meeting doesn’t take place,” Sekulow said. “So what you had is you had all this conversation about collusion. Remember this: Collusion in and of itself, there’s no crime of collusion.”

Stephanopoulos replied that collusion generally refers to cooperation or coordination, but the legal issue would be whether that conduct violated a specific criminal statute.

Sekulow’s statement reflects a distinction recognized in criminal law: “collusion” is not generally the name of a standalone federal offense. However, conduct described as collusion could potentially be investigated under laws involving conspiracy, fraud, campaign violations or other offenses, depending on the facts and evidence. A finding that people communicated or cooperated would not, by itself, establish that a crime had occurred.

Legal scholars have made similar points while discussing claims about possible coordination between political campaigns and foreign actors. Harvard law professor John Coates told PolitiFact, after Fox News host Eric Bolling made a comparable argument, that conspiring with another party to deprive someone of the intangible right to honest services can constitute a federal crime under certain circumstances.

University of California, Irvine, law professor Rick Hasen likewise said that if people participated in a scheme to fraudulently influence an election, the conduct could potentially amount to conspiracy. Whether it is labeled “collusion,” he said, is less important than whether the facts satisfy the elements of a specific offense.

The exchange therefore centered on terminology rather than establishing whether Trump, his campaign or anyone associated with it had committed a crime. Papadopoulos’s guilty plea concerned making false statements to federal investigators; it did not by itself establish that the Trump campaign had unlawfully coordinated with the Russian government.
