Sean Hannity used a Monday-night broadcast to defend President Donald Trump and criticize Hillary Clinton, the Obama administration and the Democratic National Committee.

During the segment, Hannity referred to Clinton as “President Clinton” while discussing the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. He also addressed the indictments of former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and his associate Rick Gates, arguing that media coverage should also examine Clinton-related controversies.

“This is beyond insanity,” Hannity said, according to the broadcast. “Hillary Clinton, Bill Clinton, the Obama administration allowed your national security to be compromised in what is an unprecedented way and few in the media will touch this story.”

Hannity was referring to the Uranium One transaction, a 2010 deal involving the purchase of a majority stake in a Canadian mining company by a Russian firm. The company held interests connected to uranium production in the United States.

The transaction has frequently been cited by Trump and his allies as evidence of wrongdoing by Clinton, who was secretary of state at the time. However, the deal required review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States and approval from several federal agencies. The State Department was one of nine agencies represented on the committee, but the secretary of state did not have unilateral authority to approve the transaction.

FactCheck.org has reported that there is no evidence that donations to the Clinton Foundation or payments to Bill Clinton influenced Hillary Clinton’s official actions regarding the deal. The organization also noted that Uranium One’s interests represented a portion of U.S. uranium production capacity, not ownership of all U.S. uranium.

The uranium produced by the company was sold to commercial nuclear operators, and the transaction did not transfer control of the U.S. uranium supply to the Russian government. Critics of the deal have continued to raise questions about the review process, while independent fact-checking has rejected claims that Clinton personally approved the sale or that it amounted to a national-security breach.

Hannity argued that the Uranium One matter deserved more attention and questioned whether the same standards were being applied to Clinton and Trump. He also criticized the investigation into possible coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia.

At the time of the broadcast, the indictments of Manafort and Gates concerned financial crimes alleged by special counsel Robert Mueller’s office. The charges did not themselves establish that Trump had colluded with Russia, nor did the absence of a charge against Clinton establish that she had committed a crime.

Clinton was not charged over her use of a private email server while secretary of state. The FBI investigated the matter, and then-Director James Comey said in 2016 that investigators found evidence of carelessness but did not recommend criminal charges.

The broadcast reflected Hannity’s continuing criticism of the Russia investigation and his defense of Trump. On the morning of Oct. 30, 2017, former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and his business associate Rick Gates surrendered to federal authorities after being charged in special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation. The indictment included allegations of conspiracy against the United States, money laundering and other offenses; it did not charge either man with treason.

As news outlets reported the first charges brought in Mueller’s investigation, Fox News was also airing segments on Halloween candy and an issue involving hamburger emojis at Google. ### Data Shows Most Violent Victimizations Involve Offenders and Victims of the Same Race

A federal report found that most violent victimizations in the United States involved victims and offenders of the same race, while also documenting a sharp decline in both white-on-white and black-on-black violence over the past two decades.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics report, *Race and Hispanic Origin of Victims and Offenders, 2012–2015*, examined violent victimizations experienced by U.S. residents during the four-year period. It estimated that residents experienced about 5.8 million violent victimizations each year.

According to the report, the rate of white-on-white violent victimization was 12.0 per 1,000 white residents, compared with 3.1 per 1,000 white residents for incidents involving black offenders and white victims. These figures describe victimization rates and should not be interpreted as a measure of the overall criminality of any racial group.

The report also found that violence involving victims and offenders of the same race had declined substantially since 1994. From 1994 to 2015, the rate of white-on-white violence fell 79 percent, from 52.5 to 10.8 victimizations per 1,000 white residents. Black-on-black violence declined 78 percent, from 66.6 to 14.5 victimizations per 1,000 black residents.

The findings come amid recurring political arguments about race, crime and violence. Former White House adviser Sebastian Gorka has publicly emphasized violence involving black offenders and black victims. Indiana Attorney General Curtis Hill has also spoken about the loss of black lives in homicides involving black offenders.

Such statements often omit the broader context provided by crime data, including the fact that violent crime has declined considerably across racial groups. The BJS report noted that information on the Hispanic origin of offenders was not collected before 2012.

Researchers and government agencies have continued to caution that crime statistics should be examined carefully, with attention to definitions, population rates and the limits of available data.

title: McCain Has The Best Laugh He’s Had In 80 Years When He’s Asked THIS About Donald Trump
text: It s gotta be hard these days to be John McCain. Standing up to Donald Trump is pretty unpopular among Republicans these days, and we ve seen the proof in how quickly the base turned on some otherwise solidly-conservative GOP Senators who have decided the age of Trump is just too much for them.First Tennessee s Bob Corker then McCain s fellow Arizona Senator Jeff Flake dropped out of the running for reelection, possibly dashing the GOP s hopes for holding on to the Senate in the 2018 elections. But regardless of the fact that they ve both been what old Mitt Romney might call  severely conservative,  red meat Trump voters turned on the two like villagers with pitchforks.That could be, however, because they don t have the credentials John McCain has. When he trolled Trump hard last week on the  bone spurs  he used as an excuse to dodge the draft with all of his silver spoon, private school pals, Trump tried to clap back with a warning that  people have to be careful because at some point I fight back. McCain s answer? I have faced tougher adversaries. Now, you might think Donald Trump is at least smart enough not to come at a former POW with some weak stuff like that, but you d be wrong. Here’s What Americans Could Do If Trump Moved To Fire Mueller And End The Russia Probe

As Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election continued in 2017, speculation grew over whether President Donald Trump might try to remove him. At that point, no public evidence showed that Trump was preparing to fire Mueller, and the investigation had not established wrongdoing by the president or his family.

The possibility nevertheless prompted concern among some lawmakers, legal experts and advocacy groups. MoveOn.org announced a nationwide response plan in the event that Mueller was dismissed, including demonstrations that supporters could find by searching an online map with their ZIP code. An image of the page was shared on Twitter by users discussing the issue.

Any decision to remove Mueller would have raised significant questions about the independence of the investigation and the limits of presidential power. Under Justice Department regulations, the special counsel could be removed by the acting attorney general for specific reasons, such as misconduct, a conflict of interest or incapacity. The department’s rules also provided for congressional notification if such a removal occurred.

Supporters of the investigation said the public and Congress had a responsibility to defend the integrity of the justice system and allow Mueller to complete his work. Others argued that any response should remain lawful and peaceful, including contacting elected officials, attending organized demonstrations and participating in civic debate.

Mueller’s investigation was an important part of the broader effort to determine what happened during the 2016 election and whether any crimes had been committed. At the time, its conclusions had not been reached, and claims that it would prove treason or implicate particular members of the Trump family were unsupported. If Mueller had been removed, the appropriate response would have been to seek accountability through legal and democratic institutions.

The Numbers Are In: 2018 Obamacare Premiums Reflected Both Market Pressures and Trump Administration Policy

Donald Trump said health insurance premiums were rising and blamed Democrats for the Affordable Care Act. But analyses of the 2018 individual market found that several factors were affecting premiums, including medical costs, insurer participation, uncertainty over federal policy and the administration’s decision to stop reimbursing insurers for cost-sharing reductions.

Premiums were expected to increase in many parts of the country even without the policy changes. Insurers had cited rising claims costs and uncertainty surrounding the ACA’s future when submitting their 2018 rates. However, many insurers also said the end of cost-sharing-reduction payments would require them to raise premiums, particularly for plans sold on the individual market.

An analysis published by Charles Gaba, an independent health-care data analyst, estimated that nationwide unsubsidized premiums would have risen by about 12 percent without the additional policy uncertainty. His estimate rose to roughly 16 percent under what he described as partial disruption and nearly 30 percent under a scenario in which the administration took several actions affecting the law.

Those figures were estimates based on Gaba’s methodology, rather than official government calculations. The impact varied substantially by state.

WASHINGTON: Gaba estimated that unsubsidized rates would have increased by about 26 percent without the additional uncertainty and by roughly 36 percent after accounting for the administration’s policy decisions.

VIRGINIA: His estimates were approximately 43 percent without the added disruption and 58 percent with it.

TENNESSEE: Gaba estimated an increase of about 14 percent without the added uncertainty and nearly 29 percent with it.

In North Carolina, insurers largely responded to the loss of cost-sharing-reduction payments by adding the resulting costs to premiums for silver plans. That design choice contributed to particularly large increases for some unsubsidized consumers, although the exact effect depended on the plan and rating area.

Other estimates showed similar effects. Gaba’s analysis placed New Mexico’s projected increase at roughly 15 percent without the additional policy changes and about 30 percent with them. His estimates for Arkansas were approximately 9 percent and 18 percent, respectively. For California, he estimated increases of about 12 percent without the added uncertainty and 17 percent with it. Colorado’s figures were roughly 28 percent and 34 percent.

The analysis distinguished between unsubsidized consumers and people receiving premium tax credits. Subsidized consumers were generally protected from the full effect of premium increases because the size of their tax credits also rose with benchmark premiums. Unsubsidized consumers, including some middle-income people who did not qualify for assistance, faced the largest direct impact.

The Kaiser Family Foundation also concluded that insurers’ decisions to raise premiums were influenced by the administration’s announcement that it would end cost-sharing-reduction payments. In many states, insurers added the cost to silver plans, while some states spread it across plans or used other approaches. The result was a wide range of premium changes around the country.

The market had also been affected by broader uncertainty over whether the ACA would remain in place, as well as by the administration’s decision to reduce funding for enrollment outreach and advertising. Those actions did not independently determine every rate increase, and premiums differed according to local competition, insurer participation and the health of each state’s market.

Republicans and the administration argued that the increases demonstrated weaknesses in the ACA. Democrats and consumer advocates responded that the federal government’s policy decisions had contributed to the higher rates and market uncertainty.

The 2018 figures therefore did not establish that one party alone was responsible for every premium increase. They showed that insurers were responding to both underlying market conditions and significant changes in federal policy. For consumers, the effect depended largely on whether they received financial assistance and on how their state and insurers handled the loss of the cost-sharing payments.

Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election has produced its first known criminal charges. The charges were filed under seal in federal court, according to reports, with prosecutors preparing for possible arrests as early as the following week.

The specific charges and the people facing them were not immediately disclosed. Mueller’s office declined to comment publicly. The filings marked a significant development in the investigation, which had continued while congressional committees examined Russia’s election interference and possible contacts with members of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign.

Mueller was appointed special counsel in May 2017, shortly after Trump dismissed FBI Director James Comey. His mandate includes investigating Russian interference in the election, possible coordination between Russia and the Trump campaign, and matters arising from that inquiry. The investigation has included interviews with former campaign chairman Paul Manafort, former national security adviser Michael Flynn and other current and former associates of the president.

Investigators have also examined a June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower involving Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, Manafort and a Russian attorney who was described as having damaging information about Hillary Clinton. Trump Jr. initially said the meeting concerned adoptions, but later-released emails showed that the prospect of receiving information about Clinton had been discussed before the meeting.

At the time the charges were filed, it was unclear who had been charged or what offenses were alleged. The sealed filings were expected to be unsealed once defendants appeared in court. The development represented the first public indication that Mueller’s investigation had moved from interviews and document requests to criminal proceedings.

**Questions Raised Over Puerto Rico’s Contract With Small Energy Company**

When the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority hired Whitefish Energy, a small Montana-based company, to help restore the island’s power grid after Hurricane Maria, the agreement drew scrutiny from lawmakers and local officials.

A copy of the contract released in October 2017 included provisions that limited the government’s ability to examine the company’s costs and profits. The agreement stated that government entities would not have the right to “audit or review the cost and profit elements” of the contract, prompting questions about oversight of the deal, which was valued at up to roughly $300 million.

The contract also set daily allowances for lodging and meals and established hourly rates for workers. Supervisors were to be paid $462 per hour, while linemen were to receive $319 per hour, according to the agreement. The terms attracted criticism because of the company’s relatively small size and limited prior experience with government contracts.

The contract further stated that the Puerto Rican government would waive claims against Whitefish related to delays in completing the work. Critics said the provision reduced the government’s leverage if power restoration took longer than expected.

San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz called for the agreement to be voided. After Cruz criticized the arrangement, Whitefish said on Twitter that it had 44 linemen working in the city and that additional workers had arrived, asking whether the mayor wanted them to continue.

Cruz responded that the company’s message was inappropriate and said the contract should be canceled in favor of a process that was “clear, transparent, legal, moral and ethical,” according to comments reported by Yahoo News.

The agreement also raised concerns in Congress. Reps. Rob Bishop and Bruce Westerman, the Republican chairman and chairman of a subcommittee of the House Natural Resources Committee, wrote that the contract’s size and terms, along with the circumstances in which it was formed, raised questions about PREPA’s contracting procedures.

Whitefish said it welcomed congressional inquiries and defended its ability and commitment to help restore electricity and normalcy to Puerto Rico. Before the agreement, the company’s largest government contract had reportedly been a $1.3 million project to upgrade power lines in Arizona.

The controversy intensified as federal and Puerto Rican officials examined the contract and the island’s broader response to the hurricane. PREPA ultimately canceled the agreement on October 29, 2017, after widespread criticism of its terms and the process used to award it.

Michael Flynn, who later served briefly as Trump’s national security advisor, also joined the chants and said that he would be in jail if he had done “a tenth” of what Clinton allegedly did. The Uranium One controversy concerned the 2010 approval of the sale of a majority stake in a Canadian company with U.S. uranium interests to a Russian state-owned corporation. The transaction was reviewed and approved by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which included nine cabinet-level officials. Clinton was secretary of state at the time and was a member of the committee, although the State Department has said she did not personally approve the deal.

There is no established evidence that Clinton received a personal benefit from the transaction or that she intervened in the review process. Amid continuing debate over court fees, bail and the treatment of low-income defendants, the resignation of a youth court judge in Pearl, Mississippi, has drawn attention to a case involving a young mother and her infant.

Judge John Shirley, who served on the Pearl Youth Court, resigned after issuing an order in 2016 involving a woman identified in court documents as “Mother A.” According to reporting by *The Clarion-Ledger* and legal advocates who reviewed the case, the order prevented the woman from seeing her baby while she addressed unpaid court fees. The restriction reportedly remained in place for more than a year.

The case began when Mother A and a friend were stopped by police while driving through Pearl. Both women reportedly had misdemeanor warrants related to minor offenses. Mother A had her baby with her, and a relative came to the scene to take custody of the child.

The matter was then brought before the Pearl Youth Court. Court records cited in reports said Shirley placed the infant with the grandmother and issued a no-contact order barring the mother from seeing the baby until the outstanding fees were paid. The order also reportedly limited the mother’s contact with her grandmother while the child was present.

The circumstances of the order prompted criticism from civil rights attorneys, who questioned whether a parent’s ability to pay court costs should determine access to a child. Cliff Johnson, director of the Roderick and Solange MacArthur Justice Center at the University of Mississippi School of Law, called the reported order deeply troubling and said such cases raise serious concerns about the use of monetary conditions in youth court proceedings.

The case has also renewed broader questions about how courts handle unpaid fees and misdemeanor warrants, particularly when defendants lack the resources to pay. Legal advocates have argued that financial penalties can create additional barriers for people already struggling to navigate the justice system.

Shirley’s resignation was reported after the case came to public attention. Public reports did not establish that the resignation was solely connected to the order, and the judge’s departure did not by itself resolve the questions raised about the proceedings.

title: Alt-Right Trump Lover Loses His Sh*t, Kills His Own Dad For Calling Him A Nazi
text: You might never suspect that up here in beautiful Washington State, we have one of the largest numbers of white supremacist groups in America. After all, it s gorgeous and relatively quiet, and this is a  blue  state, right? But under all of our fall colors, our lakes, our bike lanes, and our farmer s markets is the same hate you see in the Deep South or the rural Midwest or really anywhere in the United States.In fact, here in the northwest part of the Northwest, there are a surprising number of  Alt-Right  adherents. But considering how rural much of the area between Seattle and Canada is, nobody should be surprised at how many Trump supporters there are. And that seems to have been the catalyst for many people in my neck of the woods who at one time were relatively self-policing: Permission from the president to be bigots. If you listen to Donald Trump when the conversation moves to white nationalism, the subtext is almost that bigotry makes you more American, and we have got some flag wavers in these parts.So last month when my local paper covered a local murder that was, at least peripherally, connected to the Alt-Right, it really wasn t shocking to me. My (now-adult) son and I have attended any number of rallies up and down the freeway corridor we live on, and there is a strong presence of Richard Spencer wannabes and Milo Yiannopoulos sycophants at every single one. But over the fold was a face I knew: Lane Davis, a 33-year-old guy who lived a few doors down from my mom s old house. I saw him in stores and on the street. I bummed him a smoke outside the Safeway more than once.I touched that guy s hand.Image via FacebookHe killed his dad out on Samish Island, an island that s only actually an island because of a river that crosses the farmland you have have to drive through to get out there. You don t think about white supremacists on your way to Samish Island. I didn t anyway. I thought about my niece s wedding and my grandpa s funeral, both held at the Samish Island Community Center. I think about the herons and red-tailed hawks that hang out in those fields. I think about my mom sometimes. She s a Trump supporter and a bigot, but she wouldn t stab anyone like Lane Davis did.Davis worked for Milo for a little while, and he went by the online name  Seattle4Truth,  under which he posted to Reddit, his YouTube channel, and later, a super-mega-extremely-far-right website,  The Ralph Retort  (which I just won t link, so get to googling if that s your thing). And really, the link at the beginning of the last paragraph has a pretty in-depth profile of his various exploits, after The Daily Beast got their hands on the 911 call his mother made that fateful day.But it s incomplete. This is a small place, and it s personal. The judge who signed off on Davis  probable cause affidavit was the same man who gave me custody of my son. My friends are friends with Lane Davis  friends. I guarantee without texting her to ask her that the saleswoman who used to sell furniture for me knew Lane Davis personally and had possibly been to his house. When I tell you about the little place I live in, and how I casually handed out smokes to an eventual murderer, and the geography and wildlife near where that murderer lived, what I want you to do is go back to the words in bold letters a few paragraphs ago.Before Donald Trump, the white nationalists, racists, skinheads, Klan members, and just generally hateful people around here might have said something racist in public once. Maybe they had  No Trespassing  signs all over their deep-woods properties 20 miles up the Skagit River. Maybe they sported  III%  or  Prius Repellent  stickers on their giant trucks with the smokestacks tuned to blast creosote every time they leave a stoplight.Now they kill their dad because he called them a Nazi and tried to kick them out of the house when he got sick of their bullshit.Heck, Lane Davis isn t even the first murderer I ve ever known. I used to play D&D when I was a kid with a dude who killed another guy after a party back in the early 90 s. But that guy, by the time we were teens, we knew he was going to end up in prison. He was disturbed. He was morbid. He was violent.Lane Davis was just a racist until Donald Trump came along.Featured image via screen capture

Critics argued that the movement’s rhetoric helped normalize racism and harassment, while supporters described it as an alternative political current. title: WATCH: This Amazingly Aware Company Has Created A Brilliant Way To Document Trump’s Dangerous Tweets
text: Donald Trump s Twitter habit is dangerous. When one has the bully pulpit of the White House to speak from, words definitely matter. That s why it s so concerning when Trump threatens nuclear war in 140 characters or less   it s because he could actually carry it out in a matter of minutes, and the whole world knows this   and is terrified he d do it just for kicks. The same is true   albeit to a lesser degree   when Trump cozies  up to dictators like Kim Jung-un and Vladimir Putin, while insulting our allies, like his insulting phone call with Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull. Of course, these are just a few examples, as Trump spends more time tweeting than he does doing anything else.Since Trump s tweets become more alarming by the day and are far too numerous to constantly keep up with, an awesome company has found a way to help do it   and it s super rad. The good folks at Parse/Error have created the  Political Lamp,  which is an entertaining piece of decor that lights up in a lightening storm with every Trump tweet. They say they like to be politically aware, and decided that Trump s Twitter feed is important to document because of what the orange fascist represents: He perfectly embodies a dangerous era. A world where the words of one man   can endanger the fate of millions by spreading the ghost of nuclear war on the planet. Parse/Error is correct. These are dangerous times. The GOP-controlled Congress might be worrying over tax cuts because they are craven cowards who are terrified of Trump lighting them up on Twitter, but they d better serve the nation and the world   as well as their own places in history   by doing all they can to rid the world of the threat of Trump before he kills us all.In the meantime, though, this lamp is amazing, and everyone should have one! Pearson, an educational publishing company, apologized for culturally insensitive material included in its textbook *Nursing: A Concept-Based Approach to Learning*. The material grouped patients into six categories: “Arabs/Muslims,” “Asians,” “Blacks,” “Jews,” “Hispanics” and “Native Americans.” It then offered guidance on how culture might influence a client’s beliefs about and response to pain. Critics said the presentation relied on broad racial and cultural generalizations rather than emphasizing individual assessment and patient-reported symptoms.

Among the examples, the text stated that Black patients may “often report higher pain intensity than other cultures” and that Jewish patients may be “more vocal and demanding of assistance.” Critics argued that such descriptions could reinforce stereotypes and affect how health care professionals evaluate and treat patients. They also noted that racial, ethnic and religious identities can overlap and do not necessarily predict an individual’s experience of pain.

The material drew attention after a Facebook user, Onyx Moore, posted a photograph of the page on October 16, 2017. The post criticized the content as an example of inadequate cultural sensitivity and prompted discussion online.

In response, Scott Overland, Pearson’s communications director, said the company had presented an important topic “in an inappropriate manner” and apologized for the offense.

“While differences in cultural attitudes towards pain are an important topic in medical programs, we presented this information in an inappropriate manner,” Overland said. “We apologize for the offense this has caused.”

Pearson said the material had been removed from current and electronic versions of the book and would not appear in future editions. The company also said it was reviewing its nursing curriculum to identify and remove similar content in other titles.

“This material does not reflect our values as a company and how we want to serve students,” the statement said. Pearson added that it welcomed feedback from students and others who had raised concerns.

The company said it was working with its editorial teams to determine how the material had been approved for publication. Pearson’s statement focused on removing the section and reviewing related curriculum; it did not provide further details about the publication process.

**Trump Announces Release of JFK Files Under Deadline Set by 1992 Law**

On Saturday, President Donald Trump said on Twitter that he planned to permit the release of long-withheld records related to the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.

“Subject to the receipt of further information, I will be allowing, as President, the long blocked and classified JFK FILES to be opened,” Trump wrote on October 21, 2017.

The announcement drew attention because the records were already scheduled for review under a federal law enacted 25 years earlier. The President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992 required the government to disclose assassination-related records by October 26, 2017, unless the president determined that continued withholding was necessary to protect national security, intelligence operations, law enforcement or other interests.

The law was passed by Congress and signed by President George H.W. Bush in October 1992. Senator John Glenn was among the lawmakers involved in advancing the legislation, which followed renewed public interest in the assassination after the release of the film “JFK” and the creation of a records review board.

The act established a collection at the National Archives and required agencies to transfer relevant documents for review and release. Many records had already been made public over the years, while other materials remained redacted or withheld under the law’s provisions.

Trump’s statement therefore did not create the disclosure process. It signaled that his administration intended to act as the statutory deadline approached, while leaving open the possibility that some information would continue to be withheld.

On October 26, Trump authorized the release of a large number of records but also allowed some continued redactions after federal agencies argued that immediate disclosure could cause identifiable harm to national security or other government interests. He directed officials to conduct further reviews of the remaining material.

Additional records were released in subsequent years, although some information continued to be withheld or redacted. The documents have added historical detail about the government’s investigations and intelligence activities but have not produced a universally accepted alternative explanation for Kennedy’s assassination.

The release process was the result of legislation passed in 1992 and subsequent presidential and archival reviews, rather than a program initiated solely by Trump. The president had authority under the law to approve disclosure, postpone portions of the release or permit continued withholding under specified conditions.

# Reports Question Authenticity of Renoir Painting Displayed in Trump’s Penthouse

A dispute over a Renoir painting once displayed in Donald Trump’s New York penthouse centered on whether it was an original work or a reproduction of a painting held by the Art Institute of Chicago.

The painting in question is *Two Sisters (On the Terrace)*, a work by French Impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir that has been part of the Art Institute’s collection since it was donated by Annie Swan Coburn in 1933.

Trump’s biographer, Tim O’Brien, said in a 2017 interview that he saw a painting on Trump’s private jet in 2005 and asked him about it.

“ You know, that’s an original Renoir,” O’Brien recalled Trump saying.

O’Brien said he responded that the work was not authentic, explaining that he had grown up in Chicago and knew the Renoir in question was displayed at the Art Institute. According to O’Brien, Trump repeated his claim about the painting the following day.

The Art Institute has identified its painting as the authentic *Two Sisters (On the Terrace)*. The museum said the work was given to the institution by Coburn, who had acquired it from the art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel. The museum has long listed the painting as an important work in its collection.

A painting resembling the Chicago Renoir appeared in the background of an interview filmed in Trump’s penthouse at Trump Tower after the 2016 presidential election. Its presence prompted questions about whether Trump owned another version of the composition.

Richard Brettell, then chair of aesthetic studies at the University of Texas, said that, based on photographs of the painting in the penthouse, it appeared to be a copy of the Chicago work.

Richard Rand, associate director for collections at the J. Paul Getty Museum, also expressed doubt that the painting was an original. He noted that although Renoir occasionally produced variations on a composition, he generally did not make precise duplicates of his oil paintings.

“If I were presented with a picture that was an exact copy of a famous Renoir hanging in a museum, I would guess it was probably a reproduction of some kind,” Rand said in an email, according to reports.

Those comments did not establish who produced the painting displayed in Trump’s apartment or how it came to be there. They did, however, distinguish it from the documented work in the Art Institute of Chicago’s collection.

O’Brien said he believed Trump continued to describe the painting as an original despite the questions surrounding it. Trump’s representatives did not provide documentation in the reports cited here proving that the penthouse painting was an authentic Renoir.

The Art Institute’s *Two Sisters (On the Terrace)* remains the recognized work in the museum’s collection; the authenticity and provenance of the painting seen in Trump’s penthouse were not established by the accounts describing the dispute.

title: New Report PROVES Voter Suppression Handed Trump Wisconsin And Possibly The Whole Election
text: In a brand-new expos  on Mother Jones, investigative journalist Ari Berman delves into an aspect of the 2016 election that has been largely ignored in the shadow of controversies over internal DNC politics, shifting blame, and what is now known to be concrete Russian interference: Voter suppression.On the heels of a report Berman summarized back in September, his article for the November-December issue of the liberal stalwart magazine continues where he left off. Anecdotal evidence of individual voters who were prevented from voting in Wisconsin during the presidential election all adds up to a picture that explains the numbers in the University of Wisconsin-Madison study that Berman cites in his summary.The study, completed by UW-Madison s professor of Political Science, Kenneth Mayer, shows a survey in two large counties in Wisconsin that asked whether respondents were either prevented or deterred from voting in 2016 by the new Voter ID law in effect for the first time in that election. The results of the survey were stunning: More than 11 percent of respondents said they were deterred, and that 6 percent   more than half of the nonvoters   were prevented entirely. If those sound like small numbers, bear with me.In the course of research, voters were asked why they didn t vote, how engaged they were in the election, what types of ID they possessed, how confident they were in the final vote count, and their general demographics. The survey never required any respondent to answer who they may have voted for.Possibly the most distressing part of the findings was how disproportionately the Voter ID law affected low-income and minority voters: More than 21 percent of households under $25,000 of income per year were deterred; that number dropped to just over 7 percent for those above that line. The demarcation between white and black voters was even more stark, with just of 8 percent of white voters reporting trouble and 27.5 percent of African-Americans reporting the same.What does all that add up to?As Berman notes in the new piece for MJ, Wisconsin showed the second-highest voter turnout in the United States in both 2008 and 2012, but just four years later, participation was the lowest it had been in 16 years.So let s get back to those numbers.In just the two counties that were surveyed, Dane and Milwaukee, the percentage of registered voters who were adversely affected by the new Voter ID law represents a low estimate of nearly 17,000 and an upper estimate of 23,252 voters. In fact, the study points out, the 11.2 percent nonvoter estimate is actually low in itself, as it doesn t take into account voters who were deterred from even registering by the new law.If every single one of those in the study who answered that they were deterred or prevented from voting had actually cast a vote that counted, voter turnout would have increased by 2.24 percent. And that seems like an incredibly small number, until you extrapolate that across the state. The Wisconsin Election Commission estimated that 3.1 million voters turned out for the 2016 presidential election. That means 69,440 voters   under a conservative estimate   were disenfranchised entirely by the new Voter ID law.Donald Trump s margin of victory in the state? Less than a third of that.Given that the vast majority of disenfranchised voters, although they were not asked their political affiliations, were demographically more likely to vote for Hillary Clinton than for Donald Trump, it hardly requires extrapolation to conclude that, at least in the state of Wisconsin, Trump was right.The vote was rigged.Featured image via Scott Olson/Getty Images

New Report Examines Whether Wisconsin’s Voter ID Law Affected the 2016 Election

A report in *Mother Jones* by investigative journalist Ari Berman examined an aspect of the 2016 election that received less attention than disputes over Democratic Party politics and Russian interference: the effect of voter-suppression policies, particularly Wisconsin’s voter-identification requirement.

The article discussed research by University of Wisconsin–Madison political scientist Kenneth Mayer concerning the state’s voter ID law, which was used in a presidential election for the first time in 2016. The study surveyed voters in Milwaukee and Dane counties and asked whether they had been prevented or discouraged from voting because of identification requirements.

Some respondents reported that the law had made voting more difficult. The survey’s results were used to estimate that 11.2 percent of respondents had been deterred from voting and that roughly 6 percent had been prevented from voting altogether. Because the findings were based on survey responses and limited to two counties, however, they do not establish how many voters statewide were unable to cast ballots or whether the law changed the result of the election.

Participants were asked why they did or did not vote, what identification they possessed, how engaged they were in the election and about their demographic characteristics. The survey did not ask respondents which candidate they supported.

The reported effects were uneven across demographic groups. Respondents from households earning less than $25,000 a year were more likely to report being deterred than those with higher incomes. Black respondents also reported more difficulty than white respondents. Those differences are consistent with concerns raised by voting-rights advocates, who have argued that identification requirements can impose greater burdens on low-income and minority voters. They do not, by themselves, determine how those voters would have cast their ballots.

Wisconsin had recorded relatively high turnout in the 2008 and 2012 presidential elections. Turnout fell in 2016, although turnout comparisons can be affected by differences in campaign intensity, registration, voting methods and other factors in addition to election rules.

The survey’s authors used responses from the two counties to calculate possible statewide effects. One estimate put the number of registered voters in those counties who may have been deterred or prevented from voting at between roughly 17,000 and 23,000. The study also noted that its estimate did not include people who might have been discouraged from registering.

Those figures were sometimes extrapolated to the entire state, where approximately 3.1 million people voted in the 2016 presidential election. Such an extrapolation would produce a number larger than President Donald Trump’s margin of victory in Wisconsin, which was about 22,700 votes. But the comparison does not show that the voter ID law determined the state’s result.

The survey did not identify the political preferences of people who reported being deterred or prevented from voting, and it did not prove that all of them would have voted had the law not been in place. Researchers and election officials have also emphasized that estimating the effect of voter-identification requirements is difficult and that survey-based estimates can carry substantial uncertainty.

Trump won Wisconsin by a narrow margin over Hillary Clinton, while the state’s voter ID law remained the subject of legal and political debate. The research raised questions about whether the law placed unequal burdens on some voters, but it did not constitute proof that voter suppression handed Trump Wisconsin or changed the outcome of the presidential election.

The discussion began after social media users shared images from a public appearance in which Trump referred to “my wife, Melania, who happens to be right here.” One widely shared post claimed, without evidence, that the woman shown was not Melania and questioned what the president had “done with his wife.”

The posts were circulated widely, with users focusing on the woman’s facial features, clothing and expression. Some suggested that differences in appearance indicated the presence of a body double, while others treated the idea as a joke.

The White House rejected the speculation. A spokeswoman described the claims as an example of irresponsible and misleading coverage, and Melania Trump’s communications director also dismissed the story.

Images and video from the appearance showed a woman who was identified by the White House and news organizations as Melania Trump. Differences in how she looked compared with other photographs could be explained by the camera angle, lighting, sunglasses and hairstyle. No credible reporting established that a substitute had appeared in her place.

The claim nevertheless became a trending topic on Twitter, where users posted jokes, edited images and comments about the couple’s public appearances.

Some posts referred to earlier conspiracy theories promoted by Donald Trump, including false claims about former President Barack Obama’s birthplace. Others used the episode to criticize the president or to make broader comments about misinformation online.

The viral discussion illustrated how quickly an unsupported claim can spread through social media, particularly when photographs are presented without context. While online users continued to debate the images, available evidence indicated that the woman accompanying Trump was Melania Trump.

The White House did not announce any change involving the first lady, and no credible source confirmed the existence of a body double in the incident.

It s a recently uncovered video of Donald Trump back in 2007 giving a highly-paid speech to the Learning Annex. Seizing the opportunity to be the jackass he s been his whole life, skeevy Donald has the lovely young woman escorted to the stage. A beautiful girl who was 17 or 18 and applied to be a waitress. So beautiful. She s like a world-class beauty like the young lady who just asked a question about the actress. She s so beautiful. And my people came and she said,  Mr. Trump, she has no experience.  So I interviewed her anyway because she was so pretty. And I said,  Let me ask you, do you have any experience?  She goes,  No, sir.  I say,  When can you start?' Before Juliet can leave the stage, presumably having been brought on purely as a prop for his anecdote, he squeezes her and kisses her. Then he stares at her body as she leaves the stage. This isn t my  interpretation  of what Trump is doing, you ll see in the video yourself. And as if making faces, raising his eyebrows, pursing his lips as he watches her walk away isn t enough, he turns back to the microphone and explains his  addiction  to women: See now, if she worked on my plane, that s like a death wish for me, right? That s like an alcoholic. People are alcoholics. You put Scotch in front of them, it s like [Trump waves his hands around the way he did while making fun of a disabled reporter], it s like, this would be my form of alcoholism. It is so sad that the biggest trend on social media right now is people sharing their stories of abuse publicly, just to spread awareness about how pervasive the problem is  And the country is being led by one of the biggest, most public perpetrators of that kind of abuse the world has ever known.Watch the video here:Featured image via Leon Neal/Getty Images

The clip circulated as people were sharing personal accounts of harassment and assault under the #MeToo hashtag. Its release renewed discussion online about Trump’s public comments about women, as well as allegations of sexual misconduct made against him. Trump has denied those allegations.

The video was widely shared on social media during the 2017 #MeToo discussion.

**Robert De Niro Criticizes Donald Trump at Hudson River Park Gala**

Actor Robert De Niro criticized former President Donald Trump during a speech at the Hudson River Park Gala in Manhattan, where he was honored and a park bench was dedicated in his name, according to reports by *The Independent* and the *New York Daily News*.

De Niro, a two-time Academy Award winner, joked that he would keep people who did not deserve the view away from his bench, naming Trump as an example. He then used profanity while expressing his opposition to the former president and referred to him as a “low life.”

Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg also spoke at the event, joking about De Niro’s public speaking style. “It took me years before I finally got a sentence out of Bobby,” Bloomberg said, according to the *Daily News*. “He’s not a big talker.”

De Niro has repeatedly criticized Trump in public remarks. During the 2016 presidential campaign, he said he would like to punch Trump in the face and described him as “blatantly stupid.” He later called Trump a “flat-out blatant racist” and said that a more intelligent Trump would be even more dangerous.

The actor has continued to speak out against Trump’s policies and conduct, including his approach to North Korea, his decision to withdraw the United States from the Paris climate agreement, and his efforts to reverse policies associated with former President Barack Obama.

De Niro’s criticism has made him one of Trump’s most prominent celebrity opponents. Trump has also responded to the actor and other critics on social media and in public remarks.

The gala recognized De Niro’s contributions to the Hudson River Park community. A bench bearing his name was installed in the park, providing a lasting connection between the actor and the Manhattan waterfront.

Today was the perfect example of an administration that is hanging on by a thread.Earlier today, Trump displayed his blatant stupidity as he gave a speech at the conservative Values Voter Summit. During that speech, Trump shocked over 3,000 attendees (and the world) when he said he d met with the  president of the Virgin Islands.  This was Trump s direct quote: I went to Puerto Rico, and I met with the president of the Virgin Islands, these are people that are incredible people. They ve suffered gravely, and we ll be there. We re gonna be there. We have, really, it s not even a question of a choice   we re going to be there as Americans. Trump apparently doesn t know that HE is the president of the Virgin Islands, because the islands are a part of American territory! As expected, Twitter dragged Trump for this: There s really no way to gracefully fix this, but still the Trump administration had to try. In a half-ass, hilarious attempt to minimize Trump s very obvious f*ck up, the White House released a transcript of Trump s remarks   and crossed out the word  president  and replaced it with the correction of  governor of the Virgin Islands.  CNN s Kaitlan Collins made sure to share this with everyone:It s like the Trump administration didn t even try to be subtle! And how could they? Just as they put out one fire, Trump is making five more. Trump s team doesn t have time or the energy to keep cleaning up his messes   and this pathetic attempt is direct proof!Featured image via Isaac Brekken/Getty Images

The White House revised a transcript of remarks President Donald Trump made at the Values Voter Summit after he referred to the “president of the Virgin Islands.”

Speaking about the administration’s response to hurricane damage in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, Trump said: “I went to Puerto Rico, and I met with the president of the Virgin Islands. These are people that are incredible people. They’ve suffered gravely, and we’ll be there.”

The U.S. Virgin Islands are a U.S. territory led by a governor, not a president. The territory’s governor at the time was Kenneth Mapp. Trump was likely referring to Mapp when he used the term “president.”

The White House transcript initially reflected Trump’s wording but was later amended to identify the official as the “governor of the Virgin Islands.” The change drew attention online, with critics questioning why the administration had altered the transcript rather than simply noting that Trump had misspoken.

The episode came as the administration faced continued scrutiny over its response to hurricanes that had struck Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories. Trump’s comments at the summit quickly circulated on social media, prompting discussion about the accuracy of presidential remarks and official White House transcripts.

The revised transcript did not include an explanation for the change. White House officials did not immediately provide additional details about the correction.

**Puerto Rico’s Governor Responds After Trump Says Federal Recovery Aid Cannot Continue Indefinitely**

President Donald Trump said Thursday that the federal government, military and emergency responders could not remain in Puerto Rico “forever” as recovery efforts continued on the hurricane-devastated U.S. territory.

Trump wrote on Twitter that the Federal Emergency Management Agency and other agencies had done a “great job” but that Puerto Rico faced extensive debt and damaged infrastructure. He said the island’s recovery would require local officials to take a more active role.

Puerto Rico Gov. Ricardo Rosselló responded that the territory’s residents were asking for the same assistance that other Americans would receive after a disaster.

“The U.S. citizens in Puerto Rico are requesting the support that any of our fellow citizens would receive across our Nation,” Rosselló tweeted Thursday.

The U.S. citizens in Puerto Rico are requesting the support that any of our fellow citizens would receive across our Nation.

— Ricardo Rosselló (@ricardorossello) October 12, 2017

Puerto Rican officials, including San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz, have repeatedly called for additional assistance after Hurricane Maria caused widespread destruction. Cruz had previously criticized the federal response and received public criticism from Trump, who called her “nasty” in a tweet.

Cruz responded Thursday, saying the administration had a moral responsibility to help the people of Puerto Rico.

“It is not that you do not get it; you are incapable of fulfilling the moral imperative to help the people of PR,” she tweeted. “Shame on you!”

It is not that you do not get it; you are incapable of fulfilling the moral imperative to help the people of PR. Shame on you.! @POTUS

— Carmen Yulín Cruz (@CarmenYulinCruz) October 12, 2017

Vice President Mike Pence had said the previous week that the administration would continue supporting Puerto Rico until the territory was restored.

“I say to all of you gathered here today, to the people of Puerto Rico: We are with you, we stand with you, and we will be with you every single day until Puerto Rico is restored bigger and better than ever before,” Pence said.

Trump made a similar pledge in a Sept. 29 speech, saying, “We will not rest, however, until the people of Puerto Rico are safe.” He also said the administration would remain involved until residents were “safe and sound and secure.”

His comments Thursday emphasized the long-term challenges facing the territory, including its debt and damaged infrastructure, rather than announcing an end to federal recovery efforts. Trump’s businesses have filed for bankruptcy protection six times, though those filings involved corporate entities rather than a personal bankruptcy.

**WATCH: Rep. Al Green Introduces Articles of Impeachment Against Trump**

Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) took to the House floor on Wednesday and introduced articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, becoming one of the first members of Congress to pursue such action during Trump’s presidency.

“I rise today on behalf of the many who have concluded that enough is enough,” Green said in his remarks.

Green argued that Trump’s conduct and policies had harmed American society and contributed to a political environment in which hate groups and extremist movements had gained greater visibility. The resolution accused the president of conduct that Green said warranted impeachment.

Green introduced the resolution as a privileged measure. Under House rules, that designation required the chamber to take up the matter within a limited period, although it did not guarantee that the articles would advance or result in a formal impeachment inquiry.

The House was then controlled by Republicans, and GOP leaders had not endorsed impeachment proceedings against Trump. Republican lawmakers and the White House rejected efforts to remove the president, while Democrats were divided over whether impeachment was appropriate.

The introduction of the resolution did not itself impeach Trump. The House would have needed to approve articles of impeachment by a majority vote before the matter could have proceeded to a Senate trial. At the time, there was no indication that the necessary votes existed.

Green had previously criticized Trump publicly and continued to call for congressional action. His resolution reflected growing opposition among some Democrats to the administration’s policies and conduct, though it was not expected to receive sufficient support in the Republican-controlled chamber.

The debate also came amid broader concerns about the president’s handling of national security and the authority of the executive branch. However, no evidence was presented that Trump had been prevented from accessing the nation’s nuclear command system, and comparisons with the final days of the Nixon administration remained political arguments rather than established facts about the Trump presidency.

Green urged colleagues to consider his proposal and said Congress had a responsibility to act when it believed a president had violated the public trust.

The House ultimately did not move forward with impeachment based on Green’s resolution. The effort nevertheless marked an early congressional attempt to formally raise the issue of removing Trump from office.

FEMA’s role in Puerto Rico relief effort draws scrutiny after Hurricane Maria

Weeks after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico, questions continued to mount about the federal government’s response, particularly in mountainous communities that faced damaged roads, limited supplies and prolonged power outages.

On MSNBC’s *The Rachel Maddow Show*, host Rachel Maddow discussed Aibonito, a municipality in the island’s central mountains about an hour and a half from San Juan. Video shown on the program depicted roads that appeared passable, while residents and local officials said they were still seeking additional food, water and other assistance.

The report focused on the distinction between FEMA’s responsibilities and the distribution of supplies. FEMA had visited Aibonito several times, according to the program, primarily to help residents register for assistance and to assess local needs. Those visits did not necessarily mean that the agency itself was responsible for delivering all food and water directly to residents.

FEMA’s disaster response generally includes coordinating federal assistance, providing financial aid and working with territorial and local authorities, while the distribution of commodities is handled through a broader network that includes the Puerto Rico government, municipalities, voluntary organizations and other federal agencies. The division of responsibility created confusion and frustration in communities where residents were waiting for basic necessities.

After the television report, FEMA representatives again visited Aibonito and met with the mayor to discuss the municipality’s needs, according to the program. The visit was described as part of the agency’s ongoing assessment and assistance work, rather than as a direct delivery of supplies.

The federal response was taking place as officials revised estimates of the storm’s casualties and continued to address widespread damage. Hurricane Maria caused extensive destruction across Puerto Rico, leaving much of the island without electricity and disrupting communications, transportation and access to essential goods. Early death estimates were later revised as authorities examined additional storm-related fatalities.

The response also drew comparisons with federal disaster assistance provided after hurricanes in Texas and Florida. Puerto Rico faced logistical difficulties because it is an island territory with damaged infrastructure and a heavy reliance on maritime and air transportation. Restrictions under the Jones Act were temporarily waived after the storm, while officials and businesses continued to work through shipping and distribution problems.

Food assistance was another source of debate. Puerto Rico operates a nutrition assistance program separate from the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program used in the states. Federal and territorial officials considered measures to help residents obtain food while stores were closed or operating with limited supplies. Reports of high prices and shortages added to concerns about whether aid was reaching people quickly enough.

The situation highlighted the complicated roles of FEMA, Puerto Rico’s government and local municipalities during the recovery. FEMA said it was coordinating assistance and assessing needs, while local officials and residents criticized the pace of deliveries and the lack of clear information.

The difficulties also renewed debate about the treatment of Puerto Rico, whose residents are U.S. citizens but do not vote in presidential elections and have limited representation in Congress. The island’s political status, economic challenges and dependence on federal assistance became central issues in discussions of the hurricane response.

**GOP Lawmaker Says Republicans Are Concerned About ‘Dysfunction’ in the White House**

Sen. Bob Corker (R-Tenn.) received support from one of his Republican colleagues after President Donald Trump criticized the Tennessee senator. Rep. Charlie Dent (R-Pa.) said in an MSNBC interview Monday that lawmakers in both chambers had discussed their concerns about the administration.

“We have these conversations all the time,” Dent said. “We’ve had a lot of these ‘the emperor has no clothes’ moments, and I’m glad that Sen. Corker has brought voice to this.”

Dent said some Republicans were concerned about what he described as “dysfunction and disorder and chaos” at the White House. He added that tensions had eased “a bit” since John Kelly became chief of staff, but said public disputes and personal criticism were distracting from legislative work.

“We have these conversations all the time, and we have to do better,” Dent said. “I think more of my colleagues should speak up. They say things privately; they don’t say publicly. I said it publicly before I announced I wasn’t running.”

Corker, who had announced he would not seek reelection, had criticized the White House and described it as an “adult day care center.” He also warned that Trump’s rhetoric could increase tensions with other countries.

“When you’re the president of the United States, your words are policy. People take those words very seriously, and I don’t think the president has learned that yet,” Dent said. “The president, I believe, has to be much more measured in his rhetoric.”

Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.) and the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) had also publicly criticized aspects of Trump’s administration and political approach. Trump responded to criticism from Republican lawmakers through public statements and social media posts.

On Monday, Trump criticized Corker on Twitter, including by referring to the senator’s height. The exchange was part of a broader public dispute between the president and the retiring Tennessee lawmaker over the administration’s conduct and foreign-policy rhetoric.

Black Man Beaten at Charlottesville Rally Was Also Charged in Connection With the Violence

DeAndre Harris was beaten during the Aug. 12, 2017, white supremacist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. Months later, he was also charged with unlawful wounding in connection with a separate part of the confrontation, drawing criticism from his attorney and supporters.

Harris was among several people attacked in a parking garage near the University of Virginia campus as white nationalist and other far-right demonstrators clashed with counterprotesters. Video of the assault showed men striking Harris with poles and other objects as he attempted to escape.

While several people seen attacking Harris were later identified and arrested, a magistrate issued a warrant accusing Harris of injuring a man involved in the confrontation. Police said investigators had reviewed additional video that led to the charge.

Harris’s attorney, Lee Merritt, described the case as retaliatory and said Harris would surrender. Authorities, however, said the warrant was based on an investigation into Harris’s alleged conduct and not simply on material circulated online.

Journalist Chuck Modi posted video of the attack on Twitter. The footage showed Harris being surrounded and beaten in the parking garage. Modi wrote that he had intervened after seeing the assault and that Harris was injured but alive.

The video was widely shared after the rally and became part of efforts to identify people involved in the violence. Harris’s arrest generated criticism because he had also been the subject of a widely viewed assault.

Some far-right activists publicly discussed reporting Harris’s online fundraising campaign after the charge was announced. Others used the case to promote claims about the Charlottesville rally and its participants. Those comments reflected political and ideological disputes surrounding the investigation, rather than establishing who was legally responsible for each act of violence.

The rally also ended with the death of Heather Heyer, who was killed when a car struck counterprotesters. Authorities and medical officials said she died after the vehicle attack; claims that she died of a heart attack were false.

The evidence cited in Harris’s case included video that appeared to show him striking a man with a flashlight or other object during the confrontation. Harris’s defense argued that he was responding to the attack and protecting himself or another person. Whether his actions were legally justified was for the court to determine.

Daniel Borden, one of the men identified in the assault on Harris, was later arrested and pleaded guilty to malicious wounding. Other defendants were also prosecuted in connection with violence at the rally.

Harris’s charge did not erase the evidence that he had been attacked, and his arrest did not by itself establish guilt. In 2018, a judge found Harris not guilty of unlawful wounding.

Todd Womack, Corker s chief of staff, refuted the claim later in the day, saying in a statement that the President called Senator Corker on Monday afternoon and asked him to reconsider his decision not to seek reelection and reaffirmed that he would have endorsed him, as he has said many times. Trump s Corker-directed fit of tweet-rage came just days after the Senator publicly criticized the President, a move that never sits well with Trump, leading him to try and seek revenge:Senator Bob Corker "begged" me to endorse him for re-election in Tennessee. I said "NO" and he dropped out (said he could not win without  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 8, 2017..my endorsement). He also wanted to be Secretary of State, I said "NO THANKS." He is also largely responsible for the horrendous Iran Deal!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 8, 2017 Hence, I would fully expect Corker to be a negative voice and stand in the way of our great agenda. Didn't have the guts to run!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 8, 2017Senator Bob Corker is clearly the thicker-skinned of the two. However, he wasn t going to let an opportunity like this go to waste and decided to respond to the President s barbs, calling the current administration out for being exactly how many see it:It's a shame the White House has become an adult day care center. Someone obviously missed their shift this morning.  Senator Bob Corker (@SenBobCorker) October 8, 2017Corker later decided enough was enough and opted to tell it like it is in a phone interview with The New York Times on Sunday night, claiming that Trump was treating the presidency like  a reality show,  making reckless threats against other countries that put the United States  on the path to World War III. He concerns me,  Mr. Corker said.  He would have to concern anyone who cares about our nation,  he said. He was far from done.  I know for a fact that every single day at the White House, it s a situation of trying to contain him,  the Senator said in the interview.When it came to the tweets, Corker simply confirmed what we already knew. I don t know why the president tweets out things that are not true,  he said.  You know he does it, everyone knows he does it, but he does. The Senator s criticism had clearly stuck in the President s craw a little. Trump is a man who always needs to have the last word and, being unable to shake Corker s snide tweet or his brutal honesty with The New York Times, made the following tweet Sunday evening:Bob Corker gave us the Iran Deal, & that's about it. We need HealthCare, we need Tax Cuts/Reform, we need people that can get the job done!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 8, 2017Featured image via Sara D. Davis/Getty Images

**Corker and Trump Trade Barbs After Public Dispute Over Senate Race**

Tennessee Republican Sen. Bob Corker announced in September 2017 that he would not seek reelection when his term expired at the end of the following year. On Sunday, Corker and President Donald Trump engaged in a public dispute on Twitter.

The exchange began when Trump posted a series of tweets claiming that he had declined Corker’s request for an endorsement. Todd Womack, Corker’s chief of staff, disputed that account in a statement, saying that Trump had called Corker and asked him to reconsider his decision not to run. Womack said the president had also reaffirmed that he would have endorsed Corker, as he had said previously.

Trump’s posts came days after Corker had publicly criticized the president. Trump wrote that Corker had “begged” for his endorsement and claimed that Corker had decided not to run because he could not win without it. Trump also said Corker had wanted to become secretary of state, criticized his role in the Iran nuclear agreement and suggested that the senator would oppose the administration’s agenda.

Corker responded on Twitter with a pointed comment about the White House:

“It’s a shame the White House has become an adult day care center. Someone obviously missed their shift this morning.”

Later Sunday, Corker discussed the dispute in a phone interview with *The New York Times*. He said Trump was treating the presidency like “a reality show” and that the president’s threats toward other countries could place the United States “on the path to World War III.”

“He concerns me,” Corker said. “He would have to concern anyone who cares about our nation.”

Corker also said that White House officials were working to contain the president’s behavior.

“I know for a fact that every single day at the White House, it’s a situation of trying to contain him,” he said.

Addressing Trump’s allegations, Corker said he did not understand why the president posted claims that were inaccurate.

“I don’t know why the president tweets out things that are not true,” Corker said. “You know he does it, everyone knows he does it, but he does.”

Trump responded later Sunday, writing that Corker had been responsible for the Iran agreement and arguing that the administration needed lawmakers who could advance its health care and tax priorities.

title: Pence Joins Trump’s NFL Whinefest, Leaves Colts Game In A Huff Over Police Brutality Protests
text: People like to pretend that Mike Pence is the grown-up in the room compared to Donald Trump s brash childishness from the White House. However, he proved that wrong on Sunday, when he left the Indiana Colts football game because a few of the players on the team opposing the Colts chose to take a knee during the national anthem to protest police brutality against black and brown Americans. Taking a leaf out of Trump s playbook, Pence tweeted:I left today's Colts game because @POTUS and I will not dignify any event that disrespects our soldiers, our Flag, or our National Anthem.  Vice President Pence (@VP) October 8, 2017While everyone is entitled to their own opinions, I don't think it's too much to ask NFL players to respect the Flag and our National Anthem  Vice President Pence (@VP) October 8, 2017Just like Trump, Pence forgets the meaning of the First Amendment, and seems to think that his position gives him the right to try to bully owners, players, and ultimately the National Football League into following his orders. Further, it is worth noting that the Colts were playing the San Francisco 49ers, which is the former team of Colin Kaepernick, the man who started this protest before being blacklisted from the NFL for taking a stand against police brutality against people of color. Further, Pence and Trump admitted that they used the situation to divide the country and make some kind of point on the taxpayers  dime   because of course we paid for Pence to travel to that football game. For one thing, the press was kept in the van, in anticipation of Pence stirring the pot and then leaving:The media pool was kept in the vans ahead of the game instead of being led in with VPOTUS. https://t.co/NXIFZCp3fb  Vaughn Hillyard (@VaughnHillyard) October 8, 2017FLAG: Was Pence leaving Colts game a political stunt? Reporters were told to stay in van bc "there may be an early departure from the game." **Indiana Man Extradited to Charlottesville in Connection With Alleged Rally Assault**

Dennis Lloyd Mothersbaugh, 37, was arrested in Jennings County, Indiana, in late September and extradited to Charlottesville in connection with an alleged assault during the Aug. 12 Unite the Right rally, according to reports at the time.

Mothersbaugh’s identity circulated online after video from the protest appeared to show a man striking participants. Writer and activist Shaun King shared images and video while asking social-media users to help identify him. Other users posted photographs and records they said were connected to Mothersbaugh.

The online posts also focused on a shirt he appeared to be wearing, which referenced God, guns and Donald Trump. However, social-media descriptions of Mothersbaugh as a “lifelong white supremacist” or neo-Nazi were not, by themselves, established findings by authorities.

A video shared during the search appeared to show a man punching one protester and confronting another. Authorities in Virginia accused Mothersbaugh of assault in connection with the rally. The allegations were to be addressed in court, and an arrest or extradition did not establish his guilt.

The Charlottesville rally drew white nationalists, neo-Nazis and counterprotesters and ended in violence. Heather Heyer was killed when a car struck a crowd of counterprotesters, and numerous people were injured. James Alex Fields Jr., an Ohio man, was arrested and charged after the crash.

President Donald Trump drew widespread criticism for remarks in which he said there was blame “on both sides” of the confrontation. Democratic and Republican officials condemned the violence and disputed aspects of Trump’s comments.

The rally and subsequent events led to extensive efforts online to identify people shown in photographs and videos. Civil-rights groups and journalists urged the public to distinguish between documented evidence, allegations and speculation as authorities investigated possible crimes.

Mothersbaugh’s case was one of several arising from the Charlottesville demonstrations. The charges and court proceedings, rather than social-media descriptions, were to determine what conduct could be legally attributed to him.

The episode renewed debate over the presence of extremist groups at political demonstrations, the use of online investigations to identify suspects and the risks of drawing conclusions before a case has been resolved in court.

President Donald Trump’s campaign faced criticism after sending a fundraising email that referenced the mass shooting in Las Vegas.

A Michigan custody case involving a man who sexually assaulted a 12-year-old girl and fathered her child has drawn criticism from the victim’s attorney and renewed discussion about how custody and child-support proceedings handle cases involving sexual violence.

Christopher Mirasolo was convicted in connection with the assault and initially served six months in prison. He later served additional time after being convicted of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old girl.

Years later, a county child-support proceeding sought to establish whether Mirasolo was the father of the child, who was then about eight years old. According to reporting by The Detroit News, a DNA test was conducted after officials connected Mirasolo to the mother during a review of her public assistance case.

The mother said she received food assistance and health coverage for her son and did not understand why officials were pursuing the paternity matter. She also said she had not anticipated that the process could lead to Mirasolo seeking custody or visitation.

Sanilac County Circuit Judge Gregory S. Ross subsequently issued an order granting Mirasolo joint custody of the child, according to court records and news reports. The order also required the mother to return to Michigan and disclosed her address to Mirasolo, actions that her attorney said raised serious safety concerns.

“I think this is all crazy,” the mother told The Detroit News. “They never explained anything to me.”

Her attorney, Rebecca Kiessling, criticized the handling of the case and said the legal system had failed to protect her client, who was a child when the assault occurred.

“This is insane,” Kiessling said, according to the newspaper. She argued that Mirasolo should not have been given custody rights and questioned the way the original criminal case and later family-court proceedings were handled.

The case highlights the potential conflict between paternity and custody procedures and the safety needs of survivors of sexual assault. A biological parent’s status does not by itself determine custody, and courts generally consider the child’s best interests and any history of abuse or criminal conduct. The details and subsequent status of the custody order were the subject of legal and public scrutiny.

The ruling also became part of a broader debate over abortion policy. Advocates for abortion rights have argued that requiring rape survivors to continue pregnancies can create long-term legal and emotional ties to the person who assaulted them, particularly when custody or visitation is later sought.

Opponents of abortion restrictions and survivor advocates have called for laws and court procedures that account for those risks. The Michigan case underscored the difficult legal consequences that can follow when a child is born after sexual assault and the alleged or convicted offender seeks recognition as a parent.
