Trump Criticizes Late-Night Hosts, Raises Question of “Equal Time” for Republicans

President Donald Trump criticized late-night television hosts on Saturday, arguing that their programming was consistently unfavorable toward him and Republicans.

In a series of posts on Twitter on October 7, 2017, Trump wrote that late-night hosts were “dealing with the Democrats for their very unfunny & repetitive material, always anti-Trump!” He then asked, “Should we get Equal Time?”

Trump followed up by saying that “more and more people are suggesting that Republicans (and me) should be given Equal Time on T.V. when you look at the one-sided coverage?”

The comments appeared to refer to the frequent political jokes and criticism of Trump on late-night programs, including CBS’s “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.” Late-night hosts have regularly made Trump and his administration subjects of political satire since he entered national office.

Trump’s remarks revived a broader debate over whether conservative viewpoints receive comparable treatment in television news and entertainment programming. The Federal Communications Commission’s equal-time rule generally applies to broadcast stations’ political candidates and does not require comedy programs to provide comparable airtime in response to political jokes or commentary.

Presidents and other public officials have long been targets of late-night comedy, and criticism of such coverage has come from both political parties. Trump has frequently responded publicly to coverage and jokes about him, particularly on social media.

The president’s posts came as his administration faced sustained coverage of its policies and public disputes. Late-night programs, however, are entertainment shows and are not required to present politically balanced comedy.

Trump has also maintained a close relationship with some conservative media outlets and commentators, who have often defended his administration. His criticism of late-night television reflected his broader complaints about what he described as unfavorable treatment by the media.

The episode highlighted the continuing tension between the president and television comedians, who have used his statements and conduct as material for political satire. It also underscored the limits of the government’s role in regulating commentary and humor under the First Amendment.

Others saw it as a corporate marketing campaign by State Street Global Advisors, the investment firm that commissioned the statue as part of an effort to promote gender diversity.

The debate intensified later that year after State Street agreed to pay $5 million to resolve allegations by the Department of Labor’s Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs that it had underpaid 305 female employees and 15 black employees at its U.S. operations.

The settlement addressed the government’s findings but did not establish that the company or the individuals involved were opposed to feminism. State Street denied wrongdoing and said it disagreed with the government’s analysis, while agreeing to resolve the matter and provide compensation to affected workers.

The case nevertheless prompted criticism of the gap that can exist between corporate messaging and workplace practices. Social-media users were similarly divided:

Another user wrote that the statue represented “the corporate interests of State Street Corp,” while others called the pay-discrimination allegations ironic given the company’s association with a prominent feminist symbol.

Some commentators used the controversy to criticize corporate feminism more broadly. They argued that companies can adopt the language of social justice while still facing allegations involving unequal treatment in the workplace.

Other observers pushed back against that conclusion, noting that a dispute involving one company did not invalidate efforts to address gender inequality or the value that some people placed on the statue. The sculpture’s meaning remained contested: supporters saw it as a visible statement about women’s representation in corporate leadership, while critics viewed it as public relations.

The settlement did not determine whether “Fearless Girl” was an effective symbol, nor did it resolve wider arguments about corporate activism. It did, however, draw attention to the importance of matching public commitments to measurable workplace practices.

“Fearless Girl” remained a subject of debate, while State Street continued to face scrutiny over how its stated support for diversity aligned with its employment policies.

title: Thanks To Trump The U.S. Economy Lost Jobs For The First Time In 7 Years
text: After taking office, Donald Trump has repeatedly taken credit for President Obama s economy and regularly touts jobs numbers on his Twitter timeline. Now that Trump s economy is in effect, we doubt he ll be tweeting about the labor market losing 33,000 jobs last month.While some of this can be attributed to natural disasters, Trump has also failed to pass any major legislation.Job growth in August and July was revised down, to 38,000 less than previously reported. Economists expected 75,000 new jobs instead of a 33,000 job loss.The economy has added an average of 172,000 jobs a month over the past year but that has dropped to a 91,000 average over the past three months, showing a trend which is not in Trump s favor.Axios reports:Economists widely blame the disruptive effects of Hurricanes Irma and Harvey for the disappointing number, because the survey methodology dictates that folks who didn t get paid on the pay period that included September 12th are not counted as employed.But the report also revised down the two previous monthly estimates of job growth, suggested the slowdown is not all weather related.After Obama took office, he had quite a task on his hands in dealing with the cost of his predecessor s wars, but he did it. Obama s economy took an upward swing, even after natural disasters such as Hurricane Sandy and the floods which ravaged Louisiana. Throughout his campaign, Trump called Obama s economy  a disaster  but compared to other presidents, that was far from the truth.Fact: Obama took office during the worst recession since the Great Depression when the economy was losing 750,000 jobs a month and already had lost a record 9 percent of GDP. Let s see how long that lasts because the former reality show star is now making war noises toward North Korea. Also, if Trump manages to get the GOP tax proposal in the works, we ll see more reports like this one.But for a guy whose  presidency  has been based on undoing everything Obama has done, he sure did a good job of that with the first loss of jobs reported in 7 years.Photo: Alex Wong via Getty Images.

The U.S. economy lost 33,000 jobs in September, according to the Labor Department, marking the first monthly decline in payroll employment since September 2010. The report came as President Donald Trump continued to highlight employment figures during his first year in office.

The decrease was widely attributed to disruptions caused by Hurricanes Harvey and Irma, which affected businesses and prevented some workers from being counted as employed if they were not paid during the survey period. The Labor Department also revised previous estimates of job growth.

Economists had expected the economy to add jobs in September. Despite the monthly decline, employment had continued to rise over the preceding year, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.2 percent from 4.4 percent.

The September report offered a mixed picture of the labor market rather than clear evidence of a sustained reversal. Hurricane-related disruptions made the figures more difficult to interpret, while the revisions indicated that job growth before the storms may have been somewhat weaker than initially reported.

The report also renewed comparisons between Trump’s economic record and that of former President Barack Obama. Obama took office during the severe 2007–09 recession, when employment was declining sharply. The economy subsequently recorded 75 consecutive months of job growth before his presidency ended.

Trump had criticized the Obama administration’s economic performance during the 2016 campaign, while later pointing to continuing gains in employment and the stock market. The September figures reflected both the ongoing expansion and the temporary effects of major natural disasters.

**Salt Lake City Officer Shoots Fleeing Suspect During Bicycle Stop**

On Sunday, August 13, Salt Lake City police officers stopped Patrick Harmon, a 50-year-old Black man, for riding a bicycle at night without a working taillight. Body-camera footage later released by the department shows Harmon speaking with officers on the side of the road and appearing emotional during the encounter.

Officer Clinton Fox asked Harmon whether he knew about outstanding warrants, and Harmon acknowledged that he did. Fox then asked him to remove his backpack. As Harmon took off the pack, he broke away from the officers and ran down the street.

The footage shows Fox warning Harmon that he would shoot before firing three rounds as Harmon fled. Another officer appears to have a Taser drawn. Harmon fell to the ground and was heard crying as officers approached him.

Police said Harmon had a knife during the encounter. The circumstances surrounding the weapon and the shooting became the subject of public debate after officials released the body-camera video. Early accounts and reports reportedly differed on details including whether Harmon was on foot or riding a bicycle and whether he possessed a gun or a knife.

The Salt Lake County district attorney’s office determined that the shooting was legally justified. Officials said the decision was based on the circumstances known to the officer at the time, including the belief that Harmon was armed. The conclusion drew criticism from Harmon’s family and community activists, who questioned whether the use of deadly force was necessary as he ran away.

Harmon’s sister, Antoinette, traveled to Salt Lake City to join a rally organized by Black Lives Matter activist Lex Scott. Demonstrators called for the release of the body-camera footage and greater transparency in the investigation.

“This is about accountability and transparency,” Scott said at the time, according to statements reported during the protests. Harmon’s family argued that they deserved to see the video and pressed officials to explain the shooting.

After the footage was released, public attention focused on the sequence of events, including Fox’s warning, the shots fired as Harmon fled and the officers’ actions after he fell. The video did not resolve the broader dispute over whether the shooting complied with department policy or constitutional standards.

The case prompted continued calls for an independent review of police use of force and for authorities to explain discrepancies in early descriptions of the incident. The district attorney’s finding meant that Fox did not face criminal charges in connection with the shooting, though the incident remained the subject of public criticism and civil-rights concerns.

Republican Congressman Tim Murphy Resigns Amid Affair and Abortion Controversy

U.S. Rep. Tim Murphy, a pro-life Republican representing Pennsylvania’s 18th District, resigned in October 2017 after reports that he had encouraged a woman with whom he was having an affair to consider an abortion. Murphy had previously announced that he would not seek reelection in 2018.

“This afternoon I received a letter of resignation from Congressman Tim Murphy, effective October 21,” Speaker Paul Ryan said in a statement. “It was Dr. Murphy’s decision to move on to the next chapter of his life, and I support it.”

Reports said that House Republican leaders and senior Republicans had urged Murphy to step down. According to reporting by Politico, Murphy initially believed he could remain in office after the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette published text messages in which he appeared to encourage the woman to have an abortion.

The messages drew criticism because Murphy had consistently presented himself as opposed to abortion. In one text, the woman, identified in reports as Shannon Edwards, wrote: “And you have zero issue posting your pro-life stance all over the place when you had no issue asking me to abort our unborn child just last week when we thought that was one of the options.”

Murphy and Edwards were reported to have been involved in an extramarital relationship. Edwards was married at the time, and reports said she later began divorce proceedings.

Several Republican lawmakers reportedly believed the controversy could become an ethics issue and distract from the party’s priorities. Ryan met with Murphy shortly before the resignation, as congressional Republicans considered how the scandal might affect the House caucus.

Additional reports raised allegations about Murphy’s treatment of congressional staff, including claims that he yelled at aides and called them derogatory names. Former staff members also described a demanding workplace under his office’s management. The reports contributed to pressure on Murphy, although he did not face a public ethics investigation before leaving office.

Murphy’s resignation ended his congressional career before the completion of his term. He had represented the Pittsburgh-area district in the House since 2003 and had announced in September 2017 that he would retire from Congress after the 2018 elections.

The Trump administration’s Justice Department has taken the position that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 does not prohibit discrimination against transgender employees, reversing the position adopted by the previous administration.

In a filing and accompanying legal guidance, the department argued that the law’s ban on discrimination “because of sex” does not extend to gender identity. The position is based on the department’s interpretation of the statute as it was written and on the view that changes to its scope should come from Congress rather than executive agencies.

The Justice Department’s position concerns the interpretation of federal employment law; it does not make all discrimination against transgender people legal. Other federal, state and local laws may provide protections, and several courts have ruled that discrimination based on gender identity can constitute sex discrimination under Title VII.

The department’s stance also differs from the position taken by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission during the Obama administration. The EEOC had argued that Title VII protects transgender workers from workplace discrimination. The Justice Department said the earlier administration had expanded the statute beyond what Congress intended when it was enacted.

The issue remains contested in the courts. Federal appeals courts have reached differing conclusions about whether Title VII covers discrimination based on gender identity, and the Supreme Court had not yet issued a definitive ruling on the question at the time of the Justice Department’s announcement.

Civil rights organizations criticized the department’s position, arguing that discrimination against transgender workers is inherently related to sex and should be covered by federal law. Supporters of the Justice Department’s interpretation said the question should be resolved through legislation rather than judicial or executive action.

The disagreement is part of a broader legal debate over the rights of LGBTQ+ people and the meaning of federal civil rights protections. Regardless of the Justice Department’s interpretation, the status of transgender workplace protections depends on applicable state and local laws, court rulings and future action by Congress.

The Senate Banking Committee Held an Equifax Hearing, and the Monopoly Man Showed Up

The Equifax data breach in 2017 exposed the personal information of approximately 145.5 million people in the United States. The company said names, Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses and, in some cases, driver’s license numbers were accessed. The breach also involved information from about 209,000 payment cards.

Equifax Chief Executive Richard Smith had stepped down before appearing Wednesday before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about the incident. During the hearing, Smith said the company’s failure to install a security update was linked to an individual employee who did not properly communicate that the update had been applied. He also said responsibility ultimately rested with the company’s leadership.

The explanation drew criticism from lawmakers and security experts, who questioned how a major company’s systems could remain vulnerable after a patch had been made available and why internal controls had failed to detect the problem.

But Smith was not the only notable figure in the hearing room. A spectator dressed as Rich Uncle Pennybags—the character commonly known as the Monopoly Man—drew attention as the committee examined the consequences of the breach.

The person wearing the costume was Amanda Werner, an activist with Americans for Financial Reform and Public Citizen. Werner and other advocates distributed Monopoly-style “Get Out of Jail Free” cards as part of a protest against forced arbitration clauses in consumer agreements.

The groups argued that such clauses can restrict consumers’ ability to pursue claims in court and give companies substantial control over how disputes are handled. Public Citizen said the costume was intended to highlight what it described as Equifax’s disproportionate power over consumers seeking redress.

Images and video of the protest quickly circulated online as viewers reacted to the unusual appearance during the otherwise serious hearing. Social media users shared photographs of the costumed protester seated behind Smith and commented on the contrast between the character’s familiar appearance and the discussion of corporate accountability.

The protest was part of a broader response to the Equifax breach, which prompted congressional hearings, investigations by government agencies and lawsuits from consumers and state officials. Smith apologized during his testimony and said the company had taken steps to improve its security practices.

Consumers concerned about the breach were directed to information from the Federal Trade Commission and other government agencies, including guidance on monitoring credit reports, placing fraud alerts or freezes, and watching for signs of identity theft.

After Las Vegas, Some Republicans Begin To Support Restrictions On Bump Stocks

The mass shooting in Las Vegas has renewed debate over gun laws, including among some Republicans who have generally opposed broad new restrictions. The attack, in which 58 people were killed and hundreds were injured, was carried out using semiautomatic rifles equipped with bump stocks, according to investigators.

Democrats, including California Senator Dianne Feinstein, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, have called for a ban on bump stocks. The devices use a firearm’s recoil to increase the speed at which a semiautomatic weapon can fire. They had received little attention from lawmakers before the Las Vegas shooting.

The proposal has attracted support from some Republicans, although there is no indication that the party as a whole has reached agreement on the issue. Members of Congress and the administration have been considering whether bump stocks can be restricted under existing law or whether new legislation would be required.

Republican support for such a measure would still represent only an initial step toward changing federal policy. Any legislation would need to pass both chambers of Congress and be signed by President Donald Trump, whose 2016 campaign received strong support from the National Rifle Association. Trump had not committed to a ban at the time.

Representative Bill Flores, a Texas Republican and gun owner, said he supported prohibiting bump stocks after learning more about them.

“I think they should be banned,” Flores said in an interview near the House floor. “There’s no reason for a typical gun owner to own anything that converts a semiautomatic to something that behaves like an automatic.”

Other House Republicans, including Charlie Dent and Ryan Costello of Pennsylvania, Leonard Lance of New Jersey and Pete King of New York, also expressed support for restrictions.

“I’m ready to say that they should not be in public use,” Dent said. “I think they are a problem. I support a ban on bump stocks.”

title: Trump’s IRS Just Decided They’re Going To Give All Your Info To Equifax After They Got Hacked
text: Has anyone else noticed that the government sometimes seems to like awarding contracts to companies that have proven they re incapable of doing what they re supposed to be doing? Equifax s massive data breach affected most Americans with any kind of credit at all, and here comes the IRS to give Equifax a contract in the name of  fraud prevention, because Equifax has proven that they re awesome at protecting our data. Oh! And then they proved that they were totally and completely transparent and on their consumers  sides when they tried to yank away our right to sue by encouraging all of us to enroll in their own fraud protection program with very fine print binding us to arbitration.The contract, which is a $7.25 million contract to verify our identities and prevent fraud, is a  sole source order,  which means the IRS decided Equifax was the only company capable of doing this for them. Supposedly this is to help prevent an interruption in ID verification while officials try and resolve something else.Equifax s security breach involved sensitive information for over 145 million Americans, including our Social Security numbers. Congressman Greg Walden of Oregon likened the breach to the guards at Fort Knox forgetting to lock the doors. That s how bad this hack was.The IRS itself isn t exactly free of security issues, either. They ve had severe problems with tax-ID fraud and other data hacks. Senator Orrin Hatch, of the Senate Finance Committee, has said he s worried the IRS doesn t have the technology necessary  to safeguard the integrity of our tax administration system. Well, it seems Equifax doesn t either, and yet the IRS is giving up our information to them for  fraud prevention. The House Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection subcommittee called Equifax  stupid,  and said they  deserve to be shamed,  and called the breach  shocking  and  unprecedented.  Walden also said: How does this happen when so much is at stake? I don t think we can pass a law that can fix stupid. Apparently they can t regulate the stupid of the IRS, either. We should all cross our fingers and pray nothing else happens to our data now. That s literally about all we can do.Featured image via Scott Olson/Getty Images

IRS Awarded Equifax $7.25 Million Identity-Verification Contract After 2017 Breach

The Internal Revenue Service awarded Equifax a $7.25 million contract to provide identity-verification and fraud-prevention services, despite the company’s disclosure of a major data breach the previous year. The decision drew criticism from lawmakers and privacy advocates concerned about Equifax’s handling of sensitive consumer information.

The contract was issued as a “sole source” order, meaning the IRS determined that Equifax was the only provider able to meet the agency’s requirements at the time. The arrangement was intended to prevent an interruption in identity-verification services while the agency addressed other changes to its fraud-prevention systems.

The 2017 Equifax breach exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, for approximately 145.5 million people. The incident led to investigations, lawsuits and criticism of the company’s cybersecurity practices and public response. Equifax later agreed to a settlement with federal and state authorities over the breach.

The IRS has also faced persistent challenges involving tax-related identity theft and fraudulent returns. Lawmakers have questioned whether the agency has sufficient technology and security measures to protect taxpayer information and prevent fraud.

The decision to continue using Equifax prompted renewed scrutiny in Congress. Members of the House Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection Subcommittee criticized the company’s security failures and described the breach as unusually serious. Other lawmakers questioned how a company responsible for protecting credit data could continue receiving government work after such an incident.

The contract did not mean that the IRS was publicly releasing all taxpayer information to Equifax. It authorized the company to perform identity-verification services under the terms of its agreement with the agency. Nevertheless, the arrangement raised questions about how federal agencies evaluate contractors’ cybersecurity records and whether additional safeguards were needed when handling sensitive personal data.

The IRS and Equifax faced pressure to demonstrate that taxpayer information would be protected and that the services would comply with federal privacy and security requirements. The controversy also highlighted the broader risks associated with relying on private companies to verify identities and manage data used in government programs.

In a series of posts on Twitter on Sept. 30, Trump wrote that “10,000 Federal workers” were on the island and described their work as “fantastic.”

“The NRA and its supporters want easy access to weapons, while the left wants them banned,” O’Reilly wrote, describing what he presented as the competing positions in the national debate. He also argued that freedom carries risks, writing, “This is the price of freedom. Violent nuts are allowed to roam free until they do damage, no matter how threatening they are.”

O’Reilly’s comments came after a gunman opened fire from the 32nd floor of the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino in Las Vegas on October 1, 2017. Authorities said at least 58 people were killed and hundreds were injured before the gunman took his own life. Multiple firearms were recovered from the hotel room and other locations connected to the suspect.

The attack renewed debate over firearm regulations, including questions about access to high-powered weapons and devices that can increase a weapon’s rate of fire. The incident also prompted discussion of whether existing laws could have prevented the shooting or reduced its effects.

In his post, O’Reilly referred to the Second Amendment and said that Americans have a right to arm themselves for protection, including people who may later pose a danger. Critics argued that this interpretation placed too much emphasis on gun rights and did not adequately address the risks posed by people with access to large arsenals.

The shooting also intensified debate in Congress over proposed legislation concerning firearm suppressors, commonly called silencers. Supporters said the measures would reduce hearing damage for hunters and sport shooters, while opponents argued that making suppressors easier to obtain could make it more difficult to detect or respond to gunfire. Proposals were under discussion at the time, but the Las Vegas attack became part of the larger argument over whether gun laws should be tightened or loosened.

O’Reilly’s post reflected a longstanding divide in American politics. Gun-rights advocates generally argue that the Second Amendment protects individual ownership and that lawful citizens should be able to defend themselves. Gun-control advocates say that broader restrictions, stronger background checks and limits on certain weapons or accessories could help prevent mass shootings.

The tragedy prompted calls for lawmakers to review federal and state gun laws, as well as discussions about public safety, emergency response and the responsibilities of gun owners. There was no immediate agreement on which policies would have prevented the attack, and the debate continued in the aftermath.

“The time to debate gun laws is after gun violence,” a social-media account identified as Alt Sarah H. Sanders wrote in a post shared after the shooting. “The time is now.”

O’Reilly’s remarks drew criticism from people who believed his description of the shooting as a cost of freedom minimized the victims’ deaths. Supporters, however, said he was acknowledging the difficult trade-offs involved in regulating firearms while preserving constitutional rights.

NRA Faces Criticism After Las Vegas Mass Shooting

The National Rifle Association faced renewed criticism after the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history, as questions emerged about gun laws and the rapid-firing devices used by the gunman.

On the night of Oct. 1, 2017, 64-year-old Stephen Craig Paddock opened fire on attendees at the Route 91 Harvest music festival in Las Vegas, Nevada, from a suite at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino. Nearly 22,000 people were attending the concert. At least 58 people were killed that night and hundreds were injured; the death toll later rose to 60 as two victims died from their injuries.

Paddock fired into the crowd from windows of the hotel, sending concertgoers fleeing for safety. Police later found him dead in the room from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Investigators recovered numerous firearms from the suite, including rifles fitted with bump stocks, devices that can significantly increase the speed at which semiautomatic weapons fire.

The shooting prompted renewed debate over federal and state gun laws, including regulations governing bump stocks, high-capacity magazines and the purchase of large numbers of firearms. Fully automatic machine guns are tightly regulated under federal law, and the circumstances surrounding Paddock’s weapons became the subject of an investigation.

Gun-control advocates argued that stronger regulations might reduce the likelihood of similar attacks. The NRA and other gun-rights groups have generally opposed many proposed restrictions, saying that new laws should not infringe on the rights protected by the Second Amendment.

The organization did not immediately issue a detailed public response after the shooting, leading critics to accuse it of avoiding the gun-policy debate. Several days later, the NRA called for a review of regulations governing bump stocks and said that devices that allow semiautomatic firearms to fire at a faster rate should be subject to additional rules.

The shooting also prompted anger on social media, where activists and other public figures criticized the NRA and lawmakers who oppose stricter gun laws. Some accused the organization of placing political influence and gun sales ahead of public safety, while supporters of gun rights rejected those claims and argued that the actions of an individual attacker should not determine national policy.

The tragedy renewed a familiar argument over whether more firearms make communities safer or whether tighter restrictions could prevent people at risk of committing mass violence from obtaining weapons. Lawmakers and the public continued to debate those questions in the weeks after the attack.

No evidence established that the NRA directly provided Paddock with the weapons he used. The shooting instead intensified scrutiny of the broader gun industry, firearms regulations and the influence of gun-rights organizations on American legislation.

Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico on Sept. 20. On the 22nd, he decided to go golfing for four days, and rage-tweeted at the NFL the whole time. Then he rage-tweeted at the  ingrates  in Puerto Rico who aren t showing him the proper appreciation for what he s not doing. Today, he was at the Presidents Cup golf tournament, avoiding real work and participating in the trophy presentation instead.And while he was there, he decided to dedicate the trophy to the victims of Hurricanes Harvey, Irma and Maria. According to Steve Kopack of CNBC, Trump said that conditions in Texas, Florida and Puerto Rico are  really under control,  and that he was dedicating the trophy to victims of storms:For those asking, President Trump was speaking on @GolfChannel s coverage of the Presidents Cup trophy presentation. You don t dedicate a goddamn trophy, presented at a tournament full of wealthy people who are safe in their well-moneyed cocoons, to hurricane victims. You just don t. It wouldn t be surprising to start hearing more outcry from homeless, sick, and suffering Puerto Ricans   people who are already angry at the lack of response from Trump s administration and his characterization of them as lazy all over Twitter.Featured image via Elsa/Getty Images

49ers Players Kneel During Anthem in Solidarity With Colin Kaepernick (VIDEO)

Former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick began kneeling during the national anthem in 2016 to protest racial injustice and police brutality. His demonstrations drew national attention and prompted other players to join him. Kaepernick has not played in the NFL since the 2016 season.

The anthem protests received renewed attention after President Donald Trump criticized players who kneel during the national anthem. Players across the league demonstrated in various ways the following weekend, including members of Kaepernick’s former team.

The 49ers had a row of players kneeling during the anthem, while others stood nearby with their hands on the kneeling players’ shoulders. The team shared a photograph of the moment on its official Twitter account with the caption “Together.”

The demonstrations came amid an ongoing national debate over free expression, patriotism and concerns about police treatment of people of color. Trump had continued to comment publicly on the protests, while players and teams maintained that the demonstrations were intended to draw attention to racial inequality and police brutality.

Kaepernick’s protest, which began with him sitting before later switching to kneeling, has remained a subject of discussion throughout the NFL. Some players have continued to kneel, while others have supported the cause through alternative forms of protest.

The 49ers’ post showed players standing and kneeling together during the anthem. The image was shared as teams across the league responded to the controversy surrounding the demonstrations.

She later urged him to pay child support, an apparent reference to previous public disputes involving Walsh’s family obligations.

Walsh, who represented Illinois in Congress from 2011 to 2013 and later became a prominent supporter of conservative and anti-establishment causes, has frequently drawn attention for provocative political statements. His response to Che’s comments added to that record and prompted criticism from both political opponents and some commentators who objected to the language.

The episode centered on the competing use of racial insults in political commentary, but critics said treating the terms as equivalent ignored the history and severity of anti-Black language in the United States.

Her comments came after President Donald Trump criticized NFL players who knelt during the anthem. The senator also emphasized that patriotism and dissent were not mutually exclusive. In her remarks, she described public protest as part of the country’s democratic tradition and said Americans should be able to demand recognition of injustices affecting their communities.

The debate over anthem protests intensified after former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick began kneeling during the 2016 season. Other players later adopted similar demonstrations, which became a national flashpoint over racial disparities and policing.

Harris, who was one of the few Black women serving in the U.S. Senate at the time, had previously spoken about criminal-justice reform and racial inequality. Her Atlanta appearance placed those issues in the context of the growing dispute over athletes’ political expression.

Trump has, instead of trying to help them, attacked the mayor of San Juan on Twitter for begging for help to save the lives of the Americans who live there, and his disaster response has been abysmal, because, you know, brown people. And now, he sends out lying mass communications pretending that he has helped people and delivered on promises when he has done no such thing. The combination of fundraising appeals, disputes over disaster relief and attacks on the NFL protests made Trump’s handling of the period especially controversial. Critics said his rhetoric was divisive and that the administration should focus more directly on assisting Puerto Rico’s residents and restoring essential services.

As residents sought help, President Donald Trump faced criticism for golfing and continuing to post about professional football players.

Trump’s decision to golf during the crisis also drew comparisons with comments he made about former President Barack Obama in 2016.

“President Obama should have gone to Louisiana days ago, instead of golfing. Too little, too late!” Trump wrote on Twitter after flooding in that state.

The storm’s immediate effects included prolonged power failures, shortages of supplies and the displacement of residents. Officials warned that the full human and economic toll would not be clear until emergency crews could reach more communities.

**Daily Stormer Loses Icelandic Domain Over Registration Requirements**

Andrew Anglin, founder of the neo-Nazi website *The Daily Stormer*, has lost access to another domain after Iceland’s domain registry said he had failed to meet its registration requirements.

U.S. technology companies moved against the website after the 2017 Charlottesville rally, where *The Daily Stormer* published mocking coverage of Heather Heyer, who was killed when a car struck counterprotesters. Domain registrar GoDaddy terminated the site’s registration, and Google declined to provide a replacement domain.

Since then, the website has appeared under several different domain names and has faced interruptions in multiple countries. The site was previously reported to have used domains associated with Russia and Albania. More recently, it operated through an Icelandic domain.

According to *The Reykjavík Grapevine*, ISNIC, the registry responsible for .is domains, suspended the site after Anglin failed to provide information required under its terms of service. Jens Pétur Jensen, ISNIC’s chief executive, said registrants must provide proof of their identity and physical location.

The suspension was described as a registration-compliance issue rather than an action specifically based on Iceland’s hate-speech laws. ISNIC said that information provided by registrants could be shared with authorities when legally required.

Anglin has also faced legal action in the United States. A federal court in Ohio found him liable in a civil case brought by a Jewish woman who said she had been targeted by an online harassment campaign connected to his website. A judge ordered Anglin to pay damages, but he has largely remained outside the United States.

Following the domain suspension, Anglin complained about the development on Gab, a social-media platform that has attracted users banned or restricted elsewhere for extremist or offensive content.

The Daily Stormer has long been associated with white-nationalist and neo-Nazi propaganda. Its repeated loss of domain access reflects the continuing difficulty extremist publishers face in maintaining online services when registrars and hosting companies enforce contractual rules or respond to legal concerns.

title: Trump Is Too Incompetent To Handle Disaster On An Island, But Obama Handled One Just Fine
text: Trump has spent an awful lot of time whining about Puerto Rico being an island with a devastated infrastructure, claiming that s the reason our relief effort has been so slow and disorganized: The response and recovery effort probably has never been seen for something like this. This is an island surrounded by water. Big water. Ocean water. He also said: This is a thing called the Atlantic Ocean. This is tough stuff. Gee, these complaints are reminiscent of when he said nobody knew healthcare could be so complicated. With this administration,  It s really difficult, we re doing all we can,  is code for,  I don t really care about this at all unless I can find a way to make myself look good here. But are we really having problems because Puerto Rico is an island, making it different than Florida and Texas, which were also devastated by hurricanes? Current evidence suggests otherwise: Supplies are just sitting in shipping containers there because there are too few truck drives, and too many blocked roads. One has to wonder why we don t have more personnel there helping the Puerto Rican government to clear the roads so that supply lines can reopen and we can help get those supplies to where they re most needed. One person even said that the personnel who are there just seem to be modeling their uniforms. That suggests we have a lot of people who don t know what they re supposed to be doing on the ground there. That would be a failure on our part, not Puerto Rico s.But then there s how Obama handled natural disasters on islands. In 2010, Haiti, which is practically next door to Puerto Rico in the Caribbean (not the Atlantic Ocean), suffered an absolutely devastating earthquake. Despite the fact that we had no warning for that quake (we had plenty of warning for Maria), President Obama mobilized our military  as if it were going to war,  according to the Washington Post. Within two days, we had 8,000 troops on their way to the disaster-stricken country.In less than two weeks, we had 22,000 troops on the ground; 300 military helicopters dropping supplies, and 33 Navy ships aiding the relief effort. Eight days after Maria swept over Puerto Rico, we only had 4,400 troops working relief there, along with 1,000 members of the Coast Guard. Only 50 choppers were working to deliver supplies.The morning after Haiti s quake, Obama told the military that they were  going to respond in Port-au-Prince robustly and immediately, and that gave the whole government clarity of purpose.  Rajiv Shah, who led USAID when the earthquake struck, said: We were able to move more quickly in a foreign country, and with no warning because it was an earthquake, than a better-equipped agency was able to do in a domestic territory. The Posse Comitatus Act places limits on what the military can do in a state or territory, and by contrast, Haiti is a foreign country. Our military response would be considerably different just because of that. But there were over 17,000 troops from 23 states on the ground in Florida after Irma. And the administration keeps saying that Puerto Rico isn t asking for very much, despite residents running out of food, drinkable water and other supplies, and San Juan s mayor breaking down over the Trump administration saying the response has been good.There are complicating factors, it s true. But this is a level of apathy and ineptitude we can t have from the White House when responding to disasters, particularly those where people are dying. Obama showed that being an island is a lot less of a factor in relief efforts than this administration is claiming.Featured image via Chip Somodevilla and Mark Wilson/Getty Images

**Puerto Rico Response Exposed Challenges for Trump Administration, While Haiti Offers a Different Comparison**

The Trump administration faced growing criticism over its response to Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, where the storm devastated the power grid, damaged roads and communications systems, and disrupted the delivery of food, water and medical supplies. President Donald Trump repeatedly emphasized the logistical difficulties of assisting an island territory, saying, “This is an island surrounded by water. Big water. Ocean water,” and noting that the situation was unusually challenging.

The comments drew comparisons with his earlier remark that “nobody knew health care could be so complicated.” Critics argued that the administration was focusing too heavily on the obstacles rather than explaining how it would overcome them.

Reports from Puerto Rico described supplies waiting in shipping containers while fuel shortages, damaged roads, limited transportation capacity and communications problems slowed distribution. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, the Defense Department and the Puerto Rican government all faced difficulties coordinating relief. The scale of the destruction also made it difficult to move personnel and supplies beyond San Juan and other population centers.

Some officials and residents questioned whether enough federal personnel and equipment had been sent to clear roads and distribute aid. San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz sharply criticized the administration’s response and publicly disputed statements that the federal effort was working well. The disagreement became a prominent part of the debate over the recovery operation.

Comparisons were also made with President Barack Obama’s response to the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, another Caribbean disaster that required a large international relief effort. The earthquake struck without warning and caused extensive destruction in and around Port-au-Prince. According to contemporary reporting and government accounts, the United States sent thousands of military personnel, ships and helicopters to support search-and-rescue operations, security, medical care and aid distribution.

Within days, the Obama administration designated a senior coordinator for the response and expanded the military mission. At its peak, more than 20,000 U.S. service members were involved in operations connected to Haiti, including forces aboard ships offshore. The mission was larger than a conventional domestic disaster response because Haiti is a foreign country and the United States was operating alongside the Haitian government and international organizations.

Officials from the Obama administration later said that the clear direction from the White House helped agencies organize the response quickly. At the same time, the Haiti operation was not without serious problems. Aid distribution was criticized as slow and poorly coordinated, and the earthquake’s damage to roads, ports and communications created many of the same logistical obstacles that confronted responders in Puerto Rico.

The comparison between the two disasters therefore has important limits. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, making federal agencies responsible for providing assistance, but the military’s domestic role is governed by different legal and operational rules than its role overseas. The Posse Comitatus Act generally restricts the use of the armed forces for domestic law enforcement, although it does not prevent the military from providing transportation, engineering, medical and logistical support.

Florida’s response to Hurricane Irma also provided a different point of comparison. The state received extensive federal and military assistance, but it had functioning transportation networks and electrical systems in many areas, as well as greater access to nearby mainland resources. Puerto Rico’s geographic isolation, preexisting infrastructure problems and near-total power failure made its recovery especially difficult.

Those factors did not eliminate the administration’s responsibility to organize an effective response. Residents faced shortages of drinking water, food, fuel and medical supplies, and the slow restoration of basic services intensified public anger. The disaster raised questions about federal preparation, coordination and communication, as well as the territory’s longstanding infrastructure vulnerabilities.

The experience in Haiti showed that a large overseas disaster response could be organized rapidly, but it did not provide a simple model for Puerto Rico. The two operations involved different legal authorities, governments, geography and types of damage. The problems after Maria reflected both the extraordinary scale of the storm and shortcomings in the preparation and execution of the relief effort.

However, he has run the swampiest of Washington swamps that America has seen since the Watergate scandal with President Richard Nixon. Case in point- his Health and Human Services Secretary, Tom Price, being mired in scandal for taking hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of trips around the nation and world in private jets on the taxpayer dime. He has sworn, now that he is caught, to pay back every dime to taxpayers over this scandal of luxury, but that was never true. Taxpayers paid over a million dollars for these trips, but we re only getting reimbursed for Tom Price s personal seats.Well, it seems that the news coverage has gotten the best of Price, because we all know how much The Donald wants to be loved by cable news. As such, the news coverage made Trump and his administration put more pressure on Price, and that pressure has worked. Tom Price has now resigned as Health and Human Services Secretary.Under all the pressure from the public and the press, as per usual, the White House is in hiding. They released a simple statement: Secretary of Health and Human Services Thomas Price offered his resignation earlier today and the President accepted. And, in case you were wondering, no, neither Sarah Huckabee Sanders nor any other Trump Administration official came to a camera to discuss this huge development, which comes on the heels of a humiliating defeat in the FOURTH attempt from the GOP-led Congress and the Trump Administration to repeal the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. All this proves is what Democrats have been saying about Republicans all along   they are corrupt, and they are incapable of change and of governing. Donald Trump campaigned on a promise to “drain the swamp,” arguing that Washington needed greater accountability. His administration faced an early ethics controversy involving Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price, who used chartered and private aircraft for numerous trips while serving in office.

The travel came under scrutiny after reports found that taxpayers had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the flights, including trips that could have been made on commercial aircraft. Price said he would reimburse the government for the cost of his personal travel, but the reimbursement did not cover the full expense of the flights. A later review by the HHS inspector general estimated that the department had spent more than $1 million on the charter flights.

The controversy intensified as lawmakers and the public questioned Price’s travel decisions and the administration’s oversight. On September 29, 2017, Price resigned as secretary of Health and Human Services, and President Trump accepted his resignation.

The White House released a brief statement: “Secretary of Health and Human Services Thomas Price offered his resignation earlier today and the President accepted.”

Price’s departure came as the administration and Republican-led Congress were struggling to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act after several unsuccessful legislative attempts. The resignation prompted renewed debate over ethics rules, government spending and accountability within the administration.

GOP Senator Ben Sasse Criticizes White Nationalist Richard Spencer in Twitter Exchange

Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.) criticized white nationalist Richard Spencer on Twitter in September 2017 after Spencer mocked conservatives who blamed Russia for contributing to racial divisions in the United States.

The exchange followed a tweet Sasse posted about comments by Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.), who had said Russian internet operations had sought to deepen divisions surrounding President Donald Trump’s criticism of NFL players who knelt during the national anthem to protest racial inequality and police brutality.

“No one loves American-vs-American fighting more than Putin. His intel agencies stoke both sides of every divide,” Sasse wrote on September 28, 2017, linking to an article about Lankford’s remarks.

Spencer responded: “In the minds of goober conservatives, the Russians are to blame for racial divisions.”

Sasse then posted a series of replies criticizing Spencer’s views and arguing that racism, as well as foreign efforts to exploit divisions, contributed to political conflict.

“Oh let goobers & nongoobers agree on this: Racists like you are to blame. But Putin’s agencies also love using you as their divisive tool,” Sasse wrote.

In subsequent posts, Sasse challenged Spencer’s rejection of universal rights and human dignity. He argued that American political traditions recognize individuals as possessing inherent worth regardless of race, ancestry or wealth.

“Actually, that's exactly what America declares we do have: People are the image-bearers of God, created with dignity & inalienable rights,” Sasse wrote in one post.

He also criticized Spencer’s emphasis on “white culture” and identity, writing that the American ideal of universal dignity “rejects your ‘white culture’ crybaby politics” and identity-based political movements.

Sasse continued by accusing Spencer and other white nationalists of drawing on authoritarian and racist ideas. He called their arguments “hateful” and “un-American,” and concluded the exchange by writing: “Get a real job, Clown. Find an actual neighbor to serve. You'll be happier. Have a nice day.”

CNN journalist Jake Tapper also commented on the exchange, writing: “Wherein a piece of garbage is thrown into a receptacle with grace and artistry.”

The posts came weeks after the “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, where white nationalists and other far-right demonstrators gathered in August 2017. Spencer was a prominent participant in the rally. Violence broke out between demonstrators and counterprotesters, and Heather Heyer was killed when a car struck a crowd of people. Dozens of others were injured.

After the violence, Trump said that there had been “blame on both sides,” while also condemning hatred, bigotry and violence. His remarks drew criticism from Democrats, civil rights advocates and some Republicans, including Sasse, who had urged Trump to clearly condemn white supremacists and neo-Nazis.

Spencer later said he was pleased with Trump’s initial response to the Charlottesville violence. Spencer has been identified by news organizations as a leader of the white nationalist movement, a label he has embraced.

Sasse’s exchange with Spencer reflected a broader dispute among Republicans over how directly to confront white nationalism and how to describe the role of Russian influence operations in intensifying political divisions in the United States.

By and large, standards are set by the states that uphold them, with localities left to decide how best to implement those standards through lesson plans, specialized curriculum, and testing. But if you re a voter, you have at some point checked a box on a ballot for someone on a school board, or at the very least a school superintendent. That means that in a time like now, when the phrase  all politics is local  has taken on the most literal meaning you can imagine, local politics can sometimes determine what your children learn.To make matters worse, textbook manufacturers are as subject to political winds   and capitalism   as the next industry. That means they want to produce their books in markets where they can sell the most, which gives big states like California and Texas, whose student populations vastly outmatch those of other states, huge influence over education standards even outside their borders.When a state is reliably  blue,  as California is, that can shake out favorably for proponents of science, history, civics   basically everything where facts are involved. But when a state is more often  red,  as in the case of Texas, it can be bad for those same things.What happens, though, when a state is more  purple,  like New Mexico?We re finding out now. The new science education standards for the southwestern state are raising eyebrows, and that s saying something for a state in which the long-serving Public Education Secretary resigned after 7 years on the job. Hanna Skandera, who was appointed by Republican governor Susana Martinez, had faced intense scrutiny from both Democratic lawmakers and from teachers in the state over previously proposed education reforms.  A through F   grading for young elementary students and a variety of other changes Skandera had sought while serving in the same capacity in Florida under governor Jeb! Bush made her a target of teachers  unions and parent groups across the state.Martinez was very unhappy about the pressure that caused Skandera to resign.But the proposed changes to science in New Mexico were initially based on the Next Generation Science Standards, guidelines released back in 2013 and eventually passed by both chambers of the New Mexico legislature. It was when the proposed changes made it to Governor Martinez  desk that issues arose. Toward the end of my tenure at the Public Education Department, I was tasked to edit and change some of the language in the standards to make them politically sanitized. No matter whether changes come from school boards, legislatures, or directly from a governor s office, changes to education standards should never be politicized. **New Mexico Science Standards Draw Criticism Over Changes to Proposed Guidelines**

Education standards are set primarily by states, while local districts generally decide how to implement them through lesson plans, curricula and assessments. Because standards can influence the textbooks and instructional materials used across a state, disputes over their content often become political as well as educational.

That dynamic came into focus in New Mexico during a debate over new science standards. The state considered standards based largely on the Next Generation Science Standards, a set of guidelines developed by states and education organizations and released in 2013.

The proposal became controversial after Republican Gov. Susana Martinez vetoed legislation related to the standards and directed the Public Education Department to conduct additional review. The department later released a revised version, prompting criticism from educators, lawmakers and science advocates who said some changes weakened or removed references to topics including climate change and evolution.

Supporters of the revisions said the state had the authority to review and modify the proposed standards before adopting them. Critics argued that the changes reflected political concerns rather than established scientific understanding and could make New Mexico’s standards less rigorous than the model on which they were based.

The dispute unfolded amid broader disagreements over education policy in the state. Hanna Skandera, who had served as New Mexico’s public education secretary under Martinez, faced opposition from some teachers’ organizations, parents and Democratic lawmakers over proposed changes to school accountability, grading and other policies. She left the position in 2017 after several years in office.

The science standards debate was separate from Skandera’s departure but became part of the larger discussion about the role of the governor and the Public Education Department in setting policy. Some Democratic lawmakers and education advocates criticized the administration’s handling of the standards and called for a process guided more directly by scientists and classroom educators.

The final standards were the product of that review process, but the controversy highlighted a broader question: how much political influence should elected officials have over the way science is taught in public schools?

States routinely adapt national or multistate frameworks to meet their own requirements. However, scientific organizations and educators have generally argued that state standards should accurately reflect the broad consensus of the scientific community, particularly on subjects such as evolution and human-caused climate change.

New Mexico’s debate did not establish that science had been removed from the state’s curriculum. It did show how decisions about wording, emphasis and required instruction can become contentious when they involve topics with political implications.

WATCH: Gary Cohn Says $1,000 in Tax Savings Could Help Families Renovate a Kitchen, Buy a Car or Take a Vacation

Gary Cohn, then director of the White House National Economic Council, promoted President Donald Trump’s tax proposal in a September 2017 speech by describing how an additional $1,000 in take-home pay might be used by a family.

“If we allow a family to keep another $1,000, they can renovate their kitchen, they can buy a new car, they can take a family vacation,” Cohn said during remarks in Indiana.

Cohn did not say that a new car or a kitchen renovation would cost $1,000. His point was that a tax reduction of that amount could contribute toward one of those expenses, depending on a family’s circumstances. The remarks were subsequently shared widely online, where some users interpreted them as suggesting that $1,000 could cover the full cost of a car, renovation and vacation.

The comments drew criticism from people who argued that the examples did not reflect typical household costs. The average price of a new vehicle is far higher than $1,000, while kitchen renovations can range from relatively modest improvements to much more expensive projects. Vacation expenses also vary substantially based on the number of travelers, destination and length of the trip.

The tax framework promoted by the Trump administration proposed reducing individual and corporate tax rates and eliminating the estate tax. Administration officials said the changes would encourage economic growth and leave more money with families and businesses. Critics, including tax policy analysts, argued that the largest benefits would go to corporations and high-income households.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimated that the top 1 percent of taxpayers would receive roughly half of the tax cuts under the framework. Critics also said eliminating the estate tax would disproportionately benefit wealthy families, including President Trump’s family, although the proposal’s ultimate effects depended on details that had not yet been finalized.

Cohn’s statement was therefore an illustration of how a family might use additional disposable income, not a claim that a new car, a complete kitchen renovation and a family vacation could each be purchased for $1,000. The cost of a new vehicle or a major home renovation would generally be many times that amount.

**High School Policy on National Anthem Draws Debate Over Student Expression**

A Louisiana high school’s policy requiring student athletes to stand during the national anthem drew public attention in September 2017, amid a national debate over protests by professional football players.

Parkway High School in Bossier Parish said students were expected to stand “in a respectful manner” during the national anthem at sporting events in which their team was participating. According to a statement attributed to principal Waylon Bates, failure to comply could result in reduced playing time or limits on participation, at the discretion of the head coach and principal. Continued noncompliance could lead to removal from the team.

The policy said Parkway was seeking to maintain a positive environment for sporting events and avoid disruptions to athletic contests. It did not specify how the rule would be applied in every circumstance, and public reporting at the time did not establish whether any students had been disciplined under it.

The announcement came shortly after President Donald Trump criticized NFL players who protested during the anthem by kneeling, sitting or remaining in the locker room. Trump called on team owners to discipline or dismiss players who did not stand, but his comments were not a federal order requiring schools or sports organizations to adopt similar policies.

Reports said Bates described the school’s approach as an effort to keep politics out of athletics. Critics argued that a rule governing how students must behave during the anthem could itself raise questions about political expression and free speech. Some opponents also said that punishing athletes for a protest could cause additional students to participate in demonstrations.

The Louisiana High School Athletic Association has allowed schools to establish certain local policies governing their athletic programs, but that does not necessarily resolve whether a particular rule is constitutional. The authority of public schools to regulate student conduct can depend on the wording of the policy, the setting, the type of expression involved and the consequences imposed.

The debate also drew attention to a 1943 Supreme Court decision, *West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette*. In that case, the court ruled that public schools could not compel students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance when doing so conflicted with their beliefs. The decision overturned an earlier ruling that had permitted such requirements.

The plaintiffs in *Barnette* were Jehovah’s Witnesses, whose religious beliefs prevented them from saluting national symbols. The Supreme Court’s majority opinion, however, framed the case more broadly as one involving freedom of speech and belief.

Justice Robert Jackson, writing for the majority, stated that constitutional protections for speech, press, assembly and worship could not be restricted on insufficient grounds. He also wrote that public authorities could not compel individuals to “utter what is not in his mind.”

The decision is commonly cited in disputes over compelled speech, but its application to athletic participation is not automatic. Courts have recognized that schools may impose rules related to safety, order and team activities, while also limiting the government’s ability to punish students for protected expression. Whether sitting or kneeling during the anthem is protected in a specific school setting would depend on the facts and applicable law.

Some legal observers have noted that extracurricular activities are still connected to public schools and are not automatically exempt from constitutional requirements. At the same time, schools may argue that participation on an athletic team involves additional eligibility standards that do not apply in ordinary classroom settings.

The Parkway policy therefore prompted questions about the balance between team rules and students’ rights rather than establishing a clear nationwide legal precedent. The school’s action was one local response to a broader controversy over the national anthem, patriotism and racial inequality.

Trump’s remarks about NFL protests intensified that controversy in 2017, while players and their supporters said the demonstrations were intended to call attention to racial injustice and police treatment of Black Americans. The debate subsequently spread beyond professional sports to colleges, high schools and other public institutions.

Whether a student may be required to stand during the anthem, and whether a school may penalize a student for refusing, can vary according to state law, school policy and constitutional interpretation. The Parkway announcement highlighted those unresolved questions but did not, by itself, show that high schools nationwide had adopted similar rules or that the policy had been upheld by a court.

She said: The point that we re making is that we have the votes on the substance, but not necessarily on the process, which is why we are so confident that we can move healthcare forward and get it done in the spring. Huckabee Sanders, like all of Trump s minions, is well-versed in diversion tactics but still couldn t avoid exposing her boss  blatant lie. Trump does not have the votes to pass Graham-Cassidy, and he was lying through his teeth about it. No matter how Huckabee Sanders tried to conceal the truth, it was too obvious to be hidden.Many   including Republicans   already believe that Graham-Cassidy is dead. If the bill can t get enough votes on the process, the bill cannot pass. Trump’s Press Secretary Addresses Questions About Obamacare Repeal Vote

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders faced questions from reporters about President Donald Trump’s claims that Republicans had enough support in the Senate to replace the Affordable Care Act.

During a briefing, a reporter asked Sanders about the Graham-Cassidy proposal, the Republican-backed health care measure then under consideration. Sanders said the administration believed it had support for the bill’s substance, while acknowledging that procedural issues could prevent a vote.

“The point that we’re making is that we have the votes on the substance, but not necessarily on the process, which is why we are so confident that we can move healthcare forward and get it done in the spring,” Sanders said.

The distinction drew scrutiny because a bill must secure sufficient support both to advance through Senate procedures and to pass a final vote. At the time, several Republican senators had expressed opposition or reservations about the proposal, making its prospects uncertain.

Graham-Cassidy ultimately did not advance after Republican leaders concluded they lacked enough support to pass it. The episode highlighted the difficulties the Trump administration and congressional Republicans faced in fulfilling their promise to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act.

Sanders continued to defend the administration’s broader health care strategy, while lawmakers debated whether to pursue additional legislation or focus on changes to the existing law.

**Wounded Veteran Criticizes Use of His Image in Trump’s Dispute With NFL Players**

A photograph of a wounded Marine veteran became part of President Donald Trump’s criticism of NFL players who kneel during the national anthem, prompting the veteran to object to the use of military service members in political arguments.

Marine Staff Sgt. John Jones lost both legs while serving in Iraq more than a decade ago. In 2007, he posed for a photograph wearing the prosthetic legs that allow him to stand and walk.

The image resurfaced in September 2017 after Trump retweeted it while commenting on NFL protests. The accompanying message asked what the “BRAVE American” would give to stand on his “OWN two legs just ONCE MORE” for the national anthem. The post was originally shared by a Twitter user identified as Donna Warren.

Jones later criticized the use of his image in an interview with BuzzFeed, saying he was frustrated that military veterans were being used to advance political arguments over athletes’ protests. Jones works for Workshops for Warriors, a San Diego nonprofit that provides training to veterans for manufacturing careers.

“If you really want to honor the troops, listen to them,” Jones said, according to BuzzFeed. He also criticized what he described as the use of veterans to “push a political agenda,” and said he would rather see attention directed toward programs that help former service members find jobs.

Jones said the photograph should not be treated as evidence that he supported Trump’s position on the NFL protests. “I’ve got my own views about this, but that’s why I put the uniform on, so people can do whatever they want in a lawful, peaceful manner,” he said.

NFL players and other athletes who knelt during the anthem said the demonstrations were intended to draw attention to racial discrimination and police brutality. The protests began during the 2016 season, when quarterback Colin Kaepernick and other players knelt during the anthem.

Trump repeatedly criticized the demonstrations, arguing that players should stand for the anthem and accusing them of disrespecting the flag and the military. His comments intensified a national debate over free expression, patriotism and the treatment of veterans.

Kneeling during the anthem is generally protected as an expression of opinion, although professional sports leagues and teams may establish rules governing player conduct. The protests themselves are peaceful, and the First Amendment limits government restrictions on speech rather than requiring private organizations to permit all forms of expression.

Sen. John McCain, a former Navy pilot and prisoner of war, also defended the players’ right to protest during the debate. Other veterans expressed differing views, with some supporting the demonstrations and others objecting to the timing and setting.

Jones’s comments did not represent all veterans, but they underscored the disagreement among former service members over how military service and national symbols should be invoked in the dispute.

title: Trump Is So Embarrassed His Candidate Lost He’s Deleting Tweets And Praying You’ll Forget
text: Donald Trump went all in for his man Luther Strange. I mean, he tweeted   in between other pressing matters, of course   at least a dozen times in support of the incumbent Senator in Alabama.Or at least, Strange was the incumbent, until former Chief Justice of the Alabama Supreme Court and all-around douchebag Roy Moore beat him in a runoff primary last night.Trump did everything but attach himself at the hip to Strange, for a reason I ll get into in a minute. But it just wasn t enough to overcome Moore, who was backed by Trump s former right-hand man Steve Bannon, as well as a bevy of other prominent dumbass conservatives. Sarah Palin, Sebastian Gorka, Laura Ingraham and even Sean Hannity lent their support to the ultra-conservative Moore, while simultaneously being careful to tell voters that a vote against Strange wasn t a vote against Donald Trump. Bannon went so far as to say that a vote for Moore was a vote for Trump.They understand something that the president doesn t, and it s this I was alluding to as the reason Trump rolled so deep with Luther Strange. Donald Trump knows he has some kind of power over his supporters, but he doesn t know what it is. He honestly believes that he can make them do whatever he wants them to do and that they will do it happily. And above all, he believes that he is infallible in his decisions.Trump has it all backwards.In reality, it is Donald Trump who does the bidding of his fans. It s because he literally has no idea what he s doing. He has zero experience in politics. He doesn t know or even care what the people of Alabama think about or want in a Senate candidate. Let me put this plainly:If Donald Trump thought that a man like Roy Moore, who was removed from the Supreme Court of Alabama only by outside forces; who never lost the support of his constituents; who is literally the Bible-thumping, gay-hating, end-times preaching Senator that the most redneck state in America has been dreaming about since Reconstruction was going to lose this election to a career politician, well  He s a whole lot dumber than any of us give him credit for.Trump s candidate lost because he was always going to lose. Trump himself lost because he had no idea. Prior to the election, Trump was so confident of his star power and Strange s ability to win by association that he hadn t bothered to learn Moore s first name.And one thing Donald J. Trump doesn t do is lose gracefully. The president went on a deleting spree of tweets he had posted in support of Strange. He was so angry that he couldn t even remember when the general election was being held in Alabama, so when he congratulated Moore after his win, he even had to delete the first draft of that:Trump has, of course, quieted down. Unfortunately for him, the slew of tweet deletions, which may actually be illegal, just makes his timeline look like literally all he can think about is big black men on their knees.As long as nobody s sitting down during the national anthem, I suppose.Featured image via Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Trump-Backed Luther Strange Loses Alabama Senate Runoff to Roy Moore

Donald Trump strongly supported Luther Strange in Alabama’s Republican Senate runoff, using Twitter and a campaign appearance to urge voters to back the incumbent senator. But Strange was defeated Tuesday night by Roy Moore, a former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court.

Moore entered the race with support from several prominent conservative figures, including former Trump adviser Steve Bannon. Former Alaska governor Sarah Palin, conservative commentator Laura Ingraham and other national figures also endorsed Moore during the campaign.

Trump’s support for Strange reflected the president’s broader effort to influence Republican voters and maintain control over the party’s Senate candidates. Trump had endorsed Strange after then-Governor Robert Bentley appointed him to the Senate seat previously held by Attorney General Jeff Sessions.

The endorsement did not overcome Moore’s support among Alabama conservatives. Moore campaigned as a staunch social conservative and presented himself as an outsider challenging the Republican establishment. His previous tenure as chief justice ended after judicial authorities removed him from office over violations of court orders related to displays of the Ten Commandments and same-sex marriage.

Strange, who had been serving in the Senate since early 2017, argued that his experience and support from national Republican leaders made him the stronger candidate for the general election. Moore’s campaign instead emphasized cultural issues and opposition to Washington’s political establishment.

The result was a setback for Trump, who had made Strange’s candidacy a personal priority. It also represented a victory for Bannon and other conservatives who had argued that Republican voters should reject the party’s preferred candidate.

Trump later congratulated Moore on his victory and said he looked forward to helping Republicans retain the Senate seat in the December general election. Moore went on to become the Republican nominee, while Democrat Doug Jones won the general election.

The Alabama runoff demonstrated that Trump’s endorsement could not guarantee victory even in a heavily Republican state. It also highlighted divisions within the Republican Party between its leadership and activists seeking more ideologically conservative candidates.
