Trump and Clinton Clash Over Hurricane Maria Response as Navy Sends Hospital Ship to Puerto Rico

President Donald Trump had frequently criticized his former presidential rival Hillary Clinton, whose supporters had once faced chants of “Lock her up!” at Trump’s political rallies. But in the aftermath of Hurricane Maria, Clinton joined growing calls for a larger federal response to the disaster in Puerto Rico, while the Trump administration announced that additional military and medical assistance was being sent to the island.

As the destruction from Hurricane Maria became more evident, Trump faced criticism for focusing heavily on his dispute with NFL players over protests during the national anthem while residents of Puerto Rico struggled with widespread power outages, damaged infrastructure and limited access to clean water. On Sunday, Clinton used Twitter to call for a greater military response.

“President Trump, Sec. Mattis, and DOD should send the Navy, including the USNS Comfort, to Puerto Rico now. These are American citizens,” Clinton wrote on September 24, 2017.

Clinton’s message echoed requests from Puerto Rican officials and others for additional federal resources, including the USNS Comfort, a Navy hospital ship. The vessel was later ordered to Puerto Rico as part of a broader effort to expand medical and logistical support after the storm. Federal officials said the response would include additional personnel, equipment and supplies, though the timing of the deployment was not presented as a direct response to Clinton’s tweet.

Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Brock Long said the government was increasing its presence in Puerto Rico as the scale of the emergency became clearer. The Navy subsequently confirmed that the USNS Comfort would be deployed to assist with medical care.

Trump acknowledged the difficulties of delivering aid to Puerto Rico, while defending the government’s response. “It’s very tough because it’s an island,” Trump said. “In Texas, we can ship the trucks right out there. And you know, we’ve gotten A-pluses on Texas and on Florida, and we will also on Puerto Rico. But the difference is, this is an island sitting in the middle of an ocean. And it’s a big ocean; it’s a very big ocean.”

The administration’s response drew criticism from Puerto Rican officials, lawmakers and members of both political parties, who said the territory needed faster deliveries of food, water, fuel and medical supplies. Hurricane Maria caused extensive damage across Puerto Rico, leaving much of the U.S. territory without electricity and disrupting communications and transportation. Recovery and restoration efforts were expected to take months or longer in many areas.

Trump was scheduled to visit Puerto Rico the following week to meet with residents and local officials involved in the response.

title: The Worst Possible Person Just Won Alabama’s Runoff For U.S. Senate, And It’s All Trump’s Fault
text: Alabama s Republican runoff election for Jeff Sessions  vacant Senate seat has come to its end, and the candidate that will go up against Democrat Doug Jones in December s general election is none other than Roy Moore. Moore is the former chief justice of Alabama s state Supreme Court, and he s the one who ordered all of Alabama s probate judges to defy the U.S. Supreme Court s ruling on same-sex marriage in 2013.But Moore wasn t Donald Trump s candidate. Luther Strange, who has been holding Sessions  seat, was the man backed by Trump. In fact, Trump was at a political rally for Strange last Friday when he called for NFL players who kneel during the national anthem to be fired. The president s endorsement usually helps a candidate, yet it s Moore who just won. Here s a little background on Moore: He was yanked from the Alabama Supreme Court s bench in 2003 for refusing to remove a massive monument to the Bible s 10 Commandments from the grounds of the courthouse. That s considered a violation of the First Amendment since it constitutes a government endorsement of one religion.In 2012, Moore won his job back, then called same-sex relationships  sodomy,  and decried the immorality of it all in the wake of the Supreme Court legalizing same-sex marriage across all 50 states. He wanted to bar Democratic Rep. Keith Ellison from serving in office because he s a Muslim, and he accused Obama of using our military for social experiments (including wiping out  don t ask, don t tell  and allowing transgender individuals to serve).He has also defended Putin because Putin seems to agree with him on the issue of LGBTQ rights. One might think that would earn him Trump s endorsement, but somehow, it didn t.All of that should have made this election a tossup given conservatives  current love of Trump, but it didn t. Moore was polling ahead of Strange pretty much the entire time. Why?Well, Trump, for starters. That buffoon endorsed Luther Strange and bragged about it all over Twitter, up to and including through today. He boasted that Strange s numbers had skyrocketed since his endorsement, but according to NBC News, Trump s endorsement actually pushed people towards Moore. Trump won Alabama by double digits last year, but it seems they re souring towards him now.That makes this Trump s fault, at least partly. Voters claimed that his endorsement didn t affect them one way or another, but those who were influenced by Trump said he pushed them away from Strange. What that means is that some Republican voters chose Moore because Trump backed the other candidate.That s a massive blow to Trump. Maybe Alabama voters are ashamed of Trump, and they d have good reason to feel that way. For instance, speaking on the  Rick and Bubba  radio show, which is based out of Birmingham, Trump said: Luther Strange is going to be a great Senator. He loves Alabama, he loves the states and he loves the country. He will absolutely win against the Democrat.Ray will have a hard time. If Luther wins, the Democrats will hardly fight. If Ray wins, [Democrats] will pour in $30 million. Moore s first name is Roy. When Rick Burgess, one of the show s hosts, pointed out that he d gotten Roy s name wrong, Trump actually said that it s not a good sign if the president doesn t know his name. Then he said: I don t know that much about Roy Moore. Roy Moore is going to have a very hard time getting elected against the Democrat.Against Luther they won t even fight. When news of Moore s win came out, Trump tweeted the following:As noted above, the general election is December 12. text: Graham-Cassidy, the latest and worst in a line of Republican healthcare bills collectively dubbed  Trumpcare,  looks dead. Senator Susan Collins (R-ME) just joined Senators John McCain (R-AZ) and Rand Paul (R-KY) as one of the few to break party lines and refuse to vote for the bill. While not everyone is against the bill for the best of reasons, Susan Collins could not have been more clear about the many issues she had with the legislation.Here s her statement: First, both proposals make sweeping changes and cuts in the Medicaid program. Expert projections show that more than $1 trillion would be taken out of the Medicaid program between the years 2020 and 2036. This would have a devastating impact to a program that has been on the books for 50 years and provides health care to our most vulnerable citizens, including disabled children and low-income seniors.Second, both bills open the door for states to weaken protections for people with pre-existing conditions, such as asthma, cancer, heart disease, arthritis, and diabetes. Some states could allow higher premiums for individuals with pre-existing conditions, potentially making their insurance unaffordable. States could also limit specific categories of benefits for Affordable Care Act policies, such as eliminating coverage for mental health or substance abuse treatment.Third, physicians, patient advocates, insurers, and hospitals agree that both versions of this legislation would lead to higher premiums and reduced coverage for tens of millions of Americans.The CBO s analysis on the earlier version of the bill, incomplete though it is due to time constraints, confirms that this bill will have a substantially negative impact on the number of people covered by insurance.There has been some discussion that the new version of the bil includes additional money for my home state of Maine. The fact is, Maine still loses money under whichever version of the Graham-Cassidy bill we consider because the bills use what could be described as a  give with one hand, take with the other  distribution model. Huge Medicaid cuts down the road more than offset any short-term influx of money. But even more important, if Senators can adjust a funding formula over a weekend to help a single state, they could just as easily adjust that formula to hurt that state. This is simply not the way that we should be approaching an important and complex issue that must be handled thoughtfully and fairly for all Americans. There you have it   Susan Collins just hammered the final nail into Trumpcare s coffin.On September 30th, a special rule allowing Republicans to pass legislation with only a simple majority (50 votes and a tiebreak) will expire. After that, any healthcare legislation that Republicans want to pass will have to get at least eight Democrats on board.Republicans can t govern or even get their own party to agree, so good luck with that.Featured image via Alex Wong/Getty Images

Graham-Cassidy Faces Defeat as Senator Collins Says She Will Vote No

Graham-Cassidy, the latest in a series of Republican healthcare proposals sometimes referred to collectively as “Trumpcare,” appeared unlikely to pass after Senator Susan Collins (R-ME) said she would oppose it. Collins joined Senators John McCain (R-AZ) and Rand Paul (R-KY), who had also announced that they would not support the measure.

In a statement, Collins outlined several concerns about the legislation. She said the proposal would make substantial changes to Medicaid, including reductions in federal funding over time. Those changes, she argued, could affect a program that provides coverage to vulnerable people, including disabled children and low-income seniors.

Collins also raised concerns about protections for people with pre-existing conditions. Under the proposal, states could have received authority to seek waivers from certain Affordable Care Act requirements. Depending on the waivers granted, insurers could have been allowed to charge some people more or offer plans with fewer benefits, although the bill included limits on how those changes could be implemented.

The senator said healthcare providers, patient advocates and insurers had raised objections that the legislation could result in higher premiums or reduced coverage. The Congressional Budget Office had not yet issued a full analysis of the final version of Graham-Cassidy, but its earlier analysis of related legislation projected that fewer people would have insurance under that proposal.

Collins also addressed changes to the bill’s funding formula, including additional funding that could have benefited Maine in the short term. She argued that the state could still face losses over time because of reductions in Medicaid funding. She also criticized the process of changing the formula late in the debate, saying funding decisions should be made through a more consistent and transparent process.

With Collins, McCain and Paul opposed, Republicans did not appear to have enough votes to pass Graham-Cassidy through the budget reconciliation process. The bill was ultimately withdrawn from consideration in September 2017 rather than brought to a final vote.

The special budget-reconciliation process being used for the healthcare proposal was available only for a limited period, expiring at the end of the fiscal year on September 30. After that deadline, most major healthcare legislation would generally require broader bipartisan support in the Senate.

The defeat marked another setback for Republican efforts in 2017 to repeal and replace major portions of the Affordable Care Act.

Villanueva later said the moment did not unfold as he or the team had intended. According to accounts of his comments, he had asked quarterback Ben Roethlisberger whether he could stand at the front of the group with the team’s captains. When Villanueva saw the players’ positioning and the anthem began, he said he was unable to return inside without drawing further attention.

The episode led to confusion about the team’s plan. Coach Mike Tomlin had said the Steelers intended to remain in the tunnel during the anthem, rather than make a statement by kneeling or standing on the field. Villanueva’s position outside the tunnel made it appear that he had acted alone.

In discussing his military service, Villanueva said he associated the flag with the soldiers he had served alongside and with the principle that service members fight for one another. He also emphasized that his decision should not be interpreted as a condemnation of his teammates.

Villanueva accepted responsibility for the way the incident unfolded. He said the controversy had “sort of been out of control” and acknowledged that he had made Tomlin and his teammates look bad, although he said he had done so unintentionally.

He also said he felt embarrassed when he saw photographs of himself standing by himself outside the tunnel. Villanueva said the image did not accurately reflect the relationship among the players or the team’s discussions before the game.

The offensive lineman defended Tomlin against suggestions that the coach was insufficiently patriotic. Villanueva said he was offended by such claims and described Tomlin as deeply patriotic.

“We as a team tried to figure it out, obviously we butchered it,” Villanueva said, according to reports of his comments. He added that he did not view himself as having a uniquely authoritative position on the national anthem debate and said he would continue to support his teammates.

Villanueva also said he would support teammates who chose to kneel or sit during the anthem. He noted that players who had protested during anthems had approached him before or after games and thanked him for his military service.

He described his teammates as supportive and patriotic and said the team meeting held before the game had brought the players together. The Steelers’ response reflected the broader disagreement in the NFL over protests during the anthem, which players had used to call attention to racial inequality and police treatment of Black Americans.

The controversy followed public criticism from President Donald Trump, who had urged NFL owners to discipline players who knelt during the anthem. The Steelers’ decision to remain in the locker room, and Villanueva’s appearance outside the tunnel, quickly became part of that national debate.

Villanueva’s later comments made clear that he did not intend to distance himself from his teammates or to present his actions as a rebuke of players who protested. Instead, he characterized the incident as a misunderstanding and reiterated his support for the team.

WATCH: Disabled Healthcare Advocates Arrested During Senate Obamacare Hearing

Republicans were seeking to repeal and replace major parts of the Affordable Care Act through the Graham-Cassidy proposal. The legislation drew opposition from hospitals, doctors’ groups and AARP, among others, who warned that its changes to federal healthcare funding could reduce coverage and increase costs for some people. Critics also argued that the bill could weaken protections for people with pre-existing conditions.

During a Senate hearing on the proposal, Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden pressed Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, one of the bill’s sponsors, about whether it would protect people with pre-existing conditions. Cassidy discussed the legislation’s provisions, but the exchange did not resolve Wyden’s concerns.

Outside the hearing, activists with ADAPT, a disability-rights organization whose name originally stood for American Disabled for Attendant Programs Today, protested potential reductions to Medicaid. Demonstrators chanted, “No cuts to Medicaid, save our liberty!” The group has advocated for community-based services and the ability of disabled people to live outside institutions.

Sen. Orrin Hatch, the Republican chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, halted the hearing as protesters interrupted. Hatch told those who could not remain quiet to “get the heck out,” according to video of the proceedings.

“If the hearing is going to devolve into a sideshow or a forum for simply putting partisan points on the board, there’s absolutely no reason for us to be here,” Hatch said.

Capitol Police arrested a number of protesters during the demonstration. Images and video showed officers removing disabled activists from the area, prompting criticism from opponents of the bill and renewed attention to the treatment of protesters at the Capitol.

Some senators remained in the room as the arrests continued. Video posted from the hearing also appeared to show Cassidy looking tired and yawning while protesters were being removed. The footage alone does not establish what he was reacting to or whether he was responding to the arrests.

The Graham-Cassidy proposal faced significant political opposition. Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican, said he would not support the legislation, while Sen. Rand Paul also criticized it. Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska had not announced support for the bill at the time.

Public polling at the time generally showed more Americans opposing than supporting Republican efforts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, although results varied by poll and by the wording of the questions. The proposal ultimately did not receive enough support in the Senate and was not enacted.

People Debate NFL Protests While Flag Code Covers a Range of Everyday Uses

Public debate over NFL players kneeling during the national anthem has often centered on whether the demonstrations show disrespect for the American flag. The United States Flag Code, however, addresses a broader range of practices involving the flag, while offering guidance rather than generally imposing criminal penalties.

The controversy over players kneeling, sitting or otherwise protesting during the anthem intensified during the 2017 football season. Critics called the demonstrations disrespectful, while supporters said they were a form of protest against racial injustice and police treatment of Black Americans.

A Twitter user identified as HennyWise, who described himself as a third-generation veteran, used a series of posts to highlight several provisions of the Flag Code. The provisions appear in Title 4, Section 8 of the U.S. Code, rather than in a chapter numbered 10.176.

The code says that the flag should not be carried flat or horizontally, but should be carried aloft and free.

It also says that the flag should not be used as wearing apparel, bedding or drapery. In addition, the code advises that the flag should not be used for advertising purposes or embroidered on items such as cushions, handkerchiefs and similar products.

Another provision states that no part of the flag should be used as a costume or athletic uniform.

These recommendations are frequently overlooked in commercial products, sporting events and patriotic displays. The Flag Code also says that the flag should not have marks, insignia, letters, words, numbers, figures or drawings placed on it.

A separate user responding to HennyWise’s posts pointed to the same provision in discussing flags and symbols associated with the “Blue Lives Matter” movement. Whether a particular design constitutes misuse of the U.S. flag depends on how it is made and displayed; the code’s language is directed at the flag itself and does not establish a legal judgment about every related symbol.

The code also includes guidance for conduct during the national anthem. It says people present should stand at attention and face the flag, if one is displayed, with specific instructions for military personnel and civilians. It does not prescribe a criminal penalty for kneeling, and the Flag Code is generally understood as a set of standards for respectful display rather than a broad enforcement statute.

The discussion over NFL protests therefore involves both the code’s recommendations and differing views about patriotism, racial equality and the appropriate way to demonstrate during public ceremonies. While some people regard kneeling during the anthem as disrespectful, others view it as protected political expression.

The debate has also raised questions about whether criticism is applied consistently when other common flag-code recommendations are ignored in commercial or sporting settings.

text: You may not be familiar with the name  Unilever,  but there is a good chance you have some of their products in your home right at this moment. The multi-national giant owns a lot of the brands many will most likely find in both their bathroom cabinet, such as Axe and Dove, as well as in their kitchen, with brands including Hellman s, Best Foods, and I Can t Believe It s Not Butter. The corporation owns Ben & Jerry s, Klondike, Popsicle, and Slim Fast just to name a few, but they aren t the names that are paying the bills   It s what is officially known as the  Heartbrand  umbrella, available in over 40 countries under different names in order to retain a sense of regional familiarity, but always recognizable by its heart-shaped logo. This was proven after they applied to Australia s Fair Work Commission to terminate an enterprise agreement at its Heartbrand, known as  Streets,  manufacturing plant in western Sydney, Australia. You may not be familiar with the name Unilever, but many households use products associated with the multinational company. Its brands have included bathroom products such as Axe and Dove, as well as food and beverage names including Hellmann’s, Best Foods and I Can’t Believe It’s Not Butter. A leaked document was said to outline when posts about the proposed workplace changes could breach company policy, including comments and other forms of online reaction. The extent to which the guidance would affect employees’ ability to publicly criticize the proposal was disputed.

The Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union opposed the proposed changes through its “Say No to Streets” campaign. The campaign encouraged supporters to contact company representatives and express their concerns about the workplace agreement.

title: Zuckerberg Was Personally Warned About Russian Meddling By Obama And He Completely Blew It Off
text: As the investigations into how Russia meddled in our election escalate, Facebook has turned records relating to ad buys from Russian actors over to Congress. Facebook has found itself in the crosshairs of Democrats and Republicans alike because of this (and for other reasons), and Mark Zuckerberg is finally, finally wondering if maybe he should be taking a more active role in his own company.Why? Because Facebook sold over 3,000 pro-Trump and pro-right wing ads to fake accounts run by Russians and people with ties to Russia. They turned those records over to the House and Senate Intelligence Committees and to Special Counsel Robert Mueller. They re going to re-evaluate the processes they use to review political ads, and they will supposedly  offer a higher standard of transparency  on those ads than what the law requires for radio, television and other platforms.For many, it s too little, too late, though. Trump was elected, a hostile foreign power helped him win, and the true scope of how Russia used and manipulated Facebook is still unknown. When they first came under fire for allowing the proliferation of fake news following Trump s  win,  Zuckerberg s excuse was that they were a technology company, not a media company. The implication was that they couldn t be held responsible for any of that.They re only now starting to come around to the truth, but the sad thing about this is that Zuckerberg was warned about people misusing his platform to swing the election several times. In fact, none other than President Obama himself literally pulled Zuckerberg aside during a conference in Peru to practically beg him to take the threat of fake news and disinformation seriously. Obama told Zuckerberg that, unless he actually paid attention, this would only be worse in four years.But Zuckerberg blew him off. He told Obama that such messages weren t widespread on his platform, and that there wouldn t be an easy solution to it. Like his pathetic excuse of being a tech company, Zuckerberg shirked any and all responsibility for it. Obama tried. Zuckerberg didn t really seem to care.Discovering that another country would even dare to try and influence our elections should be a horrific epiphany for any American. It s true that neither Zuckerberg, nor anyone else at Facebook (or anyone really) could have sufficiently predicted that anything like this would happen. As recently as two to three years ago, most of us would have made fun of the conspiracy theorists making bizarre claims about shady and hostile foreign actors working to swing our elections to their favor. That s reality now, but early warnings like Obama s seem to have slid right off Zuckerberg s back, as he was more concerned with his product than with how his product was being misused.Russia weaponized Facebook, and it s not over. Facebook has its part to do and they need to get to it post-haste. But another part may lie with Washington, with our lawmakers. It may well be time to apply laws similar to those that govern political advertising elsewhere to social media. Facebook hasn t yet provided many details about how they ll be transparent, especially given the fact that many of their political ads don t meet current legal definitions for political ads. They are, however, talking the talk. Now they need to walk the walk, or be forced to do so under law.Featured image via Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Zuckerberg Faced Questions About Russian Election Activity, But Details Of Obama Meeting Remain Unclear

As investigations into Russia’s efforts to interfere in the 2016 U.S. election continued, Facebook turned over records of roughly 3,000 advertisements purchased by accounts linked to Russia to congressional investigators. The company faced criticism from both Democrats and Republicans over the ads, as well as over its handling of misinformation and political content on the platform.

Facebook said the advertisements were purchased by accounts associated with a Russian entity and often addressed divisive political and social issues. The company said the ads did not all explicitly support a particular candidate, and that many appeared designed to inflame existing divisions among American voters. The records were provided to the House and Senate intelligence committees, which were examining Russia’s activity and its possible impact on the election.

The company also said it would review the way it identifies and discloses political advertising. Facebook indicated that it intended to provide users with more information about who paid for political ads and to create a searchable archive of such material. Those plans were part of a broader debate over whether social-media companies should face standards similar to those applied to political advertising on television and radio.

The disclosures came after months of criticism over Facebook’s role in spreading false or misleading information during the campaign. At the time, Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg argued that Facebook was primarily a technology company rather than a traditional media organization. He later acknowledged that the company needed to do more to address misinformation, foreign influence operations and the misuse of its services.

Reports also described a meeting between Zuckerberg and former President Barack Obama at a conference in Peru shortly after the 2016 election. According to those accounts, Obama expressed concern about the spread of fabricated stories and political misinformation online. However, the precise details of the conversation, including Zuckerberg’s response, were not publicly established.

Facebook had previously said that it had not found significant evidence that Russian actors had bought political advertising on its platform. Its later review identified the thousands of ads connected to accounts that appeared to originate in Russia, prompting further scrutiny from Congress and investigators. The findings underscored the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate political activity from coordinated foreign influence campaigns.

The disclosures did not by themselves establish that the advertisements changed the result of the election. They did show that foreign-linked accounts had used Facebook to distribute political messages to American audiences, and raised questions about the company’s systems for detecting and disclosing such activity.

Facebook said it would continue cooperating with congressional inquiries and other investigations. Lawmakers, meanwhile, debated whether existing election laws adequately covered political advertising on social-media platforms. Any new requirements would need to address transparency and foreign interference while also taking account of privacy, free-expression and enforcement concerns.

title: ‘Racist, Fascist, White Supremacist’: Former NFL Star Chris Kluwe Scorches Trump Over His Attacks On Atheletes
text: Donald Trump is facing seriously fierce blowback for his attacks on black athletes who choose to protest racism and police brutality by taking a knee during the national anthem before games. Everyone from owners to players to players to former players are giving Trump a big middle finger during Suturday s games on Sunday, and former NFL star Chris Kluwe didn t stay out of the fray. During an interview with CNN host Fredricka Whitfield, Kluwe, who believes he was blacklisted in the league for speaking out for LGBTQ rights, did not hold back. First, Whitfield asked: This display of kneeling at the national anthem on a football field started a year ago with 49er s Kaepernick and now has evolved into something else or perhaps has blossomed into the same thing but in a bigger way. Chris, what statement do you see NFL teams, owners, coaches making when they kneel, touch, lock arms on display like this? Kluwe responded: Well, I think that the players and the teams are saying that they are not going to be dictated to by a racist, fascist white supremacist who currently occupies the highest place in our government. When you look at what Donald Trump has said about speaking out against Nazis, I think it s fantastic that players and owners are now taking a stand in using the platform to speak out against this because this is not what America is. America is not a fascist military state where its devotion to the flag above all. Right now our nation is not holding up its end of the social contract, especially with communities of color. It should be a baseline right now that you can walk down the street and not get shot by a police officer for carrying a toy gun or for selling cigarettes out of the back of a car. It should not be out of the ordinary to expect that. So I m glad to see these players and owners taking a stand. text: James Clapper, the Director of National Intelligence under President Barack Obama, appeared on CNN s Erin Burnett Out Front on Friday night, and he told Burnett just what many Americans have suspected since January. Speaking about Russian interference in the 2016 presidential campaign, Clapper told her that the intelligence community had met with Donald Trump prior to his inauguration. In that briefing, he and other intel chiefs discussed with Trump a joint assessment by the CIA, FBI, and NSA that concluded that the interference was significant enough to warrant concerns over the outcome of the election: Our intelligence community assessment did, I think, serve to cast doubt on the legitimacy of his victory in the election. Although Clapper didn t say it in the interview, the unspoken implication is that this message may have prompted Trump s ridiculous overreactions to his inaugural crowd size, the myth that millions of  illegals  voted in the election, and any number of other actions and statements that led to the creation of Trump s laughable  Commission on Election Integrity,  which has, thus far, served only as a vehicle for promoting voter suppression.Clapper s CNN appearance was timely. It came just a short while after Trump went back to his favorite outlet, Twitter, to vent his frustrations for the millionth time:The Russia hoax continues, now it's ads on Facebook. What about the totally biased and dishonest Media coverage in favor of Crooked Hillary?  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) September 22, 2017Unfortunately for Trump, the fact is that the Facebook ads purchased by Russia weren t even part of that discussion with Clapper. Those weren t discovered until recently, after Facebook combed through their ad sales records and discovered hundreds of fake Russian profiles buying pro-Trump and pro-conservative ads on the social media platform during the campaign. That means that completely independent of any allegations about ad buying, the intelligence community had already concretely agreed that Russia helped Trump win the election.Even after the transition to Trump s administration and Cabinet, the investigation into Russian interference produced the same responses from different intel chiefs. When Senator Mark Warner, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, asked Trump s own CIA head and his new Director of National Intelligence whether they believed that Russian intelligence agencies were responsible for the hacks and leaks that led to the investigation, both Mike Pompeo and Dan Coats agreed.Clapper told Burnett that Trump s demeanor during the January briefing has been completely different than his behavior since he was inaugurated, calling the earlier Trump  solicitous, courteous, [and] even complimentary  when he sat down with the agencies.Trump is getting more than a little nervous now, and this interview with James Clapper sheds light on his renewed efforts to brush aside the Russia investigation.Watch:Featured image via Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

WATCH: Bill Maher Discusses Trump’s Working Relationship With Schumer and Pelosi

Bill Maher recently used his HBO program, *Real Time*, to comment on President Donald Trump’s dealings with congressional Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi of California.

Maher suggested that Trump may feel more culturally familiar with Schumer and Pelosi than with some Republican leaders, pointing to their shared connections to major cities. Using the children’s story “The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse” to make his point, Maher described Schumer and Pelosi as “city mice” and said that Trump, as a longtime New Yorker, might relate more naturally to them.

Maher contrasted that relationship with Trump’s interactions with former House Speaker Paul Ryan of Wisconsin and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. In characteristic terms, he portrayed Ryan and McConnell as more socially and culturally conservative figures than Trump.

The comedian also discussed Vice President Mike Pence, whom he characterized as deeply religious and socially conservative. Maher contrasted Pence’s public image with Trump’s long-standing reputation as a New York businessman and celebrity.

Maher’s remarks came after Trump reached a bipartisan agreement with Schumer and Pelosi on a short-term government spending measure and other issues in 2017. The cooperation surprised some Republicans, particularly because Trump had frequently criticized Democratic leaders during the 2016 presidential campaign and had worked closely with Ryan and McConnell during the early months of his presidency.

The monologue also revisited Trump’s political history. Before becoming the Republican Party’s presidential nominee, Trump had been associated with the Democratic Party and had donated to candidates from both major parties. His adult children were registered Democrats during the 2016 New York Republican presidential primary, meaning they were unable to vote in that contest under the state’s rules.

Those facts have contributed to debate over the president’s political identity and the extent to which his positions have changed over time. Trump ultimately won the Republican nomination and the presidency with strong support from voters who favored his immigration, economic and cultural messages.

Maher’s comments were political satire rather than an independent assessment of Trump’s motives. The president’s cooperation with Schumer and Pelosi did not represent a formal change in party affiliation, and the two Democratic leaders continued to oppose Trump on many legislative and policy matters.

Trump Administration Plans Sunday Downtime for Obamacare Enrollment

The Trump administration has announced a schedule that will limit access to Healthcare.gov, the federal website created under the Affordable Care Act, during the 2017 open-enrollment period.

The Department of Health and Human Services said during a webinar with enrollment assisters that the website would be taken offline for maintenance for 12 hours on most Sundays during the enrollment season. The schedule was first reported by Kaiser Health News.

Websites periodically undergo maintenance, but the planned Sunday outages drew criticism because Sundays are a common time for people to handle insurance and other administrative tasks. HHS did not say that the downtime was intended to discourage enrollment, and the department characterized it as part of its operations schedule.

The administration had already announced several changes to the enrollment process. The federal open-enrollment period was shortened to six weeks, from November 1 through December 15, compared with the longer period used in previous years. HHS also reduced funding for advertising and outreach campaigns and cut grants for “navigators,” organizations that help consumers compare plans and complete applications.

The changes could make it more difficult for some consumers to learn about their options or obtain assistance, particularly those who have limited time during the workweek. Supporters of the shorter enrollment period and reduced spending have said the changes will lower costs and make the program more efficient.

The Affordable Care Act remained in effect, and consumers could continue to enroll through Healthcare.gov or state-run marketplaces. The administration’s decisions were expected to shape participation in the program, even as congressional Republicans continued debating broader changes to the health-care law.

Senator John McCain announced that he would oppose the Graham-Cassidy health care proposal, breaking with fellow Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, one of the bill’s sponsors. title: Medicaid Directors Of All 50 States Issue Joint Statement Slamming GOP Health Bill
text: On Thursday, the National Association of Medicaid Directors sent Congress a devastating letter about their planned overhaul of American healthcare. The NAMD is an organization comprised of quite literally every single Medicaid chief in the country, and any statement issued by the entirety of its body is a rare thing. Ironically, the Trump era seems to have ushered in more than one situation in which there is unanimity in opposition to his policies and positions.Medicaid directors are appointed by state governors, which means that the office is filled by partisan picks. Fully 34 of the 50 states, in fact, have Republican governors, so the joint statement isn t just bipartisan   it s almost hyper-partisan.That makes this sharp criticism of the Graham-Cassidy bill even more poignant:BREAKING: The bipartisan Medicaid Directors from all 50 states just issued this negative statement about Graham-Cassidy.Big. Very unusual. pic.twitter.com/ZtqaAI8hg1  Andy Slavitt (@ASlavitt) September 22, 2017That tweet is clickable, and each image in the tweet is clickable, but here are the important parts, in case you don t feel like popping over to Twitter. The bill makes some major changes to Medicaid funding, including a massive transfer of funds from  blue  states to  red  states, and a transition to  block grants  that do not account for increased membership in Medicaid programs. That is to say, states would get the same fixed amount of money no matter how many people signed up, making states with high membership among those with the lowest per-patient allowance. Taken together, the per-capita caps and the envisioned block grant would constitute the largest intergovernmental transfer of financial risk from the federal government to the states in our country s history. The scope of this work, and the resources required to support state planning and implementation activities, cannot be overstated. States will need to develop overall strategies, invest in infrastructure development, systems changes, provider and managed care plan contracting, and perform a host of other activities. The vast majority of states will not be able to do so within the two-year timeframe envisioned here, especially considering the apparent lack of federal funding in the bill to support these critical activities. With only a few legislative days left for the entire process to conclude, there clearly is not sufficient time for policymakers, Governors, Medicaid Directors, or other critical stakeholders to engage in the thoughtful deliberation necessary to ensure successful long-term reforms. The mostly-Republican board of Medicaid Directors also took the GOP to task for trying to pass this bill before getting a score from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office. Usually, that s the minimum a bill must have to even be considered for a vote. But Republicans are attempting to pass this bill before the end of the month, since that s the cutoff for them to do so with a simple majority. The Senate parliamentarian ruled that budget reconciliation, the process by which bills can be passed with a simple majority, expires at the end of Fiscal Year 2017. After September, votes will once again be subject to filibusters, meaning Republicans will need to muster 60 votes for anything they want to pass, unless they take Donald Trump s advice and invoke the  nuclear option  in the Senate.That s unlikely to happen, and Republicans are more desperate than ever for a win in Congress. That makes Graham-Cassidy a real danger to the future of American healthcare, despite this damning letter from the NAMD, and despite the massive opposition to the bill by every medical association, most states, nearly all consumers, and even some Republicans.Buckle up, my friends. This could get ugly.Featured image via Alex Wong/Getty Images

Medicaid Directors Raise Concerns About GOP Health Bill

On Thursday, the National Association of Medicaid Directors sent Congress a letter expressing concerns about the proposed overhaul of Medicaid in the Graham-Cassidy health bill. The association represents state Medicaid agencies, but the letter should not be characterized as a formal statement by every Medicaid director in the country.

Medicaid directors are generally appointed by state governors, and the officials who lead the programs serve under administrations from both political parties. The association’s concerns therefore focused on the bill’s potential effects on state budgets and program administration rather than on a partisan position.

The criticism came as lawmakers considered the proposal:

“Medicaid Directors from all 50 states just issued this negative statement about Graham-Cassidy,” former Obama administration health official Andy Slavitt wrote on Twitter. The wording of the tweet described the letter more broadly than the association’s formal role and membership.

In its letter, NAMD warned that the bill would make major changes to Medicaid financing. The proposal included per-capita limits on federal Medicaid funding and an option for states to use block grants. Under those arrangements, federal support would be determined through fixed formulas rather than rising automatically with enrollment or medical costs.

The association said the changes could shift significant financial responsibility from the federal government to the states. It also warned that states with growing Medicaid enrollment or higher health-care costs could face difficult budget decisions if federal funding did not keep pace.

“The scope of this work, and the resources required to support state planning and implementation activities, cannot be overstated,” the letter said. States, it added, would need to develop strategies, make infrastructure and systems changes, adjust provider and managed-care contracts, and undertake other administrative work.

NAMD also questioned whether states could complete those tasks within the proposed two-year implementation period. The organization said many states would have difficulty doing so, particularly if the legislation did not provide sufficient federal support for the planning and technical changes involved.

“With only a few legislative days left for the entire process to conclude,” the letter said, “there clearly is not sufficient time for policymakers, Governors, Medicaid Directors, or other critical stakeholders to engage in the thoughtful deliberation necessary to ensure successful long-term reforms.”

The letter came as Senate Republicans worked to advance the bill through the budget-reconciliation process. That procedure can allow certain legislation to pass the Senate with a simple majority, rather than the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster. The timetable was tied to the end of the 2017 fiscal year, creating pressure to act before September 30.

At the time, the Congressional Budget Office had not completed a full analysis of Graham-Cassidy. That absence drew criticism from opponents, who argued that lawmakers and the public should have access to an independent estimate of the bill’s effects before a vote.

The proposal faced opposition from health-care organizations, state officials and some Republican senators. Critics said its changes to Medicaid and the individual insurance market could increase uncertainty for states and for people who relied on coverage under the Affordable Care Act.

NAMD’s letter did not by itself determine the bill’s prospects in Congress, but it underscored the administrative and financial concerns state Medicaid agencies said they would face if the proposal became law.

title: Trump’s HHS Sec. Latest To Be Caught Spending HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS Of Tax Dollars On Luxuries
text: What is it with the Trump administration and spending tax dollars on things that are literal luxuries? Tom Price, Secretary of Health and Human Services, just got busted spending taxpayer dollars traveling on private planes   something to the tune of $300,000 already. Private travel on the taxpayers  dime is apparently the norm for Price   he s been doing this since he took the helm over at HHS.According to a report from Politico, Kathleen Sebelius and Sylvia Burwell, both of whom headed up HHS under Obama, tended to travel on commercial airlines when flying domestically. Price s officials claim that he only uses private jets when commercial travel isn t feasible, but most of these flights are between big U.S. cities where many airlines regularly fly. For instance, he took a private jet from Washington, D.C., to Nashville, but there are four nonstop flights per day between those two cities, with fares as low as $202.Even if he insisted on flying first class, that flight would have been considerably cheaper with average ticket prices around $1,000. His private jet from D.C. to Nashville cost $17,760.Most of his flights are to areas where he speaks about the opioid epidemic, and these engagements are planned well in advance so he could book his flights well in advance, too. It s not like most of his travel is at the last minute due to the nature of his job, or his  demanding schedule,  which is another excuse HHS officials are using.His spokespeople also claimed that he was taking private jets because he was just so amazingly busy directing recovery efforts in the hurricane-ravaged areas of Texas and Florida. However, Politico says that at least 17 of these private flights happened before Hurricane Harvey. There s no way he could possibly have been needed for recovery efforts for a hurricane that hadn t happened yet.One of those flights was from San Diego to the Aspen Ideas Festival in June. That s a swanky festival in the swanky resort town of Aspen, CO, and he spent taxpayer dollars on that. While it s true that he was speaking during a panel there, he arrived 19 hours before that panel, so it s really hard for him to claim that he had to book a private jet because this was too last minute. An average of 26 percent of the flights that go into Aspen are scheduled commercial   it s not like it s impossible to fly commercial into Aspen-Pitkin. Price s plane could have cost us as much as $7,100. Commercial flights cost well under half that.This administration is all about wasting taxpayer dollars, but cutting needed spending, while pretending to stand for regular Americans. It s absolutely sickening.Featured image via Chris Kleponis   Pool/Getty Images

Trump’s HHS Secretary Faces Scrutiny Over Use of Private Charter Flights

Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price came under scrutiny in 2017 over the department’s use of private charter aircraft for his official travel. A report by Politico said the flights had cost taxpayers hundreds of thousands of dollars, prompting questions about whether commercial service could have been used for some trips.

HHS officials said Price used charter aircraft when commercial travel was unavailable, impractical or incompatible with his schedule. However, several flights reportedly connected major U.S. cities served by regular airlines. For example, Politico reported that a charter flight from Washington, D.C., to Nashville cost substantially more than available commercial tickets.

The department said Price’s schedule included appearances related to the opioid epidemic and other public-health issues. Officials also cited his travel to areas affected by hurricanes in Texas and Florida as a reason for using charter aircraft. But the report noted that many of the flights occurred before Hurricane Harvey, raising questions about whether that explanation applied to all of the travel.

One trip took Price from San Diego to Colorado for the Aspen Ideas Festival, where he was scheduled to participate in a panel. The report questioned whether a private aircraft was necessary because he arrived well before the event and commercial flights to the area were available, although less frequently than service to larger airports.

The spending prompted criticism from lawmakers and government-watchdog groups, who said officials should use the least expensive practical form of transportation. Price said he had not personally approved the charter arrangements and offered to reimburse the government for the cost of his seat. President Donald Trump later called for Price to repay taxpayers for the expenses.

The controversy added to broader debate over travel and spending practices in the Trump administration. Price resigned as health secretary in September 2017, after the private-flight disclosures and other concerns about his use of government-funded travel.

Trump Judicial Nominee Faced Criticism Over Remarks About Transgender Students and Conversion Therapy

Donald Trump’s nominee for a federal judgeship in Texas faced criticism from LGBT rights organizations over past remarks concerning transgender students, same-sex marriage and so-called conversion therapy.

Jeff Mateer, who was serving as first assistant attorney general of Texas and had previously been general counsel of the First Liberty Institute, was nominated to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas in 2017.

Conversion therapy, which purports to change a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity, is opposed by major medical and mental-health organizations. A number of states and local governments have restricted the practice, particularly for minors.

In a May 2015 speech titled “The Church and Homosexuality,” Mateer discussed a Colorado lawsuit involving a transgender girl whose parents challenged a school’s decision to prevent her from using the girls’ restroom. According to a video of the speech, Mateer questioned whether a first-grade child could understand their gender identity.

“I submit to you, a parent of three children who are now young adults, a first grader really knows what their sexual identity?” Mateer said.

He also described the case in religious terms, saying, “It just really shows you how Satan’s plan is working and the destruction that’s going on.”

The remarks drew criticism from advocates who said they reflected hostility toward transgender children. At the time, policies governing restroom access for transgender students were being contested in courts and debated by state legislatures across the country.

In the same speech, Mateer criticized the Supreme Court’s decision recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. He speculated that the ruling could lead to broader forms of marriage, including marriages involving more than two people.

“I submit to you that there’ll be no line there,” Mateer said, according to the video. “Why couldn’t four people want to get married? Why not one man and three women? Or three women and one man?”

Mateer also referred to the term “throuple,” describing it as three people entering a relationship, and argued that the decision could contribute to what he viewed as social and religious disorder.

Later in 2015, at a conference hosted by pastor Kevin Swanson, Mateer criticized state and local restrictions on conversion therapy. He said such laws represented government involvement in religious and personal matters.

“The issue is always, it’s same sex,” Mateer said, according to CNN’s report on his remarks. “And if you’re giving conversion therapy, that’s been outlawed in at least two states and then in some local areas. So they’re invading that area.”

The comments became a focus of opposition to his nomination. Critics argued that his statements raised questions about whether he could fairly handle cases involving LGBT people and other civil-rights issues. Supporters portrayed him as a conservative Christian attorney with experience in constitutional and religious-liberty law.

Mateer’s nomination did not receive Senate confirmation. He later withdrew from consideration for the federal judgeship.

Global Survey Challenges Trump’s Claim That World Leaders Agreed With His U.N. Speech

If world leaders agreed with Donald Trump’s address to the United Nations General Assembly, public-opinion surveys suggest that support would not necessarily be shared by their citizens. A 2017 Pew Research Center survey found that confidence in Trump was generally low across the countries surveyed, although views varied and some nations expressed more favorable opinions than others.

During his speech to the United Nations this week, Trump criticized the organization as a mismanaged bureaucracy and warned that the United States might reconsider its financial and military support. He also threatened North Korea with destruction, condemned the Iran nuclear agreement and defended his administration’s decision to withdraw from the Paris climate accord.

Afterward, Trump said on Twitter that the leaders he met had agreed with much or all of his remarks.

“A great and important day at the United Nations. Met with leaders of many nations who agree with much (or all) of what I stated in my speech!” Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) September 20, 2017

There is no public evidence showing that the world leaders attending the meetings unanimously supported Trump’s positions. Diplomatic meetings and applause at the General Assembly do not provide a reliable measure of international approval, and reactions to his speech varied.

The Pew survey, conducted earlier this year, found that confidence in Trump was substantially lower in many countries than confidence in President Barack Obama during the final years of Obama’s presidency. The survey measured whether respondents had confidence in the U.S. president to do the right thing regarding world affairs; it did not determine whether governments agreed with every part of Trump’s speech.

Confidence was particularly low in several U.S. allied countries. In South Korea, for example, 17 percent of respondents said they had confidence in Trump, compared with 88 percent who expressed confidence in Obama in a comparable 2015 survey. Mexico also recorded a sharp decline in confidence after Trump took office.

The survey did not show that only two nations viewed Trump favorably. Rather, it found that opinions differed by country and by question. Some respondents in Israel and Russia expressed relatively high confidence in Trump, while other countries surveyed reported much lower levels. Favorability toward the United States also did not always move in tandem with views of the president.

Public opposition to several of Trump’s major policies was also evident in international polling. The Pew findings showed broad disagreement with some elements of his approach to climate change, trade and immigration, although the level of support or opposition varied from country to country. Such surveys measure public opinion, not the official positions of governments represented at the United Nations.

Trump’s address reflected his administration’s “America First” approach and marked a sharp break from the language traditionally used by many U.S. presidents at the General Assembly. His threats against North Korea and criticism of the Iran agreement drew international attention, while allies have expressed concern about the future of U.S. commitments on climate policy and trade.

The available evidence therefore supports a more limited conclusion than Trump’s claim. Some leaders may have agreed with portions of his speech, but international polling shows that confidence in the president was generally weak in many countries and that his policies were not broadly popular among foreign publics.

The survey results also illustrate the difference between diplomatic courtesy and genuine political support. Meetings, statements and applause can signal engagement, but they cannot establish that world leaders or their citizens agreed with “much or all” of what Trump said.

U.S. Senate Advances Defense Bill Authorizing Nearly $700 Billion in Spending

The Senate approved a major defense policy bill in September 2017 that would authorize roughly $692 billion for national defense in fiscal year 2018. The measure represented a substantial increase over the previous year’s authorization and exceeded the spending limits established under the 2011 Budget Control Act.

The National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, sets policy and authorizes spending but does not itself provide the money. Congress must approve separate appropriations legislation, and lawmakers later changed the statutory budget caps to accommodate higher defense and domestic spending.

Republicans who controlled the Senate supported the increase, while critics argued that Congress should more closely examine the military’s requirements and the effect of additional defense spending on the federal deficit. Supporters said the increase was necessary to address what they described as increasingly complex national-security challenges.

The bill also authorized the purchase of 94 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets made by Lockheed Martin. That was more than the number included in the administration’s request and more than the House version of the legislation. The additional aircraft became part of broader congressional efforts to expand military procurement.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman John McCain, an Arizona Republican, defended the committee’s decision during floor debate, saying that national-security needs should guide budget decisions. “The threats to our national security have not been more complex, severe, or daunting at any time in the past seven decades,” McCain said. He argued that Congress should provide the armed forces with the resources needed to respond to those threats.

Critics countered that the bill authorized spending above the limits set by the 2011 law and that Congress had not yet identified a long-term way to pay for the increase. Because the NDAA was an authorization measure, however, its passage did not by itself make the spending available or constitute a violation of the budget law. Congress could—and later did—change the spending limits through subsequent legislation.

The debate also renewed questions about the size and priorities of the U.S. defense budget. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the United States accounted for about 36 percent of global military spending in 2016, more than any other country. U.S. military spending was several times higher than China’s and substantially higher than Russia’s, although estimates vary depending on how countries’ defense expenditures are measured.

Some lawmakers and advocacy groups argued that a portion of the proposed increase could instead be directed toward domestic priorities, including higher education, health care, infrastructure, or deficit reduction. Estimates for such proposals vary, and comparisons between defense authorizations and social programs do not account for differences in funding structures or eligibility.

The legislation passed the Senate by a vote of 89 to 8. Senators voting against it were Bernie Sanders, Jeff Merkley, Bob Corker, Kirsten Gillibrand, Patrick Leahy, Mike Lee, Rand Paul, and Ron Wyden. The bill was part of the annual congressional process for setting defense policy and funding priorities, rather than a final determination of the military’s total spending for the year.

Study Found Refugees Had a Positive Fiscal Impact, but Trump Administration Did Not Release It

A draft federal study found that refugees generated more in government revenue than they received in public assistance over a 10-year period, The New York Times reported. The report, prepared for the Department of Health and Human Services, was completed as the Trump administration considered reducing the number of refugees admitted to the United States.

According to the draft, refugees contributed an estimated $269.1 billion in federal, state and local taxes between 2005 and 2014. The report estimated that refugees incurred about $206.5 billion in government costs during the same period, resulting in a net fiscal contribution of roughly $62.7 billion.

The New York Times reported that the draft contradicted arguments from some administration officials and refugee-policy opponents who said the program placed a significant burden on taxpayers. The issue was being debated within the administration as President Donald Trump prepared to set the annual refugee admissions ceiling.

The study did not conclude that every refugee or refugee household produced a positive fiscal balance. It examined the estimated economic costs and contributions of refugees as a group, and its findings depended on the methods and assumptions used by the researchers. Refugees may initially rely on public assistance while also contributing to the economy through employment, taxes and other economic activity.

The administration did not publicly release the draft report. Officials questioned its methodology and argued that the analysis did not provide a complete basis for evaluating refugee policy. A separate assessment requested by the White House focused more heavily on the costs of refugee resettlement and benefits received through federal programs.

The existence of the draft prompted debate over whether its findings had been excluded from the administration’s policy discussions. Reports at the time said officials involved in refugee policy had differing views about which costs and benefits should be included in an official analysis.

The study’s findings did not by themselves resolve broader disputes over refugee admissions, including questions about national security, humanitarian obligations and the capacity of federal, state and local governments to provide assistance. They did, however, challenge the claim that refugees necessarily impose a net fiscal cost on the United States.

Republican Senate Candidate Roy Moore Blames Decline of Religion for Violence

Republican Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore has drawn criticism after blaming the country’s social problems, including shootings and killings, on what he described as the removal of God and prayer from public life.

“You wonder why we’re having shootings, and killings here in 2017?” Moore said in a speech reported at the time. “Because we’ve asked for it. We’ve taken God out of everything. We’ve taken prayer out of school, we’ve taken prayer out of council meetings.”

Moore’s remarks were part of a broader argument that the United States had moved away from religious values in public institutions. He did not, in the quoted statement, say that people who do not believe in God should be shot, but critics said his comments unfairly blamed secular Americans and promoted a divisive view of the role of religion in government.

The controversy came during Moore’s campaign for Alabama’s Republican nomination for the U.S. Senate. Moore had previously served as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court and had been removed from that position twice. In 2003, he was removed after refusing to comply with a federal order involving a Ten Commandments monument in the state courthouse. In 2016, he was suspended and later resigned after directing probate judges to refuse to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples despite federal court rulings.

Moore’s supporters described him as a defender of religious liberty and traditional values, while opponents argued that his views threatened the separation of church and state. The debate over his comments reflected a larger national dispute over prayer in public institutions, religious expression by public officials and the constitutional limits on government promotion of religion.

Moore ultimately won the Republican nomination and advanced to the general election, where he faced Democrat Doug Jones. His statements continued to generate criticism from political opponents and some members of his own party.

California Assembly Advances Bill Requiring Presidential Candidates to Release Tax Returns

California lawmakers advanced legislation in 2019 that would have required presidential candidates to disclose five years of federal tax returns before appearing on the state’s primary-election ballot.

The Presidential Tax Transparency and Accountability Act, Senate Bill 27, passed the state Assembly and returned to the Senate before being sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom. The measure was backed by Democratic lawmakers who argued that tax-return disclosure would provide voters with additional information about candidates’ finances and potential conflicts of interest.

The bill targeted a longstanding political tradition rather than an existing legal requirement. President Donald Trump had declined to publicly release his tax returns, breaking with presidential candidates who had voluntarily disclosed them for decades.

Newsom signed SB 27 into law in July 2019. The law required presidential candidates to submit at least five years of tax returns to the California secretary of state in order to qualify for the state’s primary ballot.

However, the law did not remain in effect. In November 2019, the California Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the requirement violated the state Constitution because the Legislature could not add qualifications for presidential candidates beyond those established by the U.S. Constitution. The court therefore prevented the law from being enforced.

The decision meant that California could not use the tax-return requirement to keep Trump or any other presidential candidate off the 2020 ballot. Trump ultimately appeared on California’s presidential primary ballot, although he did not win the state.

WATCH: Trump Mentions Trump World Tower During Remarks at United Nations Headquarters

Donald Trump referred to one of his New York real-estate projects at the beginning of remarks at United Nations headquarters on Monday.

Trump World Tower is a residential skyscraper located across the street from the United Nations complex, where the General Assembly was meeting that week. In opening remarks, Trump said the presence of the United Nations had contributed to the success of the project.

“Thank you very much. Thank you. I actually saw great potential right across the street, to be honest with you,” Trump said. “And it was only for the reason that the United Nations was here that that turned out to be such a successful project.”

Trump also thanked then-U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley for her introduction and for advocating for American interests internationally.

ABC News Politics shared video of the remarks on Twitter.

Pres. Trump on luxury residential property by UN: “United Nations being there was reason that that turned out to be such a successful project.”  
— ABC News Politics (@ABCPolitics), September 18, 2017

The reference drew attention because Trump was speaking to diplomats and representatives gathered at the United Nations, where his broader remarks were expected to focus on international issues.

Trump World Tower, completed in the late 1990s, had been a controversial development in Manhattan. The building’s construction prompted debate over its effect on views of the East River and its proximity to the United Nations complex.

Trump’s comments highlighted his long-standing connection to New York real estate, even as he addressed a diplomatic audience. The brief reference to the building became one of the more notable moments from the opening of his remarks.

title: Your Local News Station Might Be Turning Into A Pro-Trump Propaganda Network Right Before Your Eyes
text: When Americans think about state-run television, we don t expect it to happen here. When we turn on the local news at night, we expect straight news, a rundown of the facts regarding local and national events. If we want opinion shows, we know where to go. If you re a conservative, there s a plethora of shows to watch on Fox News that offer soothing confirmation bias, such as Tucker Carlson Tonight, Hannity, or Fox and Friends. If you re a liberal, you can get the same on your side of the aisle on MSNBC with The Last Word with Lawrence O Donnell, The Rachel Maddow Show, or All In with Chris Hayes (though, to be fair, while they are opinion shows, the latter network doesn t lie, while Fox does). However, all of that could be changing.It turns out that many of America s local stations are owned by a company called Sinclair Broadcasting. That company happens to be pro-Trump. They are now going to have 174 stations around the country that will now be airing pro-Trump items on a daily basis, and those shows will be broadcast to the unsuspecting viewing public as actual news. According to Politicus USA, those shows will consist of the following:  The Terrorism Alert Desk, advertised as a daily news update about terrorist activity.  News pieces from Epshteyn, Sinclair s chief political analyst.  A clearly labeled opinion show featuring Mark Hyman, a former vice president of the company.This is especially dangerous, because Americans do not expect to be forced to watch propaganda mixed in with their news. They just want the truth, or shows that are clear opinion. That is not what this is, though. This is nothing more than the kind of stuff Kim Jung Un s regime is feeding his people in order to brainwash them. This is the kind of thing we see in authoritarian states, and it is incredibly dangerous for democracy.People keep saying not to compare Trump to a dictator, but it is becoming more and more clear that this is exactly what he is aiming to be   and he has plenty of help from his blind followers in high places.In short, beware, folks, because you re about to get a big dose of America s very own state-run propaganda.Featured image via William Thomas Cain/Getty Images

John McCain Urges Bipartisan Approach to Health Care Legislation

Sen. John McCain criticized Republican efforts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, calling for a bipartisan process rather than another bill advanced solely by one party.

McCain, an Arizona Republican who had opposed earlier GOP repeal efforts, discussed the issue in an interview with John Dickerson on CBS’s *Face the Nation*. He said he favored negotiations involving congressional leaders from both parties and President Donald Trump.

Asked about Trump’s outreach to Democrats, McCain said he was interested in a bipartisan agreement but argued that any proposal should be developed jointly by the administration and congressional leaders.

“I’m interested in that, of course,” McCain said. “This president is always full of surprises. But the problem is, John, it shouldn’t be bipartisanship. It should be both Republican, Democrat and the president.”

McCain referred to Trump’s discussions with Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi and said the president should work with both parties to develop legislation addressing problems with the health care system.

“What should take place is the three of them, both leaders, Republican and Democrat, and the president sit down and say, okay, we’ve got a problem here. We need to fix it,” McCain said.

He also criticized the way the Affordable Care Act had originally been enacted, saying it passed with Democratic votes alone. McCain argued that Republicans should not respond by moving their own proposal through Congress without broader consultation.

“That’s not the way to do it,” he said. “We’ve got to go back, if I could just say again, the way to do this is have a bill, put it through the committee. We have Patty Murray and Lamar Alexander doing fine, bring it to the floor. Have debate, have amendments.”

Murray, a Democratic senator, and Alexander, a Republican senator, were leading Senate health committee discussions at the time. McCain cited the Senate Armed Services Committee’s bipartisan work as an example of how legislation could be developed.

McCain’s comments reflected his repeated calls for a more open legislative process and bipartisan negotiations on health care. His position posed a challenge to Republican leaders, who had been seeking support for legislation to repeal or substantially change the Affordable Care Act.

The Senate had already rejected earlier Republican repeal proposals, and lawmakers continued to debate whether to replace the law, revise it or make narrower changes to stabilize the insurance market.

We have birthers on the federal bench. That s all their fault.There are no good people who are Trump voters. It s time we recognized a hard truth: There s no such thing as a good person who supports Donald Trump. Stop excusing them and start shaming them. **Debate Continues Over How to Characterize Trump Supporters**

For nearly two years, commentators have debated whether all voters who supported Donald Trump should be described as racist, misogynistic, or otherwise bigoted. The answer is not straightforward. Some people who voted for Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012 later supported Trump, while others backed Trump because of his positions on immigration, the economy, the courts, or opposition to the Democratic Party. Voting records alone do not establish every individual’s personal beliefs or motivations.

At the same time, Trump’s campaign included statements and proposals that drew widespread criticism. He was recorded in an Access Hollywood video making vulgar comments about women, called for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States, described some Mexican immigrants as criminals and rapists, and repeatedly promoted false claims questioning whether Obama was born in the United States. His campaign also proposed large-scale deportations and emphasized stricter immigration enforcement.

Those positions, along with his treatment of political opponents and various minority groups, led civil rights organizations and other critics to warn that a Trump presidency could harm immigrants, Muslims, women, racial minorities, and LGBTQ Americans. Voters who supported him had to weigh those concerns against their own priorities, including immigration, judicial appointments, economic policy, national security, and dissatisfaction with established political leaders.

That does not mean all Trump voters shared the same views. Some explicitly endorsed his rhetoric, while others said they considered him preferable to Hillary Clinton despite objections to his conduct and statements. Still others viewed their vote as a rejection of the political establishment rather than an endorsement of every position he had taken. Political researchers have repeatedly found that voters are motivated by a combination of factors, making broad judgments about their character difficult to substantiate.

Trump’s election also prompted serious debate about the consequences of his administration. His appointments and policies drew praise from conservatives and condemnation from liberals and civil rights groups. Jeff Sessions, chosen as attorney general, had faced controversy during his 1986 judicial nomination over allegations of racially insensitive remarks, which he denied. His nomination to the federal bench was withdrawn before he was later elected to the Senate. The administration also faced criticism over its response to white nationalist violence and other extremist movements.

These disputes have intensified arguments over whether Trump supporters should be held responsible for actions taken by the president and his administration. Critics say voters cannot separate their decision from the effects of the policies they helped authorize. Supporters respond that participating in an election does not indicate agreement with every statement or action by a candidate.

The continuing disagreement reflects a broader divide in American politics. It is possible to condemn Trump’s rhetoric and policies without asserting that every person who voted for him has identical beliefs or motives. Likewise, recognizing differences among his supporters does not require minimizing the concerns raised by his campaign statements or administration.

The challenge for political debate is to address those policies and their effects accurately, without turning assumptions about millions of voters into established facts.
