The couple has decided to leave their long-time church, and they did so with a statement of their own: We feel this decision is absolutely disgraceful and is a disgrace to you and all the church, especially when we have been loyal and valued members of this congregation for 10 years. You were made aware from the beginning of our proceedings that we had gay friends and also that people in our wedding party were gay. How could you assume that we would abandon them or degrade them with regards to same-sex marriage? A couple in Australia have left their church after the minister told them he would no longer perform their wedding ceremony or allow it to take place at the church, reportedly because of the bride’s public support for same-sex marriage.

The couple, who have not been identified, were called to a private meeting with Minister Steven North of Ebenezer St. John’s Presbyterian Church. Australia was at the time conducting a national postal survey on whether same-sex couples should be allowed to marry, with the result intended to inform Parliament’s consideration of the issue.

The bride had expressed support for marriage equality on Facebook, writing that she understood not everyone would agree with her position but that it reflected her beliefs and did not affect her relationship with her partner.

North later sent the couple a letter explaining his decision. “This conflict of views has practical consequences in relation to your upcoming wedding,” North wrote.

The minister’s decision appears to have been based on his interpretation of church teaching and his own position on same-sex marriage. The couple disputed that their support for marriage equality was inconsistent with their commitment to one another or their church community.

In a statement, the couple said they considered the decision deeply disappointing, particularly after being members of the congregation for about a decade. They also said the church had known from the beginning that they had gay friends and that members of their wedding party were gay.

“How could you assume that we would abandon them or degrade them with regards to same-sex marriage?” they wrote.

The couple decided to leave the church and make alternative arrangements for their wedding. Their account illustrates the tensions that emerged within some religious communities during Australia’s debate over marriage equality, as individuals and congregations differed over how their beliefs should shape their response to the proposed legal change.

Here s Trump s weak, spineless statement: We condemn the recent violence in Charlottesville and oppose hatred, bigotry, and racism in all forms. California Assembly Advances Resolution Urging Congress to Censure Trump Over Charlottesville Response

About a month after a violent white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, California lawmakers advanced a resolution criticizing President Donald Trump’s response and urging Congress to censure him.

The resolution, approved by the California Assembly, condemned Trump’s comments about the violence and called on Congress to formally rebuke the president. Assemblyman Tony Thurmond, who supported the measure, said the president should not use language that could legitimize extremist groups promoting hate.

Trump initially said that “many sides” were responsible for the violence, which left counterprotester Heather Heyer dead and injured dozens of others. Two days later, he specifically condemned white supremacists, neo-Nazis and the Ku Klux Klan. He then returned to his earlier position during an Aug. 15 news conference, saying there were also “very fine people” among those protesting the removal of a Confederate statue and that “you had some very bad people in that group,” as well as people on the other side.

The California resolution does not itself censure Trump. Instead, it calls on Congress to take that action. Censure is a formal expression of disapproval and does not remove a president from office. Congressional Republicans did not indicate that they planned to pursue such a measure.

The Assembly action came amid continuing criticism of Trump’s handling of the Charlottesville rally. In a statement issued after the violence, Trump said the country must condemn “hatred, bigotry and violence on many sides.” He later issued a more direct statement, saying racism was evil and identifying the Ku Klux Klan, neo-Nazis and white supremacists as criminals and thugs.

The California resolution reflects the broader political debate over whether Trump’s comments adequately addressed the role of white nationalist groups in the violence. Supporters said the president should have condemned those groups immediately and unequivocally. Opponents argued that the Legislature was overstepping its role and that Trump had already denounced racism and extremist organizations.

The measure was part of a series of responses from state and local officials following the Charlottesville rally. It did not require action by California’s governor and did not compel Congress to take up a censure resolution.

Juggalos, or fans of the band Insane Clown Posse, are in D.C. to protest what they call an unfair label from the FBI and Department of Justice classifying them as a  loosely organized hybrid gang. It s clear which group has the more ardent supporters, and it isn t the one I m calling (for the purposes of this piece)  the Trumpettes. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)That s the Juggalos showing up. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)You ll note from the captions that these two photos are both by Getty photographer Tasos Katopodis. WASHINGTON, DC — SEPTEMBER 16: People gather during the “Mother of All Rallies” on the National Mall on September 16, 2017, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

“The Juggalos outnumber the white supremacists at the Lincoln Memorial today,” writer Mikel Jollett posted on Twitter.

Other posts treated the two events as an unexpected contrast, with references to a hypothetical “Battle of Juggalos vs. Trump supporters.” The Juggalo March also included participants describing themselves as antifascists, according to video and photographs shared online.

The events remained separate, reflecting the different concerns of the groups involved: one focused on support for Trump and conservative politics, and the other on the FBI’s treatment of Juggalo fans.

rewritten_article_text:
What Companies May Do With Money Saved Under Trump’s Proposed Tax Break

Trump, like George W. Bush before him, argued that a tax holiday on repatriated profits would encourage major corporations holding money overseas to bring it back to the United States and invest in the economy. Supporters said the policy could increase domestic investment and potentially create jobs. Critics countered that companies may use the savings in ways that do not directly increase hiring or construction, particularly if consumer demand remains weak.

A survey conducted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch of more than 300 companies reportedly asked executives how they would use money brought back from overseas. The leading responses included paying down debt and buying back company shares.

Stock buybacks have become a central point of criticism surrounding repatriation holidays. When a company buys its own shares, the reduced number of shares outstanding can increase earnings per share and may support the stock price. Buybacks can benefit shareholders and executives whose compensation is tied to share performance, although they do not necessarily lead to new factories, stores or jobs.

The United States adopted a similar repatriation tax holiday in 2004, allowing companies to bring certain foreign earnings home at a substantially reduced tax rate. Companies repatriated roughly $300 billion under the measure. Subsequent analyses found that much of the money was returned to shareholders through buybacks and dividends rather than being used for increased domestic investment. The policy’s effect on hiring and broader economic growth has remained disputed.

Some companies that repatriated money during that period also reduced their workforces, but that does not establish that the tax holiday caused those layoffs. Corporate decisions about employment and investment are influenced by many factors, including demand, technology and industry conditions.

The same questions apply to any future tax break for repatriated profits. Companies could use the money to invest, pay down debt, increase dividends, repurchase shares or hold cash. The policy’s overall economic impact would depend on how businesses used the funds and whether the resulting activity generated additional demand.

Critics argue that policies focused on corporate tax reductions may provide greater immediate benefits to shareholders than to workers, while supporters say lower taxes can improve incentives for investment. The debate over repatriation therefore centers on whether companies would use the savings to expand their operations or primarily strengthen their balance sheets and return money to investors.

Trump Claims He Has Made More Progress Against ISIS Than Obama, but Comparisons Are Difficult

After a terrorist attack in London, President Donald Trump used a social-media post to claim that his administration had made more progress against ISIS than the Obama administration.

The United States began conducting airstrikes against ISIS in Iraq in 2014 and expanded operations into Syria that year under President Barack Obama. Nine months into his own presidency, Trump argued that his administration had achieved more in the fight against the group.

“We have made more progress in the last nine months against ISIS than the Obama Administration has made in 8 years,” Trump wrote on Twitter on September 15, 2017. He added, “Must be proactive & nasty!”

The claim is difficult to verify and depends on how progress is measured. The Obama administration oversaw the formation of an international coalition against ISIS, thousands of airstrikes and military operations that helped drive the group from large parts of Iraq and Syria.

By the time Trump took office, ISIS had lost much of the territory it controlled in Iraq, although it still held important areas in Syria and the Iraqi city of Mosul. Coalition-backed forces captured Mosul in July 2017, and operations to retake the Syrian city of Raqqa were underway during Trump’s first year.

U.S. officials and independent monitoring groups have published differing estimates of ISIS casualties and civilian deaths. Those figures are affected by the difficulty of assessing losses in active war zones, and there is no single scorecard that establishes which president made greater progress.

The Trump administration changed some rules and authorities governing military operations and increased the pace of certain actions against ISIS. At the same time, civilian-casualty monitors reported deaths from coalition operations in Iraq and Syria, though determining responsibility for individual casualties can be difficult. The administration disputed some estimates and said it took steps to avoid civilian harm.

ISIS propaganda has used U.S. military operations and civilian deaths in its messaging, as terrorist groups have done throughout the conflict. But claims that any one administration’s policies directly caused changes in recruitment are difficult to substantiate.

In military terms, Trump inherited an ongoing campaign in which ISIS had already lost most of its territorial control but continued to operate as an insurgent and terrorist organization. His administration continued and intensified that campaign, while relying on plans and partnerships developed during the Obama years.

Trump could reasonably point to battlefield gains during his first nine months, including the capture of Mosul. But the broader reduction of ISIS’s territory and military strength had begun well before he took office.

The record therefore does not support a simple conclusion that either president alone defeated ISIS. The campaign was conducted over multiple years by U.S. and allied forces under both administrations, and the group remained a threat despite its territorial losses.

Trump’s DACA and border-wall comments draw criticism from some conservative supporters (TWEETS)

President Donald Trump’s comments about negotiations over the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program and the scope of border construction drew criticism from some of his conservative supporters on Thursday.

The reaction followed reports that Trump had discussed a potential legislative agreement on DACA with congressional Democrats. Trump also said that border-security efforts could include repairing or extending existing fencing, rather than immediately constructing a continuous new wall along the U.S.-Mexico border.

No agreement had been finalized, and the administration continued to say that any immigration legislation would need to include additional border security. Still, some Trump supporters argued on social media that compromise on DACA and changes to the president’s campaign language about the wall would represent a departure from his campaign promises.

Former Illinois Representative Joe Walsh was among those who criticized the president. Walsh, who had supported Trump during the 2016 campaign, questioned whether the reported discussions were consistent with the agenda voters had backed.

“Trump: We’re close to a deal on amnesty. The wall will come later. That’s not why we voted for you,” Walsh wrote on Twitter on September 14, 2017.

In subsequent posts, Walsh questioned whether Trump’s approach represented “the art of the deal” and urged the president to remember why he had been elected.

“We voted for #MAGA, not #DACA,” Walsh wrote in another post.

Walsh also objected to descriptions of the border project that emphasized existing barriers.

“He ran on: BUILD THE WALL!” Walsh wrote. “He didn’t run on: FIX UP SOME OF THE EXISTING FENCING!”

He added that Trump, rather than congressional Republicans, should be held responsible for the decisions made by the administration. Walsh said he had supported Trump despite doubts about the president’s conservative credentials because of his positions on the wall and immigration.

Conservative commentator Ann Coulter also used Twitter to express opposition to the possibility of an agreement protecting people covered by DACA. Coulter wrote that Trump was politically finished and said she would prefer Vice President Mike Pence if the administration did not build the wall.

Other posts circulated by Trump critics and supporters similarly accused the president of abandoning campaign commitments. Some used the hashtag “#AmnestyDon,” while others said they regretted having voted for or supported Trump.

The reactions reflected a broader dispute within the Republican Party over how to address people brought to the United States illegally as children. The Obama administration established DACA in 2012, allowing eligible recipients to seek temporary protection from deportation and work authorization. The Trump administration announced on September 5, 2017, that it would end the program after a six-month transition period unless Congress acted.

Trump’s comments came after a dinner meeting with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi. The lawmakers said the discussion included DACA, border security and other issues. Trump later said that negotiations were continuing and that any agreement would need to be converted into legislation.

The president’s position created uncertainty among both supporters and opponents of DACA. Democrats and immigration advocates sought legal protections for DACA recipients, while some conservative lawmakers and activists insisted that any legislation also include stronger enforcement measures and funding for border infrastructure.

Trump had repeatedly promised during the 2016 campaign that the United States would build a wall along the southern border and that Mexico would pay for it. By 2017, the administration was pursuing funding and planning for border barriers, but much of the work involved replacing or reinforcing existing fencing. Congress had not provided all the funding required for the project, and the design and location of additional barriers remained under debate.

The tweets from Walsh, Coulter and other conservative commentators demonstrated dissatisfaction among some activists, but they did not establish how widely those views were held among Trump voters. The administration continued to negotiate with lawmakers, and no final DACA or border-wall agreement had been announced at the time.

Trump Criticizes Single-Payer Health Care Proposal, Says He Would Veto It

In a pair of tweets on Thursday, President Donald Trump criticized Senator Bernie Sanders’ proposal for a single-payer health care system and said he would veto such legislation if it reached his desk. Trump’s comments came as Republicans in Congress continued debating efforts to change the Affordable Care Act.

“Bernie Sanders is pushing hard for a single payer healthcare plan—a curse on the U.S. & its people,” Trump wrote. In a second tweet, he said he had told Republicans to approve health care legislation quickly, but added, “I will veto because I love our country & its people.”

Public opinion on the role of the federal government in health care has been divided. A Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier in 2017 found that about six-in-ten Americans believed the government was responsible for ensuring health coverage for all citizens. Support for a single-payer system was lower, with roughly one-third of respondents favoring the approach.

Sanders introduced a Medicare for All bill in the Senate in September 2017. The proposal called for a government-financed health care program that would eventually cover all Americans, replacing most private insurance for covered services. It was not expected to advance in the Republican-controlled Congress.

Universal coverage had long been viewed as a politically difficult proposal in the United States, including during the 2016 Democratic primary campaign. Hillary Clinton criticized Sanders’ approach during that contest, while Sanders continued to make single-payer health care a central part of his platform.

Following the 2016 election, several prominent Democratic senators joined Sanders in sponsoring the Medicare for All legislation. The original group of sponsors included Cory Booker, Tammy Baldwin, Richard Blumenthal, Kirsten Gillibrand, Kamala Harris, Martin Heinrich, Mazie Hirono, Tim Kaine, Patrick Leahy, Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, Brian Schatz, Jeanne Shaheen, Tom Udall, Elizabeth Warren and Sheldon Whitehouse.

The bill faced significant obstacles. Republicans held the presidency and majorities in both chambers of Congress, and the administration was supporting efforts to repeal or revise the Affordable Care Act rather than expand federal involvement in health insurance.

Trump’s statements therefore reflected his opposition to single-payer health care, but he was unlikely to face an immediate decision on whether to veto Sanders’ proposal. The measure would first have needed to pass both the Republican-led Senate and House, where it lacked sufficient support.

**Iowa Rep. Steve King Criticizes Trump’s Discussions With Democrats on DACA**

President Donald Trump’s discussions with congressional Democrats about the future of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program drew criticism from conservative lawmakers, including Iowa Republican Rep. Steve King.

In September 2017, Trump announced that his administration would end DACA, the Obama-era policy that allowed certain undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children to apply for temporary protection from deportation and work authorization. The Department of Homeland Security said the program would be wound down over six months, giving Congress time to consider legislation.

The announcement was welcomed by many immigration-restriction advocates and criticized by Democrats, immigrant-rights groups and some business leaders. DACA had provided protections to hundreds of thousands of people who met the program’s eligibility requirements.

The decision also left open the possibility of congressional action. Shortly afterward, Trump met with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi to discuss immigration legislation, border security and the status of DACA recipients.

After the meeting, the Democratic leaders said they had reached an understanding with Trump to pursue legislation protecting people covered by DACA while also considering additional border-security measures. They said a border wall was not part of the agreement. The White House later said no final deal had been reached and that any legislation would still need to be negotiated.

King objected to the prospect of granting legal status to DACA recipients. In a CNN interview, he warned that Republicans could face political consequences if the administration supported what he described as amnesty.

“The base will leave him,” King said, arguing that some of his constituents would expect Trump to maintain the immigration policies he had promoted during the campaign. King said he supported most of Trump’s agenda but opposed what he called the “amnesty piece” of any agreement.

King has long advocated stricter immigration enforcement and opposed legislation that would provide legal status or a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. He also criticized demonstrations by young immigrants seeking continued protection under DACA.

The policy applied to people who were brought to the United States as children and met requirements including age, education or military-service criteria, and limits on certain criminal convictions. DACA did not provide permanent legal status or citizenship, and recipients remained subject to changes in federal policy.

The debate over the program involved questions about executive authority, congressional responsibility and the treatment of people who had spent much of their lives in the United States. Supporters of DACA argued that recipients should not be punished for decisions made by their parents and that many had built families, careers and communities in the country.

Opponents, including King, said the program encouraged unlawful immigration and bypassed Congress’s authority to set immigration policy. The disagreement continued as lawmakers considered whether to replace DACA with legislation providing permanent protections, enforcement measures or both.

At the time of the meeting between Trump and Democratic leaders, no agreement had restored DACA or changed federal law. Any permanent resolution required action by Congress and the president.

rewritten_article_text:
The Trump administration’s Department of Education faced criticism over delays in processing student-loan forgiveness claims filed by borrowers who said they were defrauded by for-profit colleges. At the same time, the department was reviewing Obama-era rules intended to protect students and taxpayers from misconduct in the higher-education industry.

A delay in processing a claim does not necessarily mean that borrowers have been denied relief or required to continue payments permanently. However, advocates said that uncertainty could place financial pressure on students and families who took out loans based on schools’ representations about educational programs, career prospects, or job placement.

Corinthian Colleges and ITT Technical Institute, two large for-profit education companies, closed after facing financial and regulatory problems during the Obama administration. The Education Department approved hundreds of millions of dollars in loan relief for some former Corinthian students under the federal borrower-defense program. The process for reviewing additional claims continued after the change in administrations.

The Trump administration said it was examining whether some of the Obama-era regulations imposed excessive costs or applied standards unevenly to colleges. Critics, including student advocates and some lawmakers, argued that weakening those rules could make it more difficult for borrowers to obtain relief when schools misrepresented their programs or financial outcomes.

President Donald Trump’s former company also faced legal action over Trump University, a real-estate training program that was not an accredited university. In 2016, Trump agreed to pay $25 million to settle lawsuits brought by former students and the New York attorney general’s office; the settlement did not include an admission of wrongdoing.

For-profit colleges have faced scrutiny over high tuition, marketing claims, job-placement statistics, and the use of arbitration agreements that can limit students’ ability to pursue claims in court. The Education Department under Secretary Betsy DeVos said students should not be victims of fraud, while also arguing that some consumer-protection requirements needed to be reconsidered.

The debate over borrower-defense applications reflected a broader dispute about how the federal government should balance oversight of colleges, institutional access to federal aid, and protections for students who say they were misled. Student advocates urged the department to process claims promptly and provide relief when the evidence supported allegations of misconduct.

**Reports Examined Michael Flynn Jr.’s Russia Connections, but No Collusion Charge Was Filed**

Federal investigators examining Russian interference in the 2016 election looked at the activities and contacts of several people connected to the Trump campaign, including Michael G. Flynn, the son of former national security adviser Michael Flynn. However, there is no public evidence that Flynn Jr. was charged with colluding with Russia or that prosecutors established he committed a crime.

NBC News reported that Flynn Jr. accompanied his father to Moscow in December 2015, when the elder Flynn delivered a paid speech at a gala for RT, the Russian state-funded television network. Video from an associated event showed Flynn seated at the same table as Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Records later released by the House Oversight Committee showed that Michael Flynn was paid nearly $34,000 for the speech. RT also covered airfare and hotel costs for Flynn and his son during the December 9–12 trip, according to the records.

At the time, legal experts cited by NBC said special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation could examine what people involved in the campaign knew about contacts with Russia. They also suggested that potential legal exposure for individuals close to Michael Flynn could create pressure on him to cooperate. Those comments reflected analysis of investigative strategy, not confirmation that Flynn Jr. was a target or that he had engaged in wrongdoing.

Michael Flynn later pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI about his contacts with Russia’s ambassador during the presidential transition. He subsequently withdrew his plea, and the Justice Department moved to dismiss the case; President Donald Trump pardoned him in November 2020. Flynn Jr. was not charged in the matter.

Flynn Jr. also attracted attention for promoting the discredited Pizzagate conspiracy theory during the 2016 campaign. That activity, however, did not establish a connection to Russian election interference.

The broader investigation examined Russian efforts to influence the election and contacts between Russian-linked individuals and members of Trump’s campaign. Mueller’s final report said Russia interfered in the election but did not establish that the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in that effort.

Trump’s company also pursued plans for a potential Trump Tower Moscow project during the 2016 campaign. Those discussions and other contacts with Russian interests were documented, but they did not by themselves prove an agreement to interfere in the election.

The investigation generated extensive scrutiny of Trump associates, but claims that every person connected to the campaign was involved in a criminal conspiracy were not supported by the public record.

Manning and fellow active-duty Marine Sgt. Michael Chesny were accused of climbing a building and displaying a banner bearing the letters “YWNRU,” The Times-News reported. The letters have been associated with the phrase “You will not replace us,” a slogan used by Identity Evropa, a white nationalist organization founded by Marine veteran Nathan Damigo.

The slogan was also used by white nationalists at the 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. During that demonstration, chants of “You will not replace us” were reported to have changed to “Jews will not replace us.” The rally later became associated with a deadly vehicle attack that killed one person and injured at least 19 others.

Manning was reportedly in the process of being administratively separated from the Marine Corps, according to the Military Times. Capt. Joshua Pena, a spokesman for Training and Education Command, said the matter was part of an administrative process and that its results could not be released publicly.

Manning had served in the Marine Corps for about 15 years, beginning in 2002. His listed awards included the Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Iraq Campaign Medal and Afghanistan Campaign Medal. The reports did not establish the final outcome of the administrative proceedings.

A memo posted at one Pizza Hut location in Jacksonville, Florida, drew criticism after appearing to warn employees that they could face discipline if they evacuated ahead of Hurricane Irma.

According to reports, the memo instructed employees not to leave more than 24 hours before the storm and to return within 72 hours. It said that failing to report for scheduled shifts, “regardless of reason,” would be treated as a no-call, no-show and could result in documentation.

The notice said the restaurant would need employees available after the storm to help reopen the store and serve the community. The language prompted a backlash online, with critics questioning whether workers should be expected to remain in an area threatened by a major hurricane or return before conditions were safe.

Some social media users also criticized the idea of pizza delivery during or immediately after a hurricane. Others urged Pizza Hut to clarify whether the memo reflected a companywide policy.

Pizza Hut subsequently issued a statement emphasizing its commitment to the safety and well-being of its employees. The company said locations in Irma’s path were closed and would remain closed until local authorities determined that conditions were safe.

“We absolutely do not have a policy that dictates when team members can leave or return from a disaster,” the company said, adding that the manager who posted the notice had not followed company guidelines. Pizza Hut also said the local franchise operator had addressed the matter with the manager involved.

The incident highlighted the difficulties faced by businesses and workers during natural disasters, particularly when decisions about closures, evacuation and reopening are made at the local level.

title: Never Forget: Donald Trump Bragged About Having The Tallest Building In Manhattan After 9/11
text: I ll bet if you go to your kitchen and look at the calendar by your fridge, in tiny letters at the bottom of today s date it says  Patriot Day.  If not, don t worry   the official title for today s remembrance only began in 2002, the year after the terrorist attack that changed almost everything about the way our nation conducts itself. The word  patriot  means different things to different people, and we won t pretend to speak for them all here. But we know it when we see it, and we know the opposite of it, as well.Patriotism is what we see when we watched Americans coming together in grief and solidarity, helping each other in the aftermath of the attack. The opposite of it is what we saw when former New York mayor Rudy Giuliani politically invoked the attacks so much that Vice President Joe Biden once remarked that all Giuliani needed  to make a sentence is a noun, a verb, and 9/11.  Patriotism was on the face of our last President, holding a soup ladle in a national day of service in 2011. The opposite is what you call it when Rush Limbaugh attacked him and said he was  visiting the beneficiaries of his policies. Patriotism, in the words of Clarence Darrow,  hates injustice in its own land more than anywhere else. What it does not do is tout itself as superior. We see nothing but that from Donald Trump. When Trump lied on national television   one of more than a thousand times he s done so since his election   and said that he heard Muslims  cheering  the fall of the towers, perhaps what he was actually doing was projecting a little bit of his own guilt onto adherents of a religion he doesn t and has no desire to understand.Maybe, just maybe, Donald Trump felt a tiny bit bad for saying the worst thing anyone in America said on that fateful day in 2001: 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually, before the World Trade Center, was the tallest-and then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it s the tallest. What s at 40 Wall Street? The 71-story Trump Building.Listen here, if you can.Featured image via John Moore/Getty Images

**Patriot Day Remembers 9/11, While an Old Trump Comment About Lower Manhattan Resurfaces**

Patriot Day is observed each year on September 11 to remember the nearly 3,000 people killed in the terrorist attacks of 2001. Congress established the observance in late 2001, and it was first marked the following year.

The day has also become part of broader debates about patriotism, public service and the political use of the attacks. In the years after September 11, Americans came together in grief and solidarity, while public figures sometimes invoked the attacks in campaign speeches and political arguments.

Former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani frequently referred to his leadership during the attacks while seeking the Republican presidential nomination in 2007. Then-Senator Joe Biden mocked that approach during the campaign, saying Giuliani’s sentences contained “a noun, a verb, and 9/11.”

President Barack Obama also participated in national service events during his presidency, including efforts focused on community service and volunteering. Political commentators, including Rush Limbaugh, criticized some of those appearances and policies.

Donald Trump, meanwhile, made several claims about the September 11 attacks that drew public scrutiny. During his 2015 presidential campaign, he said he had seen or heard reports of Muslims in New Jersey cheering as the World Trade Center fell. Fact-checkers and news organizations found no credible evidence supporting that claim.

Trump also made a separate comment about his real-estate holdings in lower Manhattan shortly after the attacks. In a 2001 television interview, he discussed 40 Wall Street, the 71-story building he owned at the time, and said that it had become the tallest building in lower Manhattan after the World Trade Center towers were destroyed.

“40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually, before the World Trade Center, the tallest—and then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest,” Trump said. “And now it’s the tallest.”

The remarks were made in the context of discussing the damage to New York and the status of Trump’s property. They have since been revisited by critics who view them as an example of Trump emphasizing his own business interests while discussing a national tragedy. At the time, however, the building’s status as the tallest in lower Manhattan was a factual consequence of the destruction of the World Trade Center towers, not a claim that it was the tallest building in all of Manhattan.

Critics argued that the branding comment distracted from the immediate humanitarian concerns surrounding Hurricane Irma and other recent storms, including Hurricane Harvey. Others viewed it as part of Trump’s broader emphasis on the public visibility and reputation of his administration and government agencies.

The Coast Guard was among the federal agencies involved in search-and-rescue and emergency-response operations during the hurricane season. Trump’s comments did not change the administration’s stated focus on coordinating with state and local authorities as Irma moved through Florida.

CBS News shared video of Trump saying he would visit Florida soon and would continue to monitor Hurricane Irma’s progress.

Florida Republican Reps. Matt Gaetz and Ted Yoho voted against a $15 billion hurricane relief package as Hurricane Irma moved toward the state. Both lawmakers said they objected to provisions unrelated to immediate disaster assistance, including a temporary increase in the federal debt limit.

Irma was a powerful hurricane as it approached the Florida Keys, with maximum sustained winds reported at 125 mph. Forecasters warned that the storm could produce dangerous winds, storm surge and flooding across parts of Florida.

The relief package passed both the Senate and the House and was signed by President Donald Trump on Friday. It provided additional funding for the Federal Emergency Management Agency following Hurricane Harvey and amid preparations for Irma. The measure also extended the federal borrowing authority for three months and included a short-term budget to keep the government operating through December.

The agreement was negotiated by Trump and Democratic leaders including Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer of New York and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi of California. The deal drew opposition from some Republicans, who objected to combining disaster aid with a debt-ceiling increase and temporary government funding.

Gaetz and Yoho were among the House Republicans who voted against the measure. Their districts were not expected to be among the first areas affected by Irma, although Gaetz’s district includes coastal communities along Florida’s Gulf Coast.

“Snaking in a debt-ceiling increase with funding for victims and communities affected is immoral and reflective of broken leadership in Washington,” Yoho said after the vote. “I do not think it wise to extend our borrowing limit without mandatory spending reforms.”

Yoho said he would have supported a measure focused solely on assistance for people affected by Hurricane Harvey.

Gaetz also said he supported disaster assistance but opposed raising the debt limit without spending reductions. “I have a pretty strident view that I will only vote to raise the debt limit if that vote is accompanied by reductions in entitlement spending,” he said.

The vote came as officials prepared for Irma, which had already caused widespread destruction in the Caribbean and threatened to bring severe conditions to Florida. Emergency agencies and local governments urged residents in vulnerable areas to follow evacuation orders and prepare for the storm.

The legislation’s supporters argued that the additional funding was needed for recovery efforts after Harvey and for the federal response to new disasters. Opponents, including Gaetz and Yoho, said Congress should address broader spending and borrowing issues separately from emergency aid.

Americans are donating to relief efforts following Hurricane Harvey, while Hurricane Irma approaches the United States. A photograph shared on social media showed a meal consisting of vegetables, sliced meat and crackers. The image prompted complaints that the food served to some hurricane survivors was inadequate. However, there is no evidence that the meal was dangerous, and a single photograph does not establish what food was provided across the Red Cross relief operation.

Houston City Councilman Dave Martin reportedly urged residents at a council meeting to consider donating to other organizations, criticizing the Red Cross’s response and management. The money was intended to support services such as shelter, meals, emergency supplies and assistance for affected communities. Exact spending figures can change as the response continues.

Catholic Charities USA also promoted a relief campaign for people affected by Hurricanes Harvey and Irma, saying that all funds raised through that appeal would go toward the two disaster responses. As with other charitable campaigns, donors should review an organization’s financial information and the specific terms of its appeal before contributing.

The Red Cross remains one of the largest disaster-response organizations in the United States. It has provided shelter, meals and other assistance to large numbers of people affected by hurricanes, although the scale of the operation has led to criticism over logistics and the quality of some services.

A portion of the $1 million donation announced by President Donald Trump for Harvey relief was directed to the Red Cross, according to a list of recipient organizations released at the time.

The criticism surrounding the meal photograph highlights the difficult conditions faced by survivors and the high expectations placed on relief groups. Disaster agencies must provide safe, adequate food and other essential services, while donors and the public can evaluate their performance through financial reports, official updates and independent oversight.

‘Pharma Bro’ Martin Shkreli Faces Possible Bail Revocation Over Hillary Clinton Hair Offer

Martin Shkreli, the former pharmaceutical executive widely known as “Pharma Bro,” was awaiting sentencing on securities-fraud convictions when prosecutors asked a judge to revoke his bail over a series of social-media posts involving Hillary Clinton.

Shkreli offered his Twitter followers $5,000 for a strand of Clinton’s hair, claiming he wanted it for genetic testing. “On HRC’s book tour, try to grab a hair from her,” he wrote. “Will pay $5,000 per hair obtained from Hillary Clinton. Payment after the sequence matches.”

Prosecutors argued that the post and other public statements showed Shkreli could pose a danger to the community and violated the conditions of his release. They asked the court to hold a bail-revocation hearing and return him to custody while he awaited sentencing.

The request did not itself establish that Shkreli had assaulted Clinton or directed anyone to do so. It reflected prosecutors’ concern that his public offer could encourage unwanted contact with the former secretary of state.

Shkreli was later sentenced to prison after being convicted of securities fraud.

**Equifax’s Data-Breach Terms Raise Questions About Arbitration and Class Actions**

Equifax disclosed a massive data breach in September 2017, one of the largest publicly reported cyberattacks at the time. The company said criminals accessed personal information, including names, Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses and, in some cases, driver’s license numbers. Equifax initially estimated that the breach affected about 143 million U.S. consumers.

Consumers who wanted to find out whether their information was involved were directed to a company website and offered a complimentary year of identity-monitoring and fraud-protection services. Soon afterward, lawyers, journalists and consumer advocates raised concerns about arbitration language in the terms for that service.

The terms included a provision requiring certain disputes to be resolved through arbitration rather than in court and limiting participation in class actions. That led to social-media warnings that consumers could lose their right to sue Equifax or join a class action by using the breach-response website.

It was not immediately clear whether the provision applied to people who only checked the site or to claims arising from the breach itself. Equifax said the arbitration language did not apply to claims related to the 2017 security incident and later revised the terms to make that point more explicit.

The website, equifaxsecurity2017.com, was created to let consumers determine whether their information may have been affected and enroll in the company’s monitoring service. The enrollment process required users to provide personal information needed to verify their identities and administer the service.

New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman criticized the original language and said his office had contacted Equifax about removing it. Consumer advocates likewise argued that people responding to a breach should not have to accept broad legal restrictions in order to receive help.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau said the arbitration provision was troubling and that it was examining both the breach and Equifax’s response. At the time, the agency was preparing a rule that would restrict the use of mandatory arbitration clauses in certain consumer financial contracts, although the rule had not yet taken effect and would not have applied retroactively.

The controversy highlighted the difficulty consumers faced in responding to the breach while trying to understand the terms attached to Equifax’s assistance. Equifax’s subsequent clarification said that consumers would not be required to give up claims related to the breach in order to receive the offered monitoring service.

title: Five ‘All American’ Football Players Booted From Team With Black QB After KKK Display
text: The city of Creston, in the heart of Iowa, sits nestled between State Route 25 and U.S. Highway 34, only a mile from the eastern bank of Summit Lake. The seat of Union County offers two additional lakes to fish in, the glorious Green Valley State Park, and a high school football team full of terrifyingly virulent racists.At least, Creston had that last one until Thursday. Scheduled to play the Clarinda Cardinals Friday night, the Creston Panthers will suddenly find themselves without five of their starters after a viral photo of them wearing hoods and posing with a burning cross, a rifle, and a Confederate flag, made the rounds on social media earlier this week.Clearly, the players didn t do well in history at Creston High. The location of the school in Union County is a stark reminder of which side Iowans fought for in the Civil War.The boys will probably not face legal difficulties. Being a piece of shit KKK member, or even pretending to be one, is protected under the First Amendment, and in a town of fewer than 10,000, it s not likely there s a lawyer in town who could successfully argue that anyone suffered damages as a result of their racist idiocy. Not even Kylan Smallwood, the Panthers  quarterback, who is black. Sadly, Smallwood is already all too aware of the fact that this will blow over like nothing happened once the incident is forgotten. He won t forget, though: It s a bad way to put our town on the map, but I think as a community, we just have to move past it. Deal with it, I guess. I thought these guys were my friends. Like, I ve been to some of their houses before I wanted to ask them why, why they did it, but I haven t had the chance to yet. For their part, Creston High School has said that the students have been punished in addition to their removal from the team, but has not specified what that punishment was. Coach Brian Morrison called the families of each boy personally to tell them their sons were no longer playing for the Panthers.Just another day in post-racial America.Featured image via video screen capture

The allegations identify Creston, Iowa, and say the players were scheduled to face the Clarinda Cardinals. However, the report does not provide a dated school statement, law-enforcement record, or independently verified image confirming the incident or the identities of the students involved.

It also attributes remarks to Creston quarterback Kylan Smallwood, who is described as Black, but offers no recording, transcript or other source confirming that he made the quoted comments. The article further says that school officials disciplined the students and that coach Brian Morrison contacted their families, but it does not identify a school announcement or other documentation supporting those claims.

The legal discussion in the original report is also incomplete. A person’s conduct may raise First Amendment questions, but constitutional protections do not automatically prevent schools from enforcing conduct policies or imposing team-related consequences. Whether discipline is lawful would depend on the facts, the school’s policies and applicable law. A display involving weapons, fire or threats could also raise separate safety concerns.

Creston is the Union County seat in southwestern Iowa and is home to Creston High School, but those general facts do not establish that the alleged photograph or team removals occurred.

Without reliable confirmation from the school, the students’ families, law enforcement or other credible sources, the claims should be treated as unverified rather than as evidence that members of the football team were involved in racist activity or were expelled from the team.

Trump’s Decision to Work With Democrats Raises Tensions Among Republicans Over Debt Ceiling

President Donald Trump’s decision to support a short-term debt-ceiling increase and hurricane relief agreement negotiated with congressional Democrats exposed divisions within the Republican Party.

During a September meeting at the White House, Trump backed an agreement with House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to extend the federal borrowing limit for three months and provide assistance to Texas after Hurricane Harvey. The agreement also included funding for the federal government through early December.

The move surprised some Republicans, including House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who had supported a longer debt-ceiling extension. Republican leaders had also favored considering disaster aid and the debt limit separately, while Democrats pushed for a combined measure.

Trump defended the decision in a series of Twitter posts on September 8, arguing that Congress should move quickly on tax legislation and criticizing the Senate filibuster. He also pointed to the failure of Republicans to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act despite years of promises.

“Republicans, sorry, but I’ve been hearing about Repeal & Replace for 7 years, didn’t happen!” Trump wrote. He said the Senate’s 60-vote threshold for most major legislation made it difficult for Republicans, who held 52 seats at the time, to advance bills without Democratic support.

Trump also urged Republicans to begin work on tax reform immediately rather than wait until the end of September.

The debt-ceiling agreement reflected the challenges facing Republicans as they sought to advance legislation with narrow majorities in Congress. The House and Senate subsequently approved the measure, which provided temporary funding for the government, raised the debt limit and included aid for communities affected by Hurricane Harvey.

The episode also prompted discussion about whether Trump might pursue more bipartisan agreements with Democrats. While the president and congressional Democrats had reached an agreement on the immediate fiscal issues, the two parties remained divided over taxes, health care and other major policy questions.

**Donald Trump Jr. Testifies Before Senate Judiciary Committee as Questions Persist Over 2016 Russia Meeting**

Donald Trump Jr. appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday to answer questions about his June 2016 meeting with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya during the presidential campaign.

Trump Jr. has acknowledged that he attended the meeting after being told that Veselnitskaya might have information relevant to Hillary Clinton. In testimony, he said he was interested in hearing what she had to say and determining whether the information could bear on Clinton’s suitability for office. He also described the meeting as brief and said it did not produce useful information.

The testimony was held behind closed doors as part of the committee’s investigation into contacts between members of Donald Trump’s campaign and Russian figures during the 2016 election. Trump Jr. has said he did not view the meeting as a significant campaign event and that he was not aware of any effort by the Russian government to assist his father.

Before the meeting, Trump Jr. had received an email describing the proposed information as part of a Russian government effort to help Donald Trump. He later released the email chain publicly after reports about the meeting emerged.

Some of Trump Jr.’s earlier explanations focused on the possibility that the meeting concerned U.S. adoption policy and the Magnitsky Act, which imposes sanctions on certain Russian officials. He later acknowledged that the expectation of potentially damaging information about Clinton was a reason he agreed to attend. His changing descriptions have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers investigating the meeting.

Sen. Chris Coons, a Democratic member of the Judiciary Committee, circulated a memo after the testimony reminding interested parties of the federal statute concerning false statements made to Congress. The statute provides that knowingly making materially false statements in a congressional proceeding can result in criminal penalties.

Coons’ office did not publicly accuse Trump Jr. of lying in the memo. Instead, it highlighted the legal standards that apply to testimony before a Senate committee. Whether any statement made during the interview was false or materially misleading would depend on the evidence and any subsequent investigation.

The Senate Judiciary Committee is one of several congressional panels examining the circumstances of the meeting and the broader question of contacts between the Trump campaign and Russia. Trump Jr. has denied that the meeting amounted to an agreement to receive assistance from the Russian government.

The testimony provided lawmakers with another opportunity to question Trump Jr. about why he attended the meeting, what he expected to learn, and how his public explanations changed as additional details became known.

title: Vegas Cops Take Cheap Shot At Michael Bennett, Say ‘Hiding’ During Shooting Is Probable Cause
text: Now that Seahawks star defensive end Michael Bennett s harrowing story of police brutality has gone viral, the cops who arrested him are trying to cover their own asses in a PR-fueled letter to the NFL Commissioner, Roger Goodell. In the letter, Detective Steve Grammas, the president of the Las Vegas Metro Police Protective Association, asks Goodell to open an investigation into Bennett s allegations, and requests that the commissioner  take appropriate action. The irony is rich in seeing a letter asserting that the LVPD isn t racist, even as the first paragraph of it calls out the NFL for  condoning  Bennett s protest during the national anthem, a stance that only racists take.Bennett s protest, along with that of many players around the league, is specifically against police brutality when dealing with unarmed, innocent black  suspects.  To continue to insist that it is somehow disrespecting to  everything the flag symbolizes  is to ignore that the flag symbolizes justice as well.But the truly disgusting part of Grammas  letter is the reason he and the Las Vegas Police attempt to use as justification for having unlawfully detained Bennett in the first place. Grammas actually asserts that hiding behind a slot machine, then running outside during an episode in which shots are being fired is considered probable cause to arrest Bennett for  suspicious behavior. Guess what, geniuses? If Mike Bennett was running from the cops, you all just proved him right to have done so. He clearly has no gun, obviously isn t the only person in the entire casino hiding from the gunfire, and wasn t even remotely the only person running out the doors   Bennett himself said that  hundreds  of people were staging an exodus from the scene.One would think that maybe the guy with the Super Bowl ring on who kind of looks like Michael Bennett and can leap over a four-foot barrier might not be their suspect.It is my most sincere hope that Bennett and his lawyers not only sue the department, but Detective Grammas personally, for being the kind of dumbass who would send a self-contradictory letter like this in a case where he s clearly just trying to fire back at Bennett s allegations.Featured image via Mat Hayward/Getty Images

**Las Vegas Police Union Defends Detention of Michael Bennett After Casino Shooting**

The Las Vegas police union responded to Seattle Seahawks defensive end Michael Bennett’s allegations of police misconduct with a letter to NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, asking the league to review the incident and take what action it considered appropriate.

The letter, written by Detective Steve Grammas, president of the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Protective Association, also addressed the NFL’s response to players who protested during the national anthem. The union argued that the league had not adequately considered the perspective of law-enforcement officers, while Bennett and other players have said their protests were intended to call attention to racial injustice and police brutality.

Bennett said officers detained him after he ran from a Las Vegas casino during a reported shooting in August 2017. According to his account, officers ordered him to the ground, pointed guns at him and handcuffed him before releasing him. He later alleged that an officer threatened him and used unnecessary force.

Las Vegas police disputed Bennett’s characterization of the encounter. In its response, the department said officers were investigating reports of gunfire and were attempting to determine whether Bennett matched a description provided in connection with the incident. Police have said the detention was based on the circumstances officers encountered, including Bennett’s movement away from the casino.

Bennett has said he was among many people trying to leave after hearing what they believed were gunshots. He denied having done anything wrong and said the officers’ actions reflected racial profiling. The department has denied that the detention was motivated by race.

The incident prompted an internal review and became part of the broader national debate over police treatment of Black people and athletes’ protests during the anthem. Bennett’s representatives and the police union offered sharply different accounts of what happened, while the available public statements did not resolve every detail of the encounter.

Bennett has retained legal counsel in connection with the allegations. Any further claims or disciplinary action would depend on the results of investigations and potential legal proceedings.

Trump Praises FEMA Response as Hurricanes Harvey and Irma Strike the United States

President Donald Trump on Thursday praised the Federal Emergency Management Agency as Hurricane Irma approached the United States, highlighting the work of emergency personnel responding to a series of major storms.

In a morning post on Twitter, Trump wrote:

“FEMA: Hurricane Irma is raging but we have great teams of talented and brave people already in place and ready to help. Be careful, be safe! #FEMA”

Later that day, during a joint press conference at the White House with the Emir of Kuwait, Sheikh Sabah Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, Trump was asked whether FEMA was being stretched by the number of severe weather events occurring at the same time.

Trump said the agency was handling Hurricane Harvey and preparing for Irma and other storms.

“Well FEMA is doing an incredible job, as you all know,” Trump said. “I mean, you’ve been reporting it. You’ve seen how incredible they are. And there’s a great bravery to what they’re doing.”

He also described the unusual sequence of storms affecting the country.

“We’ve never had a thing like this where you get hit with Harvey, which was about as bad as it gets, certainly from the standpoint of a water dump, and then you get hit with Irma, and there’s one right behind Irma,” Trump said. “I guess you probably know, but a smaller one, but nevertheless right behind.”

Trump’s comments referred to the timing and severity of the storms, but he did not explicitly discuss climate change or connect the hurricanes to long-term changes in the climate. Scientists have continued to study how climate change may influence hurricane rainfall, intensity and other characteristics, but a single sequence of storms does not by itself establish a cause.

Hurricane Harvey made landfall in Texas in late August 2017, bringing catastrophic flooding, while Hurricane Irma was approaching Florida at the time of Trump’s remarks. The United States had also experienced multiple major hurricanes in previous years, including Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005.

Trump Tells DACA Recipients Not To Worry, Drawing Criticism Online

Days after announcing the end of an Obama-era policy that protected certain undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children, President Donald Trump said recipients of the program should not be concerned during a six-month transition period.

The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program has granted temporary protection from deportation and work authorization to roughly 800,000 people since it began in 2012. The policy did not provide a path to citizenship. Under the administration’s announcement, the government would stop accepting new applications and would phase out the program unless Congress acted.

DACA recipients were brought to the United States as minors and, in many cases, have spent most or all of their lives in the country. Immigration advocates and Democratic lawmakers criticized the decision, arguing that recipients should not be held responsible for the actions of their parents and warning that ending the program could disrupt families, education and employment.

The six-month period was intended to give Congress time to consider legislation addressing the recipients’ legal status. Whether lawmakers would reach an agreement remained uncertain.

On Thursday morning, Trump wrote on Twitter that DACA recipients had “nothing to worry about” during the transition period, prompting criticism from people who said the message did not address what could happen after the six months ended.

“For all of those (DACA) that are concerned about your status during the 6 month period, you have nothing to worry about — No action!” Trump wrote on September 7, 2017.

Trump’s message drew responses from Twitter users who questioned how recipients could feel secure when the program was scheduled to end absent congressional action.

“And then what about after 6 months? Will you kick them out of America without any notice?” Ed Krassenstein wrote.

“It’s not the Next 6 MONTHS they are worried about — It’s the REST OF THEIR LIVES!!” another account posted.

Other users pointed to the fact that many DACA recipients had grown up in the United States and might have limited ties to the countries where they were born.

“Imagine if Ivanka Came here at 2 years old from Russia. Imagine forcing her to move back to Russia w/out knowing the language or the country,” one post said.

“Obama was clear: that kids brought here by their parents should get a chance to earn their citizenship. That’s the American spirit,” another user wrote. The DACA policy itself, however, did not grant citizenship or establish a citizenship process.

Additional comments questioned the purpose of the deadline and the uncertainty it created.

“Ummm and what about after 6 months? What’s the point of creating an arbitrary deadline to mess with people’s heads?” Greg Shugar wrote.

“But after that 6 month period … you’re screwed,” another user posted.

“That’s like telling someone who has six months to live that they have nothing to worry about for six months,” Tony Posnanski wrote.

Other posts said recipients could be forced to make decisions about their education, careers and family lives while their future remained uncertain.

The end of DACA also prompted warnings about possible economic and social effects. Businesses, schools and immigrant-rights groups said the loss of work authorization for recipients could affect employers, families and communities. The broader consequences depended in part on whether Congress enacted a replacement program.

For the time being, existing DACA protections remained subject to the administration’s transition rules, while lawmakers faced pressure to determine the future of the recipients.

Trump Tells The Dakotas He Hopes The Drought Will “Go Away”

President Donald Trump told residents of drought-stricken parts of the Dakotas that his administration was working to address the conditions during a tax reform speech in Mandan, North Dakota.

“I know you have a little bit of a drought. They had the opposite, believe me,” Trump said, referring to areas affected by Hurricane Harvey. “You’re better off. You are better off; they had the absolute opposite.”

Trump said he was surprised that drought conditions could occur so far north and said federal officials were working with state authorities.

“We’re doing everything we can, but you have a very serious drought,” he said. “I just said to the governor, I didn’t know you had droughts this far north. Guess what: You have them. We’re working hard on it, and it will disappear, it will all go away.”

A federal drought monitor report issued the previous week identified long-term precipitation deficits in parts of the Dakotas, Nebraska and Montana. The report also noted that substantial portions of pasture and range conditions in the region had been rated very poor. Drought conditions had affected farmers, ranchers and livestock producers across the northern Plains.

Trump said the Agriculture Department had been working with states in the region to help reduce the drought’s effects.

“We will always stand strong with our farmers and our ranchers, the backbone of America, that I can tell you 100 percent,” he said.

The administration’s response to climate and weather issues was also part of a broader political debate. Trump had nominated Oklahoma Congressman Jim Bridenstine to lead NASA, a decision that drew criticism from some lawmakers and scientists because of his views on climate change and his limited scientific background. Bridenstine had previously questioned aspects of climate science, while NASA conducts research and monitoring related to Earth’s climate.

Trump had also previously tweeted that the concept of global warming was created by and for China to make U.S. manufacturing less competitive. During the 2016 presidential campaign, he said the post was intended as a joke.

At the time of Trump’s remarks in North Dakota, the United States was responding to the effects of Hurricane Harvey, while Hurricane Irma was moving through the Caribbean toward Florida. The drought in the northern Plains remained a separate weather-related challenge for the region’s agricultural communities.

title: Facebook Just Confirmed Russia Spent At Least $100k On Ads To Influence Election
text: Earlier today, Facebook representatives told Congress something that should shake every American to their core: A shady Russian company bought thousands of dollars worth of ads specifically targeting American voters. $100,000, to be exact. In other words, Russian actors actively sought to influence the outcome of our election.Facebook has traced the ads back to what they re calling a  Russian troll farm,  which is known to spread propaganda friendly to the Kremlin. Some mentioned both Trump and Hillary by name, while most merely worked to stoke fears about gun rights, immigration, and other issues   the same fears that Trump himself stoked during his campaign.With all the brouhaha surrounding  fake news,  and the question of how big a role social media played in the dissemination of fake news that may have unduly influenced our electoral outcome, this is a massive revelation indeed.NBC News posted Facebook s official statement on the matter to their Twitter account. It reads, in part: We have found approximately $100,000 in ad spending from June of 2015 to May of 2017 associated with roughly 3,000 ads that was connected to about 470 inauthentic accounts and Pages in violation of our policies. Our analysis suggests these accounts and Pages were affiliated with one another and likely operated out of Russia. Read their full statement below:Facebook statement: 470 inauthentic accounts  likely operated out of Russia  bought roughly $100,000 in ads between June 2015 and May 2017 pic.twitter.com/XZqvUKB0gG  NBC News (@NBCNews) September 6, 2017How utterly convenient that these ads started popping up right as Trump formally announced his candidacy. This was even before the primary season really got underway, and the GOP field was crowded. At that point, we weren t going to know for months who the GOP candidate would be. Yet, when combined with all the other evidence against Trump and his campaign, such as meetings between Don Jr. and a Russian lawyer, the Trumps  financial connections in Russia, and more, the dark picture of Russian meddling starts becoming a little clearer.Here s the thing: While the amount these Russians spent is just a tiny fraction of overall spending during the campaign cycle, and most of the ads didn t actually reference our election, the targeting was more specific than it ought to have been. That brings up questions about whether these Russian operators had help from within the U.S. when it came to targeting their ads.If they did indeed have help from inside our borders, where did the help come from? Russians already here? Or people close to some of the candidates (like, oh, say, Donald Trump and his family)? Facebook can t determine that, but hopefully investigators will be able to uncover some information about it soon.Featured image via Spencer Platt/Getty Images

Facebook Disclosed Roughly $100,000 In Ads Linked To Accounts Likely Operating From Russia

Facebook said it had identified approximately $100,000 in advertising purchased between June 2015 and May 2017 that was associated with roughly 3,000 ads and about 470 inauthentic accounts and Pages. The company said its analysis suggested the accounts were affiliated with one another and likely operated out of Russia.

The disclosure added to concerns about the use of social media by foreign actors during the 2016 U.S. election period. Facebook said some of the ads mentioned Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, while many others focused on divisive issues including gun rights, immigration and other political topics. The company did not say that all of the ads were directly related to the election or that the spending had changed the outcome.

Facebook provided the information as lawmakers and the public examined how false or misleading material may have been distributed online during the campaign. The company said the accounts and Pages violated its policies, but it did not publicly identify the individuals or organization behind them in its initial statement.

NBC News posted part of Facebook’s statement on Twitter. It reads:

“We have found approximately $100,000 in ad spending from June of 2015 to May of 2017 associated with roughly 3,000 ads that was connected to about 470 inauthentic accounts and Pages in violation of our policies. Our analysis suggests these accounts and Pages were affiliated with one another and likely operated out of Russia.”

text: One of the most feared defensive ends in football, Michael Bennett of the Seattle Seahawks, posted an account on Twitter Wednesday of his own story of police brutality, and it happened less than three weeks ago.Bennett was in Las Vegas the day after his team bested the Kansas City Chiefs in a preseason matchup. Before that game, as Bennett has the entire preseason, he sat during the national anthem in protest against police brutality nationwide. Number 72 has been an outspoken activist for years, but this year he has elected to actually join other players in protest of the treatment of people of color at the hands of police.As he did previous 2 weeks, Michael Bennett sits during national anthem. As last week, teammate Justin Britt stands at his side. #Seahawks pic.twitter.com/5ko7KG4jT2  Gregg Bell (@gbellseattle) August 26, 2017Ironic doesn t begin to cover what happened to him the very next day. With a statement far too large to fit into even a series of tweets, Bennett posted his account of what happened after the much-hyped fight between Floyd Mayweather and Conor McGregor in Las Vegas on August 26th:To be clear, Michael Bennett is a very big man. At six-foot-four and 275 pounds of pure muscle, Bennett wears a smaller version of standard NFL shoulder pads so they don t get in his way as he crushes his opponents on the field. But this beast of a man, compliant in every way, finally encountered something that made him fear for his life: The police.Any Seahawks fan   and I am one of the biggest   will tell you that Michael Bennett is the last person that would ever be a suspect in any kind of violent crime. If he seems like a monster when he gears up, it is in polar opposite to his life off the field. He lives in Hawaii with his wife and three young daughters. His brother Martellus, a tight end for the Packers, writes children s books. Michael collaborates with his brother s business, The Imagination Agency. He is a happy man.But today he is not happy. If NFL fans thought they were going to get players to stop protesting during the national anthem by complaining about their patriotism, they should seek out Michael Bennett and ask him how much he loves this country. Seattle Seahawks defensive end Michael Bennett said he was detained by police in Las Vegas after attending the Floyd Mayweather–Conor McGregor boxing match on Aug. 26, 2017.

Bennett had been sitting during the national anthem throughout the Seahawks’ preseason games as a protest against racial inequality and police brutality. During Seattle’s preseason matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs on Aug. 25, teammate Justin Britt stood beside him.

The following night, Bennett said he was leaving the fight when he heard what sounded like gunshots. According to his account, he ran with other people from the area and was stopped by police officers. Bennett said an officer pointed a gun at him, handcuffed him and ordered him to lie on the ground.

In a statement posted on social media, Bennett said he believed he was targeted because he is Black. He said the incident left him fearful and concerned about the treatment of people of color by law enforcement.

The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department said it was reviewing Bennett’s account and the circumstances surrounding the detention. Bennett’s statement did not allege that he was arrested or charged with a crime.

Bennett has been an outspoken advocate for social justice and had publicly discussed his decision to protest during the anthem. His actions were part of a broader movement among professional athletes following Colin Kaepernick’s 2016 protests against racial injustice and police treatment of Black Americans.

The incident drew attention as Bennett continued to explain why he was protesting during the anthem. He said his demonstrations were intended to call attention to inequality, rather than to criticize the military or the country.

title: Airlines Immune From Price Gouging Laws In Florida, Royally Screwing Evacuees
text: Imagine you just heard on the news that  the strongest storm ever observed in the Atlantic  was headed your way, and soon. You would, like anyone concerned for themselves and their family, want to get out as soon as possible. And the quickest way to evacuate from anywhere is the fastest method of travel on earth: Air. But you hit a small snag. You don t have the goddamn fortune that the airlines are now charging for flights that were less than half as much the day before. That has to be against the law, right?Wrong. In Florida, where Hurricane Irma is bearing down like a banshee, there are price-gouging laws like there are in every state. But airlines don t answer to specific states. They re regulated by the FAA and the Department of Transportation, which means no state or local statutes apply to them.So when Lisette Diaz tried to book a flight to get her family out of South Florida, she found that flights from the area   during what is normally a lull in the travel season in Florida   had skyrocketed from a few hundred dollars to over $3,000. Trying to get to New York, she finally settled on tickets out of Fort Lauderdale that cost upwards of $1,300 per traveler. According to the Miami Herald, there were four people traveling with her, including her mother, grandmother, adult cousin, and 11-year-old sister. $6,600 later, she had her tickets.Diaz was far from the only person to run into price gouging. Florida s Attorney General Pam Bondi activated the state s price-gouging hotline for travelers to report these egregious acts.The Herald reported that Antonio Mercurius actually got his tickets from Miami to D.C. on Monday, before the pricing spikes. Out of curiosity, he checked the price of the same ticket the next day and found it had gone up more than 800% per ticket. Said Mercurius,I understand supply and demand but the laws of capitalism should not operate in the times of catastrophic danger. What happens to the people that can t afford flights now?People trying to evacuate responsibly before the storm vented their frustration on Twitter:@AmericanAir really charging $2000 for a flight from Miami to DC. Scum I tell you.  The Last DJ Bender! (@djpushplay21) September 5, 2017Searching for flight tickets for my sister, grandma and cousin and they are over 1k from Miami   New York!  Tu Deseo ?  (@Lissette24twiny) September 5, 2017Totally unacceptable, a $358 flight from Miami to NYC went up to $3578. Why should expect anything decent from these airlines??? F ing RATS! https://t.co/rjdH6J0yOL  Joseph Pep Nodarse (@joerileyhudson) September 6, 2017Looking for flights for the last hour-plus was one of the most stressful experiences I've had in quite a while. Finally got one.  Alex Schwartz (@AlexJSchwartz) September 5, 2017Leave it to the industry that brought you fees for everything from blankets and pillows to a simple name change on a ticket to really kick evacuees while they re down. While we watch storms like Harvey and Irma bring out the best in neighbors and charities, the airline industry quietly profits for our misery.Featured image via Joe Raedle/Getty Images

rewritten_article_text:
**Airline Fares Surge as Florida Residents Seek to Evacuate Ahead of Hurricane Irma**

When a major storm is approaching, residents often try to leave as quickly as possible, and air travel can be among the fastest options. But travelers attempting to evacuate South Florida ahead of Hurricane Irma reported that fares had risen sharply, in some cases costing several times more than they had the day before.

Florida has a price-gouging law that applies during a declared state of emergency. However, its application to airline tickets is not straightforward.
