title: Senate Says ENOUGH Of Trump’s Racism, Will Force Him To Go On Legal Record Condemning White Supremacists
text: Most of the nation and world watched in horror just a couple of weeks ago as white supremacists, neo-Nazis, Ku Klux Klan members, and other various white power groups descended on Charlottesville, Virginia. Their violent, hateful rally eventually resulted in the death of a brave counter protester, 32-year-old Heather Heyer.As if that weren t bad enough, Donald Trump s response to this racist violence made the situation that had already turned the nation into a tinder box even worse. Instead of condemning white supremacy as any sane, non-bigoted person would, Trump instead made an equivocation between the vile white supremacists and the people there protesting their hate. Only when he was forced to do so did he condemn the violent hate groups by name. However, Trump, being the arrogant, bigoted jackass that he is, could not let that carefully scripted statement stand. In a freewheeling press conference for the ages, Trump ranted for more than half an hour about how the other side was just as bad as the white supremacists. Well, now, it seems that members of the United States Senate are sick of Trump s bigotry and pandering to white supremacists, and they plan to force his hand on the issue.Politico is reporting that a bipartisan group of Senators   Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mark Warner (D-VA), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), and Cory Gardner (R-CO)- have drawn up a resolution that will have Trump make a legal statement against what happened in Charlottesville. That isn t all it does, though. It also forces Trump, once and for all and on the record, to commit to  rejecting white nationalists, white supremacists, the Ku Klux Klan, neo-Nazis and other hate groups. This is an extraordinary move, considering that resolutions are usually just symbolic in nature and not controversial at all. Generally, they just recognize honorary holidays for people of note and things like that. However, this resolution   dubbed the Charlottesville Resolution   will force Trump to, once and for all, stop winking and nodding at these vile hate groups. Senator Mark Warner said: Let there be no mistake: what happened in Charlottesville was an act of domestic terrorism perpetrated by a white supremacist, one that tragically cut short the life of a young woman, Heather Heyer, who was speaking out against hatred and bigotry. We will be pressing our colleagues to swiftly and unanimously approve this resolution in order to send a strong message that the United States Congress unconditionally condemns racist speech and violence. Senator Tim Kaine said in a statement of his own: During the violent white supremacist demonstrations in Charlottesville last month, our country lost three brave Virginians in Heather Heyer and Virginia State Police officers, Lieutenant Jay Cullen and Trooper Pilot Berke Bates. This resolution honors their lives while supporting the Charlottesville community as it heals and rightfully calls on us all, including President Trump, to do better as we combat acts of hate. The beautiful thing about this is that every single Senator will have to vote in favor of it, lest they be labeled a Nazi sympathizer for the rest of their political careers. While Teflon Don gets away with being an open racist, it has been shown time and time again that these other politicians do not have cults of personality of their own and will not be so fortunate should they attempt the same sort of behavior.To that end, Trump will have no choice but to sign this Charlottesville Resolution, and it will be in the presidential records as long as this republic exists.Featured image via Zach Gibson   Pool/Getty Images

The nation watched in horror in August 2017 as white supremacists, neo-Nazis, Ku Klux Klan members and other extremist groups gathered in Charlottesville, Virginia. The rally and ensuing violence resulted in the death of Heather Heyer, a 32-year-old counterprotester, and the deaths of Virginia State Police Lieutenant H. Jay Cullen and Trooper-Pilot Berke M.M. Bates, whose helicopter crashed while responding to the events.

President Donald Trump’s response to the violence drew widespread criticism. In an initial statement, Trump condemned hatred, bigotry and violence but did not specifically name the white supremacist and neo-Nazi groups involved. After additional pressure, he later issued a statement explicitly condemning those organizations. At a subsequent news conference, however, Trump said that both sides shared responsibility for the violence, prompting renewed criticism from lawmakers and members of both political parties.

In response, a bipartisan group of senators introduced a resolution condemning the violence in Charlottesville and rejecting the ideology promoted by white supremacists and other hate groups.

The measure was sponsored by Senators Tim Kaine and Mark Warner of Virginia, along with Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Cory Gardner of Colorado. It condemned the white supremacist rally, expressed support for the Charlottesville community and honored Heyer and the two state police officers who died while responding to the events.

The resolution also called on the president and other public officials to denounce racism, white supremacy, neo-Nazism and the Ku Klux Klan. It did not require Trump to make a legal statement, nor could it compel him to sign a measure. As a congressional resolution, it primarily expressed the Senate’s position rather than creating new law.

In a statement, Warner described the Charlottesville attack as an act of domestic terrorism carried out by a white supremacist and said Congress should send a clear message condemning racist violence. Kaine said the resolution honored the victims while calling on Americans, including the president, to do more to confront acts of hate.

The Senate approved the resolution by unanimous consent, meaning no senator objected to its passage. The action reflected broad congressional condemnation of the Charlottesville violence, although it did not formally force Trump to take any particular action or establish a new legal obligation for the president.

The debate over Trump’s response continued after the Senate vote, with lawmakers and civil rights organizations pressing the administration to speak more directly against extremist groups. The resolution placed Congress on record opposing the ideology and violence associated with white supremacist organizations while offering support to those affected by the Charlottesville events.

President Donald Trump said Wednesday that his administration was preparing for Hurricane Irma as the powerful storm approached Florida, following the devastation caused by Hurricane Harvey in Texas.

Irma was forecast to bring dangerous winds, storm surge and heavy rain to parts of Florida, prompting emergency preparations and evacuation orders in some areas. Forecasters warned that the storm could cause severe damage, but its precise path and effects were still uncertain.

“Watching Hurricane closely. My team, which has done, and is doing, such a good job in Texas, is already in Florida. No rest for the weary!” Trump wrote on Twitter on September 6, 2017.

The message came as federal, state and local officials worked to prepare for Irma while continuing the response to Harvey. Trump had visited Texas after that storm and praised the work of emergency personnel and first responders.

Trump also tweeted, “Hurricane looks like largest ever recorded in the Atlantic!” The statement was not a formal assessment of the storm’s size. The administration’s handling of the storms was also being examined in light of proposed changes to federal agencies involved in disaster response and weather forecasting. The Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration were among the agencies central to preparations for Irma.

Officials urged residents to follow instructions from local authorities, secure property and prepare for power outages and possible evacuations. While Irma’s eventual effects could not yet be determined, emergency managers warned that the storm posed a serious risk to Florida and nearby areas.

**Sessions Helped Make the Case for Ending DACA as Trump Administration Announced Wind-Down**

Attorney General Jeff Sessions played a prominent role in the Trump administration’s decision to end Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, the program that protects certain immigrants brought to the United States as children from deportation and allows them to apply for work authorization.

The administration announced the policy change on Sept. 5, 2017, directing the Department of Homeland Security to begin winding down DACA and calling on Congress to determine whether to replace it with legislation. Sessions delivered a speech defending the decision, citing legal concerns about the program and broader arguments about immigration enforcement.

The announcement did not immediately remove nearly a million people from the country. Instead, it ended new applications and established a process under which existing protections and work permits would expire over time. The administration said Congress would have six months to act.

In his remarks, Sessions argued that DACA represented an improper use of executive authority. He also linked the program to a rise in unaccompanied minors arriving at the southern border and said it had reduced job opportunities for American workers.

“The effect of this unilateral executive amnesty, among other things, contributed to a surge of unaccompanied minors on the southern border that yielded terrible humanitarian consequences,” Sessions said. “It also denied jobs to hundreds of thousands of Americans by allowing those same jobs to go to illegal aliens.”

Critics disputed those arguments. The increase in unaccompanied children arriving at the border began before DACA was created in 2012, and people who arrived after the program’s eligibility cutoff generally could not qualify for its protections. Researchers and immigration advocates also challenged the assertion that DACA recipients had taken jobs from U.S.-born workers, noting that the economic effects of the program were the subject of continuing debate.

DACA was established by the Obama administration in June 2012. To qualify, applicants generally had to have arrived in the United States as children, have lived in the country for a specified period, meet educational or military requirements, and pass background checks. The program did not provide a path to citizenship or permanent legal status.

Supporters said DACA allowed recipients to work legally, attend school and contribute more openly to their communities. Business groups and immigrant-rights organizations warned that ending the program could disrupt workplaces and reduce tax revenue. The administration and its allies, however, argued that the program encouraged unlawful immigration and exceeded presidential authority.

Sessions had a long record of taking restrictive positions on immigration and had faced opposition from civil rights groups during his 1986 nomination to become U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Alabama. Coretta Scott King, the widow of Martin Luther King Jr., wrote to the Senate Judiciary Committee opposing his nomination to a federal judgeship, which was later rejected by the Senate.

The decision to rescind DACA drew criticism from Democrats, civil rights organizations, business leaders and some Republicans. They urged Congress to protect recipients, many of whom had spent most of their lives in the United States and had provided personal information to the government in order to participate in the program.

The administration’s action began a prolonged legal and political battle over DACA’s future. Courts later blocked parts of the wind-down, allowing some current recipients to renew their protections while the broader question remained unresolved.

The Dakota Free Press reported that the state’s voter-registration statistics showed substantial movement between active and inactive classifications. The September 1, 2017, tally listed 11,762 voters—2.14 percent of the August 1 active total—as removed from active status, while 11,450 voters were newly classified as inactive. The changes increased the inactive total to 42,069, after that category had declined from a March 2016 peak of 54,708 to 30,619 in August 2017.

Those figures describe changes in registration status, not the permanent removal of voters from the rolls. Voters classified as inactive generally remain registered and may be able to restore their active status by updating their information or confirming their eligibility when they vote. States commonly review registration records when voters move, fail to respond to election notices or otherwise do not appear to have current information.

The reported changes have nevertheless raised questions about how South Dakota maintains its voter lists, particularly because Krebs is also a candidate. A secretary of state oversees election administration, but the existence of a campaign does not by itself show that routine voter-registration procedures were manipulated for political purposes.

Party registration totals may show differences among categories, but they do not demonstrate that individual voters were selected for removal because of their party affiliation. Those concerns can be addressed through transparency, oversight and the consistent application of state law. They do not, on their own, prove that an election was rigged or that Krebs used her office to suppress voters.

South Dakota election officials would be responsible for following the state’s procedures for maintaining registration records, while voters can check their status and update their information before an election. Claims that Krebs personally purged Democratic voters or guaranteed herself a victory are unsupported by the registration statistics cited.

Ruiz de Guillen told the Houston Chronicle that she had hoped to travel to Houston to bury her son but was unable to enter the United States. Reports did not establish that immigration officials denied her entry specifically because of Guillen’s DACA status or because of the administration’s decision to end the program.

Speaking from her home in Mexico, she said she was asking God for strength after losing her son.

CNN Panel on DACA Draws Criticism Over Introduction of FAIR President

A CNN panel discussing the future of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program included Dan Stein, president of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, or FAIR. The segment also featured Democratic strategist Maria Cardona and focused on whether the Trump administration should end the program, which protects eligible immigrants brought to the United States as children from deportation.

Critics said CNN did not provide sufficient background on FAIR or the controversy surrounding its founder, John Tanton. The Southern Poverty Law Center and other immigration advocates have criticized the organization over Tanton’s connections to figures associated with white nationalism, eugenics and restrictionist immigration policies. FAIR has rejected allegations that it is a white supremacist organization and says it supports reducing illegal immigration through changes to federal policy.

Tanton founded FAIR in 1979 and later helped establish or support several organizations focused on immigration restriction. Critics have cited his correspondence with individuals linked to white nationalist and anti-immigration movements, as well as writings expressing concern about demographic change in the United States.

The SPLC has also pointed to statements attributed to Stein that it considers hostile toward immigrants and supportive of stricter immigration limits. Stein and FAIR have said their positions are focused on immigration policy and national sovereignty rather than race.

During the CNN discussion, Stein argued that DACA amounted to an executive amnesty program and said Democrats should support Republican priorities, including increased border security, interior immigration enforcement and changes to family-based immigration, in exchange for legislation protecting DACA recipients.

Cardona defended the program and argued that people brought to the United States as children should not be punished for decisions made by their parents. The discussion reflected the broader political dispute over whether Congress should provide permanent legal status to DACA recipients and what immigration measures should accompany such legislation.

The segment generated criticism online from viewers and immigration advocates who said Stein’s organizational background should have been explained before he appeared as a policy commentator. Others argued that FAIR’s views, while controversial, are part of the public debate over immigration and that Stein was invited to represent the organization’s position.

The episode also renewed broader questions about how cable news programs introduce political guests and provide context for organizations with disputed histories. Critics of CNN said the network should offer viewers more information about the affiliations and records of panelists, particularly during debates involving vulnerable communities.

CNN did not immediately address the criticism in the original discussion. The panel is available in the network’s video archive.

President Donald Trump’s decision to end the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties, including Oklahoma Republican Senator James Lankford.

Lankford has generally been a strong supporter of Trump and backed him during the 2016 election. However, he expressed concern about the administration’s plan to rescind DACA, which was created under President Barack Obama in 2012.

The program allowed certain undocumented immigrants who were brought to the United States as children to apply for temporary protection from deportation and work authorization. DACA did not provide a path to citizenship. More than 800,000 people had received protections under the program.

In a statement, Lankford said that people who intentionally entered the country unlawfully should face consequences, but argued that children should not be held responsible for their parents’ actions.

“However, we as Americans do not hold children legally accountable for the actions of their parents,” Lankford said. “We must confront the nation’s out-of-date immigration policy and finally resolve the issues of strong border enforcement and merit immigration.”

“Policy reform must come from the American people through Congress,” he added. “The legislative and executive branches should put aside passivity and partisanship and finally modernize our immigration laws.”

Trump’s administration said the program would be phased out over six months, giving Congress time to consider legislation addressing the status of those covered by DACA. The decision prompted protests and criticism from Democrats, immigrant-rights advocates and some Republicans.

Lankford’s statement indicated support for congressional action to protect people brought to the country as children, while also emphasizing border enforcement and broader changes to immigration policy. His comments reflected the divisions among Republicans over how to handle DACA and the future of the recipients who had relied on the program.

The administration’s decision placed pressure on Congress to reach a legislative agreement before existing protections began to expire.

In the House of Representatives, they even have a name. They call themselves the Tuesday Group. And since Donald Trump took office, it has been Republicans from that group who have been pushing back the hardest on Trump s more extreme and cruel policies. To that end, it should come as no surprise that Trump s band of trolls in his base are threatening the people in the Tuesday Group with primary challenges in 2018.At the top of the Trump trolls  list of targets is Tuesday Group co-chair Charlie Dent (R-PA). They re letting Rep. Dent know that his days are numbered in the most public of ways   by holding a huge event where they blasted their warnings to him from a park in Allentown, Pennsylvania. Adam Gingrich, who gives political advice to hard right politicians said to Dent: You re gonna get primaried. This particular rally is just the beginning. These people seem to be ready to primary anyone who has been critical of Trump and his agenda from the right. There s just one problem with that, though: They don t seem to understand some of these districts. In a place like Pennsylvania, Ted Cruz-style policies will not fly. These people have to be more moderate than say, members of the ultra conservative Freedom Caucus or they don t get elected and re-elected. There s that, and the fact that most of them seem to at least be attempting to appear reasonable. Despite these facts, though, word has leaked out that Trump himself went after Rep. Dent in a private rant, saying that Dent is destroying the Republican Party. So, as they are likely to do, the Trump Trolls came out in force on Friday in order to back their orange man up. Northampton County GOP Chairwoman Gloria  Lee  Snover said of Rep. Dent: I looked Charlie Dent in the eye and I saw the swamp. In times past, I ve supported Charlie Dent as the only alternative. But now, with his disregard and disrespect to my president   I will no longer be able to support Congressman Dent. For the first time, we finally are going to have primary challengers we can get behind. So, in other words, fall in lockstep with Trump or get out. Rep. Dent, to his credit, is pushing back, though. He says of the situation: I have repeatedly made it clear that on issues such as reforming the VA, making the regulatory environment more reasonable, improving America s infrastructure, providing necessary funding to help meet the needs of our military and spurring economic growth, I will work constructively and supportively with President Trump. At the same time. I am not a sycophant. If the president errs on issues that are important to the people of the 15th, or for the entire country, I will continue to state my opinions respectfully and civilly. The best part of this is that it could be a huge gift to Democrats. Pennsylvania is a swing state that, until 2016, always went blue. Therefore, the idea of a hard right conservative being elected there is pretty out there. We can t rule it out, of course, but if the GOP spends all of its times fighting with itself and the Democrats unify around one candidate, we win.Get it together, Democrats. Trump Supporters Target GOP Moderate Charlie Dent as Primary Challenge Speculation Grows

Moderate Republicans in Congress have faced increasing pressure from the party’s conservative base as President Donald Trump’s administration has pursued its agenda. In the House, many of those lawmakers are associated with the Tuesday Group, a coalition of Republicans that has sometimes taken positions at odds with the White House and more conservative members of the party.

Rep. Charlie Dent, Republican of Pennsylvania and a co-chairman of the Tuesday Group, has become one of the most prominent targets of that criticism. Activists opposed to Dent’s approach recently gathered in the Allentown area to call for a more conservative alternative in the 2018 Republican primary.

Adam Gingrich, a political adviser who has worked with conservative candidates, warned Dent during the event that he could face a primary challenge. The gathering reflected broader frustration among some Trump supporters with Republican lawmakers who have criticized or questioned parts of the president’s agenda.

Northampton County Republican Chairwoman Gloria Lee Snover also criticized Dent at the event, saying that she had previously supported him but could no longer do so because of what she described as his lack of support for Trump. She said conservative activists hoped to identify primary challengers who would be more closely aligned with the president.

The criticism illustrates the pressure facing Republican lawmakers in districts where voters may not share all of the positions held by the party’s most conservative activists. Dent has generally supported the Republican Party’s economic and national security policies, while also presenting himself as an independent voice on certain issues.

Dent has said that he is prepared to work with the administration on issues including veterans’ care, regulations, infrastructure, military funding and economic growth. At the same time, he has argued that supporting the president does not require him to agree with every policy or statement.

“I am not a sycophant,” Dent said in a statement, according to the remarks released at the time. He added that he would continue to express his views “respectfully and civilly” when he believed the administration was wrong on issues affecting his district or the country.

Trump and his allies have frequently criticized Republican lawmakers who have opposed or questioned the administration’s proposals. However, reports of private disagreements or calls for Dent’s removal from Congress have not been independently established in the available public information.

A primary challenge would not necessarily result in Dent’s defeat. Republican incumbents typically have significant advantages, including name recognition and access to campaign resources. Still, the episode shows how the president’s influence has encouraged conservative activists to consider challenging Republicans they view as insufficiently supportive.

The dispute could also affect the broader political environment in Pennsylvania, a competitive state that supported Democratic presidential candidates for decades before Trump carried it in 2016. The outcome of any primary contest would depend on the candidates, the district’s voters and the national political climate.

For now, the calls for a challenger remain political pressure rather than a formal change in the race. The episode nevertheless highlights the divisions within the Republican Party as lawmakers balance cooperation with the president against their own policy views and the preferences of their constituents.

The consulate’s planned closure was ordered by the Trump administration in response to Russia’s decision to reduce the number of U.S. diplomatic personnel allowed to work in Russia. The United States also ordered the closure of Russian diplomatic facilities in Washington, D.C., and New York.

The reported smoke drew attention because of the timing of the fire and the facility’s impending closure. However, there was no public evidence that the incident was connected to the diplomatic dispute or that materials unrelated to ordinary fireplace use were being destroyed.

Trump EPA’s Role in Chemical Safety Rules Drew Scrutiny After Houston-Area Explosion

In the aftermath of the historic flooding that accompanied Hurricane Harvey’s high winds and torrential rains, the Arkema chemical plant east of Houston in Crosby lost electrical power and refrigeration. The disruption affected the storage of organic peroxides, chemicals that can become unstable when kept at improper temperatures.

The facility’s stored products later decomposed and caught fire, producing loud popping sounds and smoke. Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez said the emissions were like standing over a barbecue pit, where smoke gets in your eyes, according to NBC News. Richard Rennard, a representative of Arkema, described the smoke more cautiously:

“[The emissions are] noxious, certainly. I don’t know the composition of the smoke.”

A deputy was taken to a hospital after exposure to fumes from the plant. Officials also ordered people within roughly a two-mile radius to evacuate or remain indoors, warning that additional fires or explosions were possible.

The incident prompted questions about the plant’s emergency preparations and about federal chemical-safety policy. Arkema had opposed revisions to the Environmental Protection Agency’s Risk Management Program, rules developed after the 2013 explosion at a fertilizer plant in West, Texas. The Obama administration finalized the revisions in 2017, and they were scheduled to take effect later that year.

Federal records and lobbying disclosures showed that Arkema raised concerns with the EPA and members of Congress about the rules. In comments opposing the changes, the company said they would “likely add significant new costs and burdens to the corporate audit process.” Arkema also argued that the final rule included costly changes that had not been shown to improve safety.

The company’s Crosby facility had separately been cited by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration for serious violations and assessed penalties earlier in 2017. Those citations involved workplace-safety issues, although they did not by themselves establish the cause of the Harvey-related fires.

After taking office, President Donald Trump’s EPA, led by Administrator Scott Pruitt, delayed implementation of portions of the Obama-era chemical-safety revisions while the agency reviewed them. The rules were not simply struck down, but the delay became part of a broader debate over whether chemical facilities should face more extensive reporting, emergency-planning and accident-prevention requirements.

State and federal officials also faced criticism over the limited public availability of information about hazardous chemicals stored at industrial sites. Public records and regulatory filings identified organic peroxides at the Arkema facility; officials and news organizations also examined information about other substances that could present toxic or fire hazards.

The Crosby fires renewed scrutiny of the balance between chemical-plant safety, public disclosure and regulatory costs—particularly as communities near industrial facilities dealt with the consequences of flooding and prolonged power outages.

A recent survey found that a third of Americans didn t know that the Affordable Care Act and Obamacare were one and the same. Most concerning, given Thursday s cuts, is that those between the ages of 18 and 29 were among those least likely to know the difference. That s bad. The Affordable Care Act needs younger and healthy participants, or it will smother under its own weight. Trump Administration Cuts Affordable Care Act Outreach Funding

The Trump administration announced plans to reduce federal funding for programs that help people enroll in health insurance through the Affordable Care Act, after congressional efforts to repeal and replace the law failed.

The administration said it would cut spending on advertising by about 90 percent and reduce funding for in-person enrollment assistance by roughly 40 percent. Officials described the reductions as a response to what they called diminishing returns from outreach efforts, arguing that most Americans are already familiar with the health care law.

The cuts could make it more difficult for some people to learn about their eligibility or receive help signing up for coverage. Administration officials said the largest reductions would affect enrollment organizations that had enrolled relatively few people under the law.

The Affordable Care Act remains dependent on attracting a broad mix of participants, including younger and healthier people, to help balance the costs of covering those with greater medical needs. Surveys have found that some Americans—particularly younger adults—are not fully familiar with the law or its provisions.

Consumer advocates have warned that reducing outreach could discourage eligible people from enrolling. “Sick people will find them, but getting younger and healthier people enrolled is the problem,” Timothy Jost, a consumer advocate with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, said, according to reporting cited by Vox.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized the Affordable Care Act and argued that its problems should be allowed to worsen. In a July 2017 tweet, he wrote: “As I said from the beginning, let ObamaCare implode, then deal. Watch!”

The funding reductions did not repeal the Affordable Care Act, but they represented another administration decision that could affect enrollment and the operation of the law’s insurance marketplaces.

Milwaukee County Sheriff David Clarke Resigns

Milwaukee County Sheriff David Clarke, a prominent supporter of President Donald Trump, resigned from office in August 2017 after nearly four terms in the post.

Clarke was known nationally for his outspoken political views, frequent television appearances and support for expanded policing powers. He often wore a cowboy hat in public and used social media to criticize protesters and groups including Black Lives Matter.

The Milwaukee County Clerk’s Office said it received Clarke’s resignation on Thursday afternoon. The resignation was effective immediately, according to local reports.

Clarke said he was in Nashville that day. Radio station WISN reported that he planned to take a position outside government.

Soon afterward, reports identified Clarke’s new role as a senior adviser and spokesman for America First Action, a political action committee that supported Trump’s agenda. The move prompted speculation online that Clarke might join the Trump administration or seek higher office, but there was no announcement that he had been appointed to a federal position.

Trump had publicly praised Clarke. On August 27, 2017, the president tweeted a recommendation for Clarke’s book, *Cop Under Fire: Moving Beyond Hashtags of Race, Crime and Politics for a Better America*.

A great book by a great guy, highly recommended! https://t.co/3jbDDN8YmJ

— Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) August 27, 2017

Clarke, a Democrat who became a vocal Trump supporter, spoke at the 2016 Republican National Convention in Cleveland. During his address, he promoted the phrase “Blue Lives Matter” and criticized protesters who demonstrated against police conduct.

His tenure as sheriff had also drawn criticism over conditions at the Milwaukee County Jail. Four inmates died at the facility in 2016, including Terrill Thomas, who died after spending several days in a cell without access to water. Thomas’s death was ruled a homicide by the Milwaukee County medical examiner, and the case led to lawsuits and renewed scrutiny of jail management.

Clarke denied responsibility for the deaths and defended the jail’s operations. His department also faced criticism over its handling of inmate care and oversight, though responsibility for the facility was shared with Milwaukee County officials.

Clarke attracted further controversy through public comments about race, policing and protest movements. He referred to Black Lives Matter as “Black Lies Matter” and compared the movement to the Ku Klux Klan. He also said that police brutality had largely ended decades ago, remarks that drew condemnation from civil rights advocates.

The sheriff’s resignation came without a detailed public explanation beyond his plans to leave government and pursue work in the private sector. It ended a tenure in which Clarke became a nationally recognized conservative law-enforcement figure while remaining a divisive presence in Milwaukee politics.

**The Man Donald Trump Called ‘My African-American’ Later Criticized His Approach to Black Americans**

Donald Trump has often sought to rebut criticism that his rhetoric is racially divisive by pointing to his relationships with Black supporters. One of the most widely discussed examples came during the 2016 presidential campaign, when Trump singled out a man at a California rally and referred to him as “my African-American.”

The remark drew attention because it identified the man primarily by his race. It also became the subject of further discussion after the man, Greg Cheadle, said he was not initially a Trump supporter and had attended the rally to hear the candidate in person.

Trump called out to Cheadle during a June 2016 rally in Redding, California:

“Look at my African-American over here; look at him,” Trump said while addressing the crowd.

Cheadle later told NPR that he was not offended by the comment. He said Trump had been speaking positively about Black people before making the remark, and that people around him viewed the exchange as lighthearted.

“I was not offended by it,” Cheadle said. “People around me were laughing [at the fact] that he noticed me, and everybody was happy. It was a jovial thing.”

Cheadle also said he had attended the event with an open mind rather than as a committed Trump supporter.

“I am not a Trump supporter. I went to go hear Donald Trump because I have an open mind,” he said.

Cheadle was a Republican and eventually voted for Trump in the 2016 election, saying his decision was influenced in part by his opposition to Hillary Clinton. In later comments, however, he expressed growing concerns about Trump’s policies and rhetoric concerning Black Americans.

“I would like for him just to show an interest in black people,” Cheadle said. “Why can’t he go to a black city? Why can’t he trumpet black business? Why can’t he have more black people in his administration?”

Cheadle also questioned Trump’s repeated calls for “law and order,” arguing that the phrase could be understood by some Black Americans as a reference to increased policing and arrests in their communities. He noted that he had also believed Barack Obama had not done enough for Black Americans.

Even so, Cheadle did not describe himself as having completely abandoned Trump. He said his support was “on life support” after Trump’s comments and conduct drew renewed criticism, suggesting that his view of the president remained conflicted rather than fully resolved.

The exchange at the 2016 rally continued to receive attention because it illustrated the complicated relationship between Trump and some of his Black supporters: Cheadle did not regard the original remark as offensive, but later said he wanted to see more concrete attention paid to Black communities and businesses.

Donald Trump said Wednesday that he had witnessed the destruction caused by Hurricane Harvey firsthand during his visit to Texas earlier in the week.

“He met with a number of local officials who are eating, sleeping, breathing the Harvey disaster,” Sanders said. She added that Trump had spoken extensively with Abbott, mayors and others involved in the response, describing the information he received as a firsthand account.

Trump’s visit focused on discussions with officials and emergency personnel rather than on visiting neighborhoods damaged by floodwaters. The storm had caused widespread flooding and damage across southeastern Texas, prompting evacuations and a large-scale response.

The disagreement centered on how to understand Trump’s wording: critics said it overstated what he personally saw, while the White House said his meetings with people directly managing the disaster gave him firsthand information about its effects.

title: Dan Rather: Mueller’s Russia Investigation Has Trump ‘Seized With Fear’

Speaking to MSNBC on Wednesday, Rather explained that the investigation into Trump s possible collusion with Russia has Trump scared out of his mind. Donald Trump is afraid. A political hurricane is out there at sea for him, we ll call it Hurricane Vladimir if you will, the whole Russian thing. It s still pretty far out at sea, but each day   this hurricane, this political hurricane   is building in intensity. Mueller s investigation has been steadily picking up steam. It was reported on Wednesday that New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman is now working with Mueller to take an even deeper look at Trump s former campaign manager Paul Manafort.Former national security adviser Michael Flynn has also found himself under a microscope and has even tried to cut deals for immunity to flip on Trump. So far, neither Mueller nor Congress (who is conducting their own simultaneous investigation) has taken him up on the offer. This is presumably because they don t need to let Flynn off the hook in exchange for his testimony to nail Trump s hide to the wall.Publicly, Trump still claims that the investigation is nothing more than a  witch hunt.  However, those close to him say that behind closed doors, Trump has become increasingly distraught over the intensifying investigation into his shady Russian ties.Trump should be afraid, very afraid. In fact, being terrified of what Mueller may find is probably the smartest thing he has done so far. Sooner or later, the truth is going to come out just like it always does. Dan Rather said the ongoing Russia investigation could create significant political risks for President Donald Trump, while cautioning that its ultimate findings were not yet known.

In remarks reported by MSNBC on Wednesday, Rather characterized the investigation led by special counsel Robert Mueller as a developing political challenge for the president. Rather said Trump appeared to be projecting confidence while facing scrutiny over possible contacts between his campaign and Russia. He compared the investigation to a political storm that could grow as investigators continue their work.

Mueller’s investigation has examined several figures connected to Trump’s 2016 campaign. Reports at the time said New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman’s office was cooperating with Mueller’s inquiry into former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort. The precise scope of that cooperation was not publicly established.

Former national security adviser Michael Flynn was also under investigation and had sought immunity in exchange for testimony before congressional committees. Those requests were not accepted at the time. Flynn later became a central figure in the federal investigation and pleaded guilty in 2017 to making false statements to the FBI.

Trump continued to describe the Russia investigation as a “witch hunt” and denied collusion between his campaign and the Russian government. The White House also rejected allegations that Trump had obstructed justice. Investigators had not publicly concluded that Trump or his campaign had committed a crime.

The investigation and related congressional inquiries remained active, and their findings could have political and legal consequences. However, claims about Trump’s private emotional state or predictions about the ultimate outcome were matters of speculation rather than established fact.

title: Enough About Texas, Let’s Talk Taxes: Trump’s Priorities Shift To Breaks For The Rich
text: After a brief and almost meaningless visit to Texas, during which Donald Trump didn t meet with a single victim of Hurricane Harvey, the president s cavalcade moved on to Missouri, where he returned to what he really cares about: More money for wealthy people.He s first, of course. His tweets from Wednesday morning prove unequivocally that the only victim he cares about is himself. He sent out a placating message about  horror and devastation  (which he didn t ask even one Harvey refugee about) just 25 minutes after a tweet about North Korea, and only 15 minutes before he went back into Martyr Mode :After reading the false reporting and even ferocious anger in some dying magazines, it makes me wonder, WHY? All I want to do is #MAGA!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) August 30, 2017With that much obsession on his own well-being, why wouldn t the next logical step be another campaign-style stop to try and convince people to support his awful tax plan? Did I say campaign-style? What I mean is, this was not a White House event. This was straight-up partisan. If Donald Trump operated under the rule of law, the RNC would have to reimburse taxpayers for his Missouri speech, in which he explicitly called for the ouster of a Democratic senator, Claire McCaskill. Speaking to a crowd in Springfield, Trump said,We must lower our taxes and your senator, Claire McCaskill, she must do this for you, and if she doesn t, you have to vote her out of office.That s campaigning, not laying out policy. But he doesn t have much policy yet to reveal: The GOP has yet to agree on much of what will go into their  tax reform  package. Trump himself would like to see the  business  tax rate lowered to 15%, a number so low that it would cripple the government without slashing spending on the poor. But even most Republicans oppose so low a rate, and his plans for  tax relief for the middle class and repatriating offshore profits  are, so far, still out in the ether somewhere.The bottom line is, now that he s got that awful trip to Texas out of the way, Trump is on the warpath, and his only focus is now on winning. He even warned the members of his party not to disappoint him on taxes, the way they did on Trumpcare:I am fully committed to working with Congress to get this job done, and I don t want to be disappointed by Congress. Do you understand me?Oh, we understand, Donnie. You were embarrassed by Mitch McConnell and humiliated by John McCain, so now you want a McVictory to soothe your fiery case of butthurt. Americans see through your  tax reforms,  though. The rich get richer and the poor get poorer. It s the Republican Way!Featured image via Michael B. Thomas/Getty Images

rewritten_article_text:
Trump Turns From Hurricane Response To Tax Plan In Missouri

After a visit to Texas to survey damage from Hurricane Harvey, President Donald Trump traveled to Missouri on Wednesday, where he promoted his administration’s tax proposals and urged Congress to act.

Trump’s Texas visit included stops with state and local officials and briefings on the federal response to the storm. The trip came as rescue and recovery efforts continued across the region. On Wednesday morning, Trump used Twitter to comment on both North Korea and the hurricane’s destruction, while also criticizing news coverage of his administration.

“After reading the false reporting and even ferocious anger in some dying magazines, it makes me wonder, WHY? All I want to do is #MAGA!” Trump wrote.

In Springfield, Trump delivered a speech focused largely on tax policy. The event was organized as part of his administration’s effort to build public support for a Republican tax plan, which congressional leaders were still developing.

Trump called for lower taxes on businesses and individuals and said the plan should encourage companies to bring money held overseas back to the United States. He has previously proposed reducing the corporate tax rate to 15 percent, though congressional Republicans had not reached agreement on that figure or on several other elements of the package.

Speaking to the crowd, Trump also criticized Democratic Sen. Claire McCaskill, who was up for reelection in 2018.

“We must lower our taxes and your senator, Claire McCaskill, she must do this for you, and if she doesn’t, you have to vote her out of office,” Trump said.

The remarks reflected the political stakes surrounding the tax debate. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress but faced disagreements over the size and structure of the proposed tax cuts, as well as how they would affect the federal deficit.

Trump urged lawmakers to deliver legislation and warned against another failure after the collapse of the Republican effort to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act.

“I am fully committed to working with Congress to get this job done, and I don’t want to be disappointed by Congress,” he said.

The administration said its tax proposals were intended to promote economic growth, simplify the tax code and provide relief for middle-income households. Critics, including Democrats and some policy analysts, argued that reducing business and individual tax rates could disproportionately benefit higher-income Americans and increase federal borrowing if not offset by spending cuts or other revenue.

At the time of Trump’s speech, the White House and congressional Republicans had not released a final legislative proposal. The debate was expected to continue as lawmakers worked on the details of the plan and sought support from members of their party.

text: Donald Trump is a horrible president. Everyone knew in the run up to the election that he was in no way qualified for this job. Now that he is in the Oval Office, these facts are magnified on an hourly basis a thousandfold. However, there seems to be one unlikely person who, at least secretly, shares these opinions in part: Donald Trump himself.A source close to Trump says that he is miserable. For one thing, he is angry that members of his cabinet, such as Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, are refusing to walk in lockstep on some of Trump s more controversial public statements   the comments after the violent white supremacist rally in Charlottesville that left a woman dead is a particular source of Trump s ire. Further, what really seems to get him is that there will no firings of top level cabinet officials, because no qualified person would take those jobs now. The source says of how Trump is feeling on his cabinet secretaries  public thrashings: I think that cuts him to the quick. The same source says of the laughable idea of Trump being able to replace Tillerson or any other high level member of the cabinet: I couldn t name you a guy who would take the job or get confirmed. Also, the last of the alt-right   Trump s fellow travelers in bigotry   are pretty much gone from the White House, thanks to Trump s new Chief of Staff, General John Kelly. It seems that the disciplined adult in the room has zero intention of replacing literal Nazis like Trump s ousted Chief Strategist Stephen K. Bannon and key adviser Sebastion Gorka. The source says of these developments: General Kelly has come in and done a look-see on what everyone s been working on for the first six or seven months hereSome people were ready, and some people were not. As for Trump himself? Well, he s flippin  miserable. The source says of the poor old Donald s feelings as of late: He feels like this is not what he signed up for, and his accomplishments are being underplayed. He just looks around and says,  When is this going to get better? The source goes on to say that Trump s emotional state is  the worst it s ever been.  Well, what did he expect? Sure, when you re president, you re the most powerful person on earth. But it s also the hardest job in the world. It s hard even when the occupant is actually qualified. Trump is not. He has that attention span of a gnat on crystal meth, does not read books, can t even use basic modern technology such as email, has dangerous authoritarian instincts, no impulse control, and no respect for the rule of law. Further, he is bigoted, petulant, vindictive, and petty. He s also an admitted serial sexual assaulter and adulterer. In short   Trump is everything we DON T want in a president, from his character, to his knowledge (read: lack thereof), to his ignorance and bigotry.It seems that The Donald thought he d be able to rule over the nation like some kind of mad king. It s obvious that he got a very rude awakening. Oh, if only we lived in an alternate universe where he could have seen what this would be like, and had decided against running for president.Featured image via Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

The White House said the staffing changes were part of Kelly’s effort to bring greater discipline and structure to the administration.

No independent evidence was offered to support those assertions, and Trump continued to carry out the duties of the presidency.

The presidency carries extensive responsibilities, including managing the executive branch, responding to crises and working with Congress and foreign governments. Trump’s management style and public statements had drawn sustained scrutiny, while his administration faced turnover, investigations and political opposition.

Those developments did not establish that Trump regretted running for office or intended to resign. Although reports about his frustrations circulated among political commentators, the president remained publicly committed to his administration and continued to defend his record.

The White House did not publicly confirm the claims made by the unnamed source.

title: A Judge Just Gave Sarah Palin Some Very, Very Bad News
text: Remember how Sarah Palin sued the New York Times for mistakenly saying that a concrete link had been established between her Facebook post that featured crosshairs over former Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords  district and Jared Loughner s decision to open fire on her? Well, that didn t work out so well. Don t retreat. RELOAD,  Palin famously posted on Facebook along with an image depicting gun sights over various states whose legislators she was  targeting.  Shortly after, Loughner shot Giffords in the head and pumped bullets into numerous others, killing six and wounding thirteen others.No concrete link between the two has been established   though it is reasonable to assume Palin s encouragement played a role in the shooting.Speaking of shooting, District Judge Jed Rakoff  shot down Palin s frivolous lawsuit against the Times on Tuesday. Nowhere is political journalism so free, so robust or, perhaps, so rowdy as in the United States,   Judge Rakoff wrote in his 26-page decision. But if political journalism is to achieve its constitutionally endorsed role of challenging the powerful, legal redress by a public figure must be limited to those cases where the public figure has a plausible factual basis for complaining that the mistake was made maliciously. What we have here is an editorial, written and rewritten rapidly in order to voice an opinion on an immediate event of importance, in which are included a few factual inaccuracies somewhat pertaining to Mrs. Palin that are very rapidly corrected,  Rakoff wrote. Negligence this may be; but defamation of a public figure it plainly is not. Judge Rakoff s opinion is an important reminder of the country s deep commitment to a free press and the important role that journalism plays in our democracy,  a spokeswoman for the Times said.  We regret the errors we made in the editorial. But we were pleased to see that the court acknowledged the importance of the prompt correction we made once we learned of the mistakes. This is, of course, bad news for Palin and her ally Donald Trump, who wants to  open up  libel laws to make it easier to people like Palin to file frivolous lawsuits against journalistic institutions for every little mistake even if a correction has been made.Lately, the Right has been practically masturbating over the idea of bullying anyone who reports something they don t like with expensive lawsuits as an attempt to keep criticism to a minimum.This is bad news for anyone who has recently filed a frivolous lawsuit against journalists, including  alt-Right  (a term employed by Nazis as a form of rebranding) journalist Cassandra Fairbanks, who sued a Fusion reporter for correctly reporting that she had made a hand gesture that had been adopted by the  white power  movement during a visit to the White House.Fortunately, Judge Rakoff  refused to allow Palin s farcical lawsuit to get off the ground. Hopefully, this sends a message to the Right that bullying journalists with lawsuits will not go well for them.Featured image via screengrab

Mike Pence Called for Paying for Hurricane Katrina Relief Without Adding to the Debt (VIDEO)

Hurricane Harvey struck Texas on the 12th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina and later affected parts of Louisiana. Katrina remains one of the deadliest storms in U.S. history, with about 1,800 deaths attributed to the hurricane and its aftermath. Flooding covered much of New Orleans after levees failed, forcing many residents to seek shelter on rooftops and elsewhere.

In 2005, Mike Pence, then a Republican congressman from Indiana, addressed Congress as lawmakers considered additional funding for the hurricane’s recovery.

“Mr. Speaker, Katrina breaks my heart,” Pence said. “When I consider its tragic aftermath, the ancient parable comes to mind: ‘And the rains descended, and the flood came, and the winds blew, and beat against that house; and it fell, and great was the fall of it.’”

Pence said Congress should assist victims and support rebuilding efforts, while also considering how the spending would be financed.

“For most American families, when a tree falls on your house, you tend to the wounded, you rebuild, and then you figure out how you’re going to pay for it,” he said. “Later today Congress will continue the work of funding the relief and recovery from Hurricane Katrina. And well we should, by speeding more than $50 billion to FEMA and other agencies.”

“But as we tend to the wounded, as we begin to rebuild, let us also do what every other American family would do in like circumstances and expects this Congress to do: Let’s figure out how we’re going to pay for it,” Pence continued.

“Congress must ensure that a catastrophe of this nature does not become a catastrophe of debt for our children and grandchildren,” he added.

A video of the remarks circulated online in 2017, with some posts presenting Pence’s comments as opposition to Katrina relief. The speech, however, shows him supporting federal assistance while arguing that the costs should be offset or otherwise addressed rather than added entirely to the national debt.

Pence’s position reflected a broader debate in Congress over how to finance the large emergency appropriations approved after Katrina. The remarks did not amount to a call to withhold aid from hurricane victims.

The account also alleged that an upstairs neighbor offered another resident access to an apartment in exchange for $300. No verified recording or official report establishing the claim was provided with the story.

Reports of alleged price-gouging often emerge during natural disasters, when demand for fuel, lodging, food and other necessities rises sharply. Texas law allows state authorities to investigate certain claims of excessive pricing during a declared disaster, although whether a particular transaction violates the law depends on the circumstances and available evidence.

The Texas attorney general’s office has previously encouraged consumers to report suspected price-gouging following major storms. Any complaint involving the alleged apartment payment would require corroboration before authorities could determine whether wrongdoing occurred.

The purported CNN interview and the specific account described above should therefore be treated cautiously unless verified by the network, witnesses or official records.

The Texas Senator voted against Federal funding for victims of Hurricane Sandy, the deadliest and most destructive hurricane in the Atlantic in 2012, but now he wants funds after Hurricane Harvey barreled down on his state. At least 14 people have died after Harvey hit Texas. More than 3,000 people have been rescued as responders work around the clock in devastating conditions.During a press conference on Monday, Cruz said that Trump has pledged  whatever the state needs  for water-soaked Texas. But, just after that presser, Cruz was in the awkward position of having to defend his position to MSNBC s Katy Tur on the 2012 Hurricane Sandy relief package, calling it  filled with unrelated pork. There is time for political sniping later,  Cruz said without one bit of irony or acknowledgement of his hypocrisy. It s not really political sniping, senator,  Tur shot back.  These are people who needed money and who needed funding right after that storm, I covered those people. Many of them, just like those in Houston, lost absolutely everything they owned. Cruz told Tur that hurricane relief is a  vital, central role  of the federal government and should continue to be for a long time. The problem with that particular bill is it became a $50 billion bill that was filled with unrelated pork,  Cruz said. Two-thirds of that bill had nothing to do with Sandy,  he continued.  And what I said then and still believe now is that it s not right for politicians to exploit a disaster and people who are hurting to pay for their own political wish list. Disaster relief needs to be focused on the victims of disaster relief, and I supported that for Sandy, disaster relief there, and I would support that anywhere there s a major disaster without getting distracted by political, unnecessary pork spending,  he added.The Washington Post begs to differ with Cruz:The Congressional Research Service issued a comprehensive report on the provisions, and it s clear that virtually all of it was related to the damage caused by Sandy. There may have been some pork in an earlier Senate version, but many of those items were removed before final passage. There were also some items that appear to have been misunderstood.Regardless, Ted Cruz voted against it but now he wants all that delicious disaster relief money for his state. And, Texas should get that money asap. The victims of Sandy should have, too.Image via screen capture.

**Ted Cruz Explains Why Texas Should Receive Federal Relief Money After Opposing Hurricane Sandy Aid**

U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, voted against a major federal relief package for victims of Hurricane Sandy in 2013. After Hurricane Harvey struck Texas, however, Cruz said federal assistance was an important responsibility of the government and that the state should receive the resources it needed.

At least 14 people had died after Harvey hit Texas, and more than 3,000 people had been rescued as emergency responders worked through severe flooding and dangerous conditions.

During a press conference on Monday, Cruz said President Donald Trump had pledged to provide Texas with whatever assistance it needed. Shortly afterward, Cruz defended his vote against the Sandy relief package during an interview with MSNBC’s Katy Tur.

Cruz said the $50 billion package included spending that was unrelated to the storm and argued that disaster legislation should focus on people directly affected by a disaster.

“There is time for political sniping later,” Cruz said.

Tur responded that the people affected by Sandy had needed help immediately, noting that many had lost their homes and possessions, just as residents of Houston and other Texas communities had after Harvey.

Cruz said federal disaster relief was a “vital, central role” of the government and should remain available after major disasters. He said his objection was to what he described as unrelated spending included in the Sandy legislation.

“What I said then and still believe now is that it’s not right for politicians to exploit a disaster and people who are hurting to pay for their own political wish list,” Cruz said. “Disaster relief needs to be focused on the victims of disaster.”

Cruz maintained that he supported aid for Sandy victims but opposed the broader bill because of provisions he considered unnecessary. His position drew criticism because he had voted against the final legislation while later seeking federal assistance for Texas.

The Congressional Research Service reviewed the Sandy package and found that most of its provisions were connected to recovery from the storm, although the legislation covered a range of agencies and programs. The scope of the bill, and whether some provisions were sufficiently related to Sandy, was debated at the time.

Federal disaster assistance is generally provided through established programs after a major disaster declaration, regardless of whether lawmakers previously supported a particular relief package. Texas communities affected by Harvey were eligible to seek federal help, as were communities affected by Sandy.

Cruz’s comments renewed discussion of his vote on the Sandy aid bill and of the standards lawmakers use when evaluating disaster relief for their own states. રાહ

# ICE Seeks Approval for Retention Schedule Covering Immigrant Detention Records

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, commonly known as ICE, has asked the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) to approve a schedule governing how long the agency must retain records related to its detention operations.

NARA is an independent federal agency responsible for preserving government records and making historically significant documents available to the public. ICE’s request concerns the future retention and disposal of records generated by its detention system, including documents that may be relevant to oversight of conditions and incidents in custody.

The request has drawn concern from immigration advocates and government-transparency organizations, which have long called for greater scrutiny of conditions in detention facilities. They argue that records about alleged mistreatment could be important to detainees, investigators, journalists and members of the public seeking to understand the operation of the system.

According to the proposed schedule, ICE identified multiple categories of records for potential routine disposal. These include documents related to sexual-assault allegations, deaths in custody, solitary confinement, detention-facility monitoring, detainee logs and communications from members of the public reporting possible abuses. The proposal does not itself authorize the destruction of the records; that would require approval through the federal records-management process.

The proposal has prompted criticism because the records could be relevant to investigations, lawsuits and historical research. NARA’s review considers whether federal records have sufficient long-term value to warrant permanent preservation, and not every record created during an incident is necessarily retained indefinitely. Any approved schedule would establish minimum retention periods, after which records could be destroyed in accordance with federal rules. The proposal should therefore be distinguished from an immediate decision to erase records or conceal wrongdoing.

The matter remains part of the records-schedule review process, and the treatment of documents involving deaths, sexual-assault allegations and solitary confinement will depend on the final decision and any conditions imposed by NARA.

Texas lawmakers who opposed parts of Hurricane Sandy aid seek federal help after Harvey

When Hurricane Sandy struck the East Coast in 2012, causing severe damage in New York and New Jersey and affecting communities from North Carolina to New England, Congress considered a supplemental relief package. The House ultimately approved about $50.7 billion in assistance in January 2013.

John Culberson, whose 7th Congressional District included parts of Houston, was the only Texas Republican in the House to vote for the measure, according to congressional voting records. Other Texas Republicans opposed it, citing concerns about the bill’s cost and provisions they considered unrelated to Sandy recovery.

Ted Cruz was not yet serving in Congress when the final Sandy aid vote took place. He had been elected to the Senate in November 2012 and took office the following month. During the debate, however, Cruz criticized the legislation, arguing that it included spending beyond the immediate needs created by the storm.

“Hurricane Sandy inflicted devastating damage on the East Coast, and Congress appropriately responded with hurricane relief,” Cruz said at the time, according to statements reported during the debate. “Unfortunately, cynical politicians in Washington could not resist loading up this relief bill with billions in new spending utterly unrelated to Sandy.”

In August 2017, after Hurricane Harvey caused extensive flooding and damage across southeastern Texas, Cruz and fellow Texas Senator John Cornyn wrote to President Donald Trump supporting Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s request for a major disaster declaration. Such a declaration would make additional federal assistance and emergency resources available to affected communities.

“Given the potential catastrophic impact that the hurricane may have on Texas communities, we strongly support this request and urge you to provide any and all emergency protective measures available by a major disaster declaration,” the senators wrote.

Trump issued a disaster declaration for parts of Texas as Harvey’s effects spread across the state. The declaration enabled federal assistance for recovery and emergency response, subject to eligibility and subsequent approvals.

Cruz defended his position by saying that the immediate response to the storm should take priority over political arguments about earlier votes and spending proposals.

“There’s time for political sniping later,” Cruz said. “I think our focus needs to be on this crisis and this disaster.”

Several lawmakers from New York and New Jersey said they would support federal assistance for Texas despite Cruz’s earlier criticism of the Sandy package.

“Despite my TX colleagues’ refusal to support aid in #SouthJersey’s time of need, I will support emergency disaster $$ for those impacted,” New Jersey Representative Frank LoBiondo wrote on Twitter on August 28, 2017.

“Disasters & emergencies are just that—disasters & emergencies. Must stand together as Americans, not be hypocritical based on geography,” LoBiondo added.

New York Representative Pete King also said he would support aid for Texas.

“Ted Cruz & Texas cohorts voted vs NY/NJ aid after Sandy but I’ll vote 4 Harvey aid. NY won’t abandon Texas. 1 bad turn doesn’t deserve another,” King wrote on August 27, 2017.

In another post, King wrote: “As lifelong NYer w/ NY values I will vote for emergency Harvey $ for Ted Cruz’s constituents. Above all, true Americans must stand together.”

Other commentators noted that federal disaster legislation can include funds for future preparedness as well as immediate recovery. The debate over the scope and cost of such aid continued as lawmakers considered assistance for communities affected by Harvey.

The episode highlighted the recurring political dispute over disaster relief: lawmakers often criticize broad spending packages when assisting another region, then seek rapid federal support when their own states suffer major storms.

House Proposal Would Limit Funding and Scope of Russia Investigation

A House proposal introduced by Rep. Ron DeSantis, a Florida Republican, sought to place limits on the federal investigation into possible ties between Donald Trump’s campaign and Russia. The measure would have restricted funding for the special counsel’s office after six months and limited its work to matters arising after June 2015.

The proposal did not itself end the investigation, and its effect depended on whether it was included in legislation approved by Congress and signed into law. It was also unclear whether the measure would receive a vote or gain sufficient support.

Special Counsel Robert Mueller was appointed to oversee the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible coordination with Trump campaign associates. The inquiry was also examining related matters that arose during its work, including potential financial and business issues, under the authority of the Justice Department.

Trump’s business interests in Russia have received attention because he and his company pursued projects there for years before his presidential campaign. Reporting by The Washington Post documented efforts beginning in the late 1980s to explore a hotel project in Moscow. Other proposed developments followed, although several did not come to fruition.

In the 1990s, Trump announced plans to invest in Moscow real estate. The projects were not completed, but Trump received several trademark registrations in Russia during that period. In 2005, he again expressed interest in developing a property in Moscow and described Russia as an attractive market for investment.

Donald Trump Jr. said in 2008 that Russian investors represented a significant part of the money flowing into some of the Trump Organization’s high-end properties. The comment was made before his father entered the presidential race and did not by itself establish wrongdoing.

In 2013, while the Miss Universe pageant was scheduled to take place in Moscow, Trump wrote on Twitter that Russian President Vladimir Putin might become his “best friend.” Trump also continued publicly discussing possible business opportunities in Russia during that period.

The proposed cutoff date of June 2015 was significant because Trump announced his presidential campaign that month. Supporters of the measure could argue that it would focus the investigation on the campaign and the election, while critics could say that earlier business relationships and contacts might be relevant to understanding later events.

There was no indication that the proposal alone would prevent investigators from examining earlier conduct. Its practical impact would depend on congressional action and on how any restrictions were interpreted and implemented.

DeSantis, who served on the House Foreign Affairs and Judiciary committees, did not publicly establish through the proposal alone what evidence Mueller’s team had obtained or what subjects it was investigating. At the time, the special counsel’s inquiry remained active, and the scope of its work was determined by Justice Department authority rather than by the House proposal.

In messages to Cohen, Sater said he could assist with obtaining support in Russia and claimed that President Vladimir Putin might say favorable things about Trump.

In a November 2015 email, Sater expressed confidence that the project and Trump’s presidential campaign would succeed. The proposal was discussed during the campaign, even though Trump did not travel to Russia to promote it. The Trump Organization had signed a nonbinding letter of intent related to the project, but the deal was ultimately abandoned in early 2016 after the necessary arrangements, including securing a suitable site and approvals, were not completed.

Trump later said he had no financial stake in the proposed Moscow tower and that the project was never completed. The emails and other records became part of congressional and federal inquiries into the Trump campaign’s contacts with Russia. Trump Organization representatives and Cohen did not immediately provide detailed comments on the matter.

“We’ve been covering Joe Arpaio for more than 20 years,” the publication wrote before listing examples of its reporting.

The thread noted that Arpaio had described one of his jail facilities as a “concentration camp.” The phrase referred to the tent jail opened by his office in the mid-1990s, which became one of the most recognizable features of his approach to incarceration.

The publication also cited reporting and lawsuits concerning deaths and medical care in county jails. Critics of Arpaio’s administration had long questioned jail conditions, while county officials and Arpaio disputed some of the allegations.

The New Times recalled an incident in which a jail employee was accused of using excessive force against a paraplegic inmate who requested a catheter. It also referred to a widely criticized publicity event in which Latino inmates were placed in a fenced outdoor area at the tent jail.

Other posts in the thread pointed to the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office’s former “mugshot of the day” feature, which displayed booking photographs on the agency’s website.

The publication also revisited its legal dispute with Arpaio’s office. New Times reporters were arrested in 2007 after refusing to provide information about stories concerning the sheriff, and the newspaper later reached a settlement with the county valued at $3.75 million.

It also criticized the use of public resources to investigate President Barack Obama’s birthplace. Arpaio’s office assigned investigators to examine claims that Obama’s birth certificate was fraudulent, although Obama had released a long-form birth certificate showing that he was born in Hawaii.

The New Times further referred to a 2013 federal court ruling that found the sheriff’s office had engaged in racial profiling during immigration-enforcement operations. The ruling followed a class-action lawsuit brought by Latino motorists and residents.

After the ruling, Arpaio’s office hired a private investigator to examine the judge overseeing the case and the judge’s wife. The judge later raised concerns about the investigation and the sheriff’s compliance with court orders.

The contempt case that led to Trump’s pardon centered on whether Arpaio and his department had continued immigration patrol practices barred by the court. Prosecutors said the sheriff knowingly violated the order; Arpaio argued that any violations were not intentional.

The newspaper also mentioned allegations that records relevant to the court case had not been properly preserved or turned over. The dispute over the records became part of the broader litigation surrounding the sheriff’s immigration-enforcement practices.

By 2015, Maricopa County had paid tens of millions of dollars in legal costs and settlements connected to lawsuits involving the sheriff’s office. The cases included claims involving racial profiling, jail conditions and alleged misconduct by deputies.

The New Times cited another lawsuit involving an inmate who was beaten while deputies failed to intervene. It also referred to Arpaio’s volunteer “Sheriff’s Posse,” one member of which was later arrested on child-pornography charges. The arrest was not evidence that the organization as a whole was responsible for the alleged conduct.

The thread included a report about a 2005 SWAT raid during which a police projectile ignited a fire and a family’s puppy was killed. The incident prompted criticism and litigation over the tactics used by deputies.

“So, yeah, that’s who Trump just pardoned,” the publication wrote, linking to its earlier coverage of Arpaio.

Trump’s pardon did not erase the findings in the civil-rights case, but it ended the possibility of a federal criminal sentence for contempt. Arpaio continued to deny that he intentionally violated the court’s order and said the pardon vindicated him.

The article also mentioned former Milwaukee County Sheriff David Clarke, whom Trump had praised on Twitter as a “great guy” while promoting Clarke’s book. Clarke, who was not pardoned, had drawn criticism for his public statements about the Black Lives Matter movement and for conditions at the Milwaukee County Jail.

Terrill Thomas, a Black inmate, died of dehydration in a Milwaukee County Jail cell in 2016. His death was ruled a homicide by the county medical examiner, and prosecutors later charged a corrections officer in connection with the case. Clarke was sheriff at the time, but the criminal case focused on jail staff and did not establish that Clarke personally caused Thomas’s death.

The Phoenix New Times thread placed the two sheriffs in the context of Trump’s public support for law-enforcement officials accused of misconduct. The pardon of Arpaio remained controversial because it came before sentencing and followed a federal court’s finding that his office had violated the constitutional rights of Latino residents.
