Trump Criticizes Antifa After Charlottesville, While Federal Agencies Have Also Warned About Violent White Supremacists

Following the deadly violence at a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, in August 2017, President Donald Trump faced criticism for comments that appeared to assign blame to multiple sides rather than focusing exclusively on the white supremacists and neo-Nazis who organized the event. Heather Heyer was killed when a car driven by James Alex Fields Jr. struck counterprotesters. Fields was later convicted of murder and federal hate crimes.

Trump initially condemned hatred, bigotry and violence, but his subsequent remarks about “both sides” drew criticism from civil rights groups, Democrats and some Republicans. Two days after the rally, he again argued that people on both sides of the confrontation had acted improperly. At a rally in Phoenix later that month, Trump also criticized Antifa, a loose collection of anti-fascist activists whose members had clashed with some right-wing demonstrators.

Trump did at times explicitly condemn the Ku Klux Klan, neo-Nazis and white supremacists. But his comments continued to fuel debate over whether he had adequately distinguished organized white nationalist groups from the people protesting against them. The term “alt-right” was widely used at the time to describe an online and political movement that included white nationalists, anti-Semites and others, although the movement was not a single organization with a unified leadership.

Federal law-enforcement and intelligence agencies have repeatedly identified violent white supremacists as a domestic terrorism threat. Government assessments have also warned that violence can come from a range of extremist movements, including jihadist, anti-government and other ideologies. Such reports generally distinguish between extremist beliefs, political movements and individuals who commit crimes; they do not classify the entire alt-right as a terrorist organization.

The comparison between white nationalist violence and ISIS has been part of a broader argument over how authorities and politicians describe terrorism. Critics of Trump said that white perpetrators were often portrayed as isolated individuals, while Muslim suspects were more readily associated with international terrorist groups. Supporters of Trump argued that Antifa’s use of violence and confrontations with right-wing protesters also deserved condemnation.

The Charlottesville rally exposed the difficulty of assigning responsibility for a chaotic political confrontation involving organized extremists, counterprotesters and individual acts of violence. White nationalist groups had promoted the event, and the killing of Heyer led to criminal charges against Fields. At the same time, clashes between opposing demonstrators produced additional injuries and arrests.

Trump’s response remained politically divisive. His condemnation of white supremacists was welcomed by some officials, while his repeated references to violence on “many sides” were criticized as creating a false equivalence between the groups involved. The episode continued to shape debate over domestic extremism, political rhetoric and the government’s response to far-right violence.

Trump Pardons Former Arizona Sheriff Joe Arpaio After Contempt Conviction

President Donald Trump pardoned former Maricopa County, Arizona, Sheriff Joe Arpaio in August 2017, weeks after Arpaio was found guilty of criminal contempt for violating a federal court order in a racial-profiling case. The order required his office to stop detaining people solely on suspicion that they were in the country illegally.

Arpaio, who served as sheriff for 24 years, was scheduled to be sentenced when Trump issued the pardon. The president said Arpaio had a long record of protecting the public and described him as an “American patriot.” Critics argued that the pardon undermined the court’s authority and disregarded the findings in the racial-profiling case.

The case stemmed from a lawsuit alleging that Arpaio’s deputies unlawfully targeted Latino drivers and passengers during immigration-enforcement operations. In 2013, a federal judge found the sheriff’s office had engaged in discriminatory policing and ordered changes to its practices. Prosecutors later argued that Arpaio knowingly failed to comply with that order.

Arpaio was also known for operating the Maricopa County jail system, including the outdoor facility commonly called “Tent City.” The facility attracted national attention for its harsh conditions and for the use of pink underwear for inmates, a policy promoted by Arpaio as a way to deter theft and assert control.

The former sheriff was a vocal supporter of claims questioning whether President Barack Obama had been born in the United States. Arpaio sponsored an investigation into Obama’s birth certificate, though officials and independent reviews concluded that Obama was born in Hawaii.

Arpaio lost the Republican primary for sheriff in 2016 to Paul Penzone, ending his tenure in office. His pardon remained controversial, with civil rights groups and legal commentators saying it sent a troubling message about accountability for public officials who violate court orders.

The case highlighted disagreements over immigration enforcement, racial profiling and the president’s constitutional power to grant clemency. Trump’s decision did not erase the court’s findings regarding the sheriff’s office, but it prevented Arpaio from receiving a sentence for the criminal contempt conviction.

title: RNC Staffer Assigned To Finding Positive Stories About Trump Says Take This Job And Shove It
text: Imagine for a moment that your job was to scour the media, searching for the rare news report that puts a positive spin on Donald Trump and his disastrous escapades in the White House. For one RNC staffer, this was the day to day reality he faced every morning when he clocked into work. After hanging on for several months, Andy Hemming finally decided he couldn t take it any longer and resigned. You can hardly blame the guy and have to ask, how did he stay on this sinking ship as long as he did?According to Politico, Hemming handed in his resignation on Monday. Previously, the publication had written a profile on Hemming which referred to him as the staffer the White House pays  $89,000 a year to spot and distribute positive stories from the mainstream media. Hemming was senior adviser for research at the RNC in the 2016 cycle and director of research on the Trump campaign. At the White House, he worked from 5:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. every weekday and was a regular in reporters  inboxes, blasting out stories favorable to the administration.Hemming has not yet commented on his decision to leave the position, but White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said that it was a  [m]utual decision that he could best help promote the president s agenda on the outside. Andy is smart and very talented and we wish him all the best. All administrations have people dedicated to finding and spreading news stories that show the president in a good light, but performing these duties with Trump at the helm was no doubt a unique experience. There surely isn t much positive media coverage on him these days because, in addition to being a raging bigot, he continually manages to screw up even the simplest of tasks (like not frying his retinas while watching the eclipse). How Hemming kept from completely losing his mind long before now is anybody s guess.Featured image via Chris Kleponis-Pool/Getty Images

**RNC Staffer Who Promoted Positive Trump Coverage Leaves White House Role**

Andy Hemming, a former Republican National Committee and Trump campaign research official who worked to identify and distribute favorable news coverage of the president, has resigned from his White House position, according to Politico.

Politico reported that Hemming submitted his resignation on Monday. The publication had previously profiled him as the White House staffer responsible for finding positive stories about President Donald Trump and sharing them with reporters and administration officials. Hemming served as a senior adviser for research at the RNC during the 2016 election cycle and later became director of research for Trump’s campaign.

In the White House, Hemming was described as a regular presence in reporters’ inboxes, distributing articles and other coverage viewed favorably by the administration. Politico also reported that he worked long hours in the role.

Hemming had not publicly commented on his departure at the time of the report. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the decision was mutual and that Hemming could continue supporting the president’s agenda from outside the administration.

“Andy is smart and very talented and we wish him all the best,” Sanders said.

Presidential administrations commonly have staff members who monitor news coverage and highlight favorable reports. Hemming’s departure comes as the Trump White House faced extensive scrutiny from the news media over the president’s policies, public statements and handling of controversies.

It was not immediately clear what Hemming planned to do next.

title: Trump Wants It Both Ways, But You Can’t Pass The Most Bills If ‘They’ Won’t Let You Pass Bills
text: Everybody s gotten used to Donald Trump contradicting himself. You can almost count on it, really. But with the exception of a few notable misspellings and typos, generally, his tweets that contradict previous tweets don t come on the same day, let alone in the same hour. And a contradictory pair in the span of eleven minutes? Maybe he s reprising another guy s role.Friday morning, Trump did just that. He complains all the time, but the two complaints that he tweeted just after 6:30 his time just don t go together. First, he says that 8 Democrats  control  the Senate because of the filibuster. Trump has advocated that the GOP use the nuclear option to get rid of the filibuster for some time, but most if not all Republicans are hesitant   they know that if they do, the next time voters elect a Democratic majority, their opposition will be able to ram through any legislation they like, with nothing to stop them. That s something Trump doesn t understand neither party wants.If Senate Republicans don't get rid of the Filibuster Rule and go to a 51% majority, few bills will be passed. 8 Dems control the Senate!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) August 25, 2017Just eleven minutes later, Trump came to his senses and realized if he says the GOP can t pass bills   and he is the leader of the GOP   then he can t keep saying he s passed more bills than a concert promoter on a New York subway. So he went back to that.Few, if any, Administrations have done more in just 7 months than the Trump A. Bills passed, regulations killed, border, military, ISIS, SC!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) August 25, 2017I d just like to point out the humor in calling his administration  the Trump A.  We all have the same character limit on Twitter, Donnie. Just leave out  if any  next time, so what could be admin doesn t look like ass.But complaining about the Democrats in Washington keeping him from doing what he wants is quickly becoming one of his favorite topics. There are the hilariously wrong-in-retrospect messages:Despite the long delays by the Democrats in finally approving Dr. Tom Price, the repeal and replacement of ObamaCare is moving fast!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) February 17, 2017The tweets where he can t quite get his Cabinet approved as fast as he d like:It is so pathetic that the Dems have still not approved my full Cabinet.  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) March 3, 2017The Senate Democrats have only confirmed 48 of 197 Presidential Nominees. They can't win so all they do is slow things down & obstruct!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) April 30, 2017The Obstructionist Democrats make Security for our country very difficult. They use the courts and associated delay at all times. Must stop!  Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) August 18, 2017So where are all the superlatives? You know, the best, most amazing, biggest by far in the history of the world tweets about how incredibly, ridiculously huge his successes are, which of course are the most successful of all time?Well, those are there, too, but I m not going to bore you by re-posting a bunch of tweets where Trump tries to Bannonize the old nine-iron. The point is, Trump really wants to have it both ways   that he simultaneously is the most bestest at presidenting, and that those dirty demon-dog Democrats won t let him president properly. He s not even close on the claim that no  A  has done more. He s behind Bill Clinton in bills passed and signed by about 30% for this point in his presidency.And that s just fine by me.Featured image via Drew Angerer/Getty Images

**Trump Wants It Both Ways, But You Can’t Pass Most Bills If ‘They’ Won’t Let You Pass Bills**

Donald Trump has often used Twitter to criticize Congress while also portraying his administration as unusually productive. On the morning of August 25, 2017, he illustrated that tension in two posts published about 11 minutes apart.

In the first, Trump argued that Senate Democrats effectively controlled the chamber because of the filibuster. Senate Republicans held 52 seats at the time, while Democrats and two independents who caucused with them held the remaining 48. Most legislation still required 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.

“If Senate Republicans don't get rid of the Filibuster Rule and go to a 51% majority, few bills will be passed. 8 Dems control the Senate!” Trump wrote.

Trump had repeatedly urged Republicans to use the so-called nuclear option to eliminate the legislative filibuster. Republicans had already used that procedure in 2017 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch, but they had not removed the rule for ordinary legislation. Many Republicans opposed doing so, in part because Democrats could use the same rule if they later regained control of the Senate.

Just eleven minutes later, Trump highlighted what he described as the accomplishments of his administration.

“Few, if any, Administrations have done more in just 7 months than the Trump A. Bills passed, regulations killed, border, military, ISIS, SC!” he wrote, referring to the Supreme Court vacancy filled during his first year.

The two messages reflected a recurring pattern in Trump’s public statements: he claimed credit for administrative actions and congressional achievements while also blaming Democrats for blocking his legislative agenda. The situation was more complicated than either description suggested. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress, but the Senate’s filibuster rules meant that many major bills required Democratic support.

Trump had made similar complaints earlier in the year. In February, he blamed Democrats for delays in confirming Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price while saying that efforts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act were advancing. In March, he criticized Democrats for not approving his full Cabinet.

By July, Trump was also accusing Senate Democrats of slowing the confirmation of presidential nominees. “They can't win so all they do is slow things down & obstruct!” he wrote.

Other posts portrayed Democrats as a party of obstruction and argued that their use of the courts and procedural delays was making it more difficult to address national security issues.

At the same time, Trump regularly described his administration’s performance in sweeping terms, emphasizing executive actions, regulatory changes, military policy and the confirmation of a Supreme Court justice. Those claims did not change the basic limits imposed by the Senate’s rules or the need for Congress to approve legislation.

The result was a familiar contradiction. Trump wanted to present himself as a highly productive president while arguing that congressional rules and Democratic opposition prevented him from accomplishing more. His August tweets captured both arguments, even though the two positions sat uneasily together.

title: House Dem Wants GOP On Record: Stop Gov’t Spending At Trump Properties
text: Early next month, the GOP-controlled House of Representatives will take up a spending bill that provides funding for nearly every department in the federal government. It s a must-pass bill because, without it, the government will shut down. That s a non-starter for many Republicans, who still feel the pain of the last time there was a government shutdown. Republicans were largely unable to shift blame to the Democrats as they attempted to do, and their popularity suffered as a result. But despite the GOP s absolute grip on Congress, the bill is still subject to amendments, and one Democrat from Tennessee has a doozy in mind.Representative Steve Cohen is introducing amendments to the spending plan that would ban the use of federal funds at Trump-branded properties. It covers every business listed on Trump s financial disclosure form, including hotels, country clubs, and resorts. That means events like the ones at Mar-a-Lago where Trump has hosted dignitaries and foreign leaders would either be held elsewhere, or Trump would have to provide accommodations free of charge.Such an arrangement would have prevented the Secret Service from having to stay in a trailer outside Trump Tower, where they moved after price negotiations fell apart over them staying inside while protecting the president. It also would have precluded the State Department from spending upwards of $15,000 on rooms at a hotel that Trump recently opened in Vancouver. Most of all, it might reduce the amount of money you and I pay for the president to spend more than 20% of his time in office (so far) at his own resorts.In a statement Cohen released Wednesday morning, he said:Congress should not allow the President to use his office to profit himself and his family.  The President s refusal to divest from his privately owned businesses creates a conflict of interest when steering federal spending to his resorts and other businesses  The American people should have total confidence that the President is serving their interest, not his own financial enrichment.  President Trump s refusal to disclose information to Congress or seek Congress s authorization for accepting profits from foreign governments stemming from his sprawling foreign financial interests is a brazen violation of the Constitution and a danger to our democracy.We couldn t agree more, Congressman. And while these amendments stand about a snowball s chance in hell of passing   or possibly even being brought up for a vote   it will be nice to see you force Republicans to go on record and either declare their allegiance to Donald Trump, or to the principles of conservatism.Featured image via Alex Wong/Getty Images

House Democrat Proposes Bar on Federal Spending at Trump Properties

Lawmakers were preparing to consider a broad spending measure covering much of the federal government, with a deadline for funding approaching. Failure to approve the legislation or another temporary measure could have led to a government shutdown. The bill was expected to face debate over amendments, including one proposed by a Tennessee Democrat targeting federal spending at properties connected to President Donald Trump.

Representative Steve Cohen said he planned to offer amendments that would prohibit federal agencies from using appropriated funds at businesses owned, operated or financially connected to the president. The proposal would apply to properties identified in Trump’s financial-disclosure documents, including hotels, country clubs and resorts.

If adopted, the measure could affect federal agencies that pay for lodging, meetings, security arrangements or other services at Trump-branded properties. Events involving government officials that were held at those locations could instead be moved elsewhere, unless the costs were covered without federal funds.

Cohen has argued that federal spending at the president’s businesses creates an appearance of a conflict of interest. His proposal comes amid broader scrutiny of Trump’s decision to retain ownership of his businesses while serving as president rather than placing them in a blind trust or fully divesting.

In a statement, Cohen said:

“Congress should not allow the President to use his office to profit himself and his family. The President’s refusal to divest from his privately owned businesses creates a conflict of interest when steering federal spending to his resorts and other businesses. The American people should have total confidence that the President is serving their interest, not his own financial enrichment.”

Cohen also criticized Trump over concerns involving profits connected to foreign governments and said Congress should examine whether those arrangements comply with constitutional requirements. Those issues were the subject of ongoing legal and political debate.

The amendments would need support from the Republican-controlled Congress to pass. Even if they received a vote, their prospects were uncertain, as Republican leaders generally controlled the appropriations process and could decline to bring particular amendments before the full House.

The proposed restrictions reflect a larger debate over how federal agencies should handle transactions involving businesses owned by a sitting president. Supporters said the policy could reduce potential conflicts and reassure the public that government spending was based on practical considerations rather than personal financial interests. Opponents could argue that existing procurement and ethics rules already govern such spending and that a blanket prohibition could complicate agency operations.

Cohen’s proposal was therefore unlikely to change the spending bill on its own, but it could bring additional attention to the question of whether federal money should be spent at properties tied to the president.

The article was nevertheless reposted by users on social media before the error was noted.

The incidents highlight the importance of checking photographs, captions and original sources before sharing political material. Crowd-size claims and viral political images can spread quickly, particularly when they reinforce existing views about a candidate or party.
